title: N-Acetylgalactosamine-Conjugated Small Interfering RNA Targeting Hepatic Angiotensinogen in Hypertension: A Phase I Clinical Trial With Randomized Part A and Open-Label Part B.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Angiotensinogen (AGT) is the precursor of angiotensin peptides and a key determinant of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activity. ART101 is an investigational N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA (GalNAc-siRNA) designed to durably suppress hepatic AGT synthesis.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of single ascending doses of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA in healthy volunteers and to provide an initial exploratory assessment of blood pressure effects in patients with hypertension.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This phase I study was conducted from January 2025 to April 2026 with 24-week follow-up. Part A was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, single ascending-dose trial; part B was an open-label, single-dose study. The study took place at Beijing Friendship Hospital, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China. Part A enrolled 40 healthy adults randomized 6:2 to receive the GalNAc-siRNA (25-600 mg) or placebo; 39 completed the study. Part B enrolled 8 patients with hypertension receiving the GalNAc-siRNA, 600 mg; all completed the study.
INTERVENTIONS: A single subcutaneous injection of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA (25, 75, 150, 300, or 600 mg) or placebo in part A; a single open-label subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siRNA, 600 mg, in part B.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was safety and tolerability; secondary outcomes included pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, exploratory blood pressure assessments, and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system biomarkers.
RESULTS: Among 40 healthy volunteers (27 [67.5%] male; mean [SD] age, 40.4 [7.8] years) and 8 patients (6 [75.0%] male; mean [SD] age, 47.3 [10.3] years) with hypertension, the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA was well tolerated. In part A, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 23 of 30 active-treatment participants (76.7%) vs 7 of 10 placebo recipients (70.0%); in part B, 6 of 8 patients (75.0%) had TEAEs. No serious adverse events, injection site reactions, or hyperkalemia were observed; all TEAEs were mild to moderate. Plasma exposure (maximum plasma concentration [Cmax] and area under the plasma concentration-time curve [AUC]) increased with dose over the wide dose range from 25 mg to 600 mg. Mean maximum serum AGT reductions of 93% (at 600 mg) in healthy volunteers and 90% (at 600 mg) in patients with hypertension were observed. At 24 weeks after a single 600-mg dose, the placebo-corrected 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure decreased by 12.9 mm Hg in healthy participants.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this phase I study, no serious treatment-related safety signals were identified. Sustained, dose-dependent AGT reductions and exploratory blood pressure lowering were observed. These findings support further investigation of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA as a potential long-acting therapeutic for hypertension.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: China Drug Clinical Registry Identifiers: CTR20250041 (part A) and CTR20253973 (part B).

title: Potential effect of human chorionic gonadotropin-induced extracellular vesicle RNAs on mouse ovarian granulosa cells.
abstract: Gonadotropins regulate granulosa-cell function during ovarian follicular development, and extracellular vesicles (EVs) are potential mediators of intercellular communication within the follicle. However, the regulation of EV RNA cargo following gonadotropin stimulation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)-responsive EV RNA profiles using three experimental models: two Lhcgr-expressing clones of a mouse granulosa-cell tumor-derived cell line and mouse ovaries. The cell models were treated with hCG, and immature mice were primed with serotropin, followed by hCG. EVs were isolated from these cells and ovaries and characterized by transmission electron microscopy and western blot analysis. Total RNAs from these EVs were analyzed by electrophoresis, suggesting global changes in their profiles with hCG. RNA-sequencing identified thousands of potentially differentially expressed genes, including 111 commonly upregulated and 122 commonly downregulated transcripts among all three experimental models. The 111 upregulated transcripts were further narrowed down to 27 candidates based on the abundance, and five protein-coding transcripts (Ccdc200, Gm10337, Gm614, Adad2, and Spata45) were selected for further functional validation. Interestingly, EVs carrying the overexpressed Ccdc200, Gm10337, and Gm614 mRNA significantly increased the number of ovarian cells during 3-day culture. These findings indicate that hCG modulates EV RNA cargo and suggest that EV-mediated RNAs cooperatively function as a regulatory layer of hCG signaling for intercellular communication, fine-tuning granulosa-cell proliferation or survival during follicular development.

title: Inhibiting Lactylation-Mediated Metabolic-Epigenetic Reprogramming to Potentiate Tumor Photo-Immunotherapy.
abstract: Cancer immunotherapies face limitations in treating "cold" tumors due to immune suppression driven by metabolic dysregulation within the tumor microenvironment. Research has revealed that tumor cells produce excess lactate via hypoxia-induced glycolysis, promoting histone lactylation and establishing immunosuppression-associated metabolic-epigenetic reprogramming. Here, a near-infrared (NIR)-triggered nanoplatform (RgA-L-I/P/R) has been developed to fundamentally dismantle the immunosuppression via the metabolic-epigenetic axis. Upon NIR excitation, the platform released oxygen from perfluoropentane (PFP) ("oxygen unlocking chamber") in the tumor through dual targeting of AS1411 and Rg3 ("nano-warhead"), liberating the IR-1048 and the CRISPR/Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) ("NIR immune trigger" and "metabolic nanolock"). IR-1048 induced immunogenic cell death (ICD) to trigger dendritic cell maturation and cytotoxic T lymphocyte infiltration, while CRISPR/Cas9 RNP induced LDHA (lactate dehydrogenase A) gene knockdown that locked the lactate supply and reprogrammed metabolism and epigenetics. These changes reduced histone lactylation and IL-10 expression, promoting the conversion of tumor-associated macrophages to the M1 type and synergistically downregulating hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression upon oxygen release. This nanoplatform enables synergistic photothermal immunostimulation with CRISPR-mediated metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. Rather than merely countering mild downstream immune regulation by ICD, it seeks to fundamentally eliminate the immunosuppression, offering novel therapeutic strategies through the metabolic-epigenetic pathway for poorly immunoresponsive tumors.

title: Engineered Milk-Derived Extracellular Vesicles Integrate PCSK9 Silencing and Inflammation Modulation for Hyperlipidemia Therapy.
abstract: Hyperlipidemia is a systemic metabolic disorder closely associated with chronic inflammation. Effective management requires integrated strategies that simultaneously lower lipid level and attenuate inflammation. Nucleic acid therapeutics, such as proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) siRNA, represent a breakthrough in lipid-lowering therapy. However, they either lack direct anti-inflammatory effects (GalNAc-siRNA) or are prone to triggering unintended inflammatory responses themselves such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Milk-derived extracellular vesicles (MDEs) emerge as naturally anti-inflammatory nanocarriers that suppress key pro-inflammatory cytokines by 30.0%-96.5% in vitro. However, MDEs predominantly undergo endocytic trafficking with substantial endosomal/lysosomal sequestration, which can limit productive cytosolic siRNA delivery. To address this, we developed engineered MDEs by incorporating 30.0% (w/w) probiotic-derived glycolipids into their membranes to facilitate early endosomal escape. When loaded with PCSK9 siRNA, the engineered MDEs achieved a remarkable silencing efficiency of 90.2 ± 0.2%, significantly outperforming both unmodified MDEs and conventional LNPs. In hyperlipidemic mice, systemic administration of engineered MDEs improved serum lipid profiles, reduced lipid accumulation and systemic inflammation, and showed a favorable safety profile under the conditions examined. Collectively, this work provides a promising nucleic acid delivery platform based on engineered MDEs for enhanced hyperlipidemia therapy through simultaneous lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory effects.

title: Application of Extracellular Vesicle-Based Nanocomposites in Osteoarthritis Therapy.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are lipid bilayer membranes that share lipids and proteins with parental cells, enabling the targeted transfer of bioactive molecules to recipient cells, tissues or organs for functional modulation. EV-based nanocomposites constitute an emerging delivery platform that combines the biological benefits of EVs with the tunable physicochemical features of nanomaterials, offering an opportunity for overcoming drawbacks of conventional therapeutics or delivery systems, including inefficient targeting or infiltration across biological barriers, undesirable bioavailability, and potential adverse effects. Osteoarthritis (OA), one of the most common chronic degenerative joint disorders, is characterized by cartilage degradation, synovial inflammation, and aberrant bone remodeling, and so forth. Current clinical treatments remain largely palliative or invasive, with limited efficacy to prevent disease progression. In contrast, EV-based nanocomposites, for example, can achieve cell-specific targeting of chondrocytes or synovial cells via receptor-mediated homing, enable on-demand delivery of anti-inflammatory agents, cartilage-repair molecules, or gene-editing components, and remain compatible with image-guided therapeutic precision. Herein, this review outlines recent advances, design principles, and optimization for EV-based nanocomposites, highlighting their applications in OA therapy. Current challenges and insights for future clinical translation of EV-based nanocomposites are also discussed. Collectively, this review may underscore the translational potential of EV-based nanocomposites for OA therapy.

title: From Transdermal Delivery to Immune Reprogramming: Intelligent Biomaterials for Precision Psoriasis Therapy.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory disease that causes dysregulation of keratinocyte proliferation, IL-23/IL-17-driven immune activation, oxidative stress and impaired barrier function. Biologics and targeted small molecules have improved clinical results, but systemic administration and lack of lesion specificity limit precise, long-term control of the disease. This paper revises the concept of psoriasis therapy from transdermal drug delivery to intelligent immune microenvironment reprogramming. Programmable biomaterial platforms that can actively recognize pathological signals and achieve spatiotemporal control of drug release, immune cell targeting, gene regulation and tissue remodelling have been introduced. Recently, there have been many developments in stimuli-responsive hydrogels, microneedle-based gene editing, biomimetic nanoplatforms, extracellular matrix-inspired scaffolds, and image-guided theranostic systems that link disease mechanisms, material design and therapeutic functions in a unified framework. We have further put forward the idea of cytokine blockade as a network-level immune recalibration, enhanced penetration and lesion-specific adaptive regulation, and image-guided precise intervention over empirical treatment. The three main translation problems are lesion heterogeneity, controllable immune modulation and large-scale manufacturing and long-term safety. This review provides a plan for developing intelligent, personalized biomaterial-based therapies for personalized psoriasis management.

title: Engineering Tunable Helper Lipid Architecture to Improve Messenger RNA Lipid Nanoparticle Performance.
abstract: Helper lipids are essential structural components of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), yet systematic design principles linking helper lipid architecture to messenger RNA (mRNA) delivery performance remain poorly defined. Here we identify helper lipid architecture as a major, largely unexplored design lever for optimizing LNP performance. Using a modular library of more than 80 rationally designed helper lipids, we show that systematic variation in headgroup chemistry, linker topology, and tail cardinality reshapes both LNP biophysical behavior and biological performance. Martini molecular dynamics (MD) simulations combined with multimodal structural analyses reveal that high-performing scaffolds undergo a pH-dependent transition into fusogenic inverse hexagonal-like ordering, substantially lowering the energetic barrier for endosomal escape. These performance gains persist across the clinically relevant ALC-0315 and DLin-MC3-DMA platforms, establishing helper lipid architecture as a transferable design parameter across distinct ionizable lipid chemistries. Translating these design principles into function, optimized helper lipid formulations restore hepatic protein expression in a mouse model of ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency and increase antigen expression and immunogenicity in both preclinical models and in the in vitro human MIMIC platform. Together, these findings establish helper lipids as tunable molecular actuators of potency, tolerability, and stability, offering an engineering framework for next-generation mRNA vaccines and therapeutics.

title: Bdnf mRNA-LNP Drives Nasal Epithelial BDNF Production and Improves Cognition in Aged and Alzheimer's Disease Mouse Models.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics have rapidly emerged as a transformative approach for treating a range of health challenges. Accelerated by the success of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic, this platform holds promise beyond immunisation for the transient expression of therapeutic proteins in targeted tissues. Despite this promise, non-invasive delivery of mRNA-encoded cargo to the brain remains a challenge, as most peptide drugs do not pass the blood-brain barrier. Here, we present the development of an intranasal mRNA-LNP therapeutic that drives production of neurotrophic factors in the nasal epithelium and delivery of the encoded protein to the brain. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that intranasal delivery of mRNA encoding the neurogenic factor BDNF (Brain Derived Neurotrophic Factor) enhances memory performance in both aged mice and a transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. This approach offers a promising platform for delivering therapeutic proteins to the brain and opens new avenues for treating age-related and neurodegenerative disorders.

title: In Vivo CRISPR Screen Identifies RPS19 as an Immunotherapy Target in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy, its efficacy against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains severely limited, highlighting an urgent need for novel targets and strategies to overcome immune evasion. Here, we aimed to identify key regulators of HCC immunity via unbiased functional screening and develop a targeted therapy to remodel the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed an in vivo CRISPR-knockout screen using a 4500-gene sgRNA library in syngeneic HCC mouse models. Single-cell RNA sequencing of human HCC tissues and in vivo macrophage-depletion assays were utilized to dissect cellular populations and validate underlying mechanisms. We identified ribosomal protein S19 (RPS19) as a central mediator of HCC immune evasion, whose deletion in HCC cells mitigates the immunosuppressive TME. Mechanistically, scRNA-seq pinpointed tumor-associated macrophages as the key effector subset, whereby complement C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1) transduces RPS19 signals to trigger macrophage-dependent immune suppression. We further constructed SP94-peptide-modified disulfide-bond-containing nanoparticles (SNPSS) for targeted CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. SNPSS efficiently homes to HCC cells, releases payloads within the glutathione-rich TME, downregulates RPS19, reverses immune suppression, and robustly suppresses HCC progression in vivo. Collectively, the RPS19-C5aR1-macrophage axis fuels HCC immune escape, and SNPSS-based RPS19 gene-editing offers a promising strategy to remodel the TME and boost HCC immunotherapy efficacy.

title: Chromatin Remodeling of RasGRP3 Underlies Temozolomide Sensitivity in Glioblastoma Organoids.
abstract: Acquired resistance to temozolomide (TMZ) constitutes a formidable clinical barrier in the management of glioblastoma (GBM). GBM organoid models (GBO) that faithfully mirror the parental tumor phenotype serve as powerful research instruments to overcome the limitations in this field. We established GBOs derived from primary glioma patients and their TMZ low-sensitivity counterparts. To unravel the intricate molecular underpinnings of this process, we performed an unbiased, integrated multi-omics analysis encompassing epigenomic, 3D genomic, and transcriptomic profiling, coupled with dual CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) screening of TMZ-induced enhancers (TiEns) and their cognate target genes. Our findings demonstrate that enhancer-mediated 3D chromatin remodeling drives chemosensitivity predominantly by transcriptionally activating drug-sensitivity-associated genes, such as RasGRP3, VEGFA, BTN3A2, etc. Knockdown or knockout of these genes and enhancers renders glioma cells more sensitive to TMZ, especially RasGRP3. Our work unveils a druggable "enhancer-chromatin-target" signaling axis and proposes a novel combinatorial therapeutic strategy to surmount TMZ low sensitivity in GBM.

title: Spray-Dried mRNA-LNP Powder Enabling Multi-Route Delivery With 3-Year Refrigerated Stability.
abstract: The clinical translation of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) therapeutics is constrained by limited stability of liquid formulations, necessitating ultra-cold storage and restricting global accessibility. Here, we report a spray-dried dry powder platform for mRNA-LNPs that overcomes these limitations while enabling flexible routes of administration. Systematic evaluation of pharmaceutically relevant sugars identifies trehalose as an optimal matrix former, yielding high-recovery mRNA-LNP dry powder product (DPP) with controlled particle size, low residual moisture, and preserved LNP physicochemical properties upon reconstitution. Mechanistic studies combining solid-state characterization, fluorescence tracking, and solvent extraction demonstrate that mRNA-LNPs are entrapped within an amorphous trehalose matrix core, providing protection against dehydration and rehydration stress. Reconstituted DPP (RDPP) maintains in vivo protein expression comparable to liquid control (LC) following intravenous and intramuscular administration, while supporting effective mucosal delivery via pulmonary and sublingual routes. Direct administration of DPP without reconstitution enables lung-targeted protein expression, highlighting potential for cold-chain-independent therapies. Critically, DPP preserves colloidal stability, mRNA integrity, ionizable lipid stability, and biological activity for over 3 years under refrigerated conditions, whereas liquid formulation exhibits substantial degradation within 6-9 months. These findings establish spray-dried mRNA-LNP DPPs as a robust platform integrating long-term stability with multi-route delivery for improved accessibility of mRNA therapeutics.

title: Comparative Analysis of Poly(Ethylene Glycol) (PEG) and Poly(2-Ethyl-2-Oxazoline) (PEtOx) for Organic Solvent-Free Lipid Nanoparticle Formulations.
abstract: Efficient, biocompatible, and flexible application of CRISPR-Cas9 remains a major challenge in gene therapy. This study addresses a novel formulation method, focusing on organic solvent-free lipid nanoparticles for the efficient delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 components. Therefore, novel stealth lipids comprising the lipid anchor cholesterol hemisuccinate conjugated to poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx) were synthesized and evaluated as a promising in vitro alternative to commercially available poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based lipids. Our study identified PEtOx-lipids as markedly more biocompatible compared to PEG-based analogues (12-fold reduction in cytotoxicity; 99% reduced hemolytic effect) with high efficiency for mRNA gene delivery. We demonstrate successful CRISPR-Cas9 activity ex vivo and efficient uptake of PEtOx nanoparticles by macrophages in vivo (66.5% pos. F4/80+ macrophages). Our data demonstrate that PEtOx-based stealth lipids are a promising alternative to PEG. The resulting LNPs, optimized for fully aqueous manufacturing, address key limitations of current LNP systems, including immunogenicity and the reliance on ethanol-based production processes.

title: Engineering Synthetic Molecular Operations Controlled by DNA-Binding Proteins Through Templated Proximity.
abstract: We describe a DNA-based molecular framework that enables DNA-binding proteins (DBPs) to perform diverse synthetic operations beyond their natural functions. We introduce templated proximity as a mechanism through which DBP-DNA recognition events are converted into programmable DNA strand displacement reactions. In this architecture, protein binding templates the spatial colocalization of split DNA components, generating functional nucleic acid outputs that can be propagated into downstream processes. Using representative DBPs, including EGR1, YY1, and p53, we couple protein recognition to DNA strand displacement, activation of a fluorogenic RNA aptamer, regulation of CRISPR-Cas12a and Cas13 activity, and DBP-triggered activation of hierarchical CRISPR cascades. These results establish templated proximity as a general transduction principle for integrating DNA-binding proteins into modular nucleic acid reaction networks and demonstrate that DBPs can function as programmable interfaces connecting natural biomolecular recognition with engineered DNA-based information processing, enabling modular communication layers with tailored synthetic functionality.

title: RNA Aptamer-Enabled Development of Heterobifunctionals That Chemically Induce RNA-FKBP12 Ternary Complexes.
abstract: Limitations in the druggability of challenging protein targets, coupled with recognition of the diverse roles of noncoding RNAs in cellular regulation and disease have spurred interest in RNA as a druggable macromolecule. The rapidly emerging field of RNA-targeted small-molecule therapeutics is now exploring induced proximity mechanisms in the form of RNA-targeting chimeras that recruit effector proteins to catalyze RNA decay. Inspired by "molecular glue" natural products such as rapamycin and cyclosporin A, which induce protein-protein interactions to sterically modulate protein function, we propose the new application of immunophilin recruitment to alter RNA function. Here in, we report the design and characterization of heterobifunctional molecules that induce highly cooperative RNA-FKBP12 ternary complexes and describe efforts to assess their impact on RNA metabolism. We also evaluate applications and report off-target liabilities associated with the chosen RNA ligand for our heterobifunctional series. Finally, we discuss the challenges faced and highlight opportunities for future success in the RNA space.

title: Mapping Osteosarcoma Biology With CRISPR/Cas: From Gene Function to Therapeutic Targets.
abstract: Osteosarcoma is a highly aggressive primary bone malignancy characterized by rapid proliferation, chemoresistance, and early metastasis. Recent advances in CRISPR/Cas (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated proteins) genome editing have enabled precise targeting of oncogenes, tumor suppressors, and regulators of epigenetic, metabolic, and signaling pathways, providing new insights into osteosarcoma biology. CRISPR-mediated knockout of cell-cycle regulators, including CDK11, impairs proliferation, while restoration of TP53 and suppression of TERT promoter activity inhibits tumor growth. Other line of studies has revealed that chemoresistance mechanisms mediated by ABCB1/MDR1, CD44, ATR, RAD18, and autophagy-related genes have been effectively reversed through CRISPR interventions, restoring sensitivity to cisplatin and doxorubicin. Furthermore, CRISPR applications in immune modulation, such as PD-L1 knockout, may enhance antitumor immunity. Importantly, high-throughput CRISPR screens also may identify essential genes, novel oncogenic drivers, and synthetic lethal targets, thus informing potential precision therapeutic strategies. This review aims to critically summarize CRISPR/Cas-mediated studies in osteosarcoma, focusing on targeting oncogenes and tumor suppressors, overcoming chemoresistance, modulating immune responses, regulating metabolism and autophagy, and identifying essential genes and vulnerabilities, providing a translational framework for precision therapy.

title: Costunolide-Mediated Modulation of the P2X7-NLRP3 Complex Suppresses Oligodendrocyte Precursor Cell Pyroptosis and Rescues Perinatal White Matter Injury.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Perinatal white matter injury (WMI) causes neurodevelopmental disability, driven by oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC) pyroptosis. We aimed to identify the molecular mechanism of NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in OPCs and evaluate Costunolide (Cos) as a targeted modulator of the P2X7-NLRP3 complex.
METHODS: We integrated molecular dynamics simulations, surface plasmon resonance, primary OPC cultures, single-cell RNA sequencing, and a custom CRISPR/Cas9-generated P2rx7 knockout rat model to assess Cos efficacy.
RESULTS: Cos associated with the extracellular domain of P2X7 (KD = 3.08 μM, Homo sapiens P2X7), modulating the P2X7-NLRP3 complex, thereby restricting calcium influx and preventing Caspase-1 activation and GSDMD-mediated membrane pore formation in vitro. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis identified an injury-induced P2rx7+/Nlrp3+ OPC subpopulation, revealing a previously unrecognized cell-intrinsic susceptibility to neuroinflammatory injury. Both genetic deletion of P2rx7 and pharmacological treatment with Cos markedly suppressed pyroptotic signaling in vivo, resulting in sustained restoration of myelin integrity and enhanced oligodendrocyte maturation from the acute (P7) to the developmental recovery (P14) stage.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that P2X7 may facilitate NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in developing OPCs. Consequently, modulation of this complex by Cos highlights a potential neurotherapeutic strategy for perinatal WMI.

title: Comprehensive Evaluation of Gastrointestinal Factors Influencing the Stability and Function of mRNA-Encapsulated Lipid Nanoparticles.
abstract: Owing to the intrinsic instability of mRNA, its routes of administration are limited, and to date, only injectable delivery has been clinically applied. In contrast, oral administration exposes mRNA to a variety of substances in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Despite these challenges, oral delivery remains the most familiar and convenient route for patients, making the development of orally administrable mRNA-encapsulated lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNPs) highly desirable. However, no studies have directly examined how mRNA-LNPs are affected within the GI environment. In the present study, we investigated the effects of representative GI components on mRNA-LNPs. Among several digestive enzymes, pepsin markedly reduced the protein-expression efficiency of the particles, whereas amylase had no effect. Pepsin-treated particles exhibited increased size, suggesting that structural alterations contributed to the observed functional loss. Lipase at high concentrations impaired nanoparticle function. Because lipase hydrolyzes ester bonds in lipids, we examined LNPs incorporating C12-200, an ionizable lipid lacking ester bonds, instead of SM-102. The C12-200 formulation showed reduced susceptibility to lipase-induced functional loss, indicating that enzymatic lipid degradation underlay the observed effects. Simulated gastric fluid also significantly diminished particle functionality. A detailed analysis of the relationship between functionality and pH revealed that impairment primarily occurred at approximately pH 1 but not at pH ≥ 3. Collectively, these findings identify the key GI factors that compromise mRNA-LNP integrity and provide important insights into the rational design of orally administrable mRNA-LNP formulations.

title: Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cortical neurons from monozygotic twins with the Gαo1 K278del mutation reveal disease mechanisms relevant to GNAO1-related encephalopathy.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Rare de novo variants in GNAO1 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a heterogenous display of early onset epilepsy, movement abnormalities, and global developmental delay. More than 100 pathogenic variants in GNAO1 have been identified and categorized into four groups according to their protein features. Most pathogenic variants affect both GNAO1 isoforms, whereas approximately 20% of patients have a GNAO1A-specific variant. Response to therapy is notoriously variable, even among patients harboring the same variant. Here, we set out to model GNAO1A-related encephalopathy using human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) from monozygotic twins carrying the Gαo1 K278del variant and uncovered-while taking advantage of the identical genomic setting-phenotypic features that further our understanding of the defects underlying the disorder.
METHODS: We generated hiPSCs expressing the c.832_834delAAG; p.K278del variant in GNAO1A obtained from monozygotic twins who both developed seizures 2 days after birth. For either twin, Gαo1 K278del and CRISPR-Cas9-repaired isogenic control hiPSC lines were differentiated into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and subsequently into cortical neurons. Variant-specific transcriptomic, morphological, and electrophysiological characteristics were analyzed.
RESULTS: Gαo1 K278del mutated hiPSC-derived NPCs showed disorganized neural rosette structures and revealed an altered transcriptome. In cortical neurons, the Gαo1 K278del variant caused a reduction in the size and complexity of dendrites that was accompanied by an increase in pre- and postsynaptic puncta. Multielectrode array (MEA) recordings revealed an abnormal cortical neuron bursting activity pattern with fewer bursts and more spikes per burst. The antiepileptic drug levetiracetam reduced the spike frequency and the number of spikes per burst in cortical neurons from both patients.
SIGNIFICANCE: The developed GNAO1A hiPSC-derived in vitro model uncovered key structural and functional features of GNAO1-related encephalopathy. The comparable in vitro phenotypes in neurons from both twins underscore the utility of hiPSC-derived models to investigate molecular mechanisms underlying GNAO1-related encephalopathy as well as effects of therapeutic intervention.

title: SFRP2 Editing Enhances Dermal Papilla Cell Function via Activation of the PI3K-Akt Signaling Pathway.
abstract: Secreted frizzled-related protein 2 (SFRP2) is an important molecule that regulates cell growth and development and participates in hair follicle (HF) development and homeostasis. The present study seeks to determine whether SFRP2 directly targets dermal papilla cells (DPCs), the pivotal functional cell population within HF, and characterize the intracellular signaling regulatory network triggered downstream. In this study, a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SFRP2 gene editing DPC model was established in vitro. Multi-omics analyses, including transcriptomics and metabolomics, were performed alongside functional assays to investigate the regulatory mechanisms of SFRP2 in DPCs. Among three designed single guide RNAs (sgRNAs), sgRNA3 showed the highest editing efficiency (67.0%) without off-target effects. Genetic editing of SFRP2 markedly increased the transcript levels of pivotal hair follicle‑development‑related genes (LEF1, CCND1 and Wnt2). Meanwhile, it suppressed TGF‑β1 transcription, which resulted in elevated proliferation capacity and diminished apoptotic activity within DPCs. Transcriptomic profiling identified 2288 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) enriched in PI3K-Akt, MAPK and TNF signaling pathways, while metabolomic analysis identified 185 differential metabolites (DMs) associated with apoptosis, ABC transporters, and PI3K-Akt signaling. Integrated multi-omics analysis confirmed PI3K-Akt signaling as a central regulatory axis. Western blot analysis revealed increased phosphorylation of PI3K and Akt following SFRP2 editing, indicating pathway activation. Treatment of SFRP2-edited DPCs with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 reduced the elevated phosphorylation and reversed the functional phenotypes, confirming PI3K-Akt pathway involvement. Collectively, these findings indicate that SFRP2 mediates DPC biological activities by means of PI3K‑Akt‑driven transcriptional‑metabolic networks, yielding novel perspectives on the molecular regulatory machinery controlling HF physiology.

title: Cancer-Associated Fibroblast-Derived miR-483-5p Promotes Liver Cancer Cell Proliferation and Stemness via MOAP1 Downregulation.
abstract: Within the tumor microenvironment (TME), cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) play an important role in liver cancer progression through intercellular communication, including the release of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs). This study investigated the potential mechanisms underlying the effects of CAF-associated miR-483-5p on liver cancer progression. sEV-enriched preparations were isolated from CAFs transfected with a miR-483-5p mimic or an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) and subsequently used to treat HepG2 cells. These preparations were designated as CAF-sEV-miR-483-5p-mimic and CAF-sEV-miR-483-5p-ASO, respectively. To evaluate cell proliferation and stemness, colony formation and spheroid formation assays were applied. Additionally, a subcutaneous xenograft model in nude mice was established to assess the in vivo effects of these CAF-derived sEV-enriched preparations. MiR-483-5p enhanced HepG2 cell proliferation, stemness, and migration, and higher miR-483-5p expression was associated with poorer patient prognosis. CAF-derived sEV-enriched preparations was associated with increased miR-483-5p levels in HepG2 cells, suggesting that these preparations may contribute to the regulation of miR-483-5p levels in recipient cells. The CAF-sEV-miR-483-5p mimic preparation promoted HepG2 cell proliferation and stemness while suppressing apoptosis. Luciferase reporter and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) assays supported the direct interaction between miR-483-5p and the Modulator of apoptosis 1 (MOAP1) 3' untranslated region (3'-UTR) and showed that miR-483-5p negatively regulates MOAP1 expression. MOAP1 downregulation was associated with increased proliferation and stemness in HepG2 cells. Importantly, MOAP1 overexpression attenuated miR-483-5p-induced increases in proliferation, migration, and stemness in HepG2 cells, as well as the upregulation of Wnt1, β-catenin, Nanog, Sox2, and Oct4. Furthermore, miR-483-5p ASO reversed the effects of CAF-derived sEV-enriched preparations on miR-483-5p levels, MOAP1 expression, and HepG2 cell viability. In vivo, the CAF-sEV-miR-483-5p-mimic preparation promoted xenograft tumor growth in nude mice. Collectively, CAF-derived sEV-enriched preparations may contribute to increased miR-483-5p levels and promote the growth and stemness of liver cancer cells, potentially through miR-483-5p-mediated downregulation of MOAP1. These findings suggest that the miR-483-5p/MOAP1 regulatory axis may serve as a potential therapeutic target for liver cancer.

title: Nucleic Acid Therapeutics in Rare Disease: From Precision Medicine to Programmable Platforms.
abstract: Nucleic acid therapeutics (NATs), including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics and programmable editing technologies, are reshaping the therapeutic landscape for inherited metabolic and genetic disease. Unlike conventional small molecules or biologics, NATs enable sequence-directed modulation of target gene expression and therefore provide unprecedented flexibility for targeting pathogenic mechanisms previously considered undruggable. Recent clinical successes have established proof of concept for multiple NAT modalities across neurological, hepatic, muscular and metabolic disorders. However, broader implementation remains constrained by challenges in tissue-specific delivery, biomarker validation, natural-history infrastructure and evidence generation in ultra-rare populations. In parallel, increasing platform reproducibility is beginning to challenge traditional product-based regulatory paradigms. This review examines the principal classes of NATs and proposes a practical framework for modality selection based on disease biology, tissue accessibility, durability, reversibility and clinical context. We discuss key translational bottlenecks beyond delivery, including biomarker-outcome relationships, small-population trial design and the limitations of conventional evidentiary frameworks in rare disease. A central theme of this review is the growing transition from isolated precision medicines towards increasingly programmable therapeutic platforms. We explore how advances in extrahepatic delivery, computational oligonucleotide design, artificial intelligence-assisted optimisation and programmable editing technologies may progressively support more scalable and individualised therapeutic development. Finally, we discuss emerging regulatory frameworks that may better accommodate platform-level predictability while maintaining rigorous evaluation of sequence-specific and disease-specific risks.

title: Toll-Like Receptor-Driven Neuroinflammation in Neurological Disorders: Signaling Crosstalk and Therapeutic Opportunities.
abstract: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) serve as pivotal mediators bridging innate immunity and neuroinflammation, orchestrating pathological cascades that drive neurological disorders. Beyond their sentinel role in pathogen recognition, aberrant TLR activation triggers intricate and destructive signaling networks, including activation of NF-κB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, and PI3K/AKT, alongside IRFs and type I interferon responses that converge on chronic neuroinflammation and subsequent neuronal damage. This review dissects TLRs' multilayered contribution to neuropathology, emphasizing their regulation of secondary inflammatory mechanisms, including NLRP3 inflammasome priming and activation, mTOR-driven metabolic dysregulation, SOCS-mediated feedback inhibition, inflammasome activation, and pyroptotic cell death. Critically, these signaling pathways create a pathological intersection with oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, amplifying a self-perpetuating cycle of neuronal injury that underlies conditions like Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), Huntington's disease (HD), and Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Stroke, Multiple sclerosis (MS), Epilepsy and Traumatic brain injury (TBI). Against this neuropathological landscape, this review systematically evaluates emerging therapeutic strategies targeting TLR-mediated neuroinflammation, encompassing small molecule TLR antagonists, intracellular adaptor protein inhibitors targeting myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88) and TIR-domain-containing adapter-inducing interferon-β (TRIF), biologic therapies including monoclonal antibodies and fusion proteins, natural phytochemicals and nutraceuticals, Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based genomic interventions, and cell-based immunomodulatory therapies, collectively representing a mechanistically diverse arsenal aimed at recalibrating the dysregulated innate immune response to achieve durable neuroprotection across the full spectrum of TLR-mediated neurological disorders.

title: Dimethoxytrityl-Protected Oligonucleotide Purification With On-Column Detritylation in Hydrophobic Interaction Chromatography.
abstract: State-of-the-art techniques using synthetic antisense oligonucleotides and other nucleotide-based therapeutics have transformed treatment for a wide range of diseases, including neurological, metabolic, cardiovascular, and muscular disorders, many of which were previously incurable. As the biopharmaceutical industry expands into this new therapeutic field, there is increasing demand for robust purification and analytical techniques. Therapeutic oligonucleotides are most often purified by ion pair-reversed phase (IP-RP) and anion-exchange (AEX) chromatography techniques. Here, we present a single-step chromatography approach utilizing hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC) for a 5'-dimethoxytrityl (5'-DMT)-protected 20-mer single-stranded DNA oligonucleotide. The HIC process incorporates an optimized on-column detritylation step at pH 4.0, enabling removal of the 5'-DMT protective cap from the purified oligonucleotide. This method also effectively eliminated the majority of < 20-mer oligonucleotide impurities, which were present as deprotected oligonucleotides in the crude starting material. Analytical RP and AEX chromatography methods confirmed nearly complete (99.6%) 5'-DMT removal and an oligonucleotide recovery rate of 96.9% for the final product. Moreover, an RP chromatographic depurination assay demonstrated that the acidic detritylation procedure did not result in detrimental adenine or guanine purine base loss. The all-aqueous HIC process is environmentally friendly and avoids the flammability risks associated with RP technique.

title: CRISPR Technology: From Bench to Bedside Applications.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas genome editing represents one of the most transformative advances in modern molecular biology, enabling programmable site-specific genetic modification that has revolutionized functional genomics and precision therapeutic development. Beyond canonical Cas9 nucleases, the CRISPR toolkit has diversified into precision base editors, prime editors, CRISPR-associated transposases, and Cas12/Cas13 RNA-targeting effectors, each with distinct mechanistic properties. Clinically, ex vivo CRISPR therapies for hemoglobinopathies have secured regulatory approval, while base editing, prime editing, and in vivo Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T candidates are advancing through trials for a broad spectrum of hematologic, oncologic, and rare genetic disorders. However, existing reviews largely address technical innovation or clinical translation in isolation, lacking a holistic, up-to-date synthesis of the full bench-to-bedside trajectory of CRISPR technology. This review systematically dissects the molecular mechanisms, advantages, and limitations of core CRISPR editing platforms; summarizes pivotal clinical data across hemoglobinopathies, CAR-T immunotherapy, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cardiometabolic diseases and rare monogenic diseases; evaluates delivery systems including lipid nanoparticles and viral vectors; and discusses key translational barriers such as off-target genotoxicity and immunogenicity alongside emerging optimization strategies. This work provides a holistic bench-to-bedside framework for CRISPR research, offering critical insights to advance next-generation precision genetic medicine.

title: Therapeutic and Prophylactic Agents for Viral Diseases: Current Status, Challenges, and Future Prospects.
abstract: Viral diseases remain a major global health challenge despite substantial advances in vaccination, antiviral therapeutics, and public-health interventions. However, current antiviral strategies are still constrained by important gaps, including rapid viral evolution, limited broad-spectrum efficacy, immune escape, antiviral resistance, incomplete durability of protection, and inequitable global access to prevention and treatment. This review provides a comprehensive and integrated overview of contemporary antiviral prevention and therapeutic strategies, spanning vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, direct-acting antivirals, host-targeted therapies, immunomodulators, RNA-based therapeutics, gene-editing technologies, and cellular immunotherapies. We discuss the mechanistic foundations, clinical applications, pharmacologic considerations, and translational challenges associated with each modality across major human viral pathogens, including HIV, HBV, HCV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, Ebola virus, arboviruses, and herpesviruses. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging innovations such as long-acting prophylaxis, Fc-engineered monoclonal antibodies, nanoparticle and mucosal vaccine platforms, CRISPR-based antiviral systems, and broadly protective host-directed approaches designed to overcome resistance and enhance pandemic preparedness. In addition, we highlight the growing importance of real-time genomic surveillance and equitable global deployment strategies in shaping future antiviral responses, collectively underscoring that the next generation of antiviral medicine will depend on the convergence of universal immunization strategies, durable therapeutics, precision immune modulation, and rapidly deployable platform technologies capable of addressing both endemic and emerging viral threats.

title: Inhaled Nanomedicines for Lung Diseases and Injuries: Pharmacological Advances and Clinical Translation.
abstract: Respiratory diseases remain major causes of morbidity and mortality; however, inadequate pulmonary drug exposure and systemic toxicity continue to limit treatment efficacy. Inhaled nanomedicines offer opportunities for localized, sustained, and targeted therapy. This review examines how disease biology informs pulmonary delivery design across pulmonary fibrosis, lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary infections, and acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome. It outlines anatomical and biological barriers and compares liposomes, lipid nanoparticles, polymeric and hybrid systems, biomimetic carriers, and stimuli-responsive formulations. Particular attention is given to matching therapeutic cargo and carrier properties to fibroblasts, macrophages, tumor cells, and alveolar type II cells. Emerging approaches include mRNA delivery, siRNA-mediated gene silencing, antisense oligonucleotides, and CRISPR-based editing, alongside alveolar regeneration and biomarker-guided treatment. These strategies are evaluated in relation to their delivery requirements and stage of development. The review also addresses aerosol-device compatibility, manufacturing, repeated-dose safety, regulatory considerations, and clinical outcomes. By connecting delivery mechanisms with disease-specific applications and clinical evidence, this review identifies both therapeutic opportunities and barriers to translation. This integrated perspective can guide the development of inhaled nanomedicines with more reproducible pulmonary delivery, improved treatment efficacy, and acceptable safety.

title: Alzheimer's Disease: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Advances.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative condition accompanied by widespread central nervous system damage and complex networked pathogenesis spanning molecular, cellular, and systemic dimensions. Existing studies tend to focus on individual pathological cascades or monotherapeutic approaches, while overlooking the intrinsic crosstalk among protein pathology, neuroinflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and gut-brain axis imbalance, with insufficient systematic integration of nonpharmacological strategies and multifunctional nanoplatforms. Driven by intertwined molecular aberrations, glial dysregulation and systemic metabolic disorders, AD presents profound pathological complexity. Correspondingly, multitarget pharmacotherapy integrated with hierarchical nonpharmacological and nanotherapeutic interventions has achieved substantial progress, exerting synergistic effects on alleviating AD pathological cascades and optimizing overall therapeutic regimens. We comprehensively review current evidence to delineate the mechanistic landscape of AD and update therapeutic advances, including pharmacological agents, multimodal nonpharmacological interventions, and brain-targeted nanosystems for blood-brain barrier penetration, protein modulation, microenvironment remodeling, and gene editing delivery. This study underscores major research limitations and translational obstacles in therapeutic efficacy, biosafety, and nanomedicine applications. This work emphasizes biomarker-based early stratification and staged combined interventions, providing novel integrated insights into AD pathogenesis and prospective targeted therapeutic development.

title: Adipose-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cells: Isolation, Origin, Phenotype Applications, and Challenges.
abstract: Traditional adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (AD-MSCs) research has relied on unfractionated bulk populations, whose therapeutic efficacy is constrained by cellular heterogeneity, culture-induced phenotypic drift, and rapid postengraftment functional exhaustion, resulting in inconsistent outcomes and impeding clinical translation. This review systematically examines AD-MSC developmental origins, tissue niches, isolation and purification strategies, functional phenotypes, and biomanufacturing bottlenecks. It integrates preclinical and clinical evidence for AD-MSCs and their extracellular vesicles (EVs) in bone and cartilage regeneration, chronic cutaneous diseases, neurological disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and other conditions. These therapies remodel injured microenvironments through immunometabolic reprogramming, antifibrotic signaling, angiogenesis, mitochondrial transfer, and paracrine regulation rather than direct tissue replacement. Major translational barriers include cellular heterogeneity, safety concerns, the transdifferentiation controversy, nonstandardized preconditioning, culture-induced phenotypic drift, and low cell retention after transplantation. We propose that clinical translation should be based on prospective isolation of functional subpopulations, coupled with tailored preconditioning, precision gene editing, three-dimensional biomaterials, EV engineering, and automated closed-system biomanufacturing. This framework aims to preserve potency, phenotypic stability, and paracrine function, transforming AD-MSCs and their bioactive derivatives from variable, unfractionated preparations into well-characterized, standardized, highly potent precision biologics. More broadly, it offers a mechanism-driven, function-defined, engineering-enabled, and clinically accessible roadmap for next-generation regenerative medicine.

title: Assessment of Allometric Scaling Methods for the Prediction of Human Pharmacokinetic of LNA-i-miR-221.
abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides are small synthetic DNA or RNA molecules that can be used to modulate gene expression, particularly to block the production of unwanted proteins. This makes them potentially powerful drugs to contrast cancer growth. Drug development is a long process that includes preclinical and clinical studies. Preclinical animal studies are designed to assess drug kinetics and safety before progressing to clinical trials, as they may predict the therapeutic dose to be used in the "first in human" (FIH) studies. This is usually achieved by applying allometric scaling methods that allow predicting the human pharmacokinetic (PK) parameters from those estimated in animals. Selecting the appropriate scaling formula reduces the risk of translational uncertainty and supports the design of FIH studies. The aim of this study is to compare the accuracy of different allometric scaling methods in predicting human PK of the antisense oligonucleotide LNA-i-miR-221, a powerful inhibitor of microRNA miR-221, which was found to be deregulated in several malignancies, favoring cancer progression. To do that, we exploited the availability of PK data of the drug in both Sprague Dawley rats and humans and we found that the best scaling method for both clearance and distribution volume is the simple allometry, with predictions laying within the 2-fold and 4-fold error interval, respectively. This study contributes to identifying the most accurate scaling methods among the evaluated single-species approaches to extrapolate human pharmacokinetic for LNA-i-miR-221, possibly offering a starting point for future studies involving antisense oligonucleotides.

title: Lung-Targeting Interleukin-10 mRNA Sulfonium Lipid Nanoparticles Ameliorate Acute Lung Injury.
abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the most severe manifestation of acute lung injury (ALI), characterized by diffuse pulmonary inflammation, impaired gas exchange, and high morbidity and mortality. Despite the clinical significance of ARDS, no effective pharmacological therapies are currently available. In this study, we developed a lung-targeted mRNA-sulfonium lipid nanoparticle (mRNA/sLNP) delivery system for the treatment of ALI/ARDS in a mouse model. We first examined different heads and tails to optimize sulfonium lipid structure, leading to the identification of a top-performing HOSEH formulation. HOSEH sLNP was comprehensively characterized and subsequently loaded with interleukin-10 (IL-10) mRNA, an immunomodulatory cytokine with potent anti-inflammatory activity. As a proof-of-concept, in a lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced ALI mouse model, IL-10 mRNA/sLNP demonstrated both prophylactic and therapeutic efficacy, significantly attenuating pulmonary and systemic inflammation, restoring alveolar-capillary barrier integrity, and reducing lung tissue damage. These findings highlight the potential of lung-targeted mRNA therapeutics in inflammatory lung diseases. With further development, IL-10 mRNA/sLNP may represent a promising strategy for the treatment of ALI and ARDS.

title: Genetically Encoded Engineering Switchable Circular RNA Devices for Targeted Protein Degradation.
abstract: Targeted protein degradation has shown powerful capability for diseases treatment. However, the approach is limited by the challenges in cellular internalization of synthetic degrader and potential cytotoxicity. Herein, we propose a Genetically encoded circular RNA Aptamer-based DEgrader (GRADE) to control target proteins degradation. The GRADE system is facilely constructed by integrating a transferrin receptor (TfR1) aptamer and target protein aptamer for delivering target protein into damaged endosomes and TfR1 binding, leading to target protein degradation via endosomal autophagy pathways. We show that the versatile and modular GRADE could be applied to eliminate several intracellular target proteins. Moreover, the GRADE system can be selectively activated by endogenous biomarkers for achieving highly specific protein degradation and cancer cell precise inhibition. This study presents a non-invasive, effective and general platform for intracellular protein degradation, offering new insights into controlled cell manipulation and diseases therapy.

title: Macrophages as targets for adoptive cell therapy against solid tumors.
abstract: The ability to modulate the tumor microenvironment emerges as a compelling strategy to stimulate antitumor immunity in solid tumors. In this context, innate immune cells, especially macrophages, are interesting targets for immunotherapies. Approaches based on CRISPR to delete specific suppressive molecules in these cells might lead to antitumor immunity. The target molecules to be depleted will depend on the type of tumor, since the tumor microenvironment and its immune-suppressive regulators can vary. This correspondence aims to discuss published animal models and stimulate research in this critical subject for the improvement of immunotherapies targeting macrophages. New therapeutic strategies, including epigenetic modifications to stabilize the proinflammatory phenotypes of these cells, are underscored.

title: Microbial serotonin signalling axes in irritable bowel syndrome: integrative molecular crosstalk among enterochromaffin cells, gut microbiota, neuroimmune circuits, and precision therapeutic engineering.
abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common, often disabling disorder of gut-brain interaction whose molecular basis remains incompletely defined, leaving diagnosis largely symptom-based and treatment largely non-mechanistic. We argue that the serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; hereafter 5-HT, the primary term used throughout, with "serotonin" retained in less technical contexts) signalling axis-positioned at the interface of the gut microbiota, enterochromaffin (EC) cells, enteric neurons, and the mucosal immune system-is a central, unifying integrator of IBS pathophysiology, and that reframing IBS around this axis offers a route toward mechanism-based subtyping and therapy. We first synthesise how microbiota-driven tryptophan metabolism, short-chain fatty acid and secondary bile acid signalling, and epigenetic regulation of tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1) shape EC-cell serotonin output, before examining the neuroimmune consequences of dysregulated serotonin secretion-mast cell activation, macrophage polarisation, neurogenic inflammation-and the microbiota-serotonin-gut-brain connectome linking vagal afferent signalling, blood-brain barrier permeability, and central neurotransmitter networks. We then discuss molecular stratification of IBS subtypes through serotonergic endotyping-incorporating SLC6A4 and TPH1 polymorphisms, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics-and critically evaluate next-generation therapeutic strategies, including engineered probiotic chassis, CRISPR-mediated microbial editing, and AI-guided nanomedicine, distinguishing proof-of-concept findings from clinically validated approaches. We conclude that reconceptualising IBS as a disorder of disrupted microbial serotonergic ecosystems, rather than a purely symptom-defined syndrome, offers a coherent and testable framework for biomarker discovery and precision, mechanism-directed therapy, while highlighting the causal-directionality and clinical-translation gaps that must be closed before this framework can be applied at the bedside.

title: Conditional Codon-Boundary Dinucleotide Organization in Platycerium Plastomes.
abstract: Synonymous evolution can alter both codon abundance and the placement of synonymous codons within genes. We asked whether plastid coding sequences retain non-random codon-boundary organization after protein sequence and exact codon inventory are held constant. We analysed 44 genes lacking an RNA-editing exception flag in the reference annotation across 18 Platycerium species, using exact-codon conditional randomization as the principal analysis and RSCU comparisons as supporting phylogenetic context. CpG boundaries were depleted across species and most genes, with the direction retained under reconstruction and gene-length sensitivities. TpA showed greater gene-level heterogeneity. Both patterns belonged to a coupled landscape of 16 boundary contexts, in which GpT had the lowest observed/expected ratio. These observations distinguish synonymous placement from codon abundance without identifying the evolutionary processes responsible. Shared ancestry, context-dependent mutation, and local sequence constraints remain compatible explanations. The results establish a boundary-order pattern within the sampled matrix and motivate phylogenetically informed comparisons to distinguish historical retention from continued maintenance or recurrent change.

title: Integrating RNA technologies with CAR-T cell therapy: strategies to overcome current limitations and expand clinical applications.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy has emerged as a prominent cancer treatment modality, demonstrating significant clinical success. To date, several CAR-T products have been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of hematological malignancies. Despite these advances, several challenges continue to limit the broader application of CAR-T therapy. These challenges include complex and costly manufacturing processes, safety concerns associated with integrating viral vectors, individualized production requirements, therapy-related adverse effects, and limited efficacy against solid tumors. Recent progress in ribonucleic acid (RNA)-based technologies has introduced promising strategies to improve the safety, adaptability, and therapeutic performance of CAR-T cells. This review provides a comprehensive translational perspective on the integration of RNA technologies with CAR-T therapy. Specifically, it categorizes current approaches into four key areas: RNA-driven non-viral CAR-T cell manufacturing, RNA vaccine-mediated enhancement of CAR-T activity, RNA interference (RNAi)-based modulation, and in vivo CAR-T cell generation. Among the reviewed approaches, ex vivo messenger RNA (mRNA)-based CAR-T engineering currently has the greatest clinical maturity, whereas RNA vaccine-mediated boosting shows particular promise for enhancing CAR-T expansion and persistence, especially in solid tumors. In vivo RNA-mediated CAR-T generation remains at an early stage of development, with evidence still predominantly derived from preclinical studies, but may ultimately represent the most transformative approach by simplifying manufacturing and improving accessibility.Trial registration number: Not applicable.

title: Measles-like hypermutation of a Newcastle disease virus drives fatal encephalitis during BCMA × CD3 T-cell-redirecting immunotherapy.
abstract: Newcastle disease virus (NDV or AOaV-1) is an avian paramyxovirus that typically causes only mild, self-limiting disease in humans. Here, we report fatal neuroinvasive AOaV-1 infection in a patient with multiple myeloma receiving maintenance therapy with teclistamab, daratumumab, and lenalidomide following frontline teclistamab-based treatment and autologous stem cell transplantation. Following rapidly progressive brainstem-cerebellar encephalitis and negative conventional microbiological testing, unbiased metagenomic RNA sequencing of a cerebellar biopsy identified AOaV-1 at high intraparenchymal abundance. Viral genome analysis revealed striking A-to-G and U-to-C substitutions selectively concentrated in the matrix gene, consistent with ADAR-mediated RNA editing. Long-read sequencing resolved two genetically distinct, independently hypermutated CNS haplotypes. Post-mortem analysis demonstrated widespread dissemination and continued viral diversification in multiple brain regions, whereas a peripheral urine sample contained a minimally mutated putative ancestral lineage. These findings support peripheral infection followed by CNS seeding and compartmentalized within-host evolution. The selective matrix-gene hypermutation closely parallels persistent measles virus infection in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, revealing a shared mechanism of paramyxovirus adaptation to the CNS. Profound immunotherapy-associated immune dysfunction may thus create niches enabling normally low-pathogenic zoonotic viruses to persist, evolve, and acquire severe neurovirulence.

title: Research progress of gene correction for genetic diseases via in vivo prime editing.
abstract: Curative therapies for genetic diseases caused by pathogenic mutations demand precise and safe genome editing technologies. Prime editing (PE), a CRISPR-Cas9-derived technology that enables precise base conversions without double-strand breaks (DSBs), has emerged as a transformative tool with the ability to correct 89% of human pathogenic mutations. However, transitioning PE from preclinical models to clinical applications faces critical challenges, particularly in the development of in vivo delivery systems and scalable manufacturing. This review systematically summarizes advances of in vivo PE therapeutics, focusing on the therapeutic outcomes across some retinal, metabolic, and hematologic genetic diseases. We further dissect barriers to clinical translation, including in the immunogenicity of viral vectors, off-target risks in nondividing cells, and large-scale production bottlenecks. By highlighting the unique advantages of in vivo PE and proposing actionable solutions for scalable manufacturing, the work provides a roadmap for accelerating in vivo PE-based therapies toward clinical reality.

title: Computational and experimental strategies for functional validation of non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterised by extensive genomic heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. Although recurrent coding mutations in key driver genes have been well researched, large-scale sequencing studies have identified a broad array of non-coding variants which may contribute to tumorigenesis by interfering with gene regulatory mechanisms. However, understanding the functional significance of these variants remains a major challenge due to their abundance and the complexity of non-coding regulatory structures. This review outlines current computational and experimental techniques to identify, prioritise, and functionally validate non-coding variants in PDAC. We discuss in silico methods including genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapping, colocalisation, machine learning-driven functional annotation, and the use of established computational tools, in addition to epigenomic profiling technologies including, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and CUT&RUN which define regulatory landscapes. We also emphasise new AI-based methods involving radiogenomics, AI imaging analysis and data integration, which provides novel potential to link genomic variation with phenotypic and imaging characteristics. Additionally, we highlight experimental validation techniques including reporter assays, electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), chromatin conformation capture methods, and CRISPR-based perturbation systems used to study variant functionality. Together, these complementary approaches establish a framework for correlating non-coding variation to regulatory mechanisms in PDAC.

title: Integrative CRISPR-Cas9 dependency analysis identifies CDC45 as a candidate prognostic biomarker with preliminary functional validation in prostate adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD) has become one of the most prevalent malignancies in men worldwide. Although advances in diagnostic techniques and targeted therapies have improved clinical outcomes, a significant subset of patients still develops aggressive, metastatic disease with limited treatment options. At present, identifying reliable biomarkers for early risk stratification remains a critical unmet need in prostate cancer research. This study presents a dependency-informed prognostic prioritization approach by integrating multi-omics data to enhance clinical risk stratification in prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD). Integrated analysis of CRISPR-Cas9 dependency screens and bulk RNA sequencing data prioritized tumor-dependent genes associated with PRAD cell viability. Pathway enrichment analysis indicated the involvement of these candidate genes in cell cycle regulation and tumor progression. Subsequently, an 11-gene prognostic signature was constructed via LASSO regression, effectively stratifying patients, with the high-risk cohort demonstrating significantly reduced Progression-Free Interval (PFI; log-rank p < 0.001). Among the prioritized hub genes, CDC45 exhibited marked upregulation in tumor tissues, which was confirmed by Western blotting and qRT-PCR. Collectively, this study provides a dependency-informed prognostic framework for PRAD and nominates CDC45 as a candidate prognostic biomarker, laying the groundwork for future mechanistically resolved investigations.

title: Neuroprotective effects of the petroleum ether fraction of Teucrium polium in free and lipid nanoparticle formulations on cognitive deficits and oxidative stress in an ICV-STZ-induced Alzheimer's-like rat model.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline, oxidative stress, and neuronal loss. Current pharmacological treatments provide only partial symptomatic relief. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of the petroleum ether fraction of Teucrium polium (T. polium), administered in both free and lipid nanoparticle formulations (T. polium-LNP), in a rat model of AD-like pathology induced by intracerebroventricular streptozotocin (ICV-STZ).
METHODS: Adult male Wistar rats were divided into five groups: Control, ICV-STZ, ICV-STZ + Memantine, ICV-STZ + T. polium, and ICV-STZ + T. polium-LNP. Cognitive function was assessed using the Morris water maze (MWM) and novel object recognition (NOR) tests. Serum oxidative stress markers-including malondialdehyde (MDA), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity-were measured. Hippocampal CA1 histopathology and hippocampal mRNA expression of Bax, Bcl-2, and p53 were also evaluated.
RESULTS: The ICV-STZ-induced AD-like model was associated with memory impairment, increased serum MDA levels, reduced TAC levels and SOD activity, and hippocampal CA1 neuronal damage, accompanied by increased Bax and p53 expression and decreased Bcl-2 expression. Treatment with T. polium and T. polium-LNP improved cognitive performance, particularly spatial memory in the MWM, and attenuated several pathological changes. Both treatments reduced serum MDA levels and decreased CA1 neuronal degeneration.
CONCLUSION: In this experimental AD-like rat model, both formulations of T. polium were associated with improvements in cognitive performance, serum oxidative status markers, and hippocampal tissue changes. Although T. polium-LNP showed numerically greater effects on several outcomes, direct comparisons between the free T. polium extract and T. polium-LNP were statistically significant only for CA1 neuronal damage. Further mechanistic and long-term studies are needed to clarify the potential relevance of these findings to AD-related neuroprotection.

title: The hepatic secretome-microglia axis in huntington's disease: Linking peripheral metabolic dysfunction to neuroinflammation and novel therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is traditionally regarded as a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the HTT gene, resulting in selective striatal neuronal degeneration and progressive motor, cognitive, and psychiatric impairment. However, accumulating evidence indicates that HD is a systemic disorder involving profound metabolic, mitochondrial, and immune dysfunction in peripheral organs, particularly the liver. Emerging studies suggest that hepatic mitochondrial dysfunction induced by mutant huntingtin remodels the hepatic secretome through altered secretion of hepatokines, extracellular vesicles, complement proteins, inflammatory cytokines, and metabolic mediators. These circulating factors may disrupt blood-brain barrier integrity, promote microglial immunometabolic reprogramming, enhance complement-mediated synaptic pruning, and amplify chronic neuroinflammation, thereby accelerating neurodegeneration. This review summarizes current evidence supporting the liver-brain axis in HD and discusses how hepatic metabolic dysfunction contributes to central nervous system pathology. Furthermore, we highlight therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring hepatic mitochondrial homeostasis, modulating hepatokines, extracellular vesicles, exosomal microRNAs, and complement signaling to interrupt pathological liver-to-brain communication. Finally, we discuss emerging translational approaches, including multi-omics technologies, engineered extracellular vesicles, gene-editing platforms, and precision medicine, that may facilitate the development of disease-modifying therapies. By integrating peripheral metabolic regulation with central neuroimmune mechanisms, this review presents the hepatic secretome microglia axis as a potential conceptual framework for understanding HD pathogenesis and identifies liver targeted interventions as promising therapeutic opportunities beyond conventional neuron centric strategies.

title: A comprehensive review of mixed-species biofilm infections and innovative therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Mixed-species biofilm infections are important causes of persistent and difficult-to-treat infections. Compared with monospecies biofilms, mixed-species communities contain microorganisms with different physiological and genetic characteristics that interact through metabolic cooperation, chemical signaling, competition, and modification of the local environment. These interactions, together with the EPS matrix, physiological heterogeneity, and HGT, can increase antimicrobial tolerance, contributing to treatment failure and infection recurrence. Polymicrobial biofilms are associated with chronic wounds, respiratory infections, catheter- and device-associated infections, and other persistent infections. However, treatment of polymicrobial biofilms remains challenging because their complex structure and interspecies interactions can reduce antimicrobial efficacy. This review summarizes the clinical significance, formation, and persistence of mixed-species biofilms and discusses recent therapeutic strategies for their control. We also discuss recent approaches for controlling polymicrobial biofilms, including natural compounds, QS inhibition, CRISPR-Cas-based approaches, biofilm matrix targeting, metabolic and nutrient disruption, nanotechnology, and phage therapy. Recent studies show that these approaches can inhibit biofilm formation, disrupt established biofilms, enhance antimicrobial activity, and selectively target specific microbial populations. However, their effectiveness varies with microbial composition, biofilm maturity, matrix characteristics, and treatment conditions. Overall, current evidence supports the development of targeted and combination-based strategies for mixed-species biofilms. Further studies using clinically relevant models are needed to exactly define treatment efficacy and support the translation of these approaches into clinical practice.

title: Precision gene targeting: comparative roles of siRNA, miRNA, and CRISPR technologies in gene silencing and genome editing: a review.
abstract: Precision gene targeting has emerged as a powerful approach for selectively regulating gene expression and modifying disease-associated genetic pathways. Among the principal technologies, small interfering RNA (siRNA), microRNA (miRNA), CRISPR-Cas9, and CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) provide distinct yet complementary strategies for gene regulation and genome manipulation. siRNAs mediate sequence-specific post-transcriptional gene silencing through degradation of complementary messenger RNA, enabling potent and generally transient suppression of target genes. In contrast, miRNAs are endogenous regulatory RNAs that modulate multiple transcripts through translational repression and mRNA destabilization, thereby influencing diverse cellular processes and regulatory networks. CRISPR-Cas9 expands the scope of precision gene targeting by enabling programmable modification of genomic DNA, whereas CRISPRi uses catalytically inactive Cas9 to achieve targeted transcriptional repression without introducing DNA double-strand breaks. This review provides a comparative and critical analysis of these technologies, emphasizing their molecular mechanisms, target recognition, specificity, delivery strategies, therapeutic applications, clinical development, advantages, limitations, and safety considerations. Collectively, these platforms have demonstrated therapeutic potential across a broad range of diseases, including cancer, genetic and metabolic disorders, cardiovascular and neurological diseases, infectious diseases, and ocular disorders. However, important barriers to clinical translation remain, including delivery limitations, molecular stability, target and off-target effects, immunogenicity, toxicity, genomic instability, and the need for precise and durable control of gene modulation. For CRISPR-based approaches, additional considerations include modality-specific genomic alterations, prolonged editor activity, and the ethical and regulatory implications of permanent genome modification. Continued advances in molecular engineering, delivery technologies, target-selection strategies, and platform optimization may improve the specificity, safety, durability, and therapeutic efficacy of these approaches and facilitate their responsible integration into precision medicine.

title: CRISPR interference-based gene silencing in insects: from functional genomics to prospective insect-pest management applications.
abstract: Insect-pests remain a major constraint to global agriculture, causing yield losses through direct feeding and transmission of phytopathogens. Chemical pesticides and transgenic crops expressing Bacillus thuringiensis toxins have shown initial success; however, their use is increasingly constrained by resistance, non-target effects, environmental contamination and regulatory restrictions. Although RNA interference (RNAi) presents a targeted and eco-friendly alternative, it is limited by species variability, rapid double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) degradation, inconsistent silencing and off-target effects. Nuclease-active Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) enables genetic editing, but its irreversible genome modifications raise ethical, ecological and regulatory concerns. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) offers a programmable approach for sequence-specific, reversible transcriptional suppression without inducing double-strand DNA breaks. Using catalytically inactive Cas9 (dead Cas9 or dCas9) -guided by single-guide RNA (sgRNA), CRISPRi inhibits transcription initiation or elongation while maintaining genomic integrity. Experimental studies in insect models, including disease-vector mosquitoes, have demonstrated effective suppression of coding and non-coding genes, supporting CRISPRi as a functional genomics tool. This review discusses CRISPRi mechanisms, applications, advantages and limitations in insects, comparing it with RNAi and CRISPR/Cas9. Overall, current evidences indicate that CRISPRi is a precise and non-mutagenic platform for insect-pest management, particularly where controlled, reversible and species-specific gene regulation is desirable. However, its application in agricultural pest management remains an extrapolation from functional-genomics studies and requires validation in pest species under whole-organism and field-relevant conditions.
