title: Inline Raman Spectroscopy as a Process Analytical Technology Tool for Real-Time Concentration Monitoring and Mixing Endpoint Determination of an Oligonucleotide Drug Product.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Oligonucleotide drug product manufacturing commonly relies on time-consuming offline ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analyses to confirm active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) concentration during mixing, providing limited process visibility. This study evaluated inline Raman spectroscopy as a process analytical technology (PAT) tool for real-time API concentration monitoring and mixing endpoint determination during manufacture of a model antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) drug product.
METHODS: A partial least squares regression (PLSR) model was developed from inline Raman spectra using offline UV-Vis reference concentrations. Accuracy, linearity, range, precision, specificity, and robustness were evaluated, including effects of stirring speed, probe depth, and reusable versus single-use Raman optics. The validated model was applied to four ASO drug product batches manufactured in a 50-L single-use mixer.
RESULTS: The PLSR model demonstrated good accuracy (RMSEP = 3.47 mg/mL), good linearity (R2 = 0.994 and 0.996 for calibration and independent prediction set, respectively), and precision (maximum %RSD = 1.12%). Minimal water interference supported specificity, and consistent performance across stirring speeds, probe depths, and Raman optic configurations demonstrated robustness. The procedure generated real-time ASO API concentration profiles and successfully determined the mixing endpoint for all four batches.
CONCLUSIONS: Inline Raman spectroscopy coupled with PLSR provided accurate, specific, and robust real-time API concentration monitoring during oligonucleotide drug product manufacturing. The approach enabled real-time monitoring and objective mixing endpoint determination and may reduce reliance on offline measurements while improving process visibility and supporting more timely progression of manufacturing operations.

title: Intervening in Adipocyte Senescence: Lipid Prodrugs as an Emerging Strategy for Metabolic Disease Treatment.
abstract: The accelerating aging of the global population has made aging and its related diseases major public health challenges in the 21st century. Adipose tissue is not only an energy reservoir but also a crucial endocrine organ and metabolic regulator. Its dysfunction is closely linked to aging and the development of multiple diseases. This review outlines the key characteristics of adipocyte senescence and discusses its pathological contributions to obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and cardiovascular diseases. It also summarizes current intervention strategies for adipocyte senescence, including senolytics, senomorphics, caloric restriction, physical exercise, and gene editing. We propose lipid prodrugs as promising adipose tissue delivery platforms that can be coupled with diverse therapeutic agents to increase the local concentration of drugs and minimize systemic toxicity. By utilizing the unique lipid metabolism of adipocytes, this strategy offers a new avenue for therapeutic intervention in adipocyte senescence and its associated metabolic disorders.

title: Emerging gene and stem cell therapies for hereditary hearing loss: from molecular correction to regenerative reconstruction.
abstract: Hearing loss is among the most common sensory impairments globally and remains a significant unmet clinical challenge. Current rehabilitative approaches, such as hearing aids and cochlear implants, provide partial functional compensation but fail to restore the structural and physiological integrity of the cochlea. This review summarizes progress in therapeutic development targeting key deafness-associated genes, including OTOF, GJB2, and SLC26A4, highlighting the rationale, current clinical evidence, and major translational challenges. We further discuss the potential of combining gene therapy with stem cell-based approaches to promote inner ear regeneration and restore sensorineural function. Emerging technologies such as CRISPR/Cas, adeno-associated virus, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived otic progenitors have opened new avenues for causal correction and tissue reconstruction. Integrated therapeutic models that combine gene or stem cell therapy with cochlear implants are reshaping the treatment paradigm from symptom management to biological repair. Advances in gene editing, gene delivery, and stem cell technologies are establishing these approaches as promising treatments for hereditary hearing loss, with ongoing progress expected to accelerate clinical translation despite remaining challenges in delivery efficiency, immune responses, ethics, and long-term efficacy. Collectively, these advances mark a pivotal step toward personalized and regenerative interventions for hereditary hearing loss.

title: Targeting Apolipoprotein C-III in Hypertriglyceridemia: Implications for Pancreatitis and Cardiovascular risk.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Apolipoprotein C-III (apoC-III) has emerged as a validated target for lowering triglycerides, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, and remnant cholesterol. This review summarizes the biology of apoC-III, the genetic and clinical trial evidence supporting its inhibition, and remaining questions.
RECENT FINDINGS: Loss-of-function variants in APOC3 are associated with lower levels of triglycerides and reduced cardiovascular risk. Pharmacologic inhibition of apoC-III with RNA-based agents has led to substantial reductions in apoC-III and triglycerides across familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS), severe hypertriglyceridemia (sHTG), and moderate hypertriglyceridemia (mHTG). In FCS, agents volanesorsen, olezarsen, and plozasiran have demonstrated reductions in triglycerides and acute pancreatitis. In sHTG, olezarsen has extended this benefit to a larger, multifactorial population. In mHTG, olezarsen and plozasiran lower triglycerides, remnant cholesterol, non-HDL-cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B, but an imaging study with olezarsen demonstrated neutral findings on coronary plaque composition, and cardiovascular event reduction has not been demonstrated. ApoC-III inhibition provides a potent strategy for lowering triglycerides and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Its most immediate clinical role is in FCS and sHTG, where prevention of acute pancreatitis is the main objective. Its future as a cardiovascular therapy will depend on whether reductions in remnant cholesterol and apolipoprotein B translate into fewer atherosclerotic events in a dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial.

title: Are Injectable Antihypertensives the Answer to Improving Blood Pressure Control: SiRNAs and Antisense Oligonucleotide Agents.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Hypertension remains the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality worldwide, yet blood pressure control rates remain suboptimal despite the widespread availability of effective antihypertensive therapies. Poor long-term adherence, therapeutic inertia, and the need for lifelong daily treatment continue to limit the effectiveness of current pharmacological strategies. This review examines the biological rationale, available clinical evidence, and potential role of long-acting RNA-based therapies targeting hepatic angiotensinogen synthesis in hypertension.
RECENT FINDINGS: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting angiotensinogen represent a novel therapeutic approach that suppresses production of the unique precursor of the renin-angiotensin system. Zilebesiran has demonstrated sustained reductions in circulating angiotensinogen and ambulatory blood pressure following infrequent subcutaneous administration in phase 1 and phase 2 clinical trials. Antisense strategies have provided additional clinical validation of sustained angiotensinogen inhibition, although their antihypertensive efficacy has been less consistent. Ongoing clinical development is addressing long-term cardiovascular outcomes, safety, and optimal patient selection. RNA-based antihypertensive therapies may represent an important evolution in hypertension management by combining upstream renin-angiotensin system inhibition with prolonged pharmacological activity and reduced dependence on daily medication adherence. However, their future clinical role will depend on evidence regarding long-term safety, cardiovascular outcomes, reversibility, cost-effectiveness, patient selection, and integration with conventional antihypertensive therapy.

title: Group A streptococcus vaccine strategies: virulence targets, resistance constraints and complementary control measures.
abstract: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), or Streptococcus pyogenes, causes a connected spectrum of pharyngeal, cutaneous, invasive and immune-mediated diseases. Although beta-lactams remain active, treatment alone has not controlled transmission, recurrent infection, rapid invasive progression or acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. Control is further weakened by increased macrolide and clindamycin resistance, heterogeneous diagnostic access, asymptomatic carriage, crowded living conditions and unreliable continuity of secondary prophylaxis. These limitations have shifted the field from a predominantly treatment-centered approach toward the development of vaccines as a prevention strategy. Target selection is guided by virulence functions that are required for colonization, immune evasion and tissue injury. These include the M protein, group A carbohydrate (GAC), streptolysin O, Streptococcus pyogenes cell envelope protease (SpyCEP), Streptococcus pyogenes adhesion and division protein (SpyAD), C5a peptidase and other conserved surface or secreted antigens. Current strategies include multivalent type-specific M-protein vaccines, conserved M-protein peptide vaccines, glycoconjugates, multicomponent non-M-protein formulations and mRNA-lipid nanoparticle platforms. The clinical pipeline has recently broadened. Phase I studies have been completed for StreptAnova and MJ8VAX, whereas the J8-K4S2 and p*17-K4S2 clinical trial studies have been completed, with peer-reviewed results pending. The GSK four-component vaccine initiated phase I evaluation in 2025 and remained under clinical evaluation in 2026, whereas the VAX-A1 formulation entered a first-in-human phase I study in 2026. However, no licensed GAS vaccine is available. Progress remains constrained by uncertain correlates of protection, autoimmune safety requirements, geographical emm diversity, endpoint selection and the need for trials in high-burden populations. This narrative review therefore focuses on the disease problem, targetable virulence mechanisms, limits of antimicrobial control, current vaccine pipeline and interventions required to complement future vaccine use.

title: A new CRISPR/Cas9 GALC Knockout Cellular Model Reveals Lactosylceramide Accumulation Similar to Twitcher Mice.
abstract: Krabbe disease (KD) is a lysosomal sphingolipidosis caused by the deficiency of galactocerebrosidase (GALC), leading to profound alterations in sphingolipid metabolism and severe neurodegeneration. While psychosine (Psy) accumulation is a well-established hallmark of KD, emerging evidence suggests that lactosylceramide (LacCer) may also contribute to disease pathogenesis. Here, we generated a novel human oligodendrocytic model of GALC deficiency by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated GALC knockout in MO3.13 cells and used it to investigate sphingolipid alterations associated with impaired GALC activity. GALC-/- MO3.13 cells showed a marked reduction in GALC transcript levels and enzymatic activity, confirming the successful establishment of a disease-relevant cellular model. Our results demonstrated that a) GALC knockout MO3.13 cells accumulated Psy and LacCer, and b) LacCer content was increased in the brain and heart isolated from twitcher (TWI) mice, the most widely used spontaneous animal model of KD. In parallel, AKT signalling was evaluated in both systems, supporting a link between LacCer dysregulation and altered cellular signalling pathways. Overall, these findings identify LacCer accumulation as a conserved feature of GALC deficiency across cellular and animal models and support the use of GALC-/- MO3.13 cells as a novel in vitro platform to investigate KD pathogenesis and candidate therapeutic strategies.

title: Transforming cardiac amyloidosis care: navigating the evolving diagnostic and therapeutic landscape.
abstract: Amyloidosis comprises a group of systemic disorders caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded precursor proteins, leading to progressive organ dysfunction. Cardiac amyloidosis, particularly transthyretin-related amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) has transitioned from a rare and underdiagnosed condition to a treatable disease, driven by major advances in diagnostic imaging, increased disease awareness, and the approval of disease-modifying therapies. These therapies target transthyretin (TTR) stabilization and amyloid production or deposition and have led to an evolving therapeutic landscape. As therapeutic efficacy is greatest in earlier disease stages, timely recognition is crucial. Effective management of ATTR-CM requires structured screening of high-risk populations, multidisciplinary collaboration, and longitudinal follow-up. This review provides a practical, clinician-focused framework that addresses clinical presentation and "red flags" to facilitate early detection. It offers a comprehensive overview of the diagnostic pathway, including (AI-enabled) electrocardiography analysis, (non-)invasive imaging modalities, biomarkers, and genetic testing. Additionally, emerging therapeutic strategies are discussed, encompassing supportive heart failure management, amyloid-specific treatments such as TTR stabilizers and gene silencers, and novel approaches including fibril depletion and gene-editing therapies. As the therapeutic paradigm shifts from disease stabilization toward potential reversal, early diagnosis and personalized treatment strategies are essential to improve prognosis and quality of life in patients with cardiac amyloidosis.

title: Advanced drug delivery strategies for overcoming tumor-mediated molecular hijacking: Emerging nanotherapeutics, advanced biotherapeutics, and artificial intelligence.
abstract: Recent advances in precision oncology fueled the development of nanotherapeutics,​ molecularly targeted drugs, engineered immunotherapies, RNA therapeutics, and smart biomaterials for more selective cancer treatment. However, long-term therapeutic responses remain restricted by interconnected adaptive mechanisms, including ABC transporter-mediated drug efflux, dysregulated signaling pathways, apoptosis evasion, immune escape, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and tumor microenvironment​ remodeling. In this review article, these processes are collectively framed as tumor-mediated molecular hijacking, describing malignant cell exploitation and microenvironmental pathways that promote multidrug resistance and therapeutic failure. The review critically examines nanotherapeutic and advanced biotherapeutic strategies to counteract these mechanisms, including functionalized nanocarriers, antibody-drug conjugates, CAR-T cells, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, immune checkpoint blockade, mesenchymal stem-cell (MSC)-based therapeutics, CRISPR-mediated genome editing, bispecific T-cell engagers, and RNA-based approaches. Particular focus includes drug-delivery elements such as tumour penetration, intracellular trafficking, controlled release, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and critical formulation attributes, as well as translational challenges such as manufacturability, scalability, reproducibility, stability, safety, and regulatory feasibility. Emerging biofabrication approaches enable the fabrication of adaptive and personalized delivery systems, while artificial intelligence and machine learning are utilized as tools for structure-guided design, nanocarrier optimization, treatment-response prediction, and patient-specific digital-twin modelling. This paper combines tumor-mediated molecular hijacking with drug delivery technology at the forefront and translational aspects to create a comprehensive platform for clinically relevant precision cancer therapeutics.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: Molecular dynamics simulations for lipid nanoparticles in mRNA delivery: mechanistic insights, evidence limits, and design hypotheses.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading non-viral platform for mRNA delivery, yet the molecular organization and dynamic remodeling events that determine efficiency remain difficult to resolve experimentally. This review critically synthesizes molecular dynamics (MD) studies on mRNA-LNPs and mechanistically informative surrogate systems published from 2020 through April 2026. The literature was organized around the delivery sequence: microfluidic self-assembly, mRNA encapsulation, internal nanostructure, pH-triggered remodeling, endosomal membrane interaction, and cytoplasmic release. Martini 3 coarse-grained simulations, constant-pH and enhanced-sampling strategies, evidence-calibrated interpretation of pH-responsive phase behavior, and mechanism-informed lipid optimization exemplified by Branched Endosomal Disruptor (BEND) lipids are emphasized. Findings demonstrated in intact mRNA-LNPs are distinguished from those inferred from siRNA-LNPs, short RNA oligos, RNA-free mesophases, or model membranes. Current MD has advanced from descriptive visualization to mechanistic hypothesization and design support, but predictive LNP design remains limited by force-field dependence, simplified biointerfaces, limited validation in intact mRNA-LNPs, and the absence of protein-corona models.

title: Emerging roles of circular RNAs in bovine mastitis and mammary immune regulation: mechanisms, networks and translational potential.
abstract: Bovine mastitis is a complex inflammatory disease. Somatic cell count and bacteriological culture are central to bovine mastitis diagnosis. Complementary molecular measurements could clarify processes underlying persistent mammary injury. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are relatively stable, back-spliced transcripts with context-dependent expression and potential regulatory functions, making them relevant candidates for investigating post-transcriptional control in the bovine mammary gland. This review critically evaluates circRNA evidence in bovine mastitis, with particular emphasis on Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli. It integrates findings from mammary epithelial-cell models, mammary tissue and animal studies, peripheral blood, milk extracellular vesicles and N⁶-methyladenosine-associated circRNA profiling. Available studies report changes in circRNA abundance and modification patterns under mastitis-associated conditions. Candidate circRNAs are associated with inflammatory signalling, epithelial organization, vesicle and phagosome biology, and apoptosis. One functional study also implicates a circRNA in ferroptosis. However, most reported circRNAs are supported only by differential expression, expression validation, host-gene enrichment or predicted circRNA-microRNA-mRNA networks. These findings identify candidate mechanisms but do not establish direct regulation. Functional evidence remains limited, although circPRIM2 and circ_HOMER3 demonstrate that individual circRNAs can modify inflammatory, secretory, apoptotic and ferroptotic phenotypes in bovine mammary epithelial-cell models. Milk extracellular vesicle circRNAs are analytically detectable and infection responsive, but diagnostic sensitivity, pathogen discrimination and added value beyond established tests remain unproven. Progress now depends on coordinate-based nomenclature, full-length isoform resolution, direct interaction and rescue experiments, pathogen-defined animal studies and independent longitudinal cohorts. The immediate priority is therefore to move beyond circRNA catalogues and identify a smaller set of reproducible candidates with validated mechanisms and measurable translational value.

title: Modern cell-based assays for biomedical research: from conventional methods to AI-driven high content analysis.
abstract: In vitro cell-based assays are fundamental tools in biomedical research, supporting investigations of cellular physiology, disease mechanisms, drug discovery, toxicology, regenerative medicine, and precision therapeutics. However, conventional two-dimensional (2D) cell culture models often fail to recapitulate the structural complexity and physiological functions of native tissues, prompting the development of advanced platforms, including three-dimensional (3D) cultures, organoids, organ-on-a-chip technologies, and microphysiological systems. Recent advances in cell viability and cytotoxicity assessment, functional cellular analysis, molecular profiling, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based functional genomics, high-content imaging, flow cytometry, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, and automated high-throughput screening have expanded the analytical capabilities of cell-based assays. Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted image analysis and computational biology has enhanced cellular phenotyping, biomarker discovery, and mechanistic investigation, with the potential to improve the prediction of therapeutic efficacy and toxicity. Nevertheless, challenges related to physiological relevance, technical variability, inadequate standardization, high operational costs, scalability, poor reproducibility, cell-line misidentification, batch-to-batch variation, and inconsistent reporting continue to hinder translational applications. Future progress will depend on integrating physiologically relevant models with AI-driven analytics, spatial multi-omics, digital pathology, automated screening, and microphysiological systems. Standardized protocols, harmonized reporting practices, and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to improve reproducibility, strengthen regulatory acceptance, advance precision medicine, and reduce reliance on animal experimentation. In this context, this review critically evaluates conventional and emerging in vitro cell-based assays, emphasizing their biological principles, analytical capabilities, translational applications, and practical limitations, while highlighting future opportunities to improve predictive accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical translation.

title: Base editing in livestock and aquaculture: from tool development to breeding application.
abstract: The growing recognition of base editing as a precise genome-engineering strategy for single‑nucleotide conversions without double‑strand breaks has increased interest in its application to animal agriculture, where many economically important traits are influenced by single nucleotide variants. Although recent engineering efforts have broadened the targeting scope, improved editing precision, and reduced off‑target activity, major challenges remain in translating these tools to livestock and aquaculture species, particularly with respect to delivery, mosaicism, germline transmission, and breeding-scale deployment. In this review, we outline the development of cytosine, adenine, dual, and mitochondrial base editors, and discuss their advances in livestock and fish, including trait-oriented editing in pigs and cattle, rapid functional validation in model fish, and early proof-of-concept studies in aquaculture species. We further discuss the emerging potential of mitochondrial DNA base editing for animal breeding and evaluate the extent to which current advances support the broader goal of precision breeding and sustainable animal production.

title: Macrophage Extracellular Vesicle-Camouflaged Framework Nucleic Acid Nanospheres Reprogram Lactate Metabolism-Immune Feedback Loops for Synergistic Chemoimmunotherapy of Glioblastoma.
abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-brain tumor barrier (BBTB) severely limited drug delivery into the brain, while aberrant aerobic glycolysis in the tumor microenvironment caused excessive lactate accumulation and drove immunosuppression. These factors together constituted the core obstacles to glioblastoma (GBM) therapy. From the perspective of metabolism-immune crosstalk, we engineered a brain‑targeted nucleic acid nanosphere (TE@siP‑DNS/DOX) featuring high BBB/BBTB penetrability, which orchestrated a "triple‑linked" strategy integrating glycolysis blockade, immune microenvironment remodeling, and synergistic therapeutic potentiation. The nanosphere was constructed with a self‑assembled core of PKM2‑targeting siRNA and framework nucleic acids loaded with doxorubicin (DOX), shielded by a biomimetic shell of T7 peptide‑modified macrophage extracellular vesicles. Leveraging transcytosis and T7‑mediated active targeting, TE@siP‑DNS/DOX efficiently traversed the barriers and preferentially accumulated at tumor sites. DOX simultaneously provoked chemotherapy and immunogenic cell death, igniting robust CD8⁺ T cell‑mediated antitumor immunity, whereas siRNA‑mediated PKM2 silencing curtailed glycolysis, lessened lactate production, rewired metabolic circuitry, and forced macrophage polarization toward the M1 antitumor phenotype, thereby dismantling the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (iTME). Transcriptomic analysis further confirmed that metabolic and immune-related pathways were significantly enriched following TE@siP-DNS/DOX treatment, providing transcriptional evidence for its dual modulation of the metabolic-immune feedback loop. In vivo studies substantiated that TE@siP‑DNS/DOX markedly inhibited tumor growth and prolonged survival in orthotopic GBM-bearing mice. Collectively, this nanoplatform, through a synergistic feedback loop integrating metabolic regulation and immune activation, provides a good therapeutic strategy and research paradigm for enhanced glioma therapy. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Glioblastoma therapy is impeded by a multifaceted barrier system encompassing the blood-brain barrier, metabolic dysregulation, lactate accumulation, and immunosuppression. Here, we engineered a brain-targeted nucleic acid nanosphere that integrates glycolysis blockade, immune remodeling, and chemotherapeutic sensitization via a single platform. By combining PKM2 silencing with doxorubicin-loaded framework nucleic acids and T7-modified macrophage vesicles, the nanosphere achieves efficient barrier penetration, lactate reduction, M1 macrophage repolarization, and immunogenic cell death. This metabolism-immune feedback loop synergistically suppresses orthotopic tumors and extends survival. Our study provides a paradigm for treating brain tumors through concurrent metabolic reprogramming and antitumor immunity, offering a translatable strategy for overcoming therapy resistance in glioblastoma.

title: Lipid nanoparticles and their successors: Design principles for dense tissue penetration and clinical translation.
abstract: Nucleic acid therapeutics have transformed modern medicine, enabling targeted treatments that address a wide range of diseases at their genetic roots. From RNAi-mediated gene silencing to mRNA vaccines and CRISPR-based editing, these advances offer precision strategies for previously intractable conditions. The success of these modalities hinges entirely on delivery technologies which have evolved lockstep with nucleic acid research, facilitating transport from administration site to intracellular target(s). Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the leading delivery platform for nucleic acid therapeutics which is partially due to extensive research and development of lipid-based vehicle derivatives previously developed for small molecule-based drugs. While LNPs themselves have a relatively brief clinical history, the COVID-19 pandemic propelled nucleic acid technologies into the global spotlight, accelerating public, industrial, and regulatory engagement. This surge in attention catalyzed the maturation of clinical, manufacturing, and regulatory frameworks for therapies that rely on delivery technologies like LNPs for success. While this progress has enabled a new wave of therapies, it has also underscored the limitations of LNPs, including poor penetration into dense extracellular matrix (ECM) tissues and dose-limiting toxicities driven by immunogenicity. As optimization of LNP formulations continues, a new generation of nanoparticle platforms is emerging, aiming to address these shortcomings in morphology, chemistry, and tissue specificity. These platforms are well-positioned to leverage the translational groundwork laid by LNPs, potentially accelerating their own path to clinical relevance. In this review, we examine the evolution and clinical impact of LNPs, analyze their key limitations, and explore emerging delivery platforms, such as biomimetic nanoparticles and polymeric systems that seek to overcome the physicochemical limitations of LNPs while building on the lessons and regulatory frameworks they established.

title: Toward mechanism-informed IVIVC in non-viral gene delivery: From nanoparticle transformation to therapeutic action.
abstract: Gene delivery is now a clinically established modality, but one of its central translational challenges remains: therapeutic performance emerges from a cascade of biological processes rather than from a single step. Lipid nanoparticles, polymeric carriers, and oligonucleotide conjugates undergo biological transformation, distribution and tissue access, cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, endosomal escape, and ultimately functional payload delivery. The contribution of each process to the therapeutic outcome is context dependent and may shift with formulation, route of administration, target tissue, payload, and disease state. Consequently, transfection efficiency remains a necessary and widely used endpoint, but as a single aggregate readout it cannot by itself indicate which upstream process, biodistribution, uptake, trafficking, or endosomal escape, is rate-limiting for a given formulation, route, or tissue; resolving that bottleneck is the measurable attribute an in vitro-in vivo relationship must be built around. Classical in vitro-in vivo correlation (IVIVC) concepts were developed for simpler relationships, but their underlying principle remains relevant: identifying a measurable product attribute or process that governs in vivo performance. As pharmaceutical systems have become more complex, biopredictive methodologies have logically progressed toward process-resolved assays, systems-level understanding, and mechanistic modeling. Applying this principle to non-viral gene delivery does not imply that a validated IVIVC, or a regulatory biowaiver built on one, yet exists for these systems; rather, it asks whether the same underlying logic, identifying which step in a multi-step cascade is rate limiting and can be represented by a measurable in vitro assay, can be meaningfully extended from simpler dosage forms to a biologically complex delivery process. This review proposes a pathway toward IVIVC for non-viral gene delivery as a delivery cascade comprising three interconnected layers: (i) the Nanoparticle Biodistribution Layer, spanning circulation, biological transformation, and tissue access; (ii) the Cellular Delivery Dynamics Layer, encompassing cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, and endosomal escape; and (iii) the Functional Therapeutic Action Layer, linking productive delivery to pharmacodynamic response. Each layer is matched with assays that isolate individual processes and expose where formulation performance becomes limiting. These layers have traditionally been studied by largely separate scientific communities, making their integration essential for understanding how performance gains or losses propagate through the delivery cascade. Rather than proposing a holistic IVIVC that does not yet exist for non-viral gene delivery, this framework provides a mechanistic roadmap for building it, moving formulation development from empirical screening toward stepwise biopredictive evidence and, ultimately, IVIVC for complex gene delivery systems.

title: AI-guided CRISPR gene editing for cardiovascular disease: Current progress, transitional challenges, and future directions.
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality despite major advances in pharmacological therapy, interventional cardiology, and lifestyle-based prevention. Although many current treatments reduce disease burden and improve outcomes, they often fail to address the underlying molecular and genetic mechanisms driving disease progression dot CRISPR hyphen-based gene- editing systems (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) have introduced the possibility of directly correcting, silencing, or modulating pathogenic genetic determinants involved in cardiovascular pathology. When integrated with artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled design, prediction, and optimization tools, an AI-guided CRISPR framework may assist in prioritizing editing strategies, predicting editing outcomes, and informing delivery design, although cardiovascular-specific validation of these applications remains limited. This narrative review examines the potential role of AI-guided CRISPR technologies in cardiovascular disease. It first outlines the major pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying CVD, then reviews molecular and genetic targets that may be amenable to editing. Current CRISPR applications in cardiometabolic and cardiovascular disorders are discussed, followed by an evaluation of how AI may support guide RNA design, off-target prediction, vector engineering, and therapeutic prioritization. Finally, major translational barriers are examined, including tissue-specific delivery, editing in non-dividing cells, long-term genomic safety, disease complexity, and regulatory implementation. Although early preclinical findings are encouraging, most cardiovascular applications remain in the experimental or early translational stage, and direct evidence for integrated AI-guided CRISPR applications in cardiovascular disease remains limited and largely preclinical. Progress in this field will depend on advances in delivery science, genome engineering, computational modelling, and long-term safety validation. AI-guided CRISPR should therefore be regarded as a developing precision medicine strategy with substantial future potential rather than an immediately deployable clinical solution.

title: Scaling haplospecific antisense oligonucleotides from N-of-1 to broad use in genetic disease populations by diplotyping.
abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are versatile disease-modifying therapies for genetic diseases. An accelerated US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) pathway enables ASO treatment trial initiation in an individual within a year. However, this rapid N-of-1 pathway lacks extensibility to broad use necessary for sustainability. Individualized ASOs bind pre-mRNAs encompassing an entire locus. Thus, ASOs targeting common heterozygous polymorphisms (SNPs) are potentially haplospecific in many individuals with dominant disorders. We developed haplospecific ASOs for two probands with SCN2A-complex neurodevelopmental disorder (CND) and gain-of-function (GOF) or mixed gain-loss dysfunction (GLD) variants. The ASOs targeted reference SCN2A intronic sequences containing SNPs. The probands each had SCN2A haplotypes with reference SNP alleles in cis with causal variants and alternate SNP alleles in cis with normal mRNA. Following N-of-1 demonstration of safety and efficacy, we evaluated their applicability to 21 SCN2A-CND probands using whole-genome sequencing (WGS) with haplotyping by read proximity. Ten (48%) probands had ASO-eligible diplotypes. Haplotype analysis of unrelated 1000 Genomes Project (1kGP) participants revealed 18 additional SCN2A haplotypes present in >20% of subjects, tagged by 156 SNPs. In silico assessment of specificity and potency identified additional haplospecific ASOs for validation in reprogrammed 1kGP cells heterozygous for the tagging SNPs. A combination of four haplospecific ASOs provided coverage for 76.2% of 1kGP subjects, potentially allowing scaling of N-of-1 FDA applications in future individuals with SCN2A-CND and GOF/GLD variants. Thus, population resources have potential to prepare haplospecific ASO therapies a priori for many persons and genetic diseases, with individual ASO selection by diagnostic WGS with haplotyping.

title: CRISPR, mRNA, and Beyond: Nucleic Acid Therapeutics in Allergy and Immunology.
abstract: The management of allergic and immunologic diseases has long centered on symptom management rather than disease modification. Conventional pharmacotherapy controls manifestations of the immune dysregulation but does little to treat the underlying cause. Newer monoclonal and small molecule therapies target downstream effectors of the type 2 inflammatory cascade, and allergen immunotherapy, while disease-modifying, requires years of administration for effect. Nucleic acid therapies represent a different approach that intervenes at the level of genetic information itself, at the DNA, RNA, or protein-production step. This includes mRNA treatments that direct cells to produce therapeutic proteins or modify allergen-specific immune responses; antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNAs that selectively silence disease genes; adeno-associated viral vectors for sustained gene delivery; and CRISPR-based systems that permanently edit the genome. Several technologies have advanced to clinical proof of concept including a CRISPR gene-editing therapy (lonvoguran ziclumeran) that reduced hereditary angioedema attacks by 87% compared with placebo in a randomized controlled trial. An inhaled DNAzyme targeting the intracellular transcription factor GATA3 attenuated allergen-induced late asthmatic responses by 34% in humans, and CD19 CAR-T cell therapy induced drug-free remission in severe autoimmune disease. As of 2025, 24 oligonucleotide therapeutics have received FDA approval, including donidalorsen, the first RNA-targeted prophylactic therapy approved for hereditary angioedema. This review examines each therapeutic technology, its mechanism and delivery strategy, and the evidence relevant to allergic and immunologic disease. Persistent challenges, including delivery beyond the liver, immune responses to viral vectors, and the need for long-term safety data, are addressed alongside a proposed integration with existing treatment paradigms.

title: O-glycosylation of ENO1 at serine 63 by GALNT14 promotes triple-negative breast cancer progression by enhancing ENO1 protein stability.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype with limited targeted therapeutic options. Mucin-type O-GalNAc glycosylation mediated by N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase (GALNT) family enzymes contributes to tumor progression, while GALNT14's functional substrates and mechanisms in TNBC remain largely unknown.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Expression profiling was performed using clinical tissue microarray and TCGA dataset. Cellular loss-of-function, gain-of-function and rescue experiments were conducted in TNBC cell lines. In vivo tumor growth and lung metastasis were evaluated in nude mice. Co-IP-LC-MS/MS, VVA-lectin pulldown and cycloheximide-chase assays were applied to identify interacting partners, characterize O-GalNAc glycosylation and assess protein stability.
RESULTS: GALNT14 was markedly upregulated in TNBC tissues (P < 0.05). GALNT14 knockdown inhibited TNBC cell proliferation, migration and invasion in vitro (P < 0.001), and suppressed xenograft growth and lung metastasis in vivo (tumor weight: P < 0.001; metastatic nodules: P < 0.01). α-Enolase 1 (ENO1) was identified as a novel substrate of GALNT14. GALNT14 catalyzed O-GalNAc glycosylation of ENO1 at Ser63. This modification did not change ENO1 mRNA level, yet enhanced ENO1 protein stability (P < 0.001). Under GALNT14-proficient background, glycosylation-deficient ENO1-S63A displayed attenuated oncogenic capacity compared with ENO1-WT (P < 0.05). Both ENO1-WT and ENO1-S63A rescued malignant phenotypes upon GALNT14 silencing (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: A GALNT14-ENO1 Ser63 O-GalNAc glycosylation axis drives TNBC progression, providing new mechanistic insight and candidate therapeutic targets for TNBC.

title: Loss of core 1-derived O-glycans disrupts GLUT2 cell-surface localization and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in pancreatic β cells.
abstract: Protein glycosylation is a major post-translational modification that regulates protein function. Core 1-derived O-GalNAc glycans (Galβ1-3GalNAcα1-Ser/Thr) are widely distributed across tissues and are present on membrane-bound and secreted proteins. Their synthesis is catalyzed by core 1 β1,3-galactosyltransferase (C1galt1) and requires the molecular chaperone Cosmc, encoded by C1galt1c1. Although core 1-derived O-GalNAc glycans are abundant on mucin-type glycoproteins, their physiological functions on non-mucin proteins remain poorly understood. Here, we used β cell-specific Cosmc conditional knockout (RIP-Cos) mice to investigate the physiological role of these glycans in pancreatic β cells. RIP-Cos mice exhibited impaired glucose tolerance and defective glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS), despite normal pancreatic insulin content. Because glucose uptake through glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2) contributes to glucose sensing and GSIS in mouse β cells, we examined GLUT2 in RIP-Cos islets. Immunofluorescence analysis revealed an apparent reduction in GLUT2 signal at the plasma membrane. Slc2a2 (GLUT2) mRNA expression was significantly decreased, and immunoblotting revealed a lower molecular weight form of GLUT2. These alterations were accompanied by reduced glucose-analog uptake in primary RIP-Cos islets. RIP-Cos mice also displayed resistance to streptozotocin-induced diabetes. Finally, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry identified O-GalNAc glycosylation sites within the extracellular domain of recombinant mouse GLUT2. These findings suggest that core 1-derived O-GalNAc glycosylation contributes to maintaining GLUT2 molecular properties and localization, thereby supporting β-cell GSIS. Overall, this study supports an important role for core 1-derived O-GalNAc glycosylation in β-cell glucose responsiveness and identifies GLUT2 as a target of O-GalNAc glycosylation.

title: ZFYVE21 is an essential host factor for influenza A virus by regulating endosomal acidification.
abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) remains a major global health threat, causing recurrent seasonal epidemics and sporadic pandemics. Despite extensive studies on IAV-host interactions, cellular regulation of the viral life cycle is not fully understood. Here, using genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screens, we identified zinc finger FYVE domain-containing protein 21 (ZFYVE21) as a cellular factor required for completion of the IAV life cycle. We show that ZFYVE21 acts upstream of PTEN to maintain endosomal acidification, which triggers the conformational change of viral hemagglutinin (HA) required for membrane fusion and viral uncoating. Deficiency of ZFYVE21 abrogates this acidification step, thereby blocking viral genome release into the cytosol and subsequent replication across multiple IAV strains. Importantly, ZFYVE21-deficient mice exhibit significantly lower lung viral loads, diminished histopathological damage, and markedly improved survival upon lethal IAV H3N2 challenge. Collectively, our findings uncover a critical role of ZFYVE21 in endosomal acidification-dependent IAV genome release into the cytosol and establish ZFYVE21 as a promising target for the development of broad-spectrum anti-influenza therapeutics.

title: AAV8-mediated CasRx delivery and expression in the cochlea and cochlear nucleus of mice.
abstract: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing has made substantial progress in recent years and has enabled the treatment of a variety of genetic diseases, including hearing loss in congenitally deaf mice. However, successful gene editing for hereditary deafness may still induce off-target mutations in genomic DNA, which limits its clinical translation. CasRx, also known as RfxCas13d, is a compact RNA-targeting CRISPR effector that can be packaged into AAV vectors for in vivo delivery. CasRx, a recently identified member of the type VI CRISPR system, modulates target RNA expression without altering DNA sequences, thereby avoiding permanent off-target mutations and offering broad therapeutic potential. Here, we used adeno-associated virus serotype 8 (AAV8) to deliver CasRx into the cochlea and cochlear nucleus (CN) of C57BL/6J mice and evaluated its expression pattern and short-term safety. Two weeks after viral injection, the number and morphology of neurons and other cell types in the CN remained normal. Importantly, auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds were unchanged after viral delivery, indicating that AAV8-mediated CasRx expression did not detectably impair auditory function during the short observation period. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the feasibility and short-term safety of AAV8-mediated CasRx delivery and expression in the cochlea and cochlear nucleus, providing a delivery platform for future guide RNA-directed transcript-modulation studies in auditory disorders.

title: The role of polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) in non-small cell lung cancer: molecular mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) is a highly conserved serine/threonine kinase that orchestrates key processes in mitotic progression, DNA damage repair, apoptosis, and immune signaling. Its frequent overexpression in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) correlates with tumor aggressiveness, poor prognosis, and resistance to therapy, highlighting its significance as both a biomarker and therapeutic target. This review systematically evaluates the molecular mechanisms by which PLK1 drives NSCLC pathogenesis, including its regulation by transcription factors, tumor suppressors, oncogenes, non-coding RNAs, and signaling pathways. We highlight PLK1's role in promoting cell cycle progression, chromosomal instability, metastasis, immune escape, and therapeutic resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted agents. Furthermore, we summarize preclinical and clinical advances in PLK1-directed therapies, encompassing small-molecule inhibitors, RNA interference, gene editing, PROTACs, and nanomedicine-based strategies, with an emphasis on their potential to enhance sensitivity to existing treatments. Collectively, current evidence establishes PLK1 as a central hub in NSCLC biology and a promising candidate for precision oncology. Future investigations should prioritize biomarker-driven clinical trials, combinatorial strategies, and next-generation inhibitors for overcoming resistance and improving patient outcomes.

title: AS1411-targeted nanomedicines for precision cancer therapy: Advances, mechanisms, and translational perspectives.
abstract: Conventional cancer chemotherapy is frequently compromised by nonspecific biodistribution, dose-limiting systemic toxicity, inadequate tumor accumulation, and multidrug resistance, highlighting the need for targeted nanomedicines capable of improving tumor selectivity while preserving therapeutic efficacy. The AS1411 G-quadruplex DNA aptamer has emerged as a promising targeting ligand owing to its high affinity for nucleolin, which is aberrantly overexpressed on the surface of many malignant cells. AS1411-functionalized nanocarriers can exploit nucleolin-mediated endocytosis to enhance tumor-cell uptake, intracellular drug delivery, and therapeutic selectivity while minimizing off-target exposure. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in AS1411-engineered nanocarriers, encompassing polymeric nanoparticles, micelles, liposomes, inorganic and mesoporous nanostructures, as well as bioinspired platforms such as exosomes and cell membrane-coated nanoparticles. Particular emphasis is placed on rational nanocarrier engineering, including optimization of AS1411 surface density, PEGylation, physicochemical properties, and integration of tumor microenvironment-responsive mechanisms to achieve controlled and stimuli-responsive payload release. These platforms have been explored for the targeted delivery of conventional chemotherapeutics, nucleic acid therapeutics, and nonviral CRISPR/Cas systems, and increasingly incorporate multimodal therapeutic and diagnostic functions, including photothermal, photodynamic, sonodynamic, chemodynamic, and imaging-guided approaches. Despite considerable progress, clinical translation remains constrained by heterogeneous nucleolin expression, complex tumor microenvironmental barriers, limited endosomal escape and intracellular trafficking, potential off-target interactions, formulation stability, manufacturing scalability, and regulatory challenges. Future development should prioritize mechanistic understanding of AS1411-nucleolin interactions, standardized evaluation of targeting efficiency, and rational integration of multi-responsive, dual- and multi-ligand, and bioinspired architectures. Such advances may improve the translational potential of AS1411-based nanomedicines and support their further preclinical development.

title: Physicochemical quality control of human vaccines: pharmacopeial requirements, platform-specific attributes, and advanced analytical characterization.
abstract: Physicochemical testing is a central component of vaccine control because it measures material attributes that can reveal changes in composition, structure, aggregation, particle organization, excipients, and degradation. Its role, however, must be distinguished from immunochemical, cell-based, microbiological, and animal-based tests and must be positioned within an integrated control strategy extending from starting materials and drug substance to in-process controls and the finished product. This narrative review examines physicochemical quality control of prophylactic human vaccines, with emphasis on the Brazilian Pharmacopeia and the United States Pharmacopeia and complementary World Health Organization guidance for selected vaccine categories. General compendial assays are separated from platform-specific tests for protein/subunit, toxoid, polysaccharide/glycoconjugate, viral, and mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccines. The literature is synthesized by analytical purpose rather than article-by-article, focusing on chromatography, mass spectrometry, spectroscopy, electrophoretic and particle-analysis methods, stability-indicating characterization, and the relation between critical quality attributes and potency. Advanced methods can improve specificity and mechanistic resolution, but physicochemical integrity alone does not automatically demonstrate biological potency. Their greatest regulatory value is achieved when scientifically relevant attributes are linked to manufacturing consistency, stability, and clinically qualified lots. The review also clarifies how physicochemical methods may support the consistency approach and the 3Rs without conflating them with all in vitro potency assays. Overall, modern vaccine control requires a platform-adapted analytical strategy in which finished-product testing complements, rather than replaces, appropriate drug-substance, in-process, and process-validation controls.

title: Transcription activator-like effector base editing delivered by a targeted lipid nanoparticle for therapy of lung cancer.
abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Among them, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for approximately 85% of all cases, while the mutation of KRAS oncogene plays a crucial role in its formation and metastasis. Here, we report a transcription activator-like effector (TALE) base editor that can accurately identify KRAS gene under the guide of TALE and sgRNA, convert C base to T base, thereby generating a stop codon and blocking the expression of KRAS. Besides, a targeted TALE base editing lipid nanoparticle (targeted TALE LNP) is developed by rationally designing with cancer-targeted EGFR peptide. The targeted TALE LNP exhibits a base editing effect, cancer targeting, and remarkable therapy efficacy in NSCLC cancer-bearing mice. In conclusion, the targeted TALE LNP has the potential to treat lung cancer with KRAS gene mutation through an approach of transcription activator-like effector base editing.

title: Endothelium-targeted myc silencing suppresses pathological ocular neovascularization.
abstract: Ocular neovascularization (NV) causes blindness, yet anti-VEGF therapy has limited efficacy. Myc controls endothelial cell (EC) proliferation and activation, however, its pathological role in ocular NV and therapeutic value remain unclear. In this study, we found that Myc was markedly upregulated in neovascular ECs (NV-ECs). Mechanistically, glycolytic reprogramming drove the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP), promoting Myc O-GlcNAcylation, which stabilized Myc protein. Endothelial-specific Myc knockout significantly suppressed EC proliferation, thereby alleviating NV progression and preserving visual function. To target Myc therapeutically, we engineered an endothelium targeted, cell membrane hybridized lipid nanoparticle encapsulating Myc siRNA (Lip@siMyc). This system achieved homotypic targeting, vitreal penetration, and sustained Myc gene silencing, and markedly inhibited ocular NV in mice. Notably, Lip@siMyc showed efficacy comparable to aflibercept, and combined treatment produced enhanced anti angiogenic effects. In summary, our findings establish the glycolysis/HBP/Myc axis as a critical regulator of EC proliferation and highlight endothelial Myc blockade as a promising therapeutic strategy for ocular NV.

title: Reprogramming tumor-associated macrophages through TLR4 N-glycosylation: A GnT-V mRNA delivery strategy to improve PD-1 inhibitor responsiveness.
abstract: PD-1 inhibitors have revolutionized cancer treatment, but their antitumor efficacy is limited by various constraints, including the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) driven by tumor-promoting tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). Reprogramming TAMs toward an antitumor state is a promising strategy to boost PD-1 inhibitor efficacy. However, the strategies for driving this switch remain poorly defined. Herein, we identified N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase-V (GnT-V) as a critical regulator of TAM reprogramming and PD-1 inhibitor responsiveness. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of PD-1 inhibitor-sensitive and resistant patients revealed that GnT-V expression was enriched in antitumor TAMs and positively correlated with the PD-1 inhibitor response. Validation data from spontaneous/xenograft tumors in mice and in vitro co-culture systems showed that GnT-V overexpression drives TAM repolarization toward an antitumor phenotype and enhances anti-PD-1 sensitivity. Mechanistically, GnT-V catalyzes β1,6-branched N-glycosylation of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) at Asn526 and Asn575, stabilizing TLR4 and sustaining NF-κB activation to drive antitumor TAM polarization and T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity. To translate this mechanistic axis into a therapeutic strategy, we employed a clinically relevant mRNA-loaded lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platform for in situ TAM reprogramming. The mRNA-LNP platform delivered GnT-V mRNA with high stability, achieved efficient GnT-V expression in a TAM-preferential manner, and showed no apparent systemic toxicity. Functionally, the platform-delivered GnT-V repolarized TAMs, reshaped the immunosuppressive TME, and synergized with anti-PD-1 to improve antitumor efficacy in vivo. Our findings establish the GnT-V/TLR4 N-glycosylation axis as a switch that governs TAM reprogramming and offer a promising biomaterial-based strategy that combines GnT-V mRNA delivery with anti-PD-1 therapy to overcome PD-1 inhibitor resistance.

title: From off-target to on-demand: Precision engineering and translational evaluation of next-generation base editors.
abstract: Due to the increasing demand for clinical gene therapy and the limitations of current treatment methods, there is an urgent need to develop gene-editing tools that are safer, more precise, and more clinically implementable. Deaminase-based base editors have emerged as gene-editing platforms with significant therapeutic potential because they can achieve precise single-base substitutions without inducing DNA double-strand breaks. However, the challenges of applying base editing in clinical practice extend beyond whether the intended edit can be achieved. The critical question is whether the editing system can reliably provide predictable, controllable, and verifiable outcomes across complex sequence contexts, diverse cell environments, and actual delivery conditions. This review focuses on the engineering optimization and clinical translation of base editors. We first systematically analyze the major factors affecting the clinical translation of base editors across four dimensions: editing efficiency, editing precision, safety, and delivery, together with the corresponding optimization strategies. We then summarize the applications of artificial intelligence and computational approaches in base editor design, screening, and risk assessment. We further discuss the ex vivo and in vivo pathways for clinical translation, including their respective requirements for product quality and safety evaluation. Finally, based on representative clinical programs, we discuss how editing performance, safety, and delivery factors influence development decisions for candidate base-editing systems across different therapeutic contexts, and propose minimum reporting recommendations to improve the consistency of key data and cross-study comparability.

title: Engineered CRISPR for nucleic acid imaging at the single-molecule level.
abstract: Accurate and dynamic visualization of nucleic acids at the single-molecule level is essential for elucidating cellular processes, defining disease-associated molecular mechanisms, and advancing molecular diagnostics. Conventional imaging methods often lack the sensitivity, specificity, or spatiotemporal resolution required in complex biological systems. Engineered clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) technologies, leveraging the high programmability of Cas proteins and guide RNAs, have expanded nucleic acid imaging from repetitive and non-repetitive genomic loci to sequence-variant discrimination and individual RNA imaging. This review summarizes major engineering strategies, including Cas protein labeling, guide RNA scaffold modification, and nanomaterial- or protein-assisted signal amplification platforms. We further discuss biomedical applications in live-cell tracking, spatial nucleic acid analysis, and real-time monitoring of cellular dynamics. By examining the biochemical and engineering principles underlying these platforms, we provide a framework for the rational design of CRISPR-based nucleic acid imaging strategies and identify key considerations for overcoming persistent limitations in complex biological environments. Collectively, these advances position engineered CRISPR imaging as a programmable platform for spatially resolved nucleic acid analysis; however, broader application to clinically relevant specimens will require rigorous validation of quantitative robustness and specimen compatibility, together with standardized imaging workflows.

title: The weight of memory: nutrition, diabetes, and the brain.
abstract: This issue of the Biomedical Journal explores therapeutic approaches to neuroinflammation, antimicrobial resistance, and cancer, as well as developments in laboratory testing and prognostic assessment. Experimental findings show that glibenclamide attenuates palmitic acid-induced hippocampal inflammation and memory impairment in mice. In antimicrobial research, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated elimination of resistance genes restores ertapenem susceptibility in resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates, while deep learning offers an approach to interpreting antimicrobial susceptibility tests from images. Oncology articles span molecular characterization, treatment, and prognosis: BK polyomavirus integration and aristolochic acid exposure are associated with distinct molecular features in kidney transplant-associated urothelial carcinomas; bavachinin enhances cisplatin's antitumor activity in oral cancer models; biomarker changes inform prognosis during radium-223 therapy; and external validation supports the MAGIC-D model in advanced biliary tract cancer. Furthermore, research on cartilage homeostasis examines exercise-dependent responses of Prg4-expressing cells. Correspondence addresses combined radiotherapy and systemic treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma and, in a second exchange, stewardship of short-term systemic corticosteroid use.

title: Genome engineering with base editors: Technological advancements enabling clinical translation.
abstract: Base editors (BEs) are precision genome editing tools which allow for the efficient introduction of point mutations in live cells without using double-strand DNA breaks. The two main classes of BEs are cytosine base editors (CBEs) and adenine base editors (ABEs), which can introduce C•G to T•A and A•T to G•C mutations, respectively. Since their development, BEs have been further developed and improved to address issues related to efficiency, specificity, and precision. In this review, we briefly summarize several recent notable developments in the field relevant to their path to the clinic, as well as three clinical trials from the past three years which apply BEs to the treatment of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, hypercholesterolemia, and a rare N = 1 urea cycle disorder. In these examples, base editing is used to precisely knock out genes or correct mutations back to wild-type in blood disorders and liver diseases. Through clinical trials, patients around the world are being treated with BE therapeutics, ushering in the next generation of precision medicine.

title: Advances in guide RNA engineering for endogenous ADAR-mediated therapeutic RNA editing.
abstract: Adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs) convert adenosine positioned within double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) to inosine (A-to-I). This reaction can be redirected to a specific target transcript by exogenous guide RNAs (gRNAs) that recruit abundant endogenous ADARs without the need for exogenous protein delivery. Approximately 16,000 pathogenic G > A mutations are correctable by A-to-I conversion, thus representing a broad scope for therapeutic A-to-I editing. This review covers the key advances in gRNA engineering for endogenous ADAR-mediated RNA editing. We first discuss how ADAR biology informs rational gRNA design. We then survey gRNA design strategies that increase on-target editing efficiency and diminish bystander editing. Delivery modalities are then discussed for both unmodified and modified gRNAs as a strategy to minimize transcriptome-wide off-target editing. We conclude by outlining the outstanding challenges and future opportunities, including computational gRNA design, to guide the next generation of gRNAs towards the path of approved RNA editing medicines.

title: In vivo genome-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Preclinical studies and first-in-human trial.
abstract: We report the preclinical and early clinical evaluation of in vivo genome editing for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), delivered via a single AAV9 vector. In humanized DMD mice, systemic administration achieved targeted genome editing, partial dystrophin restoration, and improved muscle function. In non-human primates, efficient on-target editing was achieved with no dose-limiting toxicity identified under the conditions tested. In an open-label, dose-escalation, first-in-human clinical trial (NCT06594094), post-treatment muscle biopsies provided early molecular evidence of hfCas12Max-mediated genome editing and detectable dystrophin expression in participants with DMD. However, at the higher dose level (1.0 × 1014 vg/kg), one participant experienced a treatment-related fatal serious adverse event, characterized by marked complement activation and systemic cytokine response shortly after dosing. This work provides initial human proof-of-concept for muscle genome editing while crucially highlighting the critical role of immunologic risks and the narrow therapeutic window of systemic adeno-associated virus (AAV)-CRISPR therapies, underscoring the need to develop safer dosing and immunomodulation strategies.

title: CRISPR mutagenesis of the MYC locus reveals a druggable ultraconserved RNA element.
abstract: Noncoding sequences comprise most of the human genome; however, their functional significance remains largely elusive. Using CRISPR tiling mutagenesis with near-PAMless, high-fidelity SpRY-Cas9, we mapped the fitness landscape of an entire human gene, the 10-kb MYC locus, at base-pair resolution. This unbiased interrogation revealed that 67% of functionally essential base pairs are noncoding. Essential noncoding base pairs are under strong constraint in the human population but show limited evolutionary conservation across species. Within this landscape, we identified an ultraconserved noncoding RNA element in the 3' untranslated region (UTR) that promotes perinuclear localization of MYC mRNA and nuclear localization of MYC protein through interaction with hnRNP L. Steric-blocking antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting this element selectively eliminate diverse MYC-dependent cancer cells and inhibit growth of patient-derived tumor organoids. Together, these findings establish noncoding sequences as major carriers of functional genetic information and identify a therapeutically actionable RNA element whose targeting disrupts MYC-driven cancer.

title: FGFR1-driven brachyury promotes endothelial-like differentiation of glioblastoma stem cells via SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling pathways.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by intensive vascular proliferation that is essential for tumor growth. Recent studies indicate the existence of tumor-derived endothelial-like cells can arise from the differentiation of GBM stem cells (GSCs). The transcription factor brachyury plays a critical role in promoting stem cell identity and vasculogenesis during normal embryonic development. However, its involvement in endothelial-like differentiation of GSCs remains unknown. By integrating clinical bioinformatics from GBM databases with preclinical in vitro and in vivo models, including patient-derived GSC cell lines and xenografts, we found that brachyury is highly expressed in GBM tissues and correlates with angiogenesis genes. Our study demonstrated that brachyury is activated by fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1), which subsequently promotes GSC differentiation into endothelial-like cells via SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling. GSCs with high brachyury expression display great sensitivity to selective FGFR inhibitors in vascular tube formation assays. In vivo pharmacological targeting of FGFR1 with inhibitor E7090 or brachyury gene editing using Cas9/gRNA suppresses GBM neovascularization and tumor growth. Furthermore, gene signature analysis of GBM patients further demonstrated that a lower FGFR1/brachyury/SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signature score significantly correlates with favorable overall survival outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of FGFR1-driven brachyury activation in GSC-derived neovascularization and suggest that targeting the FGFR1-directed brachyury/SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling represents a promising therapeutic strategy for GBM.

title: AKT as a central node integrating multidrug resistance mechanisms in ovarian Cancer.
abstract: Ovarian cancer, particularly high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), remains a leading cause of gynecologic cancer mortality. Although HGSOC responds to platinum-taxane therapy, 70-85% relapse, with acquired resistance playing a major role. The phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT)/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, centered on AKT, contributes to this resistance. Current literature examines AKT's downstream consequences in isolation, overlooking their collective contribution to tumor evolution; this review addresses that gap by separating upstream AKT activation from downstream resistance outputs. Intrinsic genomic alterations (PIK3CA mutation, phosphatase and tensin homolog [PTEN] loss) and extrinsic tumor microenvironment (TME) cues converge on AKT, which drives four emerging resistance mechanisms (metabolic reprogramming and ferroptosis evasion, epigenetic modulation of homologous recombination inhibitor sensitivity, cancer stem cell plasticity, and immune evasion, discussed with therapeutic targeting), integrated with classical mechanisms into a unified chemoresistance framework. AKT promotes chemoresistance by coordinating ATP-binding cassette transporter-mediated drug efflux, RAD51/BRCA-dependent DNA repair, and an elevated apoptotic threshold via Bcl-2-associated agonist of cell death and survivin modulation. Spatial organization and interconnections are highlighted, including amplified AKT activation at the tumor-stromal interface through cancer-associated fibroblast-derived exosomal PTEN silencing. We evaluate therapeutic strategies (AKT and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors, folate receptor alpha-targeted antibody-drug conjugates such as mirvetuximab soravtansine, and metabolic modulation through the AKT/mTORC1 axis) by targeting multiple nodes simultaneously. Patient-derived organoids, CRISPR/Cas9 screening, and circulating tumor DNA monitoring enable clinical translation, supporting rationally designed combinations over sequential monotherapy and reframing AKT from a poor-prognosis marker to a therapeutic target in recurrent, chemoresistant ovarian cancer.

title: A genome-wide CRISPR screening identifies targets that drive tolerogenic dendritic cells.
abstract: Tolerogenic dendritic cells (TolDCs) contribute to immune tolerance and have demonstrated therapeutic potential in early clinical studies of autoimmune diseases. However, the key molecular pathways driving their differentiation and tolerogenic phenotype remain elusive. Here, we investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying the functional status of TolDCs in response to different tolerizing agents and identified CD86 as a consistent and robust marker downregulated in tolerogenic state. CD86 is functionally required for TolDC-mediated suppression of T cell proliferation and cytokine secretion, supporting its use as a surrogate marker of tolerogenic potential. Leveraging CD86 expression as a readout, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen and characterized genes associated with TolDC phenotypes. This approach positions UBE2L6 as a regulator of CD86 expression through modulation of an ISG15-USP18-associated pathway, implicating its involvement in tolerogenic functions. These findings describe therapeutically targetable pathways to promote immune tolerance.

title: Heterogeneous contributions of APOBEC3 deaminases to substitution and indel mutagenesis in lung adenocarcinoma.
abstract: APOBEC3 cytosine deaminases are major sources of cancer mutations. In lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), APOBEC3 activity drives tumor evolution and therapy resistance, nominating these enzymes as therapeutic targets. Although APOBEC3A drives most APOBEC3-associated mutational signature burden across cancers, the relative contributions of individual paralogs in LUAD remain unclear. Here, we define the roles of endogenously misregulated APOBEC3 deaminases using CRISPR-Cas9 knockouts and whole-genome sequencing of 197 long-term propagated single-cell clones. APOBEC3 mutagenesis falls into three patterns, driven predominantly by APOBEC3A, by both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B, or minimal despite detectable enzyme expression. Commonly used surrogate measures, including mRNA and protein levels and in vitro deaminase activity, do not predict these contributions. We also provide the first causal evidence that endogenous APOBEC3A generates the indel signature InD9a, linking it to uracil excision following cytosine deamination. These heterogeneous contributions highlight the need for biomarkers that resolve individual APOBEC3 activities to guide therapeutic targeting.

title: IDO1 methylation by EZH2 confers resistance to its targeted therapy in colorectal cancer through tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic rewiring.
abstract: Deciphering cancer metabolic reprogramming mechanisms can identify new targets to potentiate EZH2 inhibitor efficacy. Using an in vivo genome-wide CRISPR loss-of-function screen in a CRC mouse model, we pinpointed IDO1 as a key mediator of EZH2 inhibitor resistance. EZH2 blockade remodeled CRC cell metabolism by upregulating IDO1 protein and hyperactivating the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway. Both genetic and pharmacological inhibition of IDO1 suppressed tumor growth and rescued EZH2 inhibitor resistance in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, EZH2 directly binds and methylates IDO1. Methylation of IDO1 facilitates IDO1 ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Accordingly, EZH2 inhibition stabilizes IDO1, augments tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic flux, and ultimately confers therapeutic resistance. In summary, our study identifies IDO1 as a non-histone substrate of EZH2 methyltransferase activity and validates that disrupting IDO1-mediated tryptophan metabolism is a viable strategy to overcome EZH2 targeted therapy resistance in cancers.

title: Self-amplifying RNA vaccines encoding chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinins confer immunity against phylogenetically diverse influenza A viruses.
abstract: Seasonal influenza vaccines require annual reformulation due to antigenic drift and provide suboptimal protection. Here, we evaluate self-amplifying mRNA (samRNA) vaccines encoding chimeric (cHA) and mosaic (mHA) hemagglutinins representing influenza A virus HA phylogenetic groups 1 and 2. Following prime-boost immunization, group 1 cHA vaccines (cH8/1-cH5/1) elicit broad cross-reactive antibodies and confer complete protection against diverse H1N1 strains covering decades of antigenic drift. Group 2 vaccines (cH4/3-cH15/3 and mH10/3-mH14/3) provide comparable breadth against multiple H3N2 strains and heterosubtypic H7N9 challenge, with cHA samRNA showing superior cross-group protection. Protection is associated with Fc-mediated effector functions and CD4+ T cell responses, with minimal hemagglutination inhibition and neutralizing titers. Passive serum transfer confirms antibody-mediated protection independent of cellular immunity. Protective immunity is maintained at doses as low as 0.4 μg, demonstrating the dose-sparing advantage of the samRNA platform. These results support samRNA-delivered cHA and mHA antigens as promising candidates for broadly protective influenza vaccines.

title: An engineered probiotic with integrated biocomputation and multi-molecular recording for precision theranostics of colitis.
abstract: Engineered therapeutic microbes capable of sensing and responding to diseases offer transformative potential for precision medicine. However, their capacity to intelligently process the complex and dynamic biomarkers of multifaceted diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) remains limited. Here, we design a probiotic system that executes logic computations through four stage-specific inflammatory biomarkers, enabling precise diagnosis and closed-loop treatment of colitis in mice. Integration with a CRISPR-based molecular recorder allows dynamic tracking of biomarker levels and converts inflammatory signals into quantifiable, site-specific base-editing events, thereby achieving precise diagnosis and analysis of disease progression within a living mammalian gut. We additionally develop a multimodal machine-learning classifier that utilizes both bioluminescent reporter signals and sequencing data to accurately stage intestinal inflammation with an accuracy of 0.83 ± 0.05. Together, this work provides a robust platform for in situ biocomputation and marks a significant advance toward intelligent, precision theranostics for gastrointestinal disorders.

title: Endonucleolytic mRNA decay associated with damaged tRNAs occupying the ribosome.
abstract: Aberrant events during mRNA translation trigger ribosome-dependent quality control mechanisms that tune mRNA decay and gene expression. Here, we describe endonucleolytic mRNA decay associated with damaged tRNAs at the ribosome. We provide evidence that this process is associated with a nicked tRNA that our data place in the ribosomal A-site, where it contributes to ribosome stalling. Genetic analyses suggest that the pathway is independent of canonical mRNA decay machinery, and we identify the carboxy-terminal domain kinase I (CTDK-I) complex as a critical regulator. These findings suggest that the ribosomal A-site can engage damaged tRNAs and that this engagement can trigger mRNA decay, broadening our understanding of translation elongation and tRNA biology.

title: A Point-of-Care Integrated Detection System for Rapid Mycobacterium leprae Detection Using RPA/CRISPR-Cas12a and Lateral Flow Assay.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Leprosy remains a significant public health challenge in many regions, and inadequate point-of-care (POC) diagnostics often delay treatment and lead to disability. We aimed to establish an optimized RPA/CRISPR-Cas12a POC system for M. leprae detection with integrated reagents, equipment and colloidal gold visualization.
METHODS: The workflow comprised 1 min of tissue DNA release, 15 min of incubation and amplification in the instrument, and approximately 16 min for CRISPR detection. Assay conditions were optimized (200 nM primers, 37°C, 100 nM each of Cas12a and crRNA), and analytical sensitivity and specificity against non-leprosy mycobacteria were evaluated. Clinical performance was assessed in 219 clinical samples and compared with Ziehl-Neelsen staining and PCR.
RESULTS: The detection limit was 100 copy/μL for M. leprae DNA, with no cross-reactivity with other mycobacteria. Among 179 confirmed leprosy samples, CRISPR-Cas12a detected all multibacillary (MB) samples (100%) and 65.21% of paucibacillary (PB) cases, outperforming PCR (39.13%) and acid-fast staining (0%) and comparable to qPCR (63.04%). All non-leprosy samples were negative by CRISPR-Cas12a.
CONCLUSIONS: This POC-compatible platform holds promise for early diagnosis, and the integrated reagents and equipment further enhance convenience for on-site testing in resource-limited settings, supporting timely intervention and leprosy control efforts.
