title: PIK-75 suppresses SREBP-dependent sterol-synthesis genes in PIK3CA-altered small-cell lung cancer cells, but attribution to p110α remains unresolved.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Class IA PI3K isoforms are candidate therapeutic targets in small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). The transcriptional consequences of isoform-directed inhibitors in SCLC cells have not been compared genome-wide.
METHODS: We re-analysed GEO series GSE40564, in which PIK3CA-altered NCI-H69 cells were treated for 24 h with vehicle, PIK-75 (p110α-directed) or TGX-221 (p110β-directed), with three arrays per group. Differential expression used limma, with re-processing from raw files and spike-in-anchored normalisation as sensitivity analyses. Gene sets were tested with correlation-adjusted competitive tests (camera), including a direct comparison of the two compounds. The main finding was checked against LINCS L1000 signatures of selective PI3K inhibitors and an independent alpelisib RNA-seq dataset. Isoform dependency was examined in DepMap CRISPR screens, and a PIK-75 response score was tested in 81 primary SCLCs against matched random-signature nulls.
RESULTS: PIK-75 changed 11,645 of 17,458 genes at FDR < 0.05; 316 decreased and 20 increased significantly beyond two-fold. Its clearest pathway-level effect was lower expression of SREBP-controlled sterol- and lipid-synthesis genes (SQLE, HMGCS1, HMGCR, LDLR, SCD; log2 fold-change -1.1 to -1.6). Cholesterol homeostasis was the only gene set that stayed significant after correlation adjustment (camera FDR = 0.02) and that differed significantly between PIK-75 and TGX-221 (FDR = 0.02). TGX-221 changed 358 genes, none two-fold, and its response depended on two of three replicates. In LINCS, the down-regulated genes of alpelisib and taselisib were enriched for SREBP targets (p ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁶), whereas those of TGX-221 were not, and alpelisib reduced several of the same genes in an independent dataset. PIK-75 also inhibits CDK9 and DNA-PK, and canonical FOXO targets were not induced, so the response cannot be attributed to p110α alone. SCLC lines depended more on PIK3CA than on PIK3CB in DepMap (median Chronos -0.38 vs -0.15), as did other lineages. In patients, the response score was not associated with survival beyond matched random signatures (empirical p = 0.12-0.14).
CONCLUSION: To our knowledge, this is the first genome-wide comparison of isoform-directed PI3K inhibitors in SCLC cells. PIK-75, but not TGX-221, suppresses an SREBP-dependent sterol programme in NCI-H69 cells, and public data from selective p110α inhibitors point to PI3K signalling as its most plausible source. Because PIK-75 is not selective and TGX-221 exposure was not measured, the attribution to p110α and the apparent dispensability of p110β remain preliminary.

title: Breast cancer cellular and gene-based therapies: current approaches, clinical results, and future perspectives.
abstract: Cellular and gene-based therapies are being investigated as potential strategies to address current treatment limitations in breast cancer. Adoptive cell therapies, such as CAR-T, TCR-T, TILs and NK cell-based therapies, are currently under investigation for their ability to selectively target tumor-associated antigens. Also, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing is being investigated as a strategy to enhance T cell persistence, improve tumor infiltration, and increase resistance to immunosuppressive signaling. Although cellular and gene-based therapies have transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies, their application in breast cancer remains limited by antigen heterogeneity, immune exclusion, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Among current approaches, TIL-based therapies have provided some of the clearest evidence of clinical activity selected patients, whereas the clinical efficacy of CAR-T and gene-editing strategies as standalone interventions remains uncertain. Future progress may depend on biomarker-guided, combinatorial approaches rather than single-modality therapies. This review examines the current applications, clinical evidence, and limitations of these approaches in breast cancer.

title: ACTR5 as a potential therapeutic target in AML: Preliminary mechanistic insights from integrated multi-omics analysis.
abstract: Actin-Related Protein 5(ACTR5) is essential for tumor progression in hepatocellular carcinoma(HCC), however, its function in acute myeloid leukemia(AML) remains elusive. We aim to characterize the role of ACTR5 in AML progression as well as its potential mechanism. The patient samples from TCGA and GTEx database were utilized to reveal the survival of ACTR5 high-expression(ACTR5hi) and low-expression(ACTR5low) through GEPIA online tool. ACTR5 knockout (ACTR5-KO) cell lines were generated by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing technology and ACTR5 overexpression(ACTR5-OE) cell line was obtained by plenti-CMV transfection system, to assess its impact on cell growth, apoptosis and cell cycle in vitro. Functionally essential targets were revealed via integrative analysis of multi-omics data, including RNA-seq and ATAC-seq, between wild-type and ACTR5-KO cell lines. The ACTR5hi patients showed a shorter overall survival compared to the ACTR5low patients in AML group. Besides, ACTR5 depletion inhibited proliferation, promoted apoptosis, and impaired cell cycle progression. Mechanistic studies unveiled ACTR5 as a regulator of cell cycle, including abnormal expression of checkpoints promoting G1/S phase transition(CCND2)and inhibiting S/G2 phase transition(FOS, JUNB). In addition, the functionally essential genes of DNA repair were revealed including the upregulation of RAD50, ATM, CDC20, CDC25C, TERT. Our findings highlight the potential oncogenic role of ACTR5 in poor prognosis, as well as suggesting a potential role for ACTR5 in AML pathogenesis through its association with disrupted cell cycle and DNA repair gene programs.

title: Integrated single-cell and bulk RNA-Seq analysis reveals a LCR-related prognostic signature for precision prognostication and therapeutic stratification in clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUNDS: Lysine crotonylation (LCR) is an emerging post-translational modification, yet its clinical significance and therapeutic relevance in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) remain poorly understood.
METHODS: Multi-omics data were collected from public repositories. Consensus clustering based on 18 LCR-related genes (LCRGs) was performed to define molecular subtypes. Co-expression modules identified via WGCNA were integrated into 101 machine-learning combinations to establish a LCR-related signature (LCRS). The signature was evaluated for survival prediction, immune microenvironment characteristics, and drug response across multiple cohorts, complemented by single-cell RNA sequencing. Candidate therapeutic targets and compounds were screened using DepMap CRISPR dependency data and pharmacogenomic databases (CTRP and PRISM).
RESULTS: Two distinct molecular subtypes (C1 and C2) were identified, displaying significant differences in survival, immune infiltration, and signaling pathways. Integrating WGCNA hub genes with an optimal machine-learning framework yielded a robust 15-gene LCRS, which served as an independent prognostic factor in the TCGA cohorts. Single-cell analysis localized signature genes predominantly to endothelial cells. Pharmacogenomic profiling indicated higher sensitivity to sunitinib among high-risk patients, whereas low-risk patients displayed elevated sensitivity to axitinib and pazopanib. Furthermore, dependency screening prioritized CLCNKA as a key therapeutic target along with ten candidate compounds for high-risk patients.
CONCLUSIONS: This study establishes a robust LCR-related prognostic signature and nominates CLCNKA as a novel therapeutic vulnerability, offering actionable insights for personalized stratification and treatment in ccRCC.

title: miR-221 and miR-222 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: mechanistic evidence, extracellular vesicle communication, biomarker candidates, and therapeutic prospects.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains difficult to diagnose early and treat effectively. The related microRNAs miR-221 and miR-222 share a seed sequence, but their functions and clinical evidence should be evaluated individually. Pancreatic cancer models support miR-221/222-associated TIMP-2 repression and invasion, miR-222-mediated p57 regulation, and tumor-derived vesicular miR-222 effects on p27 expression and localization. Macrophage-derived extracellular vesicular miR-222-3p has also been implicated in gemcitabine resistance through TSC1-associated signaling. By contrast, the TRPS1-ZEB2 mechanism and the vesicular SPINT1-HGF liver pathway derive from breast and colorectal cancer studies, respectively, and remain extrapolations when discussed in PDAC. Circulating miR-221 has shown exploratory diagnostic associations, but results from general miRNA panels cannot be assigned to miR-221 or miR-222 individually. Tissue prognostic associations likewise do not validate circulating assays. A first-in-human study of the selective inhibitor LNA-i-miR-221 provides early safety and peripheral-blood pharmacodynamic evidence in a mixed advanced-cancer population that included pancreatic cancer; it does not establish PDAC-specific efficacy. Translation requires independent biomarker validation, molecule-specific target-dependence studies, and confirmation of effective pancreatic tumor delivery.

title: ADAR1 p150 abundance reports interferon exposure but does not establish cancer immunotherapy resistance.
abstract: ADAR1 p150 is an interferon-inducible RNA-editing isoform that limits endogenous double-stranded RNA sensing and can protect tumor cells from inflammatory stress. Yet increased p150 expression has also been observed in immune-infiltrated tumors and in some patients responding to immunotherapy. We argue that elevated p150 abundance is consistent with an interferon-responsive state but cannot, by itself, establish functional ADAR1 dependence or immunotherapy resistance. A practical four-determinant decision framework distinguishes an interferon-exposure interpretation from a tumor-dependency interpretation by examining signaling context, cellular source and localization, treatment timing, and RNA-sensing function. Crucially, editing-independent competition for dsRNA binding can suppress PKR, making RNA-editing measurements insufficient as a sole functional assay. We specify clinically accessible measurements, the limitations of bulk assays, and functional studies required to validate the proposed decision rules. This framework offers testable hypotheses rather than a clinically validated classification system.

title: Dataset on the design and functional evaluation of INHBE-targeting small interfering RNAs.
abstract: Abdominal obesity is a major risk factor for metabolic disorders. Human genetic and transcriptomic studies have identified the inhibin beta E subunit (INHBE), a liver-enriched gene encoding activin E, as a potential regulator of body fat distribution and metabolic homeostasis. These findings highlight INHBE as a potential therapeutic target for RNA interference (RNAi)-based interventions. This study aimed to design and evaluate INHBE-targeting siRNAs. This was done by first using chemically synthesized siRNAs as a reference, followed by the establishment of an enzymatic in vitro transcription (IVT) workflow for siRNA synthesis and comparison of the gene-silencing efficiency of chemically synthesized and enzymatically synthesized siRNAs in human hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG2) cells. Gene-silencing efficiency was assessed by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) to quantify INHBE mRNA expression. Among the eight candidates, siRNA-3 and siRNA-6 produced the strongest inhibitory effects on INHBE knockdown. However, chemically synthesized siRNAs produced more consistent and reproducible knockdown effects, whereas IVT synthesized-siRNAs showed greater variability across experiments. In conclusion, the dataset includes the siRNA target sequences and corresponding INHBE expression data, providing a resource for comparing siRNA candidates and evaluating the effects of target-site selection on INHBE silencing.

title: Emerging strategies for progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) combination therapies.
abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterised by a combination of motor, ocular, cognitive, and behavioural impairment, but has a heterogeneous clinical presentation. It is a devastating and rapidly progressive atypical parkinsonian disorder with no current disease-modifying treatments. PSP is classified as a primary tauopathy characterised by abnormal accumulation of tau within neurons and glial cells, primarily in the brain stem, culminating in cell death. While genome wide association studies have been instrumental in identifying multiple risk loci, recent multi-omics studies combining brain gene expression and other omics measures have revealed a plethora of perturbed transcripts and molecular pathways that may play pivotal roles in PSP. This includes genes such as MAPT, STOM, KANK2, DDR2, LRRK2, and STX6, but their precise roles remain elusive. These genes are differentially expressed and may regulate processes including neuroinflammation, glymphatic clearance of tau, cytoskeletal maintenance, and synaptic function. In this review, we summarise current treatment strategies attempted in PSP, compile disease-modifying therapies in development, and explore potential disease mechanisms suggested by multi-omics studies. By targeting several underlying disease processes at once, combination strategies have the potential to improve both motor and cognitive function, slow neurodegeneration, and ultimately alter disease progression.

title: A single-dose membrane-anchored F1/LcrV mRNA vaccine confers protection against pneumonic plague: a preclinical study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The success of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platforms has prompted significant interest in their application against bacterial pathogens. However, adapting these platforms requires optimising host-expressed antigen structure to ensure robust immunogenicity. While membrane anchoring enhances the efficacy of viral mRNA vaccines, its application in bacterial mRNA platforms remains largely unexplored. Plague, caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Yersinia pestis, has been one of the most devastating diseases throughout human history. Despite extensive studies, there are no licenced vaccines available.
METHODS: We developed a bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccine against Y. pestis, utilising the major antigens F1 and LcrV (5 μg of each mRNA). We evaluated glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored and transmembrane (TM) variants alongside secreted native and hFc-conjugated formats to assess immunological profiles and determine protective efficacy in a murine model of pneumonic plague.
FINDINGS: Membrane-tethering of F1 and LcrV antigens improved overall immunogenicity. Whereas secreted native and hFc-conjugated variants elicited predominantly cell-mediated and serological immune responses, respectively, the membrane-anchored bivalent mRNA vaccine generated a robust, protective immune response. This dual humoural and cellular immunity facilitated robust (87.5%, 7/8 mice) protection following a single-dose vaccination.
INTERPRETATION: By progressing towards the single-dose biodefense benchmark prioritised by the World Health Organisation Target Product Profile, this membrane-anchored construct emerges as a promising translational candidate for a rapid-response plague vaccine. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that extending established antigen-tethering strategies to bacterial targets may be a highly effective approach for generating the potent immunity required to overcome complex bacterial infections.
FUNDING: This research was supported by the Israeli Science Foundation (grants 2012/20, 842/25), the Lewis Trust and the Shmunis Family Trust.

title: Long non-coding RNAs in human dental pulp stem cell differentiation: Mechanisms and therapies.
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) regulate human dental pulp stem cell (hDPSC) differentiation and stress responses, offering potential targets for dentin-pulp regeneration. This narrative review critically evaluates their roles in self-renewal and osteogenic/odontogenic commitment, distinguishing direct hDPSC evidence from findings in other cell populations. Key mechanisms include miRNA-associated networks, chromatin regulation, RNA-protein interactions, and mRNA stabilization, with effects shaped by inflammatory and hypoxic conditions. Emerging evidence links R-loop accumulation to cGAS-STING activation, increased inflammation, and impaired odontogenic differentiation; however, a causal lncRNA-R-loop pathway remains unestablished in hDPSCs. Extracellular vesicle-mediated lncRNA transfer provides an additional avenue for regenerative investigation. Current evidence remains predominantly preclinical, limited by two-dimensional models, cellular heterogeneity, and incomplete mechanistic validation. Future priorities include single-cell and spatial multi-omics, rigorous interaction and rescue experiments, standardized extracellular-vesicle studies, and organotypic and in vivo validation. Delivery specificity, RNA stability, and safety also require careful evaluation. LncRNAs thus represent promising mechanistic regulators and candidate regenerative targets, but their clinical utility requires stronger causal and translational evidence.

title: Efficacy and safety of exon skipping therapies for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by progressive muscle weakness and muscle wasting. Exon skipping therapies have been approved as part of the therapeutic arsenal for DMD, however, there is contrasting evidence regarding their clinical benefits. The aim of this study was to determine the efficacy and safety of exon skipping therapies for DMD.
METHOD: ology: A systematic review was conducted in three databases including PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Cochrane-Ovid, based on the following question using PICO strategy: What is the efficacy of exon skipping therapies for DMD? Search was limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and Open Label RCTs with reported results, published between January 2016 and December 2024, involving patients with DMD treated with any of the existing exon-skipping therapies, reporting efficacy measured by primary clinical and secondary molecular outcomes. Secondary safety outcomes were also registered. Eligible studies were assessed for risk of bias. A descriptive analysis was performed in subgroups according to variants amenable to exon 45, 51, or 53 skipping.
RESULTS: A total of nine studies were left after the final filters were applied. Studies were conducted across centers in seven different countries. Four studies used viltolarsen (exon 53), three eteplirsen (exon 51), and two golodirsen (exon 53). Trial length was heterogeneous with an average length of 119.6 weeks (±78.5). Overall, studies with exon skipping medications reported improvement in the clinical outcomes including the 6-minute walking test, time to stand and the North Star Ambulatory Assessment. Biological measurements showed an increase in dystrophin expression and exon skipping percentage. Long term follow up evidenced stabilization of both clinical and molecular outcomes in DMD patients, compared to age and treatment-matched controls.
CONCLUSION: Exon skipping therapies have evidenced improved clinical and molecular outcomes. Longer follow-up extension studies are needed to further elucidate their effect in comparison to age-matched controls.

title: Epigenetic Allostasis in Alcohol Use Disorder: A Metabolic-Chromatin Framework Linking DNA Methylation, Circuit Remodeling, and Precision Therapeutics.
abstract: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is a chronic relapsing disorder characterized by persistent dysregulation of reward, stress, and executive circuits. Although acute ethanol effects on neurotransmission are well established, the molecular mechanisms that stabilize long-term vulnerability remain unclear. Building on established allostatic and epigenetic-allostatic models, we develop an expanded framework in which repeated alcohol exposure can drive a transition from adaptive, transient chromatin remodeling toward more persistent epigenetic states across key neural circuits. We integrate evidence from histone modifications, DNA methylation, and metabolic regulation, highlighting how alcohol-induced oxidative stress and disruption of one-carbon metabolism lead to S-adenosylmethionine depletion and methylation instability. These processes converge to form a metabolic-epigenetic trap, reinforcing transcriptional repression of plasticity-related genes. We synthesize circuit-specific changes in the amygdala, prefrontal cortex, nucleus accumbens, and hippocampus, and incorporate emerging human postmortem and single-nucleus multiomic data that support cell-type-specific epigenetic remodeling. In addition, we examine neuroimmune-epigenetic interactions and developmental and sex-dependent exposures as amplifiers of epigenetic vulnerability. Finally, we evaluate therapeutic strategies ranging from selective histone deacetylase inhibition to locus-specific epigenome editing, emphasizing the critical importance of treatment timing and circuit specificity. Together, this expanded framework conceptualizes AUD as a disorder in which maladaptive genomic stability may contribute to persistent circuit dysfunction and identifies epigenetic-metabolic coupling as a testable target for next-generation therapeutics.

title: Gene Therapy for Inherited Platelet Disorders: From Proof of Concept to Clinical Translation.
abstract: Inherited platelet disorders (IPDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of rare genetic diseases affecting platelet production and/or function, with clinical manifestations ranging from mild mucocutaneous bleeding to severe hemorrhage, multisystem disease, and predisposition to hematologic malignancy. Treatment remains predominantly supportive, and curative options are limited. Future translation will require disease-specific selection of gene addition, allele-specific approaches, or precise genome editing, together with safer conditioning, efficient lineage-restricted correction, and rigorous long-term assessment of genotoxicity and clonal evolution. A shared hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells platform combined with disease-specific genetic engineering may ultimately enable curative treatment of selected severe IPDs.

title: Non-viral delivery and genome editing for CAR-NK engineering in solid tumors: from ex vivo manufacturing to in vivo reprogramming.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered natural killer (NK) cell therapy has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer treatment, offering advantages over CAR-T cells such as a lower risk of cytokine release syndrome and graft-versus-host disease and the potential for off-the-shelf manufacturing. Viral vectors have long served as effective tools for CAR-NK engineering, but their dependence on complex manufacturing procedures, considerable production costs, and the potential risks associated with genomic integration has encouraged increasing interest in non-viral alternatives. Recent advances in genetic engineering technologies have facilitated the development of CAR-NK platforms, particularly through non-viral delivery approaches including electroporation, transposon systems and lipid nanoparticles, while CRISPR-based tools enable targeted genome editing. Meanwhile, an increasing number of clinical trials have begun to evaluate the safety and therapeutic potential of CAR-NK cells in both hematological malignancies and solid tumors. However, challenges such as limited NK-cell persistence, antigen heterogeneity, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment remain. In this review, we summarize recent progress in non-viral CAR-NK engineering strategies, analyze the current landscape of preclinical and clinical trials, and discuss key challenges and future directions for advancing CAR-NK therapy. Collectively, these advances suggest that non-viral engineering technologies may serve as an important technological foundation for next-generation CAR-NK therapies, enabling more flexible ex vivo manufacturing and potentially supporting the future development of in vivo CAR-NK generation strategies for solid tumors.

title: Simple heat-assisted method for mRNA loading into empty lipid nanoparticles enables robust in vitro and in vivo delivery.
abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (LNP) have emerged as a versatile modality, enabling diverse applications by changing encoded mRNA sequences. However, the conventional mRNA-LNP preparation process poses significant barriers to non-specialists because it requires specialized equipment and technical expertise. In this study, we aimed to report a simple post-encapsulation approach where mRNA is mixed with preformed empty LNP in solution to form mRNA-LNP for effective in vitro and in vivo delivery. Process optimization revealed that heating mRNA and empty LNP at 75°C and pH 4.0 achieved approximately 90% mRNA encapsulation while maintaining an LNP size of approximately 100 nm. The resulting post-encapsulated LNP were comprehensively compared with conventional LNP prepared via microfluidic mixing. Both LNP formulations exhibited over 90% cellular uptake and comparable concentration-dependent expression in vitro. The intravenous administration of post-encapsulated LNP in mice resulted in robust luciferase expression in the liver and spleen at 0.01 mg/kg, with no notable changes in serum chemistry at 1 and 3 mg/kg. However, the activity of the post-encapsulated LNP was slightly reduced compared with that of the conventional LNP. Sucrose density gradient centrifugation indicated that post-encapsulated mRNA-LNP formed heterogeneous populations with varying mRNA/lipid ratios, in contrast to conventional mRNA-LNP. These findings support a working hypothesis that this heterogeneity could contribute to the reduced in vivo activity. Our simple post-encapsulation method potentially could lower entry barriers for non-specialists in this field and accelerate RNA-LNP research through its compatibility with 96-well-format preparation.

title: Machine learning-guided chondrocyte membrane-camouflaged lipid nanoparticles for intra-articular SOX9 mRNA therapy of osteoarthritis.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) progression involves cartilage matrix loss and persistent inflammation. This study developed a machine learning-guided and chondrocyte membrane-camouflaged lipid nanoparticle carrying messenger RNA (CM-LNP@mRNA) platform for intra-articular SOX9 delivery. Random forest analysis identified the nitrogen-to-phosphorus and SM-102 ratios as primary determinants with feature importance values of 0.57 and 0.32 respectively. Following ML-guided formulation selection and experimental membrane-coating optimization, the final CM-LNP@mRNA formulation showed an encapsulation efficiency of 95.50% and a particle size of 133.70 nm. Compared with the conventional reference formulation prepared under the same final coating condition, encapsulation efficiency increased from 89.20% to 95.50% and particle size decreased from 145.40 nm to 133.70 nm. Membrane coating shifted the zeta potential from -25.57 mV to -35.07 mV. This transition provided biophysical evidence of successful surface modification. In interleukin-1β-stimulated chondrocytes, CM-LNP@mRNA increased the relative expression of Col2a1 and Acan from 0.20 to 0.33 and from 0.50 to 0.73, respectively, while reducing the relative expression of Mmp3 and Adamts5 from 10.50 to 7.80 and from 4.00 to 2.50, respectively. These alterations indicated a shift toward a matrix-preserving transcriptional state. Downstream matrix metalloproteinase 3 and prostaglandin E2 concentrations decreased from 37.10 ng/mL to 18.50 ng/mL and from 113.70 pg/mL to 76.50 pg/mL by day 7. This reduction demonstrated effective suppression of catabolic and inflammatory activity. In OA rats, CM-LNP@mRNA reduced the osteophyte volume from 4.00 mm3 to 2.00 mm3 and prolonged the thermal response latency from 7.50 s to 11.80 s. These improvements linked cellular metabolic regulation to functional joint recovery. These findings establish a strategy integrating formulation optimization with biomimetic membrane coating to modulate the OA microenvironment.

title: Enhancing mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine-induced T cell responses by simple supplementation with class B CpG oligodeoxynucleotides.
abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines can elicit robust T cell responses; however, these responses remain insufficient, particularly in the context of cancer vaccine therapy. Although several types of adjuvants reportedly enhance T cell responses induced by mRNA-LNP vaccines, few comprehensive side-by-side comparisons exist, and it remains unclear which adjuvants are most suitable. Herein, we screened 15 adjuvants. The addition of class B CpG oligodeoxynucleotides (ODNs) markedly augmented T cell induction in an interleukin-12-dependent manner and promoted the antitumor effects of mRNA-LNP vaccines in mice. Class B CpG ODN-adjuvanted mRNA-LNP vaccines induced more potent T cell responses than the mRNA-LNP vaccine administered at a 10-fold higher dose, while exhibiting a more favorable safety profile. However, this approach also reduced the cellular uptake of mRNA-LNPs and antigen expression. As a possible mechanism underlying this reduced delivery efficiency, we found that class B CpG ODNs adsorbed onto LNPs and altered their particle characteristics. These findings demonstrate that supplementation with class B CpG ODN is a simple, safe, and readily implementable approach for enhancing mRNA-LNP vaccine-induced T cell responses. This study also highlights that adding auxiliary components to mRNA-LNPs can potentially affect the performance of LNPs as delivery carriers.

title: Inhaled biologics: A paradigm shift in drug delivery for proteins, vaccines, and gene-based therapeutics.
abstract: Pulmonary drug delivery has emerged as a promising platform for the administration of biologics, offering direct access to the respiratory tract while minimising systemic exposure and associated adverse effects. Recent advances in inhalation technologies, formulation engineering, and carrier systems have significantly expanded the scope of inhaled biologics beyond conventional therapies. This review provides a comprehensive overview of emerging inhaled biologics, including proteins, peptides, monoclonal antibodies, gene therapies, mRNA therapeutics, siRNA, CRISPR-based systems, vaccines, and nanocarrier-enabled delivery platforms. Key physiological barriers to pulmonary delivery, such as mucociliary clearance, alveolar macrophage uptake, mucus penetration, and epithelial transport, are critically discussed along with contemporary strategies to overcome these challenges. Recent developments in lipid nanoparticles, polymeric nanoparticles, liposomes, exosomes, and inhalable dry powder systems are highlighted for their role in enhancing stability, targeting efficiency, and therapeutic outcomes. The review also examines clinical translation, regulatory considerations, aerosol performance, pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic relationships, and the integration of artificial intelligence in formulation design and precision delivery. Marketed inhaled biologics remain limited to a few products, including inhaled insulin. In contrast, most inhaled monoclonal antibodies, gene-based therapies, gene-editing approaches, and pulmonary vaccine platforms remain investigational, with evidence derived primarily from clinical studies at different stages or from preclinical models. This review distinguishes marketed products from clinical-stage candidates and preclinical proof-of-concept studies to clarify the current state of pulmonary biologic delivery.

title: Engineering mRNA lipid nanoparticle for protein replacement in rare genetic diseases - current advances and future challenges.
abstract: Rare genetic diseases affect over 350 million patients worldwide and have long posed significant challenges in modern medicine. Although messenger RNA (mRNA) was initially considered unsuitable due to its instability, immunogenicity, and inability to cross biological barriers, the COVID-19 pandemic established mRNA as a clinically validated therapeutic. Advances in mRNA synthesis and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) design have since improved stability, translation, safety, and scalability, offering a modern strategy, alongside advances in our understanding of rare diseases. By enabling the production of functional proteins without modifying the genome, mRNA-LNP offer a flexible solution to restore proteins lost through rare genetic diseases. Despite this promise, their application for rare genetic diseases remains at early stages, with most candidates in preclinical developments or early Phase 1/2 trials. This review underlines recent advances in mRNA-based protein replacement for rare genetic disorders, integrating innovations in mRNA design combined with LNPs optimization. It also discusses current challenges, emerging innovations, and future perspectives. While early clinical programs have mainly targeted liver-based disorders, the field is expanding toward pulmonary, hematologic, and neuromuscular diseases. Continued multidisciplinary efforts may establish mRNA nanotherapies as a transformative treatment option for patients with rare genetic disorders.

title: Systematic excipient selection as a tool to optimize solid state properties and aerosol performance of spray dried RNA loaded lipid nanoparticles.
abstract: The advancement of RNA therapeutics, particularly small interfering RNA (siRNA), offers promising new approaches for the treatment of pulmonary diseases driven by aberrant gene expression and chronic inflammation like asthma and COPD. In this study, we systematically engineered dry powder inhaler (DPI) formulations containing low (0.8%) and high (2%) siRNA-loaded lipid nanoparticle (LNP) concentrations using spray drying. The matrix-forming excipients, lactose, mannitol and trehalose were combined with varying concentrations of L-leucine (3% to 30% relative to the sugar or sugar alcohol) and trileucine (3%) as dispersion enhancers. The goal was to address key formulation hurdles: maintaining siRNA gene-silencing efficiency, optimizing solid-state properties, and achieving efficient aerosolization for pulmonary delivery. Lactose and trehalose-based spray-dried powders exhibited yields over 70% and preserved siRNA bioactivity, with gene silencing efficiencies exceeding 95% in vitro. Physicochemical characterization revealed that these formulations containing low to moderate leucine or trileucine content solidified in the glassy state, displaying glass transition temperatures over 76 °C and residual moisture levels below 7%, favorable for long-term stability and pulmonary delivery. In contrast, mannitol-based formulations were highly crystalline and less compatible with LNPs, resulting in low yields, larger, irregular shaped particles and poor aerosolization efficiency. In vitro aerosol performance was assessed using two breath-actuated DPIs in a laser diffraction inhalation setup. Our findings highlight that successful pulmonary delivery of siRNA-LNP powders not only depend on powder attributes but also on the interplay between formulation and DPI device. Optimizing excipient selection with regard to a device's powder dispersion principle is essential to achieve robust aerosol performance, efficient lung deposition, and preservation of therapeutic activity in solid-state siRNA-LNP dry powder formulations.

title: Precision drug delivery for ulcerative colitis: engineering the colonic microenvironment for site-specific and responsive therapy.
abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory bowel disease characterised by continuous inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa, resulting from complex interactions among genetic susceptibility, environmental factors, intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and dysregulated immune responses. Although conventional therapies, including aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunomodulators, biologics, and small-molecule drugs have improved disease control, their clinical utility remains limited by incomplete therapeutic responses, adverse effects, loss of efficacy, and difficulties in achieving sustained remission. The present review offers an in-depth view of the emerging trends in molecular pharmacology and future drug-delivery systems for UC. UC-relevant molecular targets and pathological features of the colonic microenvironment be matched to site-specific or stimulus-responsive delivery strategies to improve local therapeutic exposure while limiting systemic toxicity, and clinical translation have been described. We discuss recent therapeutic advances targeting key inflammatory pathways (e.g. TNF-α, JAK-STAT, TYK2, IL-23/Th17, S1P receptors and PPAR-γ) and microbiome-directed approaches (e.g. faecal microbiota transplantation, microbial metabolites and postbiotics). Biomarker-driven approaches, such as faecal calprotectin and microbiota profiling, are emphasised as key components of precision medicine and treatment monitoring. Advanced Drug delivery mechanisms such as liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, solid lipid nanoparticles, hydrogels, microparticles, nanogels and multifunctional theranostic systems provide opportunities for colon-specific drug delivery, controlled release, improved bioavailability, improved mucosal targeting and decreased systemic exposure. New approaches based on RNA-based therapeutics, CRISPR/Cas technologies and artificial intelligence-assisted drug delivery system design further increase the possibilities of personalised treatment. To summarise, the combination of molecularly targeted pharmacology with intelligent and site-specific drug-delivery technologies is an exciting avenue for enhancing therapeutic efficacy and reducing treatment-related toxicity and for furthering personalised management of UC. However, translation to widespread clinical practice will need to overcome challenges related to biocompatibility, gastrointestinal variability, scalability, manufacturing, controlled release, and regulatory approval.

title: TRIM2 facilitates macrophage mediated anti-tumor immunity in renal cell carcinoma through enhancing SIRPA ubiquitination and degradation.
abstract: SIRPA delivers an anti-phagocytic "don't-eat-me" signal through its expression on macrophage membrane surface and promotes tumor progression via membrane-independent mechanism. However, current CD47- and SIRPA-targeting agents only disrupt cell-surface inhibitory signaling, highlighting the therapeutic potential of degrading SIRPA. Here, we identified that E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM2 interacted with SIRPA in vitro. Clinically, elevated TRIM2 expression is associated with prolonged overall and progression-free survival in renal-cell carcinoma (RCC) patients. Mechanistically, TRIM2 catalyzes K48-linked poly-ubiquitination of SIRPA, promoting its proteasomal degradation and reducing SIRPA protein levels. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of TRIM2 in macrophages upregulated SIRPA, significantly impairing phagocytosis of tumor cells. TRIM2 deficiency also promoted tumor growth by increasing intratumoral infiltration of M2-type macrophage, reducing accumulation of anti-tumor M1-like and antigen-presenting macrophages, and impairing effector CD8+ T-cell recruitment. Importantly, combined TRIM2 overexpression and PD-L1 blockade synergistically enhance anti-tumor immunity. Together, these results suggest that targeting TRIM2 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy against RCC by degrading SIRPA in macrophage and provide a roadmap for clinical application.

title: Tonlamarsen, a Hepatocyte-Directed Antisense Oligonucleotide Targeting Angiotensinogen: Phase 1 and 2a Clinical Studies.
abstract: Tonlamarsen, a hepatocyte-directed antisense oligonucleotide targeting angiotensinogen (AGT), produced rapid, dose-dependent reductions in circulating AGT in healthy participants and patients with uncontrolled hypertension. A single dose reduced AGT by up to 75.2%, while monthly dosing achieved reductions of up to 79.0% after 4 doses. Tonlamarsen was generally well tolerated, with no clinically meaningful effects on platelet count, potassium, renal function, liver enzymes, or hypotension. Exploratory analyses demonstrated lower systolic blood pressure with tonlamarsen than placebo. These findings support further evaluation of hepatic AGT suppression as a novel therapeutic strategy for hypertension. A Study to Assess the Safety, Tolerability, and Efficacy of Monthly Subcutaneous Administration of ION904 in Participants With Uncontrolled Hypertension: NCT05314439).

title: Identification of mitophagy inducers for Alzheimer's disease via high-throughput endogenous ATP5B tagging system.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Mitophagy, the selective clearance of defective mitochondria via the autophagy-lysosome pathway, is essential for maintaining mitochondrial health and cellular homeostasis. Dysregulation of mitophagy is strongly implicated in aging-related pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's), cancer, and metabolic disorders, highlighting the significance of elucidating its regulatory mechanisms. While existing methods using exogenous reporters enable genome-wide and high-throughput screening for mitophagy regulators, they constrain discoveries to specific pathways and introduce artifacts through ectopic expression.
OBJECTIVES: To overcome these limitations, we developed an effective and rapid platform for identifying mitophagy modulators by targeting endogenous proteins.
METHODS: Using CRISPR-Cas9 technology, we engineered HeLa cells expressing small molecular tags (GFP or NanoLuc) fused to the C-terminal of ATP5B, a mitochondrial inner membrane protein. Genome-wide screening for mitophagy regulatory genes were performed using a genome-wide CRISPR library coupled with flow cytometry. Additionally, an FDA-approved kinase inhibitor library was used to screen for mitophagy inducers. To evaluate the efficacy of a screened drug in Alzheimer's disease, cognitive behavior, pathological features and mitophagy events in 3 × Tg-AD mice with or without treatment were examined using the Morris water maze assay, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
RESULTS: These ATP5B-tagging cells provided a robust readout of mitophagy and enabled high-throughput genetic or pharmacological screening. With this platform, we identified several promising genes that regulate mitophagy and are significantly associated with Alzheimer's disease. Moreover, the FDA-approved drug Flupentixol emerged as a novel mitophagy inducer that acts by promoting adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) localization to mitochondria and exhibited strong therapeutic potential in a model of Alzheimer's disease.
CONCLUSION: This study establishes a novel system for identifying mitophagy modulators, with the potential to accelerate the discovery of therapeutic strategies for Alzheimer's disease.

title: Uncovering the lymphatic uptake, pharmacokinetics, and biodistribution of mRNA-lipid nanoparticles after intravenous and subcutaneous injection.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations have enabled the in vivo delivery of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) vaccines and therapeutics yet the delivery of RNA remains relatively inefficient. In order to improve LNP design there is a need to better understand how current mRNA-LNP formulations are trafficked and expressed in vivo. Importantly, no prior work has quantified mRNA-LNP transport through lymphatics. In the current study we profile the thoracic lymph uptake, plasma pharmacokinetics (PK), and tissue protein expression after intravenous (IV) and subcutaneous (SC) administration in rats of three common LNP formulations (ALC-0315, SM-102 and MC3 ionizable lipids) containing muGFP-P2A-nLuc reporter mRNA. After IV administration, the SM-102 and MC3 LNP formulations provided the most effective protection of mRNA in plasma. Despite this, tissue NanoLuc® Luciferase (nLuc) expression at 32 h post-dosing was relatively similar across formulations with highest expression seen in the liver and spleen. After SC injection, all formulations supported relatively low bioavailability of mRNA (0.42-0.87% dose) and slightly higher bioavailability of ionizable and PEG lipid (<5% dose) with PK profiles of the ionizable lipid and PEG lipid not completely matching the mRNA PK profiles. There was also greater lymphatic recovery of all ionizable lipids (3.1-4.3% dose) compared to mRNA (0.62-1.4% dose) and PEG lipid (1.9-2.0% dose). Together this data suggests that mRNA is lost prior to or during lymphatic transport. Importantly, concentrations of all mRNA-LNP components were 10-1000 fold higher in thoracic lymph compared to plasma after SC injection. At 32 h after SC injection, highest nLuc expression was seen in lymph nodes and tissues near the dosing site and in the liver and spleen. These findings demonstrating that mRNA-LNPs predominantly traffic from tissue injection sites via lymphatics, mRNA-LNP components may traffic separately from each other in both lymph and blood, and tissue protein expression reflects the PK of mRNA-LNPs at early timepoints.

title: Overcoming technological and biological barriers to pulmonary mRNA delivery with lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles.
abstract: Delivering mRNA to the lungs promises treatment of genetic, infectious and non-communicable lung diseases. Yet, conventional lipid nanoparticle formulations lack the stability needed to endure the harsh mechanical stress during nebulization. Additionally, once deposited in the respiratory tract, gene delivery systems may first have to overcome the mucus barrier, before actually transfecting the target cells. To overcome these challenges, we utilize lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles (LPH), merging the stability of pharmaceutical polymers with the transfection efficiency of cationic and ionizable lipids. LPH are produced in a robust microfluidic process, accomplish near-complete encapsulation efficiency, even after nebulization, and confer high transfection efficiency in A549 cells. To provide colloidal stability after aerosolization, we developed a coating strategy with hyaluronic acid (HA) and poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), ensuring ideal nebulization stability by steric shielding. This formulation showed good transfection efficiency of air-liquid interface grown Calu-3 cells, producing and covered by mucus. The potential of LPH to deliver mRNA to mammalian cells was first shown in primary human lung fibroblasts in vitro and could also be confirmed after intratracheal administration to mice in vivo. Together, these findings validate LPH as a versatile and aerosolizable mRNA delivery platform, overcoming the key technological and biological barriers in pulmonary gene delivery.

title: mRNA folding facilitates efficient and spleen-targeted delivery by highly branched poly(β-amino ester)s.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics hold great promise in preventing and treating various diseases. However, the instability and high immunogenicity of raw mRNA molecules, along with the inefficient delivery vectors, strictly limited the proteins translation and therapeutic applications. In this work, we successfully engineered a folded structural mRNA for enhancing its stability by leveraging a magnesium ion (Mg2+)-mediated charge neutralization and structural compression strategy. Further, a functionalized highly branched poly(β-amino ester)s (HPAEs) was utilized to efficiently deliver the folded mRNA, achieving specifically targeting to the spleen. Notably, compared with polyplexes containing non-folded mRNA, the optimal folded mRNA-based polyplexes exhibited stronger mRNA encapsulation, smaller size, and a more homogeneous morphology; ultimately, demonstrated higher mRNA transfection efficiency up to 85.4% across five different cell types, maintaining high cell viability. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that Mg2+-mediated mRNA folding strategy dramatically enhanced the folded mRNA-formulated polyplexes cellular uptake and endosomal escape. Encouragingly, when administered systemically, the representative folded mRNA-based polyplexes demonstrated robust protein expression, yielding 3-fold enhancement in spleen, compared to the unfolded mRNA-based nanoparticles, showing superior biosafety in vivo. Collectively, the work establishes a new class of the folded structure mRNA polymer delivery system, and provides a foundation for the next generation of RNA-based therapeutic drugs for spleen-related diseases.

title: Exploring lipid nanoparticle design spaces using self-regulating microfluidic machines and multiplexed in vivo biodistribution.
abstract: Delivering therapeutic mRNA relies on lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Finding optimal process parameters for new lipid combinations in LNP formulations remains a challenge. We used an automated, self-regulating microfluidic formulation platform developed for PEG-containing LNPs that actively changes process parameters to meet preset LNP diameters, and now explore how this automated production setup can be expanded to LNPs decorated with poly(2-oxazoline) (POx)-lipids. We also examine how the choice of lipopolymer affects the resulting physicochemical properties and in vivo biodistribution of the resulting LNPs. For that, we tested new LNPs by swapping poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) lipopolymers for alternatives based on poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline) (PMeOx) and poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx). For both POx-lipid variants, the platform independently identified optimal production conditions in four or fewer iterative cycles, yielding particles of the preset size and high mRNA encapsulation. Small-angle X-ray scattering revealed that smaller LNPs modified with PEtOx had greater structural surface variety and higher mRNA loading efficiency. When multiplexing these formulations in mice, the PEtOx-containing LNPs accumulated more in bone marrow and liver (and less in spleen and pancreas), compared to those with PEG, indicating trends that the chemistry of the lipopolymer affects the biodistribution of the resulting LNPs. By combining automated formulation and in vivo multiplexed testing, our approach provides a practical way to rapidly plan, formulate, and evaluate large pharmaceutical design spaces to select excipients and process parameters yielding optimal biological performance of LNPs.

title: Macrophage-targeted GAS6 siRNA delivery by a multifunctional mannan-peptide nanocarrier attenuates pulmonary fibrosis progression.
abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a fatal interstitial lung disease with limited treatment options. Here, we investigated MR3, a macrophage-targeted polysaccharide-peptide delivery system, for the pulmonary delivery of siRNA against growth arrest-specific protein 6 (GAS6). MR3 facilitated effective siRNA endosomal escape, while intratracheal administration ensured sustained lung retention with targeted uptake by macrophages. Functionally, siGAS6@MR3 selectively downregulated macrophage GAS6 expression to inhibit profibrotic M2 polarization, thereby improving survival, restoring lung function, and reversing histological and molecular indices of fibrosis in IPF models. Furthermore, MR3 conferred intrinsic antioxidant protection that enhanced macrophage survival under oxidative stress. siGAS6@MR3 was well tolerated in long-term repeat-dose studies, with no evidence of systemic toxicity. These findings identify GAS6 as a promising antifibrotic target and establish MR3 as a versatile, macrophage-selective siRNA platform for fibrotic and other macrophage-driven diseases.

title: Stimuli-responsive CRISPR-based genome editing delivery system for cancer treatment: A review of fundamentals and applications.
abstract: Cancer remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Conventional modalities, namely surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy, continue to face substantial limitations. The advent of gene therapy, particularly CRISPR-based genome editing, offers new opportunities to overcome these barriers. Nuclease systems such as CRISPR/Cas9 enable precise excision of mutant alleles and targeted insertion of exogenous sequences by harnessing endogenous DNA-repair pathways, achieving durable and accurate genomic modification; derivative tools including CRISPRi, base editing, and prime editing enable diverse forms of gene regulation or precise genome modification through transcriptional repression, base conversion, or related editing mechanisms. To enhance the efficiency, specificity, and spatiotemporal control of CRISPR editing in vivo, sophisticated delivery platforms have been engineered to respond to endogenous tumor-microenvironment cues (e.g., pH, redox potential, hypoxia, ATP, enzymes and microRNAs) or exogenous triggers (e.g., light, ultrasound and magnetic fields). Distinct from material-centric classification schemes, this review organizes these stimuli-responsive systems according to their pathological relevance to the tumor microenvironment (TME), establishing a conceptual framework that links specific TME aberrations with corresponding delivery paradigms. These stimuli-responsive systems represent a major innovation and markedly expand the therapeutic potential of genome editing in oncology. In this review, we summarize the mechanistic basis of CRISPR-based editing, delineate design principles and engineering strategies for stimuli-responsive delivery, and highlight recent advances, outstanding challenges, and future directions toward clinical translation. We aim to provide a concise reference to guide the rational design of gene-editing cancer therapeutics.

title: Lipid nanoparticles supplemented with oligocationic lipids and pH-releasable PEG show enhanced siRNA delivery.
abstract: The composition of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) strongly affects the nucleic acid loading, the interactions with biological targets, the effective endosomal escape, and the cytosolic release at the target site. To integrate these requirements and evaluate the effect of excipients commonly used in LNP production, we comparatively screened a set of LNP formulations containing nucleic acid condensing tetraArginine-[G2]-distearoyl glycerol (OCE), and different fusogenic/ionizable commercial lipids: DOPE, DODAP, D-Lin-MC3-DMA, ALC-0315, and SM-102. Three PEGylated agents were investigated to evaluate their effect on colloidal stability and transfection performance: pH-sheddable DSPE-hydrazone-PEG2kDa (DSPE-Hz-PEG), diffusible DMG-PEG2kDa (DMG-PEG) and non-releasable DSPE-PEG2kDa (NR-DSPE-PEG). The combination of OCE with the commercial lipids yielded LNPs with ~100 nm sizes, and + 35/40 mV z-potentials, and high siRNA loading efficiencies (~90%), nearly doubling those of OCE-free formulations. LNPs containing OCE and the ionizable lipids D-Lin-MC3-DMA, ALC-0315, and SM-102 yielded the highest gene silencing in eGFP-expressing H1299 cells, with IC₅₀ values between 0.32 and 0.47 nM. In contrast, all OCE-free formulations and formulations containing OCE in combination with DOPE or DODAP, yielded remarkably lower gene silencing. LNPs obtained with OCE and SM-102 coated with 3 and 5 mol% DSPE-Hz-PEG and NR-DSPE-PEG produced colloidally stable formulations also in presence of serum. The 5 mol% DSPE-Hz-PEG coating provided effective charge shielding at pH 7.4 while PEG detached under endosomal conditions (pH 5.5). This behavior enhanced cytosolic siRNA delivery, achieving an eGFP silencing IC₅₀ of 3.22 nM owing to efficient OCE-LNP endosomal escape enabled by spatially controlled, pH-triggered cleavage of the PEG-lipid. NR-DSPE-PEG showed reduced endosomal escape and transfection (IC₅₀: 82 nM) while DMG-PEG exhibited poor serum stability due to premature detachment, making it a less effective stealth agent.

title: mRNA-LNP vaccine encoding for Fc-scaffold antigen drives FcγR-independent immunity.
abstract: While clinical translation of messenger RNA (mRNA) lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technologies has redefined vaccinology, the development of potent platforms against complex bacterial pathogens is often limited by the transient expression kinetics and rapid clearance of encoded antigens. One well established approach to enhance immunogenicity is the fusion of an Fc fragment to an antigen. However, the mechanism of Fc-mediated potentiation within mRNA-LNP systems is, yet, undefined, specifically regarding the necessity of receptor-mediated interactions. Here, we demonstrate that an mRNA-LNP vaccine, encoding an Fc-fragment fused to the Yersinia pestis F1 antigen, drives robust, protective immunity against the lethal bubonic plague by functioning as a pharmacokinetic stabilizer. Through systematic architectural design, variation of Fc isotypes, species-matched scaffolding, and glycosylation profiling, we reveal that Fc-integration extends systemic antigen bioavailability by over 300-fold, providing a sustained kinetic window for immune priming. Remarkably, immunogenicity is preserved in Fcγ receptor (FcγR)-deficient mice, as well as with a reduced FcγR-binding Fc variant, suggesting that protective immunity is independent of classical FcγR engagement in this model. These findings decouple Fc-mediated enhancement from receptor-mediated interactions, identifying structural stabilization and prolonged persistence as the primary drivers of efficacy in mRNA-LNP vaccines. Altogether, our results provide a mechanistic framework for the design of high-potency mRNA vaccines through engineered protein stability.

title: Z-RNome profiling uncovers dysregulated Z-RNA with implications in systemic lupus erythematosus pathogenesis.
abstract: RNA molecules adopt diverse secondary structures for distinct functions. Among them, the left-handed RNA double helix (Z-RNA) regulates innate immunity and has been implicated in autoimmune disorders. However, accurate, fine-scale Z-RNome profiling remain lacking, and its role in autoimmune diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is poorly understood. Here we develop AMAZE-seq for fine-scale profiling of the human Z-RNome. AMAZE-seq leverages the Zα domain for specific recognition of Z-RNA and a fused APOBEC1 enzyme to edit Z-RNA regions for subsequent detection. Using AMAZE-seq, we reveal that Z-RNAs predominantly form on intramolecular double-stranded RNA rich in pyrimidine/purine alternations, with nearly half originating from non-repetitive regions, substantially expanding the known repertoire of Z-RNA-forming regions. Knockout and rescue experiments support the role of ADAR1 p150 in suppressing Z-RNA through both binding and RNA editing. AMAZE-seq profiling of SLE patient-derived cells reveals a dysregulated Z-RNome. Mechanistically, elevated Z-RNA formation activates ZBP1 and induces RIPK3-MLKL-mediated necroptosis and caspase-dependent apoptosis, potentially triggering the release of immunogenic Z-RNA species and aberrant immune responses in SLE patients. Our results define the landscape, features, regulatory mechanisms, and disease relevance of Z-RNA, establishing AMAZE-seq as a transformative tool for dissecting Z-RNA biology in health and disease.

title: Liver biopsy confirms precise and efficient correction of SERPINA1 after in vivo base editing in a patient with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
abstract: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) caused by the PI⁎ZZ genotype (Glu342Lys) is characterized by hepatic accumulation of misfolded AAT-Z protein and reduced circulating AAT levels, leading to progressive liver disease and pulmonary emphysema. Gene correction therapy represents a potentially curative approach by directly correcting the underlying genetic defect. We report the first clinical case with direct assessment of hepatic gene correction by liver biopsy following in vivo base editing in a 66-year-old male patient with PI⁎ZZ AATD who underwent gene correction therapy within the YOLT-202 phase I/Ia clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT07193615). Ten weeks after treatment, a liver biopsy was performed to assess hepatic histology in the context of pre-existing F2 fibrosis identified by elastography before treatment. Liver tissue was analyzed for correction of the PI⁎ZZ variant using Sanger and Illumina sequencing, including assessment of bystander and off-target editing. Serum levels and biological activity of AAT were assessed longitudinally using an elastase inhibition assay. Liver biopsy showed no evidence of hepatic inflammation and demonstrated correction of the PI⁎ZZ variant in 54% of alleles by Sanger and 57% by Illumina sequencing without detectable off-target signals. Following a transient post-treatment increase in transaminases, liver enzymes returned to baseline. Monthly measurements demonstrated sustained circulating AAT levels with preserved biological activity, as assessed by elastase inhibition, throughout follow-up. In vivo base editing achieved substantial and precise hepatic correction of the pathogenic SERPINA1 PI⁎ZZ variant, without concerning histological findings or detectable bystander or off-target editing. Sustained biologically active AAT levels support the feasibility and potential of this approach for the treatment of AATD.

title: The σ subunit identity, rather than RbpA, is the major determinant of M. tuberculosis RNA polymerase sensitivity to fidaxomicin.
abstract: Fidaxomicin is a narrow-spectrum antibiotic that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) at an early stage of transcription initiation. Fidaxomicin is used for treating Clostridioides difficile infections and has demonstrated in vitro efficacy against drug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). Fidaxomicin derivatives are currently the focus of extensive research to develop novel antibacterial agents. Previous studies showed that region 3.2 of the RNAP primary σ factor and the mycobacterial transcriptional activator RbpA modulate fidaxomicin potency through poorly understood mechanisms. Moreover, the impact of the structurally distinct extracytoplasmic function (ECF) σ factors on fidaxomicin potency has never been explored. Here, using DNA scaffold-based in vitro transcription assays, we found that RbpA-dependent primary σ factors from Mtb enhance fidaxomicin potency, whereas ECF σ factors render Mtb RNAP resistant to fidaxomicin. Contrary to the prevailing assumptions, RbpA has only a marginal effect on fidaxomicin potency. Our structural analysis and molecular dynamics simulations support a model in which ECF σ factors obstruct fidaxomicin binding by changing the configuration of the RNAP RNA channel. Conversely, the direct interaction between fidaxomicin and RbpA-dependent primary σ factors does not affect drug binding. Our findings identify the σ factor as a key modulator of fidaxomicin potency and provide a framework to explore σ factor structural diversity for designing pathogen-specific fidaxomicin analogs. Moreover, these results highlight fundamental mechanistic differences between the modes of action of housekeeping and ECF σ factors during transcription initiation.

title: An unexpectedly well-organized ligand-free conformation provides an alternative view of theophylline aptamer recognition.
abstract: A theophylline-binding RNA aptamer has been extensively studied as a model for RNA-ligand interactions. While previous structural analyses have provided insights into its binding mechanism, the precise nature of ligand recognition remains unclear. In this study, we present a crystal structure of a novel ligand-free conformation of the theophylline aptamer. Unlike previously reported ligand-free conformations within Fab-RNA complexes, the ligand-binding region adopts a well-organized structure in which the space occupied by theophylline in the ligand-bound state is instead filled by an RNA nucleotide. Structural evaluation with a residue-separation-based statistical potential revealed that the newly identified ligand-free conformation shows greater consistency with statistically preferred intramolecular atomic arrangements than the other ligand-bound and ligand-free conformations examined. These findings provide new insights into the conformational landscape underlying theophylline recognition.

title: Frailty as a determinant of mRNA vaccine efficacy.
abstract: Frailty, an age-related state of increased vulnerability, is associated with greater susceptibility to infection and impaired vaccine response. In this Review, we examine how frailty-associated immunosenescence, including altered haematopoiesis, chronic inflammation, and dysfunction of innate and adaptive immune responses, can affect the immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety of lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines. Evidence from COVID-19 lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines and other vaccines suggests that people living with frailty can mount weaker or less durable responses than non-frail peers, although findings remain heterogeneous and frailty-specific evidence is scarce. The high customisability of lipid nanoparticle mRNA platforms creates opportunities for frailty-tailored vaccination. We discuss optimisation of lipid nanoparticle composition, targeting and dosing, mRNA cargo and combination-vaccine approaches, alongside host-directed measures addressing comorbidities, nutrition, and immune dysfunction. Integrating frailty into vaccine design, evaluation, and deployment could support safer, more effective, and more individualised vaccination strategies for older adults.

title: Beyond off-target editing: the emerging landscape of Cas9 cytotoxicity and immunogenicity across biological systems.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 has transformed agricultural biotechnology, microbial engineering, and human therapeutics within a decade, yet biosafety assessment remains focused on editing accuracy and off-target cleavage. A second, neglected question is what the high-molecular-weight Cas9 effector protein does to expressing systems. This review integrates evidence from eukaryotic cell lines, microbial hosts, transgenic mammals, and dietary exposure models. In isolated cells Cas9 injures the host by three routes, only one requiring DNA cleavage: TP53-dependent genotoxic stress at susceptible loci, modified by cell sex and p53 status; guide-independent binding to ribosomal proteins that activates the PI3K-mTORC2 axis; and promiscuous association with host transcripts inducing a p53-linked stress programme. In GC-rich bacteria, PAM density and limited double-strand break repair make basal expression lethal. Intact mammals tolerate tissue-restricted Cas9 expression, although nervous system and germline compartments are exceptions, and dietary exposure carries no measurable toxicological or allergenic risk. Pre-existing anti-Cas9 immunity is the dominant translational barrier. Proteasomal, SUMO-regulated and autophagic pathways together set Cas9 half-life. Transient ribonucleoprotein delivery, anti-CRISPR, degron-based control, and lower-toxicity orthogonal nucleases each narrow this exposure window. We conclude that Cas9 toxicity is not intrinsic but contingent on expression kinetics, delivery format, host repair, proteostatic capacity, and immunological history. Biosafety is therefore a tunable design parameter, and this review provides a mechanism-based framework for matching nuclease, delivery route and temporal control to the intended application.

title: Recent Progresses in Immune Cell Therapy for Tuberculosis.
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading cause of global mortality. Its prevention and control face major challenges, including a large latent infection reservoir, high transmissibility, complex treatment protocols, rising drug-resistant TB (notably multidrug-resistant TB, MDR-TB), and comorbidities. MDR-TB has severely undermined conventional pharmacotherapy, with suboptimal global treatment success rates. Thus, novel strategies are urgently needed to accelerate elimination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and shorten treatment duration. Immune cell-based therapies, acting through multiple targeted mechanisms, align well with the complex demands of TB treatment. When integrated with advanced technologies such as genetic engineering and nanotechnology, immunotherapy holds substantial promise for developing novel regimens. This review systematically delineates major immune cell types involved and their mechanisms of action, critically assesses current technical bottlenecks, and explores future innovative directions. It also critically evaluates recent encouraging clinical trials in TB immunotherapy. Collectively, these efforts aim to establish a robust theoretical and practical translational framework, overcome existing limitations, accelerate clinical translation of immune cell-based therapies, provide new options for patients, and advance the field toward personalized and precision medicine.

title: Molecular insights into the long terminal repeat regions of therapeutic staphylococcal Twortvirinae phages.
abstract: Staphylococcal bacteriophages with proven therapeutic efficacy in anti-staphylococcal therapy have large (~140 kb) genomes and belong to subfamily Twortvirinae. Representatives of four genera (Kayvirus, Silviavirus, Sepunavirus, and Twortvirus) are the most intensively studied and are advancing toward clinical applications. However, the functions of many of their genes remain unknown and cannot be predicted from sequence homology alone. The least explored and most diverse genomic regions are the long terminal repeats (LTRs), which comprise ~10% of the virion DNA. These regions were often omitted from early genome assemblies or misplaced in genomic maps. Only recent studies have shown that LTRs encode genes expressed immediately upon infection and involved in host takeover, genome establishment, and interactions with bacterial defense systems, highlighting their critical role in successful infection during phage therapy. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genomic architecture, transcriptional organization, and molecular functions of LTR regions in Twortvirinae phages. By integrating comparative genomics with recent transcriptomic and phage-host interaction studies, we identify LTRs as key regulatory and evolutionary hubs in Twortvirinae biology and highlight major knowledge gaps concerning their roles in bacterial immunity and phage genome evolution. The enrichment of LTRs in targets of bacterial anti-phage defense systems, together with their dynamic evolution through gene gain, loss, and diversification, suggests a central role in phage adaptation to diverse hosts. Finally, our synthesis of available data allows us, for the first time, to infer which end of the phage genome enters the host cell first during infection.

title: Integrated engineering of antibiotic-marker-free cyanobacterial chassis for enhanced recombinant protein accumulation and intestinal localization.
abstract: Engineered cyanobacteria are promising microbial chassis for recombinant protein production and oral delivery, but low intracellular accumulation, expression-associated physiological burden, and residual antibiotic-resistance markers limit their application. Here, we developed an integrated protein-production and marker-removal strategy in Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 and evaluated chromosomal reporter expression in Arthrospira platensis NIES-39. The CpcB-based expression configuration at the native phycocyanin locus resulted in markedly higher mVenus accumulation than free expression at the NSC1 neutral site, accompanied by reduced culture growth and altered photosynthetic characteristics. Incorporation of a tobacco etch virus protease recognition site, together with chromosomal TEV protease expression, enabled partial intracellular cleavage of the fusion protein. Sequential CRISPR-Cpf1 editing and SacB counterselection enabled the removal of targeted antibiotic-resistance cassettes in Synechocystis, as supported by locus-specific PCR and Sanger sequencing. Chromosomal mVenus expression was also established in A. platensis, although the complete marker-removal strategy was not successfully transferred to this host. Under zebrafish-oriented in vitro intestinal conditions, engineered Synechocystis exhibited pronounced structural disruption, whereas A. platensis filaments fragmented more gradually, accompanied by the release of intracellular components. Following zebrafish feeding, reporter-associated fluorescence was detected in the examined intestinal sections at 6 h after administration. Together, these results establish a Synechocystis engineering framework integrating enhanced recombinant protein accumulation, protease-mediated intracellular processing, and targeted antibiotic-marker removal, with complementary assessment of intestinal mVenus-associated fluorescence following oral administration.

title: CRISPR-Cas Systems in Protozoan Parasites: Genome Editing, Functional Genomics, Gene Regulation and Emerging Applications.
abstract: Protozoan parasites possess complex genomes, unusual DNA-repair mechanisms, multiple developmental stages, and, in several species, intracellular or vector-dependent life cycles that complicate functional genetic studies. CRISPR-Cas9 has become a central tool for functional genomics in these organisms, enabling targeted gene disruption, replacement, tagging, nucleotide modification and genome-wide functional screening. However, editing efficiency and outcomes vary substantially among parasite species and depend not only on Cas9-mediated double-strand break formation but also on target accessibility, guide design, delivery method, parasite stage, DNA-repair capacity, donor availability, selection and the biological cost of the induced lesion. This review focuses primarily on experimentally established Cas9-mediated genome editing in Plasmodium, Leishmania, Toxoplasma gondii, Trypanosoma, Babesia, Theileria and Cryptosporidium. We compare plasmid-based and transient expression, ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, electroporation/nucleofection, stage-specific delivery, guide and donor design, selection strategies, editing outcomes, and molecular and functional validation. Particular emphasis is placed on homology-directed repair (HDR), canonical non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) and single-strand annealing (SSA), which determine whether editing results in indels, precise sequence replacement, tagging or larger genomic deletions. Species-specific differences are illustrated by efficient NHEJ-mediated disruption in Toxoplasma, donor-dependent repair in Plasmodium and Cryptosporidium, SSA-associated repair in Leishmania, efficient homologous recombination in trypanosomatids, precise editing in Babesia, and stage-specific delivery constraints in Theileria. The review further examines the progression from single-gene editing to marker-free manipulation, base editing, conditional approaches and genome-wide functional screens. Cas12a, CRISPRi/a, prime editing and related systems are discussed as emerging extensions. Overall, this repair- and delivery-centred framework explains why CRISPR editing differs among protozoan parasites and identifies the experimentally validated limitations that currently shape their genome-engineering potential.

title: Small genomes, big lessons: What viruses teach us about structure-based riboregulation.
abstract: RNA viruses encode multiple layers of information within a single molecule, which functions simultaneously as a template for protein synthesis and as a structured regulatory RNA. These structures control key aspects of viral gene expression, govern host interactions, and mediate immune evasion. Although the prevalence of RNA structure in viral genomes is now well established, only recently have functional and mechanistic studies begun to uncover how these elements act as regulatory modules that shape infection outcomes. With their compact genomes and experimentally tractable life cycles, RNA viruses represent powerful model systems for uncovering the fundamental building blocks of riboregulation and illuminating principles of gene control conserved across eukaryotes. Here, we review current mechanistic understanding of RNA structure-based regulation across diverse viral families and draw parallels to structure-mediated gene control in eukaryotic transcriptomes, highlighting RNA structure as a central regulatory layer in gene expression with broad therapeutic and synthetic biology potential.

title: An SMN2 splicing-correcting antisense oligonucleotide promotes gene looping and transcription activation.
abstract: We have previously proposed a combined therapy for spinal muscular atrophy based on the upregulation of exon 7 (E7) inclusion into SMN2 mRNA by the antisense oligonucleotide nusinersen (ASO1) together with histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Using a CRISPR-deadCas-based strategy in a human cell line, we show here that targeting histone acetylation at the SMN2 E7 region duplicates the HDACi effect, which overcomes pleiotropic effects. Most noticeably, targeted acetylation at the E7 region causes acetylation and activation of the 30-kbp-distant promoter. Since the nusinersen target site maps near the SMN2 gene 3' end, this crosstalk between the two ends of the gene prompted us to use chromosome conformation analysis (3C) to find that ASO1 promotes gene looping. This unpredicted property of ASOs in modulating chromatin 3D configuration depends on cohesin, CTCF, cleavage/polyadenylation factors, and a canonical poly(A) signal and causes promoter activation at a long distance, which expands the therapeutic potential of splicing-correcting ASOs.

title: The NADHX epimerase NAXE governs PARP1-DNA retention to maintain poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation homeostasis.
abstract: PARP1 is a crucial enzyme involved in DNA-damage repair and other biological processes through poly(ADP-ribose) modification (PARylation), but persistent activation can trigger parthanatos. Despite extensive research, the precise mechanisms governing PARP1 activity remain elusive. Here, through multiple CRISPR-Cas9 screens, we identified NAXE, an NADH hydrate (NADHX) epimerase, as a key regulator of PARP1 activity homeostasis. We show that NADHX inhibits PARP1-DNA binding, while NAXE lowers NADHX levels to promote PARP1 recruitment and DNA repair. PARP1 activation, in turn, induces PARylation that binds and inhibits NAXE, forming a negative feedback loop that restrains PARP1 aberrant activation. Notably, knockout of NAXE in mice and C. elegans disrupts PARylation homeostasis, leading to sustained DNA damage and PARP1 activation, ultimately resulting in parthanatos-driven catastrophic neural injury. These findings uncover a metabolite-mediated feedback mechanism that preserves PARylation homeostasis and highlight NAXE as a potential therapeutic target in PARP1-related neurological disorders.
