title: Progress and applications of microneedle-based gene therapy.
abstract: Gene therapy holds considerable promise for treating a wide range of intractable diseases through the modification of specific genes. However, gene therapeutics such as plasmid DNA, messenger RNA, and CRISPR-based systems are susceptible to degradation, face challenges in crossing cellular barriers, and may induce immune-related adverse effects, thereby limiting their clinical translation. Microneedles create microchannels that penetrate tissue barriers and, when combined with various carrier materials, enhance nucleic acid stability and intracellular delivery efficiency. This review summarizes the compatibility of different microneedle configurations with gene-delivery vectors, compares the effects of various fabrication processes on the activity of therapeutic agents, and elucidates the mechanisms underlying barrier penetration and delivery by microneedles. Recent advances in the application of microneedle-based gene therapy in dermatology, oncology, and nucleic acid vaccination are also discussed. Finally, current challenges, including drug loading, mass production, and safety evaluation, are analyzed, and the prospects for smart, responsive, and integrated diagnostic and therapeutic microneedles are highlighted.

title: Reprogrammed macrophage-derived nanovesicle-lipid nanoparticle hybrids for cardiac siRUNX1 delivery: Therapeutic evaluation in Ang II-induced cardiac remodeling.
abstract: Targeted delivery of small interfering RNA (siRNA) to the heart remains challenging because conventional lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) predominantly accumulate in the liver following systemic administration. To improve cardiac siRNA delivery, we developed a biomimetic hybrid nanoplatform by co-extruding siRUNX1-loaded LNPs with reprogrammed macrophage-derived nanovesicles (rMNVs) obtained from sequentially LPS/TGF-β1-treated RAW264.7 macrophages, followed by surface functionalization with a cardiac-targeting peptide (CTP). The sequentially treated donor cells exhibited a phenotypic shift characterized by reduced M1-associated markers and enhanced M2-associated features. The resulting CTP-hLNPs maintained a nanoscale spherical morphology, high siRNA encapsulation efficiency, and retained donor-cell-derived membrane components, including CD206. In vitro, CTP-hLNPs showed reduced uptake by RAW264.7 macrophages while maintaining cellular internalization and siRUNX1 activity in H9c2 cardiac-derived cells. Following intravenous administration, CTP-hLNPs exhibited reduced liver-associated fluorescence and increased heart-associated fluorescence at 24 h compared with conventional CTP-LNPs. Therapeutic efficacy was subsequently evaluated in an angiotensin II (Ang II)-induced mouse model of cardiac remodeling. CTP-hLNP@siRUNX1 reduced cardiac RUNX1 mRNA expression and improved left ventricular systolic function, as indicated by increased left ventricular ejection fraction and fractional shortening. Treatment also attenuated cardiac hypertrophic remodeling, including reductions in the heart weight-to-body weight ratio and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area. In addition, CTP-hLNP@siRUNX1 reduced myofibroblast-associated α-SMA expression, collagen deposition, and myocardial fibrotic area. Collectively, these findings support rMNV-LNP hybridization combined with CTP functionalization as a potential delivery strategy for cardiac RNA interference therapy and demonstrate its therapeutic effects in Ang II-induced cardiac remodeling.

title: Gene-activated matrices as nanomedicine platforms for bone regeneration: Delivery, translation and patent landscape.
abstract: Protein biologics are constrained in critical-size bone defects not by insufficient potency, but by rapid clearance and the inability to sustain therapeutic signaling at the repair site. Dose escalation does not overcome this pharmacokinetic limitation and instead increases the risk of ectopic bone formation, osteolysis, and soft tissue toxicity. Sustained, localized delivery, not higher dosing, is the unmet requirement. Gene-activated matrices (GAM) address this problem by integrating nucleic acid cargo and delivery vectors within an implantable scaffold, converting infiltrating host cells into local sources of regenerative signals. This review examines GAMs as nanomedicine platforms for bone regeneration, tracing their development from scaffold bioactivity and the limitation of protein biologics to nucleic acid-based delivery. We compare viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, polymeric polyplexes, calcium phosphate nanoparticles, and scaffold-integrated systems across transduction efficiency, expression kinetics, immunogenicity, and bone-site retention. We then examine how scaffold composition, architecture, and fabrication govern vector retention, release, and substrate-mediated transfection. This review then evaluates nucleic acid cargo selection and coordinated osteogenic and angiogenic gene delivery, including pDNA, mRNA, siRNA, miRNA, and explores emerging multi-factor, stimuli-responsive, and CRISPR-based GAMs alongside their translational constraints. A distinct feature of this review is its claim-level patent analysis, which identifies substantial intellectual-property white space in GAM development. Despite strong preclinical evidence, no GAM platform has simultaneously achieved scalable manufacturing, regulatory readiness as a combination product, and validation in a human-scale bone defect model. Clinical translation will require coordinated optimization of vector-scaffold interactions, manufacturing scalability, safety, and clinically relevant validation.

title: Naturallyoccurring phytosterols in lipid nanoparticles induce rigidity reshape and endosome retention to enhance intracellular mRNA processing.
abstract: Although lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have been widely used for mRNA delivery, understanding how cholesterol analogues modulate LNP properties and intracellular trafficking to enhance transfection efficiency remains essential for the rational design of next-generation delivery systems. This study investigated their structure-activity relationships and effects on mRNA delivery. We hypothesized that C-24 alkyl-substituted phytosterols enhance transfection by modulating LNP physicochemical properties and interactions with intracellular transport proteins. These phytosterols altered LNP mechanics and morphology, promoting cellular uptake. In vitro results and molecular dynamics simulations revealed differential interactions between phytosterols and Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1), a late endosomal membrane protein involved in intracellular cholesterol transport. These interactions influenced the late-endosomal retention of phytosterol-substituted LNPs and contributed to enhanced transfection. Furthermore, rather than simply prolonging retention, phytosterol substitution modulated LNP trafficking kinetics, establishing a formulation-dependent optimal intracellular residence window. In vivo results demonstrated reduced serum levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines in mice receiving phytosterol-substituted LNPs. Collectively, these findings elucidate how cholesterol analogues regulate LNP physicochemical properties and intracellular trafficking, providing mechanistic insights and design principles for developing more efficient and precise mRNA delivery systems.

title: AAV peptide-conjugated LNPs highlight bottlenecks in LNP-mRNA delivery to photoreceptors.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) can enable efficient delivery of mRNA for gene editing, making LNPs a promising vector for therapeutic treatment of inherited retinal degenerations (IRDs). Currently, LNP targeting of photoreceptors is inefficient and inconsistent between different cargos. We aimed to mimic the photoreceptor tropism of viral vectors by attaching adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsid surface peptide derivatives to LNPs. We identified the most promising AAV capsid-derived peptides for photoreceptor uptake by confocal microscopy of retinal cross-sections. We generated LNP variants by surface conjugation of top performing peptides to maleimide-polyethylene glycol (PEG)-lipids. Peptide-conjugated LNPs delivered mRNA to photoreceptors and retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) in mice, with GS4, a peptide derived from the AAV9 capsid, as the top performer. Subretinal delivery of 1.0% peptide conjugated GS4-LNPs encapsulating Cre mRNA shows an 8.7-fold increase in photoreceptor transfection in the treated area compared to standard LNPs, respectively. However, when GS4-LNPs encapsulated Cas9 mRNA and sgAi9 editing was restricted to the RPE, reaching 10.9% editing of the total RPE and 31.3% editing within the treated area. Our novel GS4-LNP formulation demonstrates the feasibility for AAV peptide conjugation to LNPs and illuminates the bottlenecks in LNP-mRNA delivery to photoreceptors across mRNA payloads.

title: Epitranscriptomic regulation contributes to multiple myeloma biology and offers potential therapeutic targets.
abstract: RNA modifications are being investigated as contributors to multiple myeloma (MM) biology alongside genomic lesions and bone marrow interactions. This narrative review examines N⁶-methyladenosine (m⁶A), 5-methylcytosine (m⁵C), adenosine-to-inosine editing, and pseudouridylation, with emphasis on the distinction between MM-specific findings and mechanisms proposed from other systems. Functional studies in MM cells and animal models link METTL3, WTAP, FTO, ALKBH5, and YTHDF2 to selected growth, metabolic, and treatment-response programs. Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) has been implicated in GLI1 editing and regulation of double-stranded RNA sensing during lenalidomide exposure. Patient expression and outcome associations support clinical relevance but do not establish that these regulators determine disease behavior. Evidence for m⁵C is more limited, including an NSUN2-exosomal MALAT1 mechanism in myeloma bone disease, while the pseudouridylation studies discussed here largely concern non-myeloma cancers. Stage-specific regulatory changes across precursor disease and relapse remain hypotheses requiring longitudinal testing. Therapeutic approaches include enzyme inhibition, targeted protein degradation, and RNA-directed strategies; most remain preclinical, and several have been evaluated mainly outside MM. Plasma cell-free RNA studies provide early diagnostic observations, but modification-aware liquid biopsy has not been clinically validated for MM risk stratification, treatment selection, or relapse prediction. Progress will depend on disease-specific target validation, selective delivery, assessment of normal hematopoietic effects, and prospective clinical studies. Epitranscriptomic regulation therefore offers a useful research framework for understanding and potentially targeting MM, without displacing the established contribution of genomic and clinical risk factors.

title: PRKN-independent mitophagy regulators in dopaminergic neurons identified by genome-wide CRISPR screening.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the development of PD. PRKN/Parkin is known to play an essential role in mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy. Indeed, mutations and inactivation of this gene are associated with hereditary and idiopathic forms of PD. Despite extensive studies on PRKN-dependent mitophagy, the molecular regulators of PRKN-independent mitophagy in dopaminergic neurons remain incompletely understood. We generated a PRKN knockout iPSC-derived dopaminergic neuronal line expressing the fluorescent mitophagy biosensor mito-SRAI, which reports the delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes as an increase in the TOLLES/YPet fluorescence ratio. We used this cell line to conduct a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen to reveal genetic regulators involved in PRKN-independent mitophagy. Dozens of genes were identified whose knockout increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in an uncoupler-dependent manner. Of these, several genes emerged as candidates with potential therapeutic implications, one of which was Cathepsin F (CTSF). CCCP treatment increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in neurons with siRNA-mediated CTSF knockdown, and CTSF knockdown partially preserved the proportion of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons after paraquat exposure. These results suggest that CTSF is a candidate regulator of PRKN-independent mitophagy and that this lysosomal enzyme may represent a potentially druggable candidate target for PD.

title: Antisense oligonucleotide silencing rescues neurodevelopmental deficits in AMPA receptor gain-of-function mice.
abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for neuronal development and brain function. We investigated the role of a recurrent AMPAR GluA1 variant (GRIA1 p.A636T) identified in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using a Gria1-A636T knock-in mouse model, we show that this variant is sufficient to produce core ASD/ID-like behaviors and cause selective hippocampal vulnerability characterized by progressive dendritic atrophy and neuronal loss. Despite a reduction in GluA1-containing complexes, synaptic AMPARs exhibit hyperexcitability and fail to transition from calcium-permeable to calcium-impermeable AMPARs during development, resulting in persistent excitotoxicity. To explore potential therapeutic interventions, we developed an allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively silence the mutant transcript. A single neonatal ASO dose prevents hippocampal pathology and rescues behavioral deficits. These findings define a mechanism of developmental excitotoxicity driven by a GRIA1 gain-of-function channelopathy and support RNA-targeted precision therapy for AMPAR-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: SCN2B Drives Depression-like Phenotypes in Mice by Suppressing BDNF Signaling via Its Intracellular Domain NICD.
abstract: The rising global burden of depression necessitates novel mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets. Voltage-gated sodium channel β2-subunit (Navβ2, coded by SCN2B) has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, yet its role in depression remains unexplored. Here, we identify SCN2B as a previously unrecognized driver of depression-like pathophysiology. Using SCN2B-overexpressing (SCN2B-OV) mice across different ages (1, 12, and 20 months) and CRISPR- engineered Navβ2V173A,V175K mice with selective reduction of the Navβ2 intracellular domain (NICD), we combined behavioral phenotyping, electrophysiology, neurotransmitter profiling, and molecular analyses, with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) as an environmental challenge. SCN2B-OV mice exhibited accelerated depression-like phenotypes, including anhedonia (sucrose preference 52.42% reduction, P<0.05), behavioral despair (forced swim test immobility 67.42% increase, P<0.05), and cognitive deficits (Y-maze alternation 50.90% reduction, P<0.05), independent of natural aging. Electrophysiologically, SCN2B overexpression induced a striking prefrontal-hippocampal imbalance: prefrontal cortex (PFC) became hyperexcitable (glutamate release increased by 64.7%; sEPSC amplitude increased 2.05-fold, P<0.05), whereas the hippocampus showed synaptic suppression (GABA release reduced by 32.65%; sIPSC frequency reduced by 66.67%, P<0.05). Mechanistically, SCN2B overexpression suppressed BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/AKT signaling axis (BDNF reduced by 53.17%; p-TrkB reduced by 63.62%, P<0.05), accompanied by decreased synaptic proteins (PSD95 43.45%, synapsin I 40.31%, P<0.05). Remarkably, NICD-reduced Navβ2V173A,V175K mice were fully resistant to CUMS-induced behavioral and neurotransmitter deficits, establishing NICD as a critical mediator of stress vulnerability. Collectively, these findings unravel a causal pathway in which SCN2B overexpression drives NICD-dependent suppression of BDNF signaling, leading to region-specific excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, synaptic disintegration, and depression-like phenotypes. Targeting Navβ2 proteolysis to block NICD generation may thus represent a novel therapeutic strategy for mood disorders.

title: AI-Enhanced CRISPR-Cas9 Therapeutics: Advances in Precision, Safety, and Delivery.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has transformed biomedical research and is advancing toward clinical translation. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) offers improved precision in guide RNA design, off-target prediction, and delivery optimization. This review synthesizes recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9 for medical applications, covering core mechanisms, engineered variants, base and prime editors, and therapeutic applications including CAR T-cell and CAR-NK engineering, genetic disorders, infectious diseases, and regenerative medicine. Delivery strategies are evaluated with emphasis on AI-driven optimization. AI applications are highlighted across deep learning architectures for guide RNA design, AI-designed nucleases such as OpenCRISPR-1, structure-guided and AI-assisted design of compact high-fidelity SaCas9 variants, reinforcement learning for pipeline optimization, and roles in CAR T-cell therapy and safety assessment. Safety challenges are examined, including off-target effects, chromosomal rearrangements, immunogenicity, and regulatory concerns. Future directions emphasize multi-scale modeling, explainable AI, clinical validation, and integration with synthetic biology, single-cell sequencing, organoids, and nanomaterials. The convergence of AI and CRISPR-Cas9 holds substantial potential for personalized medicine.

title: Emerging strategies targeting the Hippo-YAP/TEAD pathway and the translational relevance in solid tumors.
abstract: The Hippo-YAP/TEAD signaling axis regulates tissue growth, cellular identity, and organ homeostasis. Dysregulation of this pathway, through NF2 loss, LATS1 or LATS2 inactivation, or YAP1- or WWTR1-derived gene fusions, results in persistent nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ, driving TEAD-dependent transcriptional programs. NF2-deficient and YAP1/TAZ-driven tumors, such as mesothelioma, schwannoma, meningioma, and epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, exemplify Hippo-pathway dependency and are potential therapeutic targets. Targeting TEAD disrupts transcriptional circuits sustaining tumor growth, plasticity, and immune suppression while modulating metabolic and stromal dependencies. Pharmacologic interventions targeting YAP/TEAD include TEAD palmitate-binding pocket inhibitors, direct YAP/TEAD protein-protein interaction disruptors, PROTAC-mediated TEAD degraders, and YAP-directed antisense oligonucleotide strategies. Early-phase trials have demonstrated preliminary clinical activity, particularly with TEAD palmitate-binding pocket inhibitors in mesothelioma and have been associated with mild drug-related toxicities, such as proteinuria. YAP/TEAD inhibition may also be a rational combinatorial approach given the emergence of adaptive resistance mechanisms to EGFR/KRAS inhibitors and immunotherapies. Collectively, these findings provide rationale and early proof-of-concept for the pharmacologic targeting of the YAP/TEAD pathway. In this review, we describe the biological underpinnings of the YAP/TEAD pathway in cancer medicine, the anti-cancer strategies targeting this pathway, and discuss future directions in the field.

title: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity switches: Molecular design, pharmacology, and therapeutic considerations.
abstract: Genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems are chemogenetic tools that utilize small molecules to regulate protein association, higher-order assembly, and dissociation. Over the past three decades, an expanding repertoire of these systems has transformed the study of protein function and cellular signaling by enabling rapid, reversible, and tunable manipulation of protein localization, assembly, activity, and downstream physiological processes. As these technologies advance from experimental tools toward therapeutic applications, their translational potential depends not only on molecular switch performance but also on the properties of the chemical inducer and engineered protein components. In this review, we summarize the major classes and design principles of representative genetically encoded chemically controlled proximity systems, with particular emphasis on the pharmacological determinants that define their therapeutic operating window, including pharmacodynamic orthogonality, pharmacokinetics, tissue exposure, endogenous target engagement, and clinical readiness. We also examine how the biological origin and engineering of the chemogenetic modules influence immunogenicity and long-term compatibility. We further discuss exemplary applications, including pharmacological control of CAR-T cell activity, programmed cell death, CRISPR-based genome and epigenome engineering, and on-demand secretion of therapeutic proteins. Finally, we consider the delivery and coordinated expression of chemically regulated protein components as major remaining barriers to therapeutic implementation and highlight clinically compatible inducers, compact and minimally immunogenic protein modules, de novo protein design, and advances in viral and nonviral delivery as promising directions toward more reliable and pharmacologically tractable chemically controlled therapies.

title: Title: Topoisomerase I Inhibition Serves as a Tumor Vaccine by Inducing the ERVs-dsRNA-Interferon Pathway.
abstract: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) can activate potent anti-tumor immunity, but its clinical translation remains challenging. We sought to identify clinically applicable strategies to induce endogenous dsRNA and enhance anti-tumor immune responses. Here, we integrated genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening data with the Therapeutic Target Database (TTD) and identified Topoisomerase I (TOP1) as a potential inducer of dsRNA. Mechanistically, we found that TOP1 was associated with suppression of endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) in an enzyme activity-dependent manner, and this was accompanied by "viral mimicry" through the induction of dsRNA. Pharmacological inhibition of TOP1 using Irinotecan (CPT-11) triggered dsRNA accumulation across cancer models, including patient-derived organoids (PDOs), activating the RIG-I/MDA5-MAVS pathway and antiviral interferon responses (Type I/III IFNs, ISGs). scRNA-seq revealed that CPT-11 remodeled the tumor microenvironment, promoting infiltration of dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and T cells. Combining CPT-11 with PD-1 blockade in "cold" tumors dramatically improved survival. CPT-11 also generated a potent in situ vaccine effect, establishing immunological memory that prevented tumor rechallenge. Moreover, tumor cells pretreated with CPT-11 in vitro were also able to exert a vaccine-like effect, inhibiting the growth of subsequently inoculated tumors. Collectively, our findings support the repurposing of TOP1 inhibitors such as CPT-11 to harness dsRNA-mediated immune activation for more effective cancer therapy.

title: A Transgenic Pig Model for human Metabolic Disorders Defines the relationship between the colon pathological phenotype of metabolic disease, the microbiota and the intestinal barrier.
abstract: Metabolic disorders are increasingly associated with intestinal dysfunction and colorectal diseases, yet the pathological characteristics and underlying mechanisms of intestinal injury under metabolic stress remain poorly understood. Here, we established a transgenic (TG) Bama pig model by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of three humanized susceptibility genes and subjected the pigs to a high-fat, high-sugar diet (HFHSD) for 4, 8, or 12 months to investigate metabolic disorder-associated colonic dysfunction. HFHSD intervention induced marked alterations in serum biochemical parameters and disrupted colonic mucosal architecture, characterized by glandular disorganization and crypt distortion. Colonic tissues from TG pigs exhibited reduced populations of goblet cells, CD8⁺ T cells, and CD79A⁺ B cells, accompanied by pronounced activation of mitophagy, indicating impaired epithelial barrier integrity and mucosal immune homeostasis. In parallel, microbial diversity and IgA levels were reduced in the colonic contents of TG pigs, accompanied by an increased abundance of potentially pathogenic bacteria, particularly Escherichia-Shigella. Metabolomic profiling of colonic contents further revealed significant alterations in the intestinal metabolic landscape, including decreased levels of isobutyric acid and isovaleric acid and an increased level of myristic acid, a metabolite associated with autophagy-related processes. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that metabolic disorders are associated with coordinated alterations in colonic mucosal integrity, mucosal immunity, mitochondrial quality control, gut microbiota, and intestinal metabolism. The humanized TG Bama pig model provides a clinically relevant large-animal platform for investigating the pathophysiology of metabolic disorder-associated colonic diseases and may facilitate the development and preclinical evaluation of therapeutic strategies targeting intestinal dysfunction.

title: Coupled RNA editing and splicing within plant chloroplasts by the MORFs-CFM2 interaction module.
abstract: RNA editing and splicing are two important post-transcriptional processing steps in plant chloroplasts. Evidence gathered in recent years indicates that these two steps are often tightly connected, although the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here, we elucidate that the splicing protein CFM2 is associated with the MORF2/MORF9 editors and is involved in editing-splicing coupling within plant chloroplasts. Using immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS) and in vitro/in vivo interaction assays, we identified the chloroplast splicing factor CFM2 as a direct physical interactor of the core editosome components MORF2 and MORF9. Disruption of CFM2 in Arabidopsis thaliana results in an albino-lethal phenotype, accompanied not only by impaired splicing of specific group II introns (e.g., ycf3.1, ndhA, and ndhB) but also by severe defects in RNA editing across multiple chloroplast sites, phenocopying morf2 and morf9 mutants. Conversely, mutations in the MORF genes analogously compromise splicing efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this mechanistic coupling is evolutionarily conserved between dicots and monocots, as loss of the rice homolog OsCFM2 drastically impairs site-specific editing. Together, our findings provide compelling evidence that, the MORF-CFM2 complex forms a physical association, coordinating the dual maturation of chloroplast transcripts to ensure photosynthetic function and plant viability.

title: mRNA chemical modifications in model and crop plants.
abstract: Post-transcriptional RNA modifications have emerged as a crucial layer of epigenetic regulation in eukaryotes, profoundly influencing mRNA processing, stability, and translational efficiency. As RNA modification research expands from mammalian systems to plants, its significance for crop improvement and environmental adaptation is becoming increasingly evident. This review synthesizes current research on the plant epitranscriptomic landscape-primarily focusing on N6-methyladenosine (m6A), alongside N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C), 5-methylcytosine (m5C), 1-methyladenosine (m1A), 7-methylguanosine (m7G), and pseudouridine (Ψ). By exploring the dynamic machinery of specific "writers," "erasers," and "readers," we highlight how these epitranscriptomic marks orchestrate plant growth, developmental phase transitions, and adaptive responses to abiotic stresses in model species and major crops. Rapid advances in detection methods, from conventional chromatography to third-generation single-molecule sequencing, have largely driven these biological insights. Although regulatory mechanisms and cross-species conservation of most modifications beyond m6A remain poorly understood, their translational potential is undeniable. Ultimately, we discuss how leveraging gene-editing technologies to manipulate these epitranscriptomic pathways offers a transformative strategy for molecular breeding, aiming to enhance crop yield, nutritional quality, and abiotic stress tolerance.

title: Beyond diagnostic categories: A narrative review of transdiagnostic mechanisms in neurodevelopmental disorders.
abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) represent a heterogeneous class of early-onset conditions marked by impairments in cognition, reduced social function, hyperactivity and repetitive-stereotyped behaviour. Traditionally classified as discrete clinical entities, NDDs such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disability (ID) are now increasingly understood as overlapping, multifactorial conditions shaped by converging genetic, epigenetic, immune, and environmental influences. This review synthesizes current evidence challenging categorical diagnostic boundaries and instead proposes a transdiagnostic and mechanistic framework that integrates shared disruptions in neural circuits, excitatory/inhibitory balance, synaptic architecture, and immune-metabolic signalling. We explore how genes and environment interact during early development, how epigenetics influences long-term outcomes, and how these insights are driving a shift toward precision medicine guided by biomarkers and patient-derived models. Emerging therapies include neuromodulation, immune and microbiota-based interventions, and gene editing, supported by insights from animal and iPSC models. A time-sensitive and biologically grounded approach is needed, moving beyond symptom-based classifications to allow for earlier diagnosis, personalized treatment, and the development of innovative interventions. This paradigm shift aligns with precision approaches already transforming other biomedical domains and holds the potential to more effectively address the complex and lifelong challenges posed by NDDs.

title: The OVCA1-A2BR-ROS axis drives gastric cancer aggressiveness and identifies an actionable precision target.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Gastric cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, underscoring the urgent need for novel therapeutic targets. Ovarian cancer gene 1 (OVCA1) has been implicated as a tumor suppressor in various malignancies; however, its clinical relevance and mechanistic role in gastric cancer progression remain poorly defined.
METHODS: We assessed OVCA1 expression in a large clinical cohort (n = 616) and performed prognostic analyses (n = 417). The functional consequences of OVCA1 knockdown, overexpression, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout were evaluated in gastric cancer cell lines. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic profiling, together with in vivo xenograft and peritoneal metastasis models, were utilized to elucidate the downstream molecular mechanisms. Furthermore, the therapeutic potential of the selective adenosine A2B receptor (A2BR) antagonist BAY-545 was tested both in vitro and in vivo.
RESULTS: Low OVCA1 expression was significantly associated with aggressive clinicopathological features and shorter patient survival. Functionally, OVCA1 loss promoted proliferation, invasion, and cell-cycle progression, whereas its overexpression reversed these phenotypes. Multi-omics integration linked OVCA1 deficiency to purine metabolism remodeling, marked by CD73/NT5E upregulation and selective elevation of the adenosine receptor A2BR. OVCA1-deficient tumors exhibited increased ROS accumulation and upregulation of MMP14 and VEGF. Notably, pharmacological A2BR inhibition with BAY-545 effectively mitigated the enhanced malignancy of OVCA1-knockout cells, suppressed ROS production, and significantly reduced tumor growth and peritoneal dissemination in vivo.
CONCLUSION: Our findings identify a novel OVCA1-A2BR-ROS axis contributing to gastric cancer aggressiveness. Given that A2BR blockade robustly reverses OVCA1-loss-associated phenotypes, this study supports A2BR as a potential actionable target and provides a preclinical rationale for its further evaluation in OVCA1-deficient gastric cancer.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated RNA delivery enables protein expression in chicken testes.
abstract: RNA-lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are emerging tools for poultry vaccination, but methods for local protein expression in reproductive tissues remain underdeveloped. Here, we established RNA delivery to chicken testes using LNPs formulated with the ionizable lipid DLin-MC3-DMA (MC3) and multifocal intratesticular injection through an intercostal surgical approach. Bilateral injections were completed in all six chickens in a surgical-feasibility cohort, with postoperative recovery during the 7-day observation period. At an equal RNA mass dose of 80 µg per testis, conventional messenger RNA (mRNA) encoding enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) produced detectable reporter signals at days 1, 3, and 7, with the highest measured signal at day 3. An eGFP self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) construct showed delayed detectable expression at days 3 and 7. Delivery of mRNAs encoding CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) and the epitope-tagged recombination-related proteins DNA meiotic recombinase 1 (DMC1) and RAD51 recombinase (RAD51) also produced detectable proteins in testicular tissue. Following local delivery, testicular architecture was preserved, with minimal apoptosis and only a modest inflammatory response. These findings establish the feasibility of local RNA-LNP delivery for short-term protein production in chicken testes, providing a platform for future studies of male reproduction and genome editing.

title: CTRP3 disruption promotes a tendon-like matrix signature in tenogenically induced canine adipose-derived stem cells.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tendon injuries heal through disorganized extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition rather than the restoration of native collagen architecture, thus resulting in suboptimal functional recovery. Although adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) are attractive for tendon regeneration because of their accessibility and expandability, their tenogenic differentiation efficiency is lower than that of tendon-derived stem cells (TDSCs). C1q/TNF-related protein 3 (CTRP3) is an adipokine implicated in ECM remodeling and fibrosis; however, its role in tendon lineage regulation is unknown.
OBJECTIVE: CTRP3 (C1q/TNF-related protein 3) contributes to extracellular-matrix remodeling and, in tendon, is associated with a pathological fibrotic matrix signature; we therefore reasoned that reducing CTRP3 would favor a more mature tendon-like matrix. Using a loss-of-function approach based on clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), we investigated whether CTRP3 disruption alters tenogenic marker expression, at both the transcript and protein levels, and the tendon-associated ECM marker profile of canine ADSCs relative to wild-type ADSCs and native TDSCs.
METHODS: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs were generated and validated using sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, and Western blotting. Wild-type ADSCs, CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs, and TDSCs were subjected to tenogenic induction for 0-3 weeks. Tenogenic transcriptional and ECM markers were analyzed at mRNA and protein levels.
RESULTS: CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs showed increased collagen type I and tenomodulin (TNMD) expression during tenogenic induction compared with wild-type ADSCs. COL III expression showed a transient increase followed by a decline, with lower expression in CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs than in WT cADSCs at week 2. CTRP3 disruption increased early Mkx and Scx expression at the earliest time points but did not consistently alter the early transcriptional program, which rose comparably across all groups. CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs showed partial, marker- and time-point-dependent overlap with native cTDSCs, mainly for selected late ECM markers rather than across the overall transcript and protein profiles.
CONCLUSION: CTRP3 disruption shifted the tendon-associated ECM marker profile during the tenogenic differentiation of ADSCs, with reduced COL III accumulation, rather than uniformly enhancing tenogenic differentiation. Although early transcriptional changes were observed, the more consistent differences were found in late tendon-associated ECM markers. The modulation of CTRP3 may represent a candidate strategy worth further investigation for stem cell-based tendon regeneration in veterinary medicine.

title: Autocatalytic split-crRNA Cas12a circuit coupled with phosphorothioate G-quadruplex fluorescence for ultrasensitive ctDNA analysis.
abstract: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as an important biomarker for early cancer diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring; however, the ultrasensitive detection of low-abundance single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) remains highly challenging. Herein, we developed an autocatalytic split-crRNA Cas12a fluorescence platform, termed AutoSCas, for highly sensitive detection of EGFR L858R mutant ctDNA. Upon recognition of trace EGFR L858R ctDNA, activated split-crRNA Cas12a (SCas12a) cleaved the loop region of a cascade hairpin probe, resulting in the release of functional spacer RNA (sRNA) molecules. The liberated sRNA further activated additional SCas12a complexes in the presence of assistant DNA, thereby establishing a positive-feedback autocatalytic nucleic acid circuit for exponential-like signal amplification. Simultaneously, a phosphorothioate-modified G-quadruplex hairpin probe was introduced as a low-background "signal-on" fluorescence reporter. Activated SCas12a continuously cleaved the loop region of the probe, releasing phosphorothioate-modified G-quadruplex that subsequently bound Thioflavin T to generate strong fluorescence signals. Benefiting from the synergistic integration of autocatalytic amplification and low-background signals, AutoSCas achieved ultrasensitive and highly specific ctDNA detection with a detection limit as low as 2 aM. Therefore, AutoSCas platform provides a pre-amplification-free strategy for highly sensitive SNV analysis and expands the design of split-crRNA-based CRISPR sensing systems.

title: Unlocking genetic accessibility in Halomonas bluephagenesis: A high-efficiency transformation chassis enables linear DNA-mediated genome editing.
abstract: Halomonas bluephagenesis has emerged as a promising chassis for industrial biotechnology distinguished by its halophilic robustness and capacity for open and continuous fermentation. However, its poor transformability has substantially limited rapid, iterative, and automatable strain engineering. Here, we develop a "restriction release" strategy that increases transformation efficiency from approximately 102 to 107 cfu/μg DNA, rivaling the efficiency of standard laboratory Escherichia coli. A spontaneous IS30 insertion disrupting the type II restriction endonuclease gene notI increased plasmid transformation efficiency by about 2000-fold. Targeted deletion of notI reproduced this phenotype, confirming its role as a major barrier. Further deletion of the DNA phosphorothioation restriction locus dptFGH yielded an additional 10 to 37-fold improvement, generating the highly transformable ΔEPSΔFlgΔNotIΔPTRes chassis. Notably, the enhanced chassis further facilitated two linear-DNA-based editing strategies: direct RecET-mediated pyrF deletion using a linear donor coupled with phenotypic selection, achieving a recombination efficiency of 16.7%, and CRISPR/Cas9-assisted ribDHBA promoter replacement via co-delivery of a gRNA plasmid and a linear donor, achieving an efficiency of 11.1%. Together, these results identify endogenous restriction systems as primary barriers to genetic manipulation in H. bluephagenesis. Stepwise restriction release markedly improves plasmid transformation and enables linear DNA-mediated genome editing, providing an improved genetic platform for the iterative engineering of this industrial halophile. More broadly, this study suggests a practical strategy for overcoming the genetic inaccessibility of other non-model microorganisms and accelerating iterative strain engineering.

title: A genetic engineering toolkit for the probiotic yeast Saccharomyces boulardii.
abstract: Saccharomyces boulardii (S. boulardii) is the only yeast probiotic widely used in clinical practice and consumer products. It combines gastrointestinal robustness, intrinsic antibiotic tolerance and eukaryotic protein-processing capacity, making it an attractive chassis for engineered probiotics, in situ biomanufacturing and live biotherapeutic delivery. However, host-specific characterization of regulatory elements, candidate genomic integration sites, and multicopy integration strategies remains limited in the clinically used S. boulardii CNCM I-745 background. Here, using S. boulardii CNCM I-745 as the host, we developed and characterized a genetic engineering toolkit that integrates transcriptional control elements with genome-integration strategies. We first quantified the activities of 20 endogenous constitutive promoters, two inducible promoters and six terminators. We then established a markerless CRISPR-Cas9 workflow and evaluated 10 chromosomal integration loci; six of which showed Editing efficiency above 80% while supporting comparable transgene expression without detectable growth penalties. Finally, we constructed an rDNA-repeat-based multicopy integration system that increased transgene expression by 9.8- to 22.6-fold relative to single-copy integration and revealed a significant positive but non-proportional association between estimated copy number and reporter output. Together, this toolkit provides S. boulardii with a set of tunable promoters and terminators, candidate chromosomal integration sites compatible with a markerless CRISPR-Cas9 workflow. These resources expand the genetic accessibility of this probiotic yeast and provide a foundation for developing engineered S. boulardii strains with enhanced probiotic, therapeutic and biomanufacturing functions.

title: Evaluation of the minipig as an alternative model based on cross-study comparisons with rabbit in mRNA vaccine safety assessment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Robust non-clinical safety models are crucial to the development and evaluation of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA)-based drugs and vaccines. In this study, we leveraged cross-study data to explore whether the Göttingen minipig could serve as an alternative to the rabbit, a commonly used species in vaccine safety assessment.
METHODS: Results from two independent toxicity studies of lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA encoding the hemagglutinin H3 antigen, administered at equivalent dose levels, were qualitatively compared. Clinical observations, local reactions, body weight, food consumption, body temperature, clinical pathology, immunogenicity, inflammatory biomarkers, and anatomical pathology endpoints were evaluated.
RESULTS: Both species exhibited expected vaccine responses, with minor differences in local reactogenicity and body temperature. The vaccine candidate was well tolerated at the injection site in both species. However, mild and transient vaccine-related effects (i.e., injection site induration and increased body temperature) were observed only in minipigs. Transient increases in neutrophil, fibrinogen, and C-reactive protein levels were observed in both species following vaccination, consistent with an inflammatory response. Microscopic findings (i.e., inflammation at the injection site and increased germinal center cellularity in the draining lymph nodes) were comparable between species and aligned with expected immune activation following vaccination.
CONCLUSIONS: This qualitative comparison provides preliminary, supportive evidence for the potential use of the minipig as an alternative to the rabbit in non-clinical safety evaluation of mRNA vaccines, with the added benefit of larger blood volume for sampling and availability of validated key inflammatory markers.

title: A multipathogen view of Epstein-Barr virus pathogenesis and tumorigenesis.
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects more than 95% of the global population and contributes to multiple human cancers and autoimmune diseases. Co-infection with pathogens including Helicobacter pylori, human immunodeficiency virus, human papillomavirus, and Plasmodium falciparum can reshape host immunity and the EBV latency-lytic balance and, in some settings, promote reactivation. Collectively, these interactions may exacerbate chronic inflammation, immunosuppression, and epigenetic dysregulation to accelerate disease progression and tumor formation. Existing clinical treatments control only the active pathogens but fail to target latent EBV. Emerging strategies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) gene editing and EBV-targeted immunotherapy aim to eliminate latent viral reservoirs. This review outlines the synergistic mechanisms of EBV co-infection in oncogenesis, highlighting that further research on pathogen interactions is vital for developing better prevention and treatment options.

title: MANF promotes cell fitness and attenuates bortezomib sensitivity in multiple myeloma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a clonal plasma cell malignancy in which disease relapse and treatment resistance remain major clinical challenges. Identifying molecular dependencies that support myeloma cell fitness may reveal therapeutic vulnerabilities beyond recurrent genomic alterations. Mesencephalic astrocyte-derived neurotrophic factor (MANF) is an endoplasmic reticulum-resident, stress-responsive protein, but its clinical and biological significance in MM remains poorly defined.
METHODS: Publicly available DepMap CRISPR dependency data were analyzed to identify candidate MM-preferential dependencies. MANF expression and prognostic associations were examined in the MMRF CoMMpass cohort. Single-cell RNA sequencing and in silico perturbation analyses characterized its cellular distribution and predicted functional associations. MANF knockdown and genetic rescue using an siRNA-resistant MANF construct were performed in RPMI-8226 and OPM-2 cells to assess proliferation, cell-cycle distribution, and bortezomib sensitivity. Transcriptomic profiling characterized gene expression changes following MANF knockdown, while measurements at multiple time points assessed the temporal patterns of IRE1α-XBP1s-associated readouts.
RESULTS: MANF was identified as a candidate MM-preferential dependency. Higher MANF expression was associated with advanced ISS stage and inferior overall survival, with the survival association retained after adjustment for established clinical and cytogenetic risk factors. Single-cell analysis localized MANF expression predominantly to plasma cells, while virtual knockout predicted changes involving ER protein processing, proteasome function, and metabolism. MANF knockdown inhibited proliferation, increased G0/G1 accumulation, and reduced MYC/E2F-associated transcriptional programs and cell-cycle regulatory proteins. Time-course analyses revealed early enhancement followed by later attenuation in selected IRE1α-XBP1s-associated readouts. MANF knockdown also increased bortezomib-induced apoptosis and reduced its IC₅₀. MANF re-expression partially reversed proliferation and cell-cycle phenotypes, restored IRE1α-XBP1s-associated protein abundance, and attenuated bortezomib sensitization.
CONCLUSION: These findings identify MANF as a previously underexplored candidate myeloma-associated dependency that supports proliferative fitness and modulates bortezomib sensitivity in the tested MM models. MANF depletion is associated with dynamic changes in IRE1α-XBP1s-related readouts. These results support further investigation of MANF as a candidate therapeutic vulnerability in MM.

title: mRNA-LNPs encoding Ornithodoros moubata antigens induces humoral and cellular immune responses and tick resistance in rabbits.
abstract: Ornithodoros moubata and Ornithodoros erraticus are important vectors of African swine fever virus and relapsing fever Borrelia spp., highlighting the need for effective and sustainable control strategies. In this study, six previously identified O. moubata vaccine candidates, including salivary and/or midgut antigens cyclophilin (OmCPH), peroxiredoxin (OmPXR), hypothetical protein 275 (OmH275), aquaporin 23 (OmAQP23), subolesin (OmSUB) and Om85, were evaluated as messenger RNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccines. Rabbits received three intradermal immunisations with individual mRNA-LNP formulations, and humoral, cellular, and protective immune responses were assessed. All mRNA-LNP constructs induced antigen-specific IgM and IgG responses and generated antibodies capable of recognising native proteins in tick salivary glands and/or midgut tissues. Antigen stimulation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells revealed antigen-specific cellular responses characterised by increased expression of IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-8, CXCL10, IL-2, and IL-4, although the extent of these responses varied among antigens. OmCPH induced the strongest IL-8 response, OmSUB markedly increased CXCL10, IL-2 and IL-4 expression, and OmH275 elicited consistent IFN-γ and TNF-α responses. Vaccination adversely affected tick feeding, reproduction, development, and survival, with the most pronounced effects observed on female oviposition and fertility. Vaccine efficacies against O. moubata reached 19.8% (OmCPH), 3.7% (OmPXR), 25.6% (OmH275), 10.1% (OmAQP23), 25.2% (OmSUB), and 38.5% (Om85), while efficacies against O. erraticus reached 0%, 26.5%, 6.2%, 11.7%, 10.6%, and 18.5%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that mRNA-LNP vaccination induces both humoral and cellular immune responses against Ornithodoros antigens and provides measurable protection against tick infestations, supporting the application of mRNA technology for the development of multivalent anti-tick vaccines.

title: Establishment of a RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a system-based nucleic acid detection method for avian reticuloendotheliosis virus.
abstract: Reticuloendotheliosis virus (REV) is an immunosuppressive and oncogenic pathogen that causes substantial economic losses in poultry production. In the absence of commercial vaccines and specific therapeutic agents against REV, early and accurate detection is essential for REV control and eradication. In this study, a visual RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay was established for REV detection based on a conserved 552-bp region of the pol gene. RAA primers and crRNA were screened, and the reaction conditions were systematically optimized. The assay was completed at 37 °C with 20min of RAA amplification and 40min of Cas12a reaction, and results were read visually under blue/UV light. The limit of detection was 10 copies/μL. The assay showed no cross-reactivity with other common avian pathogens and exhibited good repeatability. When 90 clinical samples were tested, the RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay detected 50 positive samples (55.55%), whereas qPCR detected 43 positive samples (47.77%). The overall agreement was 85.56% (77/90), with a positive agreement of 93.02% (40/43), a negative agreement of 78.72% (37/47), and a Cohen's kappa of 0.713. These results indicate that the RAA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay is a rapid, specific, and visual method for REV detection and provides a complementary tool for REV screening, although further validation with live birds and other sample types is required.

title: mRNA encoding norovirus VP1 produces antigenically functional virus-like particles in vitro.
abstract: Human norovirus is a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis worldwide across all age groups, yet no licensed vaccine is available. The major capsid protein, VP1, self-assembles into highly immunogenic virus-like particles (VLPs) that have shown promise in clinical studies. Recently, mRNA has emerged as a compelling platform for norovirus vaccination. However, whether VP1-encoding mRNA can drive authentic VLP formation in human cells relevant to the vaccination environment has remained unknown. In this study, we used multiple human cell lines, including THP-1-derived macrophage-like cells, to model the post-vaccination environment. Transfection with norovirus GII.4 VP1 mRNA or lipid nanoparticle-formulated VP1 mRNA induced both intracellular and extracellular VP1 expression. Sucrose gradient purification and electron microscopy confirmed VLP assembly. These particles retained key antigenic and functional properties, including recognition by norovirus-specific antibodies in human serum and binding to histo-blood group antigens. Collectively, our findings provide direct evidence that VP1-encoding mRNA can generate structurally and functionally relevant norovirus VLPs in physiologically relevant human cell systems. These results strengthen the mechanistic rationale for mRNA-based norovirus vaccines and support their continued development.

title: mRNA-LNP vaccines targeting mutation-derived BRCA2 and p53 elicit antigen-specific immune responses in beagles.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines are next-generation platforms capable of eliciting potent cellular and humoral immunity through intracellular expression of tumor-associated or mutation-specific antigens. Canine mammary gland tumor (CMT), commonly encountered in female dogs, frequently harbors mutations in the BRCA2 and p53 genes, which are also relevant to human breast cancers. We aimed to design mutation-targeted mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines encoding canine BRCA2 and p53 variants using in silico epitope prediction and evaluate their immunogenicity and safety. Three mRNA constructs encoding BRCA2 and p53 mutations were synthesized and encapsulated in ionizable-lipid-based LNPs. The resulting mRNA-LNP formulations, namely canine BRCA2-10204ins candidates (cBR2-Cand), canine BRCA2-p53 28-mer epitopes (cBR2-p53), and canine BRCA2-partial (cBR2-Part), were then admixed to prepare the cBR2-cocktail, a mixed mRNA-LNP vaccine designed to enhance mutation-specific immune responses. In vitro expression was confirmed in HeLa cells. In vivo immunization in mice induced strong interferon (IFN)-γ secretion, particularly against BRCA2 H143R, K801R, and T1425P mutations. Beagles immunized with cBR2-cocktail mRNA-LNPs exhibited increased IFN-γ production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells after repeated dosing, without significant hematological or biochemical abnormalities. Mutation-derived mRNA-LNP vaccines safely induced mutation-specific T-cell responses in vivo. Although anticancer efficacy was not assessed, we established a preclinical foundation for developing mutation-targeted mRNA immunotherapies for CMT and underscored the translational relevance of the canine model for human BRCA2/p53-related cancers.

title: A Virus-like particle system based on parainfluenza virus PIV5-L for CRISPR-Cas9 and RNAi delivery.
abstract: Nucleic acid-targeting technologies based on CRISPR-Cas or small-hairpin RNA (shRNA) are essential for functional genomics and therapeutic development, yet a delivery platform that simultaneously ensures high efficiency, safety, modularity, and broad cell compatibility remains lacking. Here, we report L-VLP, a virus-like particle platform derived from a B-lymphoma-isolated strain of parainfluenza virus PIV5-L. This single-cycle, replication-deficient VLP functions as a dual-mode delivery system, capable of carrying either Cas9/sgRNA for CRISPR-mediated gene editing or shRNA for RNA interference, and achieves effective target gene knockdown or knockout in both breast cancer and B-lymphoma cells. Notably, the sgRNA or shRNA cassettes in L-VLP can be readily exchanged for any sequence of interest without altering the core vector architecture, providing a modular and versatile design. Functional assays confirm that L-VLP-mediated UBR5 silencing significantly inhibits tumor cell growth in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, our work establishes L-VLP as a flexible and efficient platform for manipulating gene expression, with promising applications in both basic research and cancer target therapeutics.

title: An ESCRT-engineered mRNA-VLP vaccine elicits humoral and cellular immunity against Lassa virus.
abstract: Lassa virus (LASV) causes severe hemorrhagic fever across West Africa, yet no licensed vaccine is available. A major barrier to LASV antigen design is that its sole neutralization target, the glycoprotein complex (GPC), lacks intrinsic late-domain motifs required to engage the host ESCRT machinery for particle release. Here, we report a rational design strategy that confers autonomous budding capacity to LASV GPC by appending a synthetic ESCRT-recruitment cassette to its cytoplasmic domain. Systematic screening of a sixteen-construct matrix identified a lead candidate, VLPdEm5. This construct integrates the ESCRT cassette, an optimized furin cleavage site, and a heterologous H1N1 transmembrane-cytoplasmic domain to support efficient particle assembly and proper display of conformational neutralizing epitopes. Delivered via lipid-nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA (mRNA-LNP), VLPdEm5 drives efficient in situ virus-like particle (VLP) self-assembly, eliciting rapid, high-titer binding antibodies with broad cross-reactivity across six major LASV lineages, robust germinal center B-cell activity, and memory T-cell responses. Crucially, VLPdEm5 mRNA-LNP provides dose-dependent protection against pseudovirus challenge in vivo. This work establishes an effective LASV vaccine candidate and validates an ESCRT-engineered mRNA-VLP platform broadly applicable to non-budding viral envelope proteins.

title: Protocol for engineering primary human and mouse T cells using peptide-assisted genome editing.
abstract: Efficient engineering of human and murine primary T cells without perturbation of cellular function is crucial for immunotherapy and immunology research. Here, we present a protocol for genome editing of primary T cells with minimal toxicity using peptide-assisted genome editing. We describe key steps required for primary T cell isolation and activation, CRISPR ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assembly and delivery mediated by peptide, and assessment of editing efficiency. This protocol maintains T cell proliferative capacity and functional potency. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Zhang et al.1.

title: CRISPR-based pipeline for generating and validating multi-kb deletions and indels in iPSCs.
abstract: Here, we present a CRISPR-Cas9 protocol for generating both small indels and multi-kilobase deletions to enable genome editing in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We describe steps for a ribonucleoprotein (RNP)-based approach that integrates guide RNA selection, electroporation, and multi-tiered screening to accurately identify indels, deletions, inversions, and mixed genotypes. Human iPSCs provide a versatile genome editing platform due to their capacity for clonal expansion and differentiation. This protocol provides a scalable framework for genome editing and quality control. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Hamerlinck et al.1.

title: Protocol for cell-type-specific manipulation of histone acetylation in developing mouse cortex using CRISPR-based epigenome editing.
abstract: Epigenetic regulation controls transcriptional programs that govern cortical neurogenesis. Here, we present a protocol for locus-specific manipulation of histone acetylation using a CRISPR-dCas9-Kat2a epigenome-editing system. As an example, we describe the design and validation of single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs), assembly of a Cre-dependent all-in-one CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) vector, validation of promoter-specific H3K9 acetylation in Neuro2A cells, and targeted delivery of epigenome-editing constructs into the embryonic mouse cortex by in utero electroporation (IUE). For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Sokpor et al.1 and Kerimoglu et al.2.

title: Protocol for generation, immunophenotyping, and live-cell cytotoxicity analysis of primary human CAR-NK cells using CRISPR-SaCas9 and AAV6.
abstract: Targeted gene editing enables controlled integration and consistent expression of a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) in natural killer (NK) cells. We present a protocol for homology-directed repair-mediated CAR knockin into the AAVS1 safe-harbor locus of expanded human NK cells using CRISPR-SaCas9 ribonucleoprotein electroporation and AAV6 donor-template delivery. We also detail the phenotypic analysis of CAR-NK cells using a 23-marker flow cytometry panel including CAR detection and describe a live-cell imaging assay to evaluate CAR-mediated and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity kinetics.

title: Endothelial small extracellular vesicle-derived lncDLX1 facilitates bone repair by recruiting RBMX to activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
abstract: Interface integration failure after implanting bone repair material is a core challenge in treating bone defects. This study aimed to investigate the molecular mechanism by which endothelial cell-derived small extracellular vesicles (EC-sEVs) deliver lncRNA DLX1 (lncDLX1) to regulate the osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs through both in vitro and in vivo experiments. The results showed that lncDLX1 expression was significantly downregulated in an inflammatory microenvironment and that overexpression of lncDLX1 promoted BMSC osteogenic differentiation while inhibiting inflammatory responses. Mechanistic studies revealed that lncDLX1 binds to RBMX, which then transcriptionally activates β-catenin expression and enhances its mRNA stability by binding to the CTNNB1 promoter region, thereby activating the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. Functional experiments confirmed that EC-sEVscould be effectively taken up by BMSCs and functionally deliver lncDLX1, and GW4869 treatment attenuated this regulatory effect, supporting the involvement of sEVs. In vivo experiments showed that hydroxyapatite materials loaded with lncDLX1-overexpressing BMSCs significantly promoted bone repair in a rat femoral defect model. In summary, this study reveals the central role of the EC-sEVs/lncDLX1/RBMX/Wnt/β-catenin signaling axis in bone repair, providing a new theoretical basis for the development of sEV-based lncRNA bone repair strategies.

title: Comparative mitogenomics of Hippophae reveals conserved gene content, repeat-mediated structural variation, and limited phylogenetic resolution.
abstract: Plant mitochondrial genomes retain conserved coding content but evolve rapidly in structure. We assembled mitogenomes of four Hippophae taxa from long reads and compared them with four published mitogenomes. Gene content and codon usage were largely conserved, whereas the assemblies of closely related taxa differed by up to four inversions and two translocations. Long reads spanning repeats of 1.3-9.6 kb supported both assembled and recombinant arrangements, and allowing for repeat-mediated isomers removed all inversions among the seven records compared. RNA-seq identified 80-262 candidate editing sites per taxon, and mitogenome-plastome homologous fragments made up 12.54-12.77% of each assembly. A 31-gene phylogeny supported Hippophae monophyly but weakly resolved relationships within the genus (16 parsimony-informative sites). Only nad4 showed a Hippophae-specific increase in ω; its fixed C-to-T substitutions and intron loss point to retroprocessing rather than positive selection. Most structural differences among Hippophae mitogenomes can be explained by repeat-mediated isomerization.

title: A DNA-free CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein electroporation protocol for efficient knockout generation in cardiac and skeletal muscle cell lines.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Efficient, reproducible gene knockout in cardiomyocyte-related cell models is critical for cardiovascular research but remains challenging because of cell-type-specific sensitivity to genome-editing workflows.
METHODS: We developed an optimized CRISPR-Cas9 genome-editing protocol using electroporation of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes to generate knockout lines in cardiac and skeletal muscle cells. We also provide practical guidance for gRNA design, genotyping, and clonal line generation. Using human AC16 cardiomyocyte-like cells and rodent muscle-derived cell lines (C2C12, L6, and H9C2), we optimized electroporation conditions to maximize editing efficiency while maintaining viability.
RESULTS: SpCas9-single-guide RNA (sgRNA) RNPs targeting the lipid-trafficking regulator SAR1B/Sar1b produced high-frequency frameshift indels and marked loss of target protein expression in all models. A composite knockout score that combines editing efficiency and cell survival identified optimal electroporation settings of 1400 V, 10 ms, and 3 pulses for AC16 cells, and 1500 V, 10 ms, and 3 pulses for C2C12, L6, and H9C2 cells.
CONCLUSIONS: This protocol combines rational sgRNA design, chemically modified sgRNAs for efficient RNP assembly, and standardized genotyping to improve reproducibility. The framework is transferable to other cardiomyocyte and muscle-derived cell types and supports both pthe olyclonal and monoclonal CRISPR-Cas9 knockout approaches.

title: Development of an Efficient and Precise TadA-based C-to-G Base Editor Mi-zCGBE.
abstract: C-to-G base editors (CGBEs) offer the potential to correct 11% of pathogenic single-nucleotide variants. While APOBEC-based CGBEs are highly efficient, they are limited by high indel rates and off-target activity. In contrast, TadA-based CGBEs offer greater precision but currently suffer from suboptimal editing efficiency. In this study, we first developed zCGBE, a TadA-based variant that achieves editing efficiency comparable to APOBEC-based editors while maintaining low Cas-independent off-target activity. To further reduce residual on-target indels, we engineered mi-zCGBE by fusing Brex27, a 36-amino-acid-long RAD51-recruiting peptide, to zCGBE. Mi-zCGBE preserves high C-to-G editing capacity and low Cas9-independent off-target activity while significantly reducing both on-target indels and guide-RNA-dependent off-target effects. We demonstrated the potential utility of mi-zCGBE by correcting the CFTR-N1303K mutation in Cystic Fibrosis patient-derived bronchial epithelial cells, achieving high rates of base correction and minimal indels or off-target edits, leading to restored CFTR protein expression and functional chloride channel activity. These results establish mi-zCGBE as an efficient and precise tool for gene editing research and future therapeutic applications.

title: Mosaic Hemagglutinin-Based Influenza B mRNA-LNP Vaccine Induces Strong Humoral Immune Response in Non-Human Primates.
abstract: Developing broadly protective influenza vaccines remains a major challenge for global public health. Influenza B viruses cause about one-third of all annual influenza virus infections and current vaccines only show moderate effectiveness against matched virus strains, therefore, development of more effective and broadly protective vaccines against them is important. Chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinin (cHA and mHA) immunogens are under investigation as broadly protective influenza B vaccine candidates. The lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated nucleoside-modified mRNA technology has recently revolutionized vaccination and gained widespread interest due to its successful use in the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. Here, we evaluated influenza B cHA and mHA mRNA-LNP vaccines in non-human primates and compared their immunogenicity to a quadrivalent seasonal influenza virus vaccine. mHA mRNA-LNPs induced high binding antibody titers against antigenically distant influenza B virus strains, with significant hemagglutination inhibition and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity activity and provided protection in mice in a serum transfer challenge experiment. This approach shows great promise for developing broadly protective influenza B vaccines.

title: FLT3 Kinase Inhibition Reshapes the Neuronal Transcriptome to Suppress Seizures.
abstract: Approximately one-third of individuals with epilepsy are refractory to current anti-seizure medications, highlighting the need for new, mechanism-based therapeutic approaches. Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3), a receptor tyrosine kinase classically studied in hematopoiesis and leukemia, is also expressed in neurons, although its function in the brain remains largely unexplored. Our prior work identified small-molecule FLT3 inhibitors (FLT3i) as unexpected enhancers of potassium-chloride cotransporter 2 (KCC2), a neuron-specific chloride transporter essential for maintaining GABAergic inhibition. Here, we applied a functional genomics framework in mouse primary neurons and human stem cell-derived neurons to define FLT3i-induced transcriptional programs, revealing conserved gene networks governing synaptic function and ion channel regulation. A complementary CRISPR/Cas9-based screen of candidate transcription factors identified FLT3-responsive neuronal gene regulatory networks linked to epigenetic remodeling and neuroinflammatory signaling. We further demonstrate that KW-2449, an orally bioavailable FLT3 inhibitor, penetrates the blood-brain barrier, elevates KCC2 expression in vivo for up to 24 hours, and significantly reduces seizure susceptibility in a kainic acid-induced mouse model of epilepsy. Together, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for FLT3 in neuronal function and establish proof-of-principle for FLT3 inhibition as a mechanistically supported candidate strategy warranting further development as a next-generation anti-seizure therapy.

title: SOLO-CD47: an all-in-one AAV strategy for localized CRISPR-Cas12f-mediated CD47 editing in cancer immunotherapy.
abstract: Localized CRISPR-mediated CD47 ablation represents a potential alternative to systemic antibody-based therapy, with the possibility of reducing systemic toxicity associated with CD47 targeting. However, clinical translation is constrained by the limited cargo capacity of AAV vectors, which precludes packaging conventional Cas9/Cas12a systems into a single AAV vector. Here, we evaluated and optimized existing hypercompact CRISPR-Cas12f systems for efficient CD47 disruption and localized single-AAV delivery. Through systematic benchmarking, we identified AsCas12f-HKRA as a suitable editor for mouse Cd47 editing, achieving >60% editing efficiency comparable to enAsCas12a-HF while maintaining a favorable specificity profile. CD47 ablation enhanced macrophage phagocytosis in vitro and suppressed tumor growth in vivo. We then developed SOLO-CD47 (Single-AAV Optimized for Localized On-target-editing of CD47), an all-in-one AAV strategy incorporating a tandem dual-sgRNA expression cassette to overcome limited sgRNA expression from a single cassette. Intratumoral delivery of SOLO-CD47 suppressed tumor growth without detectable short-term hematologic abnormalities, and immune profiling revealed increased frequencies of F4/80+ CD86+ macrophage-associated cells and CD8+ T cells in SOLO-mCD47-treated tumors. The human-targeting strategy of SOLO-CD47 also achieved >60% CD47 editing across multiple human cancer cell lines. Collectively, these findings provide proof-of-concept for localized CRISPR-Cas12f-mediated CD47 editing using a single-AAV strategy in cancer immunotherapy.

title: A Two-Step Strategy Based on Fpg Recognition and RCA-CRISPR/Cas12a for Ultrasensitive Detection of Gene Mutation.
abstract: Accurate detection of gene mutations is crucial for acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) diagnosis and treatment. Although CRISPR/Cas systems enable sensitive mutation detection, their adaptability is constrained by dependence on restriction endonucleases. Herein, we propose a two-step strategy, termed Fpg-RCA-CRISPR/Cas12a for ultrasensitive detection of the p53 R175H, which integrates formamidopyrimidine DNA glycosylase (Fpg)-mediated recognition with rolling circle amplification (RCA)-coupled CRISPR/Cas12a technology. Validation confirmed that Fpg exhibits minimal activity when adenine (A) is opposite the damaged site. Based on this finding, we designed a padlock probe with a site-specific 8-oxoguanine (8-oxoG) modification. This modification enables selective recognition of G > A mutations. For the target TP53 c.524G > A (p53 R175H), the G > A substitution opposite the 8-oxoG site blocks Fpg cleavage, facilitating probe circularization and subsequent RCA. The resulting RCA products then activate the trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a, enabling cascade signal amplification and generating a strong fluorescence output. For wild-type p53, Fpg-mediated cleavage prevents circularization and amplification, yielding weak fluorescence. Taking advantage of the high specificity of the Fpg enzyme and the cascade amplification effect of the RCA-CRISPR/Cas12a system, this method achieves a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.29 fM and covers a linear range from 0.8 fM to 800 pM, along with high reproducibility, excellent selectivity, and negligible background interference. Notably, the assay can detect mutation frequencies as low as 0.1% in excess wild-type p53. Crucially, its clinical feasibility was confirmed by analyzing human serum samples, yielding results consistent with standard assays and thus demonstrating its practical reliability and translational potential.

title: An Integrating Sphere Based Method for Quantifying RNA Encapsulation Efficiency in Lipid Nanoparticles without Lysis.
abstract: Encapsulation efficiency (EE) is a critical quality attribute of lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-RNA formulations, determining the fraction of active RNA payload available for delivery and influencing therapeutic potency, dose accuracy, and product consistency. Conventional fluorescence-based EE assays, such as RiboGreen (RG), require detergent-mediated LNP lysis, which can introduce systematic bias arising from incomplete particle disruption and additional sample handling steps. Here, we report a lysis-free method for direct EE determination using Scatter-Free Absorption Spectroscopy (SFAS) within an integrating sphere. In this approach, RG fluorescence appears as a quantitative negative absorbance feature in the SFAS spectrum, enabling direct quantification of free RNA from intact LNP suspensions in a single measurement. Applied to SM-102 LNPs loaded with polyA or mRNA in PBS or Tris/sucrose buffers, the method yielded EE in close agreement with conventional plate-reader measurements. This approach provides a practical, formulation-independent, and potentially more robust strategy for standardized routine EE analysis and LNP quality-control workflows.

title: Modular Cell-Surface-to-Solution CRISPR-Cas12a Platform for Wash-Free Quantification of Cell-Surface Proteins on Living Cells.
abstract: Cell-surface proteins are important biomarkers for cell phenotyping, disease diagnosis, therapeutic evaluation, and drug screening. However, their quantitative analysis on intact living cells remains challenging because conventional methods often require cell lysis, fixation, repeated washing, extensive sample processing, or bulky instrumentation. Herein, we developed a modular and reconfigurable cell-surface-to-solution CRISPR-Cas12a platform for wash-free quantitative analysis of cell-surface proteins on intact living cells. Aptamer recognition of extracellularly accessible targets deblocks a DNA activator, thereby activating Cas12a trans-cleavage in solution and converting localized cell-surface recognition into amplified fluorescence while maintaining a low background in the absence of targets. Using EpCAM as a model target, we engineered a split dual-aptamer architecture that enabled cooperative target recognition, efficient activator deblocking, and low-background signal amplification. The platform achieved sensitive EpCAM detection with a limit of detection of 32 fM and enabled live-cell analysis down to 2 cells/μL. It distinguished cell populations with different surface EpCAM levels and quantitatively monitored epithelial-mesenchymal transition-associated changes in cell-surface EpCAM abundance. Coordinated redesign of the target-responsive nucleic acid components extended the platform to PTK7 detection and the analysis of drug-induced cell-surface PTK7 remodeling. Coupling the system to a lateral flow readout enabled portable visual detection. This work establishes a modular and reconfigurable CRISPR-Cas12a sensing strategy for wash-free amplified quantification of cell-surface proteins on living cells, providing a convenient tool for investigating their dynamic remodeling during physiological and pathological processes and therapeutic responses, as well as for drug screening.

title: Synthesis and Characterization of Aminooxy Click Chemistry-Mediated Bis-Conjugates of siRNAs and Evaluation of Their RNAi Activity.
abstract: Previously, we used an aminooxy click chemistry (AOCC) strategy to introduce pairs of ligands into oligonucleotides during solid-phase synthesis by using nucleoside and non-nucleoside building blocks. However, the standard oligonucleotide synthesis conditions were incompatible with the incorporation of certain complex ligands. In this report, first, a post-oligonucleotide synthesis solution-phase AOCC approach was developed to address this issue. Different pairs of ligands were conjugated to oligonucleotides through an O-amino building block incorporated during the solid-phase synthesis. Second, a small interfering RNA with a sense strand conjugated using the AOCC strategy to target the ApoB gene using a receptor-targeting ligand (GalNAc) and a pharmacokinetic enhancer (C16 alkyl) was evaluated in mice. The bis-heteroconjugate had a longer duration of action and higher level of silencing than the siRNA carrying only the receptor-targeting ligand.

title: Modular Peptide Coatings Regulate the Multistep Biological Performance of Lipid Nanoparticles for Enhanced mRNA Delivery.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading platform for mRNA delivery, yet improving their performance often requires complex chemical modification or reformulation of core components. Here, we report a modular peptide-coating strategy for post-formulation engineering of LNP interfaces through physical assembly. A modular multifunctional peptide (MFP) library was developed to systematically investigate how peptide composition, secondary structure, chirality, and concentration regulate coating assembly and delivery performance. In vitro, MFP coatings enhanced cellular uptake, endosomal escape, and mRNA translation. In vivo, optimized coatings improved mRNA delivery across multiple LNP formulations and promoted receptor-mediated tumor-specific accumulation and expression. In an IL-12 mRNA immunotherapy model, MFP-coated LNPs elicited potent antitumor immune responses and inhibited tumor growth without observable systemic toxicity. This work establishes a modular peptide surface engineering strategy for regulating LNP biological performance and provides an expandable framework for developing a tissue- and disease-specific nanomedicine platform through the tailoring of peptide functional modules.
