title: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Palindromic Repeats-Cas Genome-Editing Systems in Filamentous Fungi: Current Tools, Optimization Strategies, and Future Perspectives.
abstract: Filamentous fungi are important microbial cell factories for producing antibiotics, organic acids, enzymes, and other valuable products, with broad applications in food, agriculture, and medicine. However, inefficient and imprecise genome editing remains a major bottleneck limiting rational strain engineering. This review summarizes major genome-editing tools in filamentous fungi, including Cre-loxP, TALENs, and CRISPR-Cas systems, with emphasis on their mechanisms, advantages, and limitations. We highlight CRISPR-Cas9 as the predominant platform and discuss optimization strategies involving sgRNA design, engineered Cas9 variants, promoter engineering, AMA1-based replicative plasmids, and ribonucleoprotein delivery. Emerging technologies, including base editing, prime editing, Cas12a, and Mad7, are also discussed for their potential to broaden editing capabilities. Finally, we outline future perspectives focusing on extending the application of existing genome-editing systems in filamentous fungi and discovering novel genome-editing tools from large-scale omics data sets. This review will accelerate the development of filamentous fungi as versatile platforms for biomanufacturing.

title: Insights into Composition-Induced Structural Shifts in Lipid Nanoparticles.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading platform for nucleic acid delivery, yet current formulations typically suffer from rapid in vivo clearance and limited extrahepatic delivery. Recent experiments demonstrate that increasing the helper lipid content (e.g., to 40% 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine [DSPC]) can significantly improve mRNA stability, prolong circulation, and enhance transfection efficiency. In this study, we used coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to provide mechanistic insight into the structural changes driving these improvements. Our simulations confirm that an elevated helper lipid content fundamentally alters the internal morphology of the LNP. Consistent with experimental observations, at high DSPC levels, the core transitions from a compact, disordered, predominantly lipid state to an extended structure with distinct lamellar-like elements encompassing lipid-rich and water-rich regions. This structural reorganization can be used to rationalize the enhanced stability and delivery properties reported in the experiments. These findings provide a molecular-level understanding of the composition-morphology relationship and suggest that coarse-grained modeling can inform the design of novel LNP formulations.

title: Recent Advances in Peptide-Oligonucleotide Conjugates for Enhanced Therapeutic Efficacy.
abstract: Oligonucleotide therapeutics have emerged as next-generation therapeutics. However, targeted delivery of oligonucleotides to extrahepatic tissues, such as skeletal and cardiac muscles and the central nervous system, at efficacious yet well-tolerated doses remain a major challenge for their clinical translation. Although antibody-oligonucleotide conjugates are promising for the treatment of genetic disorders, inadequate tissue penetration and immunogenicity have constrained their therapeutic efficacy. By combining the advantages of cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) or cell-targeting peptides (CTPs) with those of oligonucleotides, peptide-oligonucleotide conjugates (POCs) display enhanced cellular uptake, endosomal escape, and extrahepatic delivery. The therapeutic efficacy of POC was increased through conjugation with CPPs, endosomal-escape peptides (EEPs), fusogenic peptides, nuclear localization signal peptides, or CTPs. In this perspective, innovative molecular designs such as multivalent, cyclic, and chimeric peptides, and combinations of CPPs and EEPs, were explored, highlighting key advancements in POC development and providing insights into future directions for the development of novel POCs.

title: Enhanced Sampling of Ligand Binding Coupled to RNA Base-Flipping Dynamics.
abstract: Noncoding RNAs have recently emerged as promising targets for therapeutic drugs. However, their high conformational flexibility presents significant challenges in structure-based rational drug discovery. Therefore, it is essential to gain detailed mechanistic insights into the millisecond-time scale ligand recognition process coupled to RNA conformational dynamics. Enhanced sampling simulations can help investigate these intricate dynamical processes by effectively exploring the rugged conformational landscapes of RNA-ligand complexes. In this study, we applied the on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling algorithm and its flooding variant to compute the free energy surface, kinetics, and binding mechanism for three different natural and synthetic ligands to a prototypical RNA aptamer. Our simulations revealed the dynamic coupling between ligand recognition and the base-flipping transition. In addition to reproducing the relative trends of binding affinities and residence times, our results uncovered a competing effect between the conformational selection and the induced fit mechanisms. The preference for one mechanism over the other is influenced by the binding affinity. By integrating these mechanistic insights with the binding affinity and kinetics derived from our simulations, we provide an atomistically detailed understanding of the RNA-ligand recognition process.

title: RNA-Adjusted TUFM Protein State Captures Mitochondrial Proteome Organization in Lung Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Matched transcriptome-proteome measurements can reveal protein-state information not represented by RNA abundance. We integrated four lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) proteogenomic cohorts, two longitudinal osimertinib transcriptomic systems, and DepMap CRISPR screens to test whether the TUFM protein captures coordinated mitochondrial proteome organization beyond TUFM RNA. In discovery LUAD, the RNA-adjusted TUFM protein state (TUFM_PT) added substantial explanatory information beyond its transcript for mitochondrial-translation and oxidative-phosphorylation (OXPHOS) protein programs. Across three independent cohorts (n = 292), TUFM_PT replicated with pooled Spearman rho values of 0.564 and 0.620 for mitochondrial translation and OXPHOS, respectively, and ranked 40th and 23rd among 5,242 externally benchmarked RNA-adjusted protein states. Associations persisted after copy-number, clinical, tumor-purity, and background-proteome adjustment. Highest-ranked human TUFM_PT proteomic partners were enriched in an independent CRISPR codependency network, including after the exclusion of prespecified mitochondrial genes, demonstrating cross-modal convergence at the network tail. Longitudinal osimertinib data provided complementary temporal context: early drug tolerance suppressed mitochondrial translation and OXPHOS transcripts, followed by later recovery without universal TUFM mRNA recovery. Together, these findings identify TUFM_PT as a reproducible, network-embedded proteomic readout of mitochondrial organization beyond TUFM RNA, while the longitudinal transcriptomes define the treatment-stage context rather than treatment-linked TUFM protein dynamics.

title: Dual Antifibrotic Modulation via CTGF Silencing and Peptide Amphiphile Nanofibers for Topical Treatment of Skin Fibrosis.
abstract: Skin fibrosis is driven in part by transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling and the matricellular protein connective tissue growth factor (CTGF). Elevated CTGF expression is a hallmark of fibrotic skin lesions and contributes to pathological extracellular matrix remodeling. In this project, an antisense oligonucleotide (AON) delivery system was developed for the treatment of skin fibrosis. In this respect, two antifibrotic agents, i) AON against CTGF and ii) antifibrotic polypeptide amphiphile, were self-assembled into nanofibers to enhance antifibrotic efficacy. The nanofibers were encapsulated in chitosan nanoparticles (CNPs) for protection and sustained release. Loaded CNPs were characterized by morphology, size, endosomal escape, and skin penetration using a transwell-based 3D skin model. The nanoparticles exhibited an average size of 220 nm. The encapsulation efficiency of CNPs was 52%, providing sustained nanofiber release over 7 days. With the use of nanoparticles, clear reduction trends were observed in CTGF, α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA), and collagen expression. CNPs penetrated the skin model gradually, revealing no cytotoxicity to skin cells. Overall, these results reveal the potential of the designed nanofibers as a therapeutic agent and the CNPs as the carrier of the nanofibers. The developed delivery system can be used as an alternative approach for the treatment of lesions in fibrotic skin.

title: SecAntiGami: A Secondary-Antibody-Inspired RNA Origami for Qualitative Aptamer Validation.
abstract: RNA aptamers are short, single-stranded RNA molecules that fold into specific three-dimensional structures and selectively bind molecular targets. Despite applications in therapeutics, diagnostics, and biosensing, tools for aptamer validation remain scarce compared to well-established pipelines for other biomolecular binders such as antibodies. Here, we introduce SecAntiGami─a secondary-antibody-inspired RNA origami─as a modular tool for signal enhancement and aptamer characterization. SecAntiGami binds aptamers of interest through programmable kissing-loop interactions and carries a fluorescent aptamer for visualization. It amplifies aptamer-dependent size increases in dynamic light scattering assays and enables fluorescence-based aptamer localization. We rationally design three different variants of a biotin-binding aptamer and use SecAntiGami to demonstrate that all of them retain their functionality, enabling efficient integration of aptamers into RNA origami structures. SecAntiGami serves as a versatile tool for qualitative aptamer validation for synthetic biology, structural RNA nanotechnology, RNA therapeutics, and diagnostics.

title: GSH/pH Dual-Responsive Zwitterionic mRNA Nanocomplexes for Tumor-Enriched mRNA Delivery in a B16F10 Melanoma Model.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapy offers a programmable route to melanoma treatment, but its translation is limited by nuclease degradation, off-target biodistribution and endolysosomal trapping. Here we report a glutathione (GSH)/pH dual-responsive mRNA nanocomplex (mRNA-NC) fabricated by one-pot in situ polymerization of N-(3-aminopropyl)methacrylamide (APMA), 1-vinylimidazole (VI), N,N'-bis(acryloyl)cystamine (BACA), and 2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine (MPC) on the mRNA template. At an N/P ratio of 40, the carrier reached an encapsulation efficiency of 92.7 ± 2.1% and a loading capacity of 87.4 ± 3.2 μg mg-1, forming monodisperse particles of 126.4 ± 7.2 nm (polydispersity index, PDI, 0.14). The zwitterionic corona limited plasma protein adsorption to 12.6 ± 1.5 μg mg-1 (4.6-fold lower than jetPEI/mRNA), kept hemolysis at 0.8 ± 0.2%, and extended the serum half-life of the mRNA to ≈27.4 h, roughly 9-fold longer than naked mRNA. Release was gated by both triggers: 86.5 ± 3.7% of the cargo was released within 8 h under 10 mM GSH, whereas leakage under physiological conditions remained ≤ 12%; in a 4 h matrix, pH 5.5 plus 10 mM GSH released 85 ± 6.8% versus 12 ± 1.5% at pH 7.4 without GSH. In B16F10 cells, the nanocomplex was taken up in a dose- and energy-dependent manner, entered the lysosomal compartment, and escaped over time in a manner consistent with imidazole-mediated proton-sponge buffering (a hypothesis; intralysosomal pH was not measured directly), producing a peak firefly luciferase (FLuc) expression of 56,140 ± 3280 RLU mg-1 protein at 24 h, about 1.5-fold higher than jetPEI/mRNA, with 93.6 ± 3.9% cell viability and 6.7 ± 1.2% lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release. In B16F10-bearing albino C57BL/6 mice, a single intravenous dose produced tumor-dominant bioluminescence (peak 5.7 × 106 photons s-1 at 6 h), a tumor enrichment index of 1.22 ± 0.18 (vs 0.31 ± 0.03 for jetPEI/mRNA) and 2.42 × 107 FLuc mRNA copies μg-1 tumor RNA at 12 h, while all 7-day safety indicators remained at phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) levels. These results demonstrate that a single zwitterionic nanocomplex can integrate stealth, dual-triggered release, and endosomal escape for safe, tumor-enriched mRNA delivery. While this study focuses on delivery performance and reporter gene expression, it lays a solid foundation for future therapeutic applications with functional mRNA.

title: Pooled Screening of Cancer Cell Lines Identifies Vulnerability to Polyunsaturated Fatty-Acid-Induced Ferroptosis.
abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are essential nutrients supporting numerous cellular processes in normal and neoplastic cells, yet PUFA-containing phospholipids predispose cells to ferroptosis. How cancer cells from various lineages or genetic backgrounds proliferate in the presence of PUFA remains poorly understood. Here, by systematically profiling various fatty acids using a barcoded and pooled cancer cell line library, we show that a subset of cell lines is sensitive to PUFA treatment at concentrations comparable to physiological levels. We demonstrate that PUFA treatment alone is sufficient to induce ferroptosis in these cell lines that are also vulnerable to GPX4 inhibition. By correlating patterns of PUFA sensitivity with cancer cell line features including basal mRNA transcript levels, we show that PUFA sensitivity is positively associated with fatty acid binding protein 1 (FABP1) expression. Additionally, by profiling a diverse collection of fatty acids and analogs, we find that ferroptosis in cancer cells can be effectively induced by conjugated linolenic acids, in addition to PUFAs containing 1,4-pentadiene groups. Genome-wide CRISPR modifier screens in the PUFA-sensitive ES2 cells reveal a pro-ferroptosis pathway defined by enzymes that convert PUFAs to membrane-associated phospholipids, and an anti-ferroptosis pathway that segregates PUFAs by delivering them to lipid droplets. Together, we present the first comprehensive data set of PUFA-induced ferroptosis sensitivity in a collection of 554 cell lines from 19 primary lineages and suggest a potential therapeutic avenue to induce tumor cell ferroptosis using dietary metabolites.

title: All Roads Lead to Rome: Non-canonical Modulators of RNA Metabolism in ALS Pathogenesis.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive motor neuron loss. Aberrant RNA metabolism is one of its most consistent molecular features, and ALS has long been framed as a disease of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), given that mutations in RBPs are among the most frequent genetic causes of ALS. However, a growing number of ALS-associated genes encode proteins that lack canonical RNA-binding domains; nonetheless, their mutations also disrupt RNA homeostasis. This review examines how these non-canonical disease modulators perturb RNA metabolism. We group these factors into three functional classes. One includes proteostasis regulators, whose dysfunction impairs protein quality control and promotes the accumulation of aggregation-prone RBPs in cytoplasmic inclusions and persistent stress granules. Another involves factors that elicit RNA toxicity or disrupt ribonucleoprotein organization, including GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9ORF72 and CAG repeat expansion in ATXN1. The third class comprises factors governing axonal RNA granule transport. Across these categories, a shared consequence is the disruption of mRNA processing, stability, localization, and translation in motor neurons. We further discuss how epitranscriptomic dysregulation, particularly altered m6A and m1A modification states, may contribute to ALS pathology. We also discuss the therapeutic implications of this mechanistic convergence in defective RNA metabolism in ALS.

title: Adenovirus-Derived Virus-Like Particles Enable Rapid Encapsulation and Delivery of Functional Antigen Cargo.
abstract: Adenoviral vectors have been widely validated as effective vaccine platforms for both infectious diseases and cancer due to their strong immunostimulatory properties. However, their application to personalized cancer vaccines and other time-sensitive antigens is limited by the prolonged production time required for conventional vector generation. Here, we developed an adenovirus-derived virus-like particle (Ad5VLP) platform that enables modular incorporation of antigen cargo without reconstruction of a complete antigen-encoding adenoviral genome. Ad5VLPs successfully packaged and delivered foreign mRNA, although mRNA-derived antigen expression remained insufficient to induce robust antigen-specific immunity in vivo. In contrast, direct encapsulation of protein or peptide antigens substantially improved intracellular antigen delivery and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I antigen presentation. Following subcutaneous prime-boost immunization in mice, antigen-loaded Ad5VLPs induced robust antigen-specific interferon-γ (IFN-γ) responses, with functional activity preferentially enriched within CD44hi CD8+ T cells and accompanied by effector-associated CD8+ T-cell differentiation. Importantly, robust cellular immune responses were also observed using an E0771 tumor neoantigen, demonstrating that the platform extends beyond the model ovalbumin (OVA) antigen. Protein-loaded Ad5VLPs also elicited antigen-specific and antivector humoral responses. Vaccination was well tolerated over the 14 day study period, with no substantial changes in body weight, clinical observations, serum markers of hepatic or renal injury and systemic inflammation, or broad splenic inflammatory transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings demonstrate that Ad5VLPs enable modular delivery of protein and peptide antigens and induce robust cellular immune responses, supporting further investigation for personalized cancer vaccination and other time-sensitive vaccine applications.

title: In Vivo Blood Kinetics and Transcript Integrity of Three mRNA-Lipid Nanoparticle Vaccines in Humans.
abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines are detectable in human blood after vaccination, but platform-specific differences in systemic persistence and transcript integrity remain poorly defined. We analyzed serial blood samples from 73 participants receiving Moderna mRNA-1273 (three formulations), Pfizer/BioNTech BNT162b2, or an investigational receptor-binding domain (RBD) mRNA vaccine (three different doses). Using droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) assays, we quantified total and long-range linked ("intact") vaccine mRNA, and we measured vaccine-specific ionizable lipids by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Across platforms, mRNA decay was fastest for mRNA-1273, intermediate for BNT162b2, and slowest for the RBD vaccine, with ionizable lipid decay following the same rank order. Notably, intact spike mRNA declined 2-fold faster after mRNA-1273 than BNT162b2 vaccination. Kinetics modeling revealed platform-dependent coupling of mRNA and lipid kinetics: intact mRNA tracked closely with SM-102 for mRNA-1273, whereas ALC-0315 persisted longer than intact mRNA for BNT162b2. A ten-fragment linkage ddPCR panel spanning the spike transcript showed lower linkage toward 3'-proximal regions that mirrored the administered mRNA-1273 formulation. Together, these data provide a quantitative framework for benchmarking mRNA-LNP platform kinetics and transcript integrity in humans.

title: Poly(acrylamido) PEG-Alternative Lipids Rescue mRNA Efficacy during Repeated Dosing and Enhance Immune Cell Delivery.
abstract: Following the successes of the messenger RNA (mRNA) lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines against COVID-19, mRNA-LNPs are being explored for varied multidose applications including cancer immunotherapies and protein replacement therapies. LNPs rely on poly(ethylene glycol)-lipid (PEG-lipid) coatings for stability, but increasing anti-PEG antibody prevalence threatens repeat-dose efficacy and increases pseudoallergic risk, creating an urgent need for alternatives. Here, we introduce poly(acrylamido) lipids (PAM-lipids), a family of polymer lipids that effectively replace PEG-lipids in mRNA-LNP formulations. Systematic variation of monomer chemistry, molar mass, and end group reveals critical structure-activity relationships determining LNP size, polydispersity, and transfection efficiency. Varying PAM monomer chemistry allows minimization of antipolymer antibody cross-reactivity, with multiple PAM-lipids demonstrating no anti-PEG antibody binding. Several PAM-LNPs exhibit superior mRNA transfection efficacy to PEGylated clinical benchmarks in vitro and in vivo across multiple cell types, organs, routes of administration, and mRNA cargos. In particular, lead PAM-LNPs enhance mRNA delivery to dendritic cells (up to 120-fold in vitro and 3-fold in vivo) and macrophages (4-fold in vivo), with 2.5-fold superior lymph node expression, driven in part by increased cellular association and lymphoid targeting. Crucially, PAM-LNPs evade circulating anti-PEG antibodies to rescue lost mRNA efficacy after repeated dosing, resulting in 300% mRNA expression relative to that of PEG-LNPs. These findings demonstrate PAM-lipids as a chemically varied, immunologically compatible family of PEG alternatives for mRNA-LNP therapeutics.

title: CRISPR-AsCas12a with crRNA-Free Collateral Cleavage Activity for Electrochemical Diagnosis of HER2-Positive Breast Cancer.
abstract: The CRISPR-Cas12a system has revolutionized molecular diagnostics; however, the strict requirement of crRNAs and target DNA for collateral cleavage activation restricts its flexibility in non-nucleic acid diagnostics. Herein, we demonstrate that AsCas12a exhibits an RNA-free collateral cleavage activity with the presence of manganese ions (Mn2+), which preferentially cleaves single-stranded DNA efficiently. Mechanistically, kinetic analyses reveal that AsCas12a exhibits a significantly higher binding affinity for Mn2+ than for magnesium ion (Mg2+), while molecular dynamics simulations suggest that Mn2+ coordination induces conformational changes to expose the RuvC endonuclease domain. Harnessing this unique property, an enzymatic cascade-amplified electrochemical biosensor integrating manganese nanoflowers is reported for the diagnosis of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive breast cancer. By equipping screen-printed gold electrodes with DNA reporters, this diagnostic tool enables high-precision HER2 quantification and successfully distinguishes various HER2-related cell lines. Furthermore, the biosensor has been extended to analyze HER2-positive exosomes, facilitating the dynamic tracking of serum exosome levels in tumor-bearing nude mice to evaluate therapeutic efficacy and accurately distinguish HER2-positive breast cancer patients in clinical samples. This RNA-free Cas12a system may provide new insights into CRISPR-based non-nucleic acid detection, emerging as a powerful tool for dynamic tumor monitoring and precision oncology.

title: Engineering Escherichia coli Nissle as a Safe Chassis for the Production of Therapeutic Peptides.
abstract: Synthetic biology enables the installation of programable genetic functions in microorganisms, positioning them as versatile platforms for therapeutic applications. However, clinical translation requires chassis organisms that integrate safety, genetic stability, and precise control over the activity. Here, we present an innovative engineering framework for the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle (EcN) that transforms EcN into a safe, efficient, and non-proliferative chassis for therapeutic production. The native EcN plasmids pM1 and pM2 were cured and repurposed to encode two functional modules: a CRISPR-Cas12 chromosome-shredding device that prevents bacterial propagation and a programable circuit for payload expression, thereby generating a non-proliferative therapeutic-producing system. To broaden the range of therapeutic payloads, we developed an artificial-intelligence-guided bioinformatic pipeline to predict anticancer cell-penetrating peptides (ACCPPs). As a proof of concept, a candidate identified through this workflow was produced in the engineered EcN chassis and evaluated in human cell culture for anticancer activity. Collectively, this strategy established a modular platform that integrates computational therapeutic discovery with engineered probiotic production, paving the way for the future development of safer microbial therapies and their clinical applications.

title: Programmable and Dynamic DNA Localisation at Synthetic Cell Membranes.
abstract: Spatial and temporal organisation of membrane-associated components is fundamental to cellular signalling, yet remains difficult to engineer in minimal synthetic systems. In synthetic cells, DNA and RNA nanotechnology offer programmable molecular organisation at membranes, while in vitro transcription (IVT) enables gene expression-driven regulation. However, integrating these systems within cell-like compartments, such as giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs), remains challenging due to undesirable interactions between transcription machinery and nucleic acid assemblies. Here, we present a modular strategy that couples in situ RNA production to dynamic DNA localisation at GUV synthetic cell membranes. RNA strands, transcribed within GUVs, function as linkers that recruit DNA-conjugated cargo to lipid membranes, enabling programmable spatial organisation. Using this framework, we achieved reversible membrane localisation through toehold-mediated strand displacement and RNase H-mediated degradation. This work establishes a gene expression-driven platform for programmable and dynamic control of membrane-associated components in synthetic cells, providing a foundation for constructing dynamic signalling assemblies and higher-order cellular behaviours.

title: Tumor-Specific Gene Editing Enhances Cancer Immunogenicity through Succinate Metabolism-Mediated MHC-I Reprogramming.
abstract: Impaired expression of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) greatly compromises cytotoxic T-cell-mediated anticancer immunotherapy. Existing MHC-I activation strategies are greatly challenged by poor tumor specificity and off-target toxicity. Herein, we report a dual tumor-specific CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system that can precisely knock out succinate dehydrogenase subunit C (Sdhc) to activate the MHC-I pathway via epigenetic and transcriptional regulation. A tumor-specific gene editor is first engineered via reversible shielding of sgRNA using an apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1)-responsive, complementary ssDNA, yielding AP-sgRNA with blocked editing activity in normal cells yet completely restored activity in APE1-overexpressing tumor cells. Subsequently, tumor-targeted delivery of AP-sgRNA and Cas9 mRNA (mCas9) is achieved using dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated lipid nanoparticle (DLNP), which upon bioorthogonal click reaction can anchor cancer cells that are prelabeled with azido groups using the unnatural sugar DCL-AAM. Thus, AP-sgSdhc/mCas9@DLNP enables efficient and selective Sdhc editing in tumor cells, leading to epigenetic and transcriptional activation of MHC-antigen processing and presentation genes and thereby provoking robust antitumor efficacy in the B16-OVA melanoma model through enhanced, T cell-mediated immune responses. Moreover, it completely suppressed pulmonary metastasis after combination with aPD-L1 in the 4T1 lung metastasis model. This study provides an enlightened paradigm for precision gene editing and renders a promising mechanism for potentiating cancer immunotherapy.

title: Mediator kinase inhibition exposes a transcriptional vulnerability and synergizes with venetoclax in AML.
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a heterogeneous and aggressive hematologic malignancy associated with poor survival despite recent therapeutic advances. To identify novel anti-leukemic agents, we performed a high-throughput viability screen of 10,000 small molecules across 56 genetically diverse primary AML samples. Compounds with similar activity profiles were grouped into Compound Correlation Clusters (CCCs), leading to the identification of CCC163, which includes AML874, as a potent and selective hit. Integrated pharmacological and CRISPR-Cas9 approaches identified the Mediator complex as the molecular target of AML874. We demonstrated that AML874 acts as a selective CDK8/CDK19 inhibitor, disrupting Mediator-dependent transcription. FLT3-mutated AML showed increased sensitivity to AML874, suggesting a subtype-specific vulnerability. Notably, CDK8 inhibition synergized with venetoclax in AML cell lines and patient-derived xenograft models, resulting in enhanced anti-leukemic activity in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish CDK8/CDK19 inhibition as a therapeutically relevant strategy in AML.

title: GluD1 modulates GluN2B-containing NMDAR function and plasticity at subicular synapses.
abstract: Dysregulation of the delta-type glutamate receptor GluD1 and N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) is implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders including schizophrenia and intellectual disability, and GluD1 modulates NMDAR responses in hippocampal neurons. However, the precise mechanisms by which GluD1 influences specific NMDAR subtypes remain undefined, representing a critical gap given the reliance of synaptic plasticity and cognition on NMDAR composition. GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing NMDARs are essential for synaptic long-term potentiation (LTP) and contextual learning and memory. Here, we used CRISPR/Cas9 to generate GluD1 knockout (KO) in cultured hippocampal neurons and observed a selective decrease in GluN2B-containing NMDAR responses. In acute hippocampal slices, GluD1 KO similarly reduced GluN2B-containing NMDAR currents at ventral CA1→subiculum synapses and impaired LTP at these synapses. In vivo, region-specific GluD1 deficiency in the ventral subiculum disrupted long-term contextual memory, indicating a critical role for GluD1 in cognitive processes. These findings demonstrate that GluD1 is indispensable for preserving GluN2B-containing NMDAR function, synaptic plasticity, and memory, providing molecular insight into how GluD1 regulates NMDAR subtypes implicated in synaptic dysfunction in neuropsychiatric disorders. Understanding this mechanism will guide the development of therapeutic strategies that selectively target GluD1-dependent modulation of NMDAR subtypes in brain disease.

title: DCST1 drives cisplatin resistance via non-canonical ubiquitination and stabilization of NFAT5 to suppress PANoptosis in bladder cancer.
abstract: Cisplatin-based chemotherapy constitutes the cornerstone of first-line treatment for muscle-invasive and metastatic bladder cancer (BCa); however, the frequent emergence of chemoresistance presents a formidable clinical obstacle. In the present study, by combining a systematic CRISPR-Cas9 E3 ligase library screen with drug sensitivity data from the GDSC database, DCST1 (DC-STAMP Domain Containing 1) was identified as a pivotal driver of cisplatin resistance. DCST1 expression was found to be markedly upregulated in chemoresistant BCa tissues, and its elevated expression served as an independent predictor of poor patient prognosis. Functionally, DCST1 deficiency sensitizes BCa cells to cisplatin in vitro and in vivo by triggering PANoptosis (simultaneous apoptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis). Mechanistically, DCST1 functions as an atypical E3 ubiquitin ligase to catalyze the K11/K27-linked polyubiquitination of NFAT5 at residue K450. This non-canonical ubiquitination stabilizes NFAT5 by preventing its lysosomal degradation and promotes its nuclear accumulation. Nuclear NFAT5 then transcriptionally activates SOD2, orchestrating an anti-PANoptotic program that ensures BCa cell survival under chemotherapeutic stress. Furthermore, through molecular docking and CETSA validation, digoxin was identified as a potent pharmacological inhibitor of NFAT5 that overcomes DCST1-mediated chemoresistance and synergistically restores cisplatin sensitivity. Collectively, these findings unveil a previously unrecognized ubiquitination-dependent mechanism of chemoresistance and establish the DCST1-NFAT5 signaling axis as a promising therapeutic target for overcoming drug resistance in BCa.

title: A 5' tRNA-derived fragment tDR-Glu-TTC exacerbates intestinal ischemia/reperfusion injury via ADAR1/autophagy/ROS/necroptosis signaling axis.
abstract: Transfer RNA-derived small RNAs (tDRs) are a class of functional small non-coding RNAs, many of which are induced by stress conditions and have been implicated in tissue injury and disease pathogenesis. However, their role in intestinal ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury remains unclear. Using tDR sequencing, we identified that tDR-Glu-TTC was significantly upregulated in intestinal tissues, plasma, epithelial cells, and human clinical samples; and its levels positively correlated with the severity of intestinal injury. Functionally, tDR-Glu-TTC exacerbates intestinal mucosal damage by activating TNF pathway-mediated necroptosis in intestinal epithelial cells. Mechanistically, tDR-Glu-TTC directly binds to and suppresses the RNA-editing enzyme ADAR1, impairing adenosine-to-inosine editing of autophagy-related transcripts (ATG18 and Lamp2). This inhibits autophagy, leading to the accumulation of damaged mitochondria, and the release of reactive oxygen species (ROS). The elevated ROS subsequently promotes TNF-α secretion, triggering TNF pathway-mediated necroptosis. Furthermore, increased ROS downregulates TRMT6/61A-dependent m¹A methylation of tRNA-Glu-TTC, increasing tDR-Glu-TTC biogenesis and forming a pathogenic positive feedback loop. Thus, therapeutic dual-target intervention using N-acetylcysteine combined with tDR-Glu-TTC-antagomir synergistically mitigated I/R-induced intestinal injury in vivo. In summary, our study unveiled a previously unrecognized mechanism by which tDR-Glu-TTC exacerbates intestinal I/R injury via the ADAR1/autophagy/ROS/necroptosis signaling axis, offering a promising therapeutic strategy for combating intestinal I/R injury.

title: Deciphering the regulatory code of RNA inosine through enzymatic precision mapping and an explainable deep learning model.
abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing is one of the most abundant RNA modifications and is involved in multiple critical biological processes; however, the precise localization of inosine and the mechanisms governing their selective editing remain incompletely understood. Integrating high-accuracy detection technologies with deep learning models can accelerate our understanding of the selective positioning and functional implications of A-to-I editing. To address these challenges, this study simultaneously developed RNA inosine sequencing by endonuclease V (EndoV) and XRN-1 (REX-seq), a highly sensitive and accurate detection method for inosine sites, and Inosine Deep Residual Enhanced Attention Model (InoDREAM), a predictive deep learning framework. REX-seq combines EndoV cleavage specificity with XRN-1 exonuclease activity to enable comprehensive A-to-I editome profiling while maintaining accurate gene expression quantification. Using this method, we identified 590,249 high-confidence inosine sites in HEK293T cells, including 84,645 novel sites. Leveraging the high-confidence A-to-I editing sites identified by REX-seq, we developed InoDREAM, which successfully predicted multiple regulatory proteins that exhibit specific binding affinity to A-to-I edited transcripts while simultaneously identifying disease-associated mutation sites and relevant cis-regulatory elements that are functionally linked to RNA editing events. These findings provide novel mechanistic insights into both the molecular regulation of RNA editing and its pathophysiological implications in disease development.

title: Genotoxic safety and long-term engraftment dynamics of efficient translational CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for β-haemoglobinopathies from bench to clinical trials.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing targeting the BCL11A erythroid enhancer has transformed therapeutic approaches for transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia (β-thal) and sickle cell disease (SCD). Even though clinical efficacy is well demonstrated, translating these therapies to global patient populations requires a strong evidence-based framework to address critical concerns regarding long-term genotoxic safety and long-lasting engraftment dynamics.
METHODS: Following the 2020 PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic review of 21 key clinical and preclinical studies (published during 2014-2026) to evaluate CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing in β-thal and SCD. The inclusion criteria focused on studies reporting foetal haemoglobin (HbF) induction, transfusion independence (TI) and safety outcomes.
RESULTS: Clinical data indicate high efficacy, with exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) achieving TI in 91% of β-thal patients and a vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC)-free status in 97% of SCD patients. Safety profiling confirmed that severe adverse events, including febrile neutropenia and stomatitis, are primarily associated with busulfan-based myeloablation rather than gene editing. Gene-editing safety and conditioning toxicity are interlinked because conditioning is part of the process, and edited clones might interact with stress pathways during long-term repopulation. Preclinical benchmarks substantiate molecular reliability, with negligible off-target activity reported in most validated platforms. However, rare instances of complex structural rearrangements and intergenic off-target indels highlight the necessity for in-depth, unbiased long-term genomic surveillance.
CONCLUSION: CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for β-thal and SCD treatment constitute a treatment option within current clinical frameworks. These therapies need continuous surveillance. Rather than establishing a perfect plan, this systematic review highlights that while current platforms are thought to have short-term molecular precision, the use of Multilayer Safety Risks Screening and Surveillance for pretransplant conditioning is critical. This approach helps address long-term genotoxic concerns and ensures the safety and scalability of gene-editing therapies for global β-thal and SCD patient care.

title: Cholesterol dysregulation contributes to hematopoietic failure in parn-mutant zebrafish with implications for dyskeratosis congenita.
abstract: Germline mutations in PARN cause dyskeratosis congenita (DC), an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by multilineage cytopenia and progression to myeloid disease. The mechanisms underlying this malignant transformation have not been fully elucidated. Here we show, using a loss-of-function CRISPR-Cas9 zebrafish parn mutant, hematopoietic stem and progenitor (HSPC) expansion and reduced mature hematopoietic cells across various lineages. Cholesterol biosynthesis was transcriptionally activated; a finding recapitulated in patient-derived iPSCs with PARN mutations. Inhibiting cholesterol biosynthesis rescued HSPC expansion and anemia in parn mutants. Concurrent myeloid differentiation therapy or Wnt inhibition reduced HSPCs to varying degrees. We further demonstrate a role for activated Erk signaling in impairing erythrocyte differentiation and show robust rescue with trametinib treatment. Overall, our findings uncover unrecognized roles for Parn in regulating cholesterol metabolism and Erk signaling and provide preclinical evidence for targeting these pathways to restore hematopoiesis in DC.

title: Positional replication fork instability drives PARP inhibitor cytotoxicity.
abstract: Although poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) show promise for treating homologous recombination-deficient cancers, the observed PARPi hypersensitivity in additional genetic contexts expands their potential use in precision oncology. Yet, the DNA lesions driving PARPi-induced cytotoxicity remain poorly defined. Here we uncover distinct replication-fork lesions in specific genomic regions as key determinants of PARPi cytotoxicity. Using CRISPR screens, we identify that loss of replication-coupled cohesin acetyltransferase ESCO2 confers PARPi hypersensitivity independently of homologous recombination deficiency. Quantitative single-molecule imaging reveals that ESCO2 loss promotes accumulation of G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures at a subset of replication-associated sites, associated with PARP1 activation and engagement of fork protection factor TIMELESS to mitigate G4-induced stress. Notably, these G4 lesions localize to fragile pericentromeric regions and engage the G4 helicase DDX11. PARP inhibition disrupts this protective G4-processing response by preventing PARP1-dependent engagement of TIMELESS and DDX11, leading to G4 accumulation, DNA damage and chromosomal instability. Together, our findings define the G4-PARP1-TIMELESS-DDX11 axis as a critical safeguard of replication fork stability at hard-to-replicate loci and reveal ESCO2 as a therapeutic target for promoting synthetic lethality in PARPi-treated cancers.

title: Rational design of lipid nanoparticles for brain delivery of RNA therapeutics.
abstract: Effective delivery of RNA therapeutics to the brain remains challenging due to the multiple barriers of the central nervous system (CNS). To probe molecular scaffolds that could help overcome these barriers, we analysed the pharmaceutical profiles of over 100 CNS-active drugs and identified hydroxyzine (HX) as a promising scaffold for designing ionizable lipids with improved brain-targeting properties. Specifically, HX1 liquid nanoparticles (LNPs) achieved robust mRNA delivery to the brain through multiple trafficking pathways across CNS barriers. HX1 LNPs also enabled efficient gene editing in mouse brains via co-delivery of CRISPR mRNA and guide RNA and effectively delivered luciferase mRNA to the brain of a non-human primate. Moreover, HX1 LNPs carrying Il10 mRNA mitigated radiation-induced brain injury in mice, highlighting their potential for preventive treatment in the presence of intact CNS barriers. These findings establish HX1 LNPs as a promising translational platform for delivering therapeutic mRNAs and genome-editing components to the brain.

title: Immunogenicity risk assessment of novel modalities using new approach methodologies.
abstract: A new generation of medicines that includes gene therapies, cell-based treatments and gene editors have the potential to treat a vast range of diseases. However, the clinical success of these novel modalities is limited by unwanted immune responses, which can compromise both safety and efficacy. Regulatory agencies have recently emphasized reducing animal testing in preclinical safety studies and envisioned a strategic approach for basing regulatory decisions on scientifically validated new approach methodologies (NAMs). These methods encompass mathematical models, artificial intelligence tools, organ-on-a-chip systems, and advanced in vitro and ex vivo assays. In combination, these approaches seem potentially well suited for assessing unwanted immune responses of the novel modalities. Key challenges to be addressed include predicting the immunogenicity risks from transgene products, delivery vehicles and gene-editing machinery; managing pre-existing immunity; overcoming barriers to repeat dosing; and establishing robust long-term monitoring strategies. In this Perspective, we critically evaluate how the current NAMs toolkit, originally developed for protein therapeutics, can be adapted to assess the unwanted immune responses of novel modalities. We provide a forward-looking framework for developing and validating the next generation of predictive immunogenicity tools required to safely unlock the full therapeutic potential of these revolutionary medicines.

title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies, but its efficacy remains limited by multiple negative regulatory mechanisms intrinsic to T cells1-4. Here we perform a high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double-knockout (DKO) CRISPR screen, and identify multiple DKO gene pairs that are both effective and synergistic. The top pair, NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO, has multiple favourable immunological features. Whole-transcriptome profiling and in vivo single-cell RNA sequencing reveal that NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO specifically upregulates metabolic pathways in CAR-T cells, which show significantly higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity. NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO CAR-T cells and T cells exhibit exceptionally potent antitumour efficacy and long-term tumour control across different tumour models without compromising safety features. NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO outperforms several benchmark single-gene and dual-gene modifications in T cells and CAR-T cells5-9. These data demonstrate high-throughput in vivo CAR-T DKO screening for rapid discovery of combination targets, and establish NR4A1-SOCS3 as a promising pair of intracellular checkpoints to engineer high-performance CAR-T therapies against cancer.

title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury.
abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3-5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

title: In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering.
abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease1. Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model2,3. Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor-encapsulated within a GalNAc-lipid nanoparticle-leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells.
abstract: Rubella virus (RuV) causes rubella and, when acquired during pregnancy, congenital rubella syndrome1. Despite its clinical significance, the cellular entry mechanism of RuV remains poorly characterized, owing to limited identification of host receptors2, which hinders pathogenesis research and therapeutic development. Here, using proximity biotin labelling-based proteomics coupled with CRISPR-Cas9 validation, we identify nectin-4 as a functional RuV entry receptor. Ectopic expression of nectin-4 conferred susceptibility to RuV in non-permissive cells, whereas blocking or genetic ablation of nectin-4 reduced infection, results that demonstrate that nectin-4 is a major entry factor. Mechanistically, nectin-4 directly interacts with the RuV envelope glycoprotein heterodimer and facilitates receptor-mediated endocytosis following initial calcium-dependent viral attachment to cellular lipids. In polarized airway epithelial models, nectin-4 mediates basolateral entry of RuV and supports apical progeny release, a finding that provides a molecular mechanism for respiratory transmission. In placental models, nectin-4 is highly expressed on syncytiotrophoblasts and facilitates infection at the maternal-fetal interface, although additional nectin-4-independent pathways contribute to infection of other trophoblast populations. Together, these data establish nectin-4 as a key factor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of RuV and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of rubella and related diseases.

title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA.
abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4-8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

title: An mRNA-lipid nanoparticle vaccine against H5N1 influenza virus protects lactating dairy cows from infection.
abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 virus has recently emerged in dairy cattle in the USA, leading to mastitis and sharp reductions in milk production. The main site of H5N1 viral replication is the mammary tissue rather than the respiratory tract and viral transmission between animals is thought to occur through viral shedding in milk. Here, we generate an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccine encoding the hemagglutinin (HA) of A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024, representative of circulating bovine H5N1 viruses, and assess its immunogenicity and efficacy in lactating dairy cows. Eight cows were divided into vaccinated and control groups, receiving two intramuscular doses of the vaccine or saline, followed by intramammary viral challenge. Vaccination elicited HA-reactive and neutralizing antibodies in serum and HA-reactive antibodies in milk. Following viral challenge, vaccinated cows had ~1,000-fold lower peak viral RNA in milk and a lower occurrence of mastitis and mammary fibrosis.

title: A CD7-targeted AAV variant enables efficient T and NK cell engineering in vivo.
abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have been applied for precise genome engineering in human T cells but poor tropism restricts their efficiency and translational potential. Here, through directed evolution of the AAV6 capsid in primary human T cells, we identified a family of variants containing an APR motif at residues 455-457. The lead candidate, AAV.APR31, enabled robust transduction of primary T and NK cells at nearly 100-1,000-fold lower doses than AAV6 and outperformed the human T cell-tropic capsid AAV-hT7. CRISPR screening identified CD7 as a lineage-specific entry enhancer alongside the canonical AAVR pathway and structural analysis suggested that the APR motif facilitates CD7 engagement. Unlike existing delivery systems confined to one engineering mode, AAV.APR31 enabled transient transgene delivery, site-specific knock-in and transposon integration in human T and NK cells, generating CAR-T cells functionally equivalent to lentiviral vector-manufactured products. Systemic administration of AAV.APR31-generated CAR-T cells in vivo resulted in potent tumor control in hematologic and solid tumor mouse models.

title: Aptamer-mediated multivalent endogenous ADAR1 recruitment for highly efficient RNA editing.
abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing mediated by endogenous ADAR enzymes represents a promising therapeutic strategy because it can correct mutations at the transcript level without inducing permanent changes to the genome. However, existing systems face challenges, particularly the limited editing efficiency, which limits their practical applications. Here we introduce MARRS (multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system)-an efficient and specific RNA editing platform that leverages engineered multivalent RNA aptamers to robustly recruit endogenous ADAR1 enzymes. By optimizing aptamers targeting the Zα domain of ADAR1 p150 and embedding them in a circular RNA scaffold, MARRS enables near-complete adenosine-to-inosine editing of RNA targets in cultured cells and mouse models, achieving efficiencies up to 100% in vitro and 84% in vivo. MARRS also exhibits remarkable versatility across a range of transcript targets while maintaining high specificity with minimal off-target effects. Operating without the need for exogenous enzymes, the MARRS system offers a safe, efficient and programmable platform.

title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Structural mechanism of programmable gene integration by the R2 retrotransposon coupled with CRISPR-Cas9.
abstract: R2 retroelements are non-long-terminal-repeat retrotransposons that primarily insert into 28S ribosomal DNA loci across diverse eukaryotes. R2 elements home to their target sites through target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT), in which the R2 protein recognizes and nicks the target DNA to prime reverse transcription using an R2-encoding RNA as the template. The avian R2 system from Taeniopygia guttata (R2Tg) can insert a payload sequence within an RNA template into 28S ribosomal DNA loci in human cells. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of the R2Tg-template RNA-target DNA complex in the TPRT initiation state, both alone and bound to a Cas9-guide RNA complex. These structures provide mechanistic insights into R2Tg-mediated TPRT in its natural context and in the programmable gene integration system STITCHR (site-specific target-primed insertion through targeted CRISPR homing of retroelements). Furthermore, we combine these structural insights with computational protein design methods to engineer an enhanced STITCHR system.

title: Widening the BRCAness therapeutic window for its synthetic lethality effects with PARP inhibitors.
abstract: This review examines the expanding role of PARP inhibitors in cancer therapy, moving beyond the traditional model of single-strand break repair inhibition and BRCA-dependent synthetic lethality. We highlight emerging evidence that PARP inhibitors induce cytotoxicity through replication-associated DNA damage, including defects in Okazaki fragment maturation and replication gap accumulation. By integrating recent mechanistic insights with findings from CRISPR-based screens, we outline how disruptions in DNA replication and repair pathways define a broader BRCAness phenotype. We further emphasize the clinical implications of these discoveries, including novel combination strategies that extend the therapeutic applicability of PARP inhibitors beyond prevailing treatment regimens.

title: GALE is a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint of Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated killing.
abstract: Vγ9Vδ2 T cells mediate HLA-independent targeting of tumor cells, offering unique opportunities for cancer immunotherapy, yet their therapeutic efficacy remains limited. Here, using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify UDP-galactose 4-epimerase (GALE) as a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint that restricts Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated killing. GALE is a key nucleotide-sugar metabolic enzyme that controls the interconversion of UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose, thereby supporting protein glycosylation and cell-surface glycan remodeling. Mechanistically, GALE promotes complex N-glycosylation of CD155 and CEACAM1, favoring their engagement with the inhibitory receptors TIGIT and TIM3, respectively, while limiting CD155 binding to the activating receptor CD226. GALE loss potentiates Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated tumor killing in multiple mouse models and colorectal cancer patient-derived organoids. Together, these findings reveal how nucleotide-sugar metabolism shapes tumor-immune communication through complex N-glycan remodeling and identify GALE and its downstream receptor-ligand interactions as potential therapeutic targets for enhancing Vγ9Vδ2 T cell antitumor activity.

title: BAZ2A-induced epigenetic states in cancer cells fuel palmitate accumulation in the tumor microenvironment driving CAR-T cell exhaustion.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy shows limited efficacy in solid tumors, partly owing to poorly defined tumor-intrinsic resistance mechanisms. Here we show that the epigenetic regulator BAZ2A drives resistance to CD70-targeted CAR-T therapy by reprogramming tumor lipid metabolism. Using an in vivo CRISPR screen in a mouse renal cell carcinoma model, we identify BAZ2A as a key mediator that promotes the production and accumulation of palmitic acid, a saturated fatty acid in the tumor microenvironment. Excess palmitic acid is taken up by CAR-T cells and impairs mitochondrial fitness by inhibiting PGC-1α activity, thereby enforcing a dysfunctional state. Pharmacologic inhibition of BAZ2A reduces lipid accumulation and restores CAR-T cell activity in vivo. These findings reveal an epigenetic-metabolic mechanism of immune resistance and suggest that targeting tumor lipid remodeling represents a therapeutic strategy to overcome CAR-T resistance in solid tumors.

title: Temporal proteomics maps concealed-stage remodeling and reveals early mitochondrial alteration as an intervention target in a model of PKP2-arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.
abstract: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is a heritable cardiac disorder commonly linked to alterations in desmosomal proteins. While desmosomal dysfunction is a recognized pathogenic mechanism, the early molecular remodeling that precedes clinical manifestations remains unclear. Here we used a mouse model with inducible cardiomyocyte-specific knockout of Pkp2 (encoding plakophilin-2) and performed time-resolved mass spectrometry-based proteomics to map disease progression from early PKP2 loss to structural remodeling. Molecular changes preceded phenotypic abnormalities, and spatial asymmetry was evident, with earlier and more pronounced proteome remodeling in the right ventricle despite comparable PKP2 depletion in both ventricles. Downregulation of protein networks spanning desmosomes, sarcomeres and mitochondria suggests their functional coupling, with mitochondrial remodeling emerging as an early and progressively worsening feature. Intervention with honokiol attenuated changes across the major protein networks, highlighting mitochondrial pathways as promising therapeutic targets and honokiol as a potential strategy to delay arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy progression. Our findings provide critical insights into the concealed stage of disease progression and identify molecular targets for early intervention.

title: A transient modified mRNA encoding Myc and cyclin T1 improves cardiac function after myocardial injury.
abstract: Myc is an evolutionarily conserved transcription factor that is necessary for the restoration of tissues in multiple regenerative species. The adult mammalian heart lacks regenerative capacity and cardiomyocytes fail to divide following damage-induced signaling. Transgenic expression of Myc and cyclin T1 can drive substantial adult cardiomyocyte proliferation to replace lost cardiomyocytes. Here, using transgenic models and a prototypical mRNA therapeutic, we show that Myc and cyclin T1 require transient induction for cardiomyocyte proliferation that leads to myocardial repair and functional recovery after myocardial infarction in mice. This research provides a strategy to translate Myc-cyclin T1 coexpression for cardiac regeneration to address serious unmet needs in the treatment of cardiovascular disease.

title: AND-gate CRISPR/Cas13a-assisted colorimetric assay for dual microRNA monitoring of cervical spondylosis prognosis and auricular point pressing therapy evaluation.
abstract: Simultaneous detection of dual microRNA biomarkers is crucial for accurate prognosis and treatment monitoring of cervical spondylosis, yet remains challenging due to the lack of stringent logic control and high-fidelity signal amplification. Herein, we report an AND-gate-controlled colorimetric assay that integrates target-recycling strand displacement amplification, CRISPR/Cas13a/crRNA-mediated trans-cleavage, and self-priming cyclic amplification for sensitive and specific analysis of two cervical spondylosis-associated miRNAs (miRNA-221 and miRNA-146a). Only when both targets are present does the cascade proceed, producing double-stranded amplicons that trigger SYBR Green I-catalyzed TMB oxidation, yielding a naked-eye-visible blue signal. The assay exhibits a broad linear range from 10 fM to 500 pM, a detection limit of 2.12 fM, excellent selectivity, and good repeatability. Importantly, we applied this method to clinically evaluate the therapeutic effect of auricular point pressing (ear acupressure), a traditional Chinese medicine intervention for cervical spondylosis. In a 4-week study of 20 patients, the treatment group receiving auricular point pressing showed significant downregulation of both miRNAs compared to baseline, while the control group showed no notable change. Results correlated well with RT-qPCR, confirming reliability. This logic-controlled CRISPR/Cas13a platform offers a robust, equipment-free strategy for early prognosis of cervical spondylosis and objective monitoring of auricular point pressing therapy.

title: A programmable aptamer-triggered B-PER/CRISPR cascade amplification platform for ultrasensitive detection of Staphylococcus aureus.
abstract: Rapid and sensitive detection of Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is critical for food safety and public health. Herein, this work developed an ABC (aptamer-B-PER-CRISPR) cascade detection platform, where B-PER stands for bidirectional primer exchange reaction, that integrates aptamer-mediated target recognition, B-PER isothermal amplification, and CRISPR/Cas12a trans-cleavage for highly sensitive and specific detection of S. aureus. Upon target recognition, the trigger strand T is released from the aptamer-T duplex, initiating B-PER to generate abundant products containing sequences recognized by the guide RNA (gRNA), which activate Cas12a to cleave the reporter probe, generating a detectable fluorescence signal. Under optimized conditions, the platform exhibited a linear range of 102 to 1010 CFU per mL with a regression equation of F520 nm = 575.36 log C + 3246.47 (R2 = 0.9992) and a limit of detection of 13 CFU per mL. The assay showed excellent specificity for S. aureus, with negligible cross-reactivity toward Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Salmonella. Recovery tests in spiked milk samples yielded average recoveries of 98.9-100.7%. Overall, the ABC platform offers high sensitivity, excellent specificity, robust anti-interference capability, and operational simplicity, demonstrating great potential for rapid and reliable detection of foodborne pathogens in complex matrices.

title: Rational optimization of lipid nanoparticles enables efficient and low-activation mRNA delivery to platelets.
abstract: Advances in gene delivery technologies have opened new avenues for modulating platelet function and expanding their applications in cell-based therapies. However, as anucleate cells, platelets have long faced the dual challenge of low transfection efficiency and susceptibility to activation during genetic manipulation. Here, we report a rationally optimized lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation for efficient and low-activation mRNA delivery to platelets by systematically tuning the 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC)/cholesterol molar ratio. Five LNP formulations composed of ALC-0315, DOPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG2000 were prepared and evaluated in terms of physicochemical properties, mRNA encapsulation, platelet activation, and transfection efficiency. We found that varying the DOPC/cholesterol ratio was associated with differences in nanoparticle morphology, platelet responses, and delivery efficiency, with F3 showing the highest reporter expression among the five formulations tested. The optimized formulation enabled efficient expression of functional superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2) mRNA in platelets without inducing significant activation. Functional studies showed that SOD2 overexpression markedly reduced mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) and total ROS levels while preserving platelet ultrastructure and aggregation function. This study establishes a platelet-compatible LNP platform for functional mRNA delivery and provides new insights into the structure-activity relationship of LNP formulations in platelet gene delivery.

title: Microfluidic channel engineering for mRNA-LNPs: a systematic review of mixing strategies, nanostructures, and biological performance.
abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNPs) have revolutionized nucleic acid therapeutics, yet their clinical success relies heavily on precise manufacturing processes. This review comprehensively explores the critical intersection between microfluidic channel design, lipid self-assembly biophysics, and the subsequent biological performance of mRNA-LNPs. First, we analyze the fundamental fluid mechanics driving representative microfluidic mixers, elucidating how different channel architectures dictate solvent exchange rates and nanoparticle assembly kinetics. We then systematically examine how these specific mixing regimes modulate essential physicochemical characteristics, including lipid distribution, internal nanostructure, particle morphology, size distribution, and overall colloidal stability. Crucially, we bridge the gap between manufacturing and pharmacology by evaluating how mixing-induced physicochemical differences directly translate into distinct biological outcomes, such as cellular uptake mechanisms, endosomal escape efficiency, and systemic pharmacokinetics. By integrating microfluidic engineering principles with biological evaluation, this review provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how continuous-flow assembly processes program the functional behavior of mRNA-LNP systems. Ultimately, we highlight emerging design principles essential for developing the next generation of robust, highly efficient nucleic acid delivery platforms.

title: Translational nanotechnology for precision gene therapy delivery systems.
abstract: Gene therapy is one of the breakthrough strategies for treating genetically acquired and complicated disorders owing to its potential in regulating the expression of genes precisely. Nevertheless, the success of any gene therapy will depend upon the development of a safe and efficient system for gene delivery. Nanotechnology has brought about great changes in the field of non-viral gene delivery systems by providing carriers that increase stability, facilitate cellular uptake, allow endosomal escape, and have tissue specificity without causing systemic toxicity. This review examines the basic concepts underlying the design of nanocarriers for the delivery of plasmid DNA, mRNA, siRNA, and the CRISPR-Cas genome editing system. The current review provides an overview of different viral and non-viral delivery platforms for plasmid DNA, mRNA, siRNA, and CRISPR-Cas genome editing systems. The discussion focuses on adenoviral, adeno-associated viral, lentiviral, retroviral, herpes simplex viral and virus-like particle delivery platforms, as well as non-viral nanocarriers. The review further highlights clinically validated examples, such as liposomal nanoparticles used for the delivery of RNA-based therapies and discusses some of the translational challenges that still exist in terms of transfection efficiency, long-term safety issues, manufacturability at a large scale, and regulatory acceptance. Finally, some of the latest trends in gene delivery, such as artificial intelligence-assisted nanoparticle design, smart multi-responsive nanoparticles, and personalized nanomedicine, have been outlined as the most important driving forces in developing the next generation of gene delivery technologies.

title: Nano-amorphous dispersions with microenvironmental stabilization enable sustained niclosamide solubilization.
abstract: Niclosamide suffers from poor oral bioavailability due to acid-induced precipitation and colloidal instability. We developed a nano-stabilized amorphous solid dispersion using PVP-VA and MgO, which maintained supersaturation, suppressed precipitation, and enhanced oral absorption. The formulation improved dissolution (>3-fold) and significantly increased systemic exposure and plasma half-life in mice.

title: Orthogonal ensemble and single-particle characterisation of antisense oligonucleotide lipid nanoparticles.
abstract: Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) remain underexplored relative to siRNA and mRNA LNPs. Using an orthogonal workflow (DLS, NTA, AF4), we show that ionisable lipid identity and microfluidic flow rate govern key LNP attributes. Replacing SM-102 with MC3 increased size and reduced ASO recovery, while lower flow rates increased LNP size and improved recovery, highlighting formulation-property relationships for ASO LNP optimisation.

title: Ultrasensitive endogenous miRNA imaging in live cells by an allosteric orthogonal CRISPR probe.
abstract: Sensitive and multiplexed visualization of endogenous RNA in living cells remains challenging because of insufficient signal amplification, background activation, and interference between parallel readout pathways, particularly for low-abundance regulatory RNAs. Many current CRISPR-based RNA imaging strategies rely on stoichiometric RNA binding, limiting sensitivity and often yielding a poor signal-to-background ratio for low-abundance endogenous microRNAs (miRNAs). Moreover, limited orthogonality between sensing modules and readouts complicates interference-free multiplexing. Inefficient intracellular delivery further limits their applicability in complex biological environments. Here, we introduce an allosteric CRISPR probe for orthogonal and amplified miRNA imaging in living cells, which is built on an allosterically gated crRNA that integrates a CRISPR-Cas12a system with a Zn2+-dependent DNAzyme module. Mechanistically, miR-210 selectively unlocks the caged crRNA to activate Cas12a trans-cleavage, providing amplified red (Cy5) fluorescence, while miR-21 independently activates DNAzyme cleavage to generate green (FAM) fluorescence with minimal cross-talk. Black phosphorus nanosheets serve as a biocompatible nanocarrier for efficient intracellular probe delivery. This orthogonal architecture enables precise discrimination of breast cancer subtypes in living cells and clinical tissue sections. Together, this work overcomes a central limitation of live-cell miRNA imaging by enabling sensitive and multiplexed visualization of endogenous miRNAs, opening new possibilities for dissecting RNA-mediated regulation in complex cellular systems.

title: A targeting delivery platform for the mapping of responses to p53-independent intervention in heterogeneous patient cancer cells.
abstract: Developing new cancer therapeutic strategies has become a central focus in precision oncology. However, a major challenge is the lack of robust models to accurately assess target vulnerability in patient-specific heterogeneous cancer cells, which limits the translation of research findings into effective clinical therapies. In this study, we developed an ex vivo blood-based model utilizing a versatile nano-delivery platform to evaluate the responsiveness of MDM2 knockout as a representative therapeutic approach in circulating malignant cells (CMCs) from patients stratified by their p53 status. In our genome editing plasmid delivery system (p@RPA), protamine sulfate was combined with a cell-penetrating peptide to condense the CRISPR-Cas9 plasmid into nano-cores. These nano-cores were then coated with chondroitin sulfate shells functionalized with the AS1411 aptamer, enabling the selective recognition of CD44 and/or nucleolin overexpressing malignant cells. Using the same vector, a molecular beacon delivery system (MBs@RPA) co-loaded with MBMDM2 for probing MDM2 mRNA, MBTP53 for probing TP53 mRNA and MBTP73 for probing TP73 mRNA was constructed for the in situ evaluation of biomarker changes induced by genome editing. p@RPA demonstrates satisfactory efficacy in mediating gene editing for MDM2 knockout in malignant cells. Notably, the knockout of MDM2 induces cell cycle arrest and leads to a marked upregulation of anti-tumor TAp73 irrespective of their p53 status. With efficient gene editing and mRNA probing achieved in patient-derived CMCs, we establish an ex vivo platform capable of in situ therapeutic efficacy assessment at single-cell resolution to explicitly reveal the underlying cellular heterogeneity across individual CMCs.

title: Rational design of polycationic, biodegradable nanogels for intracellular siRNA delivery to microglia.
abstract: Targeted modulation of microglial activation with siRNA in neuroinflammatory diseases presents a compelling therapeutic strategy by enabling precise gene silencing while preserving beneficial immune responses. However, the immune-sensitive nature of microglia creates unique barriers to safe and efficient siRNA delivery. Dual pH- and redox-responsive polycationic nanogels with tunable molecular architectures are developed to overcome these barriers, enabling spatiotemporal delivery and intracellular degradation. Varying hydrophilic and hydrophobic monomer ratios tunes nanogel molecular architecture to control particle size, pH-responsive behavior, and therapeutic release. Disulfide crosslinkers enable selective degradation of polymer networks into fragments at intracellular glutathione levels, enabling controlled release and intracellular degradation. Increased hydrophobic composition yields smaller hydrodynamic size, optimal pH swelling profile for endosomal escape, and surface charge shifts that balance membrane disruption and biocompatibility. Degradation studies confirm redox-responsive crosslinks selective fragmentation at intracellular glutathione levels. Systematic siRNA loading studies demonstrate electrostatic interactions dominate, achieving high loading efficiency. Release studies mimicking intracellular environmental shifts confirm the spatiotemporal siRNA delivery from dual-responsive nanogels. Nanogels demonstrate first-pass cytocompatibility (MTS and LDH assays) with microglia at therapeutic concentrations. Both formulations achieve intracellular accumulation of carboxyfluorescein (FAM)-labelled siRNA in microglia, with higher efficacy for the more hydrophobic formulation. Future work will investigate the platform's innate immune response in microglia and functional knockdown of disease-relevant genes with target specific siRNA to modulate microglia's neuroinflammatory response. Collectively, these dual-responsive nanogels provide a foundational rational design framework for vectors that balance biosafety and delivery efficacy for siRNA therapies to microglia for targeting neuroinflammation.
