title: The Therapeutic Pipeline: Future Treatments and Precision Medicine.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: rare interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) represent a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by various pathogenic mechanisms, clinical presentations, prognoses, and therapeutic challenges. Among these, acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (ASMD), pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (PLCH) exemplify rare pulmonary diseases driven by distinct biological mechanisms, including lysosomal dysfunction, impaired surfactant homeostasis, and activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK) pathways. Recent advancements in molecular biology, genomics, and translational research boosted the development of precision medicine strategies and disease-specific therapies for these conditions.
STUDY DESIGN: this narrative review was conducted in accordance with the SANRA guidelines. A thorough literature search of the PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus databases was performed from January 2000 to June 2026.
RESULTS: significant progress has been made in treating all three diseases. In ASMD, enzyme replacement therapy with olipudase alfa has greatly improved visceral and lung symptoms, while research in gene therapy, gene editing, and metabolic treatments is ongoing. For PAP, inhaled granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) is now the primary disease-specific treatment, now supported by phase III trial evidence for inhaled molgramostim, complemented by potential therapies such as immunomodulation, macrophage transplantation, and gene-based strategies. In PLCH, the discovery of recurrent MAPK pathway variants has supported the use of genotype-targeted treatments with BRAF and MEK inhibitors. Under these conditions, advances in molecular diagnostics, circulating biomarkers, quantitative HRCT, radiomics, and artificial intelligence (AI) are poised to enhance diagnosis, patient stratification, prognosis, and treatment decisions.
CONCLUSIONS: ASMD, PAP and PLCH are entering into an era of precision medicine, in which disease-specific molecular mechanisms play an increasing role in guiding diagnosis and treatment. Ongoing integration of genomics, biomarkers, advanced imaging, AI, and targeted therapies could revolutionise the management of conditions such as ASMD, PAP, and PLCH, leading to better long-term patient outcomes.

title: Extended Analyses of Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a).
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pelacarsen is an antisense oligonucleotide that reduces serum levels of lipoprotein(a). In a randomized placebo-controlled trial in patients with established cardiovascular disease, pelacarsen did not reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared to placebo. We further investigated the association of pelacarsen treatment with cardiovascular outcomes.
METHODS: We report the association of pelacarsen treatment with a primary composite end point of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization. Analyses included on-treatment, uninterrupted treatment, total primary end point events (first and recurrent events), landmark analyses classified by changes in and achieved lipoprotein(a) at 3 months, and key subgroups including baseline lipoprotein(a), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP), and time from qualifying event to enrollment.
RESULTS: For participants on treatment, a primary end point occurred in 434 participants (10.4%) randomly assigned to placebo and 380 participants (9.1%) assigned to pelacarsen (hazard ratio, 0.98; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.85 to 1.12). When evaluating participants with uninterrupted treatment, a primary end point event occurred in 167 participants (11.0%) in the pelacarsen group and 204 participants (10.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.89 to 1.34). When evaluating total primary end point events, there were 644 events in the pelacarsen group and 646 events in the placebo group (rate ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.14). In landmark analyses evaluating participants alive and free of the composite end point at 3 months, when compared to placebo there was no association between pelacarsen treatment and the primary end point either in participants with reduction in lipoprotein(a) greater than or equal to the median (170 nmol/l) (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.92 to 1.29) or in participants who achieved lipoprotein(a) lower than or equal to the median (69.5 nmol/l) (hazard ratio, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.93 to 1.29). There was also no association between pelacarsen treatment and the primary end point in any of the evaluated key subgroups including classification by median baseline lipoprotein(a), LDL cholesterol, high-sensitivity CRP, or time from qualifying cardiovascular disease to enrollment.
CONCLUSIONS: Pelacarsen was not associated with a reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events when evaluated by treatment exposure, changes in or achieved lipoprotein(a) levels at 3 months, considering total events, or within subgroups of baseline lipoprotein(a), LDL cholesterol, or high-sensitivity CRP levels.

title: Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a).
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide, reduces serum levels of lipoprotein(a). However, the effect of pelacarsen on cardiovascular outcomes remains uncertain.
METHODS: We conducted an international, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease and a lipoprotein(a) level of at least 70 mg per deciliter. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous pelacarsen (80 mg) administered monthly or matching placebo. The primary end point was a major adverse cardiovascular event, defined as a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization.
RESULTS: A total of 8350 patients underwent randomization, with 8322 included in the efficacy analysis; 4157 patients were assigned to receive pelacarsen, and 4165 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 59.7 years, and 27.0% were women. The median lipoprotein(a) level at baseline was 236 nmol per liter. At 12 months, the lipoprotein(a) level was 64.4 nmol per liter in the pelacarsen group and 233.4 nmol per liter in the placebo group. The median follow-up was 4.7 years. A primary end-point event occurred in 511 patients (12.3%) in the pelacarsen group and in 503 (12.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90 to 1.15, P = 0.76). Among patients with a baseline lipoprotein(a) level of at least 90 mg per deciliter, a primary end-point event occurred in 402 of 3266 patients (12.3%) in the pelacarsen group and in 403 of 3274 (12.3%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.15; P = 0.99). Serious adverse events occurred in 1553 of 4166 patients (37.3%) who received pelacarsen and in 1709 of 4154 (41.1%) who received placebo.
CONCLUSIONS: Pelacarsen did not result in a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events than placebo at a median follow-up of 4.7 years. (Funded by Novartis; Lp[a]HORIZON ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04023552.)See also in NEJM Evidence: Extended Analyses of Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a).

title: A genome-wide senescence synthetic lethality screen identifies PARP16 as a senolytic target.
abstract: Accumulation of senescent cells is increasingly viewed as a significant contributor to aging and age-related diseases. To date, the elimination of senescent cells through small molecule senolytic agents has largely relied on a limited number of repurposed agents, often leveraged from previous oncological applications. Here, we describe a CRISPR-based, genome-wide, synthetic lethal screen for senescent cells. From this screen, we identify a number of genes whose deletion appears to be well tolerated in normal proliferating cells, but whose deletion is lethal in the context of senescence. We further characterize one promising candidate gene encoding the ER-resident protein PARP16. Knockdown of PARP16 does not affect the viability of mouse or human cells but results in the death of a wide range of senescent cells. Furthermore, two distinct small molecule PARP16 inhibitors have little effect of normal cell growth but result in the selective death of senescent cells in culture and in freshly isolated human donor lung tissue explants. Together, these results demonstrate a rational strategy to identify novel senolytic therapies that could have potential applications for a wide range of age-related conditions.

title: T-cell clonality and TCR repertoire dynamics during germinal center responses: A comprehensive review of regulatory mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: T-cell receptors (TCRs) are pivotal for antigen recognition within germinal centers (GCs), which are essential for B-cell maturation and high-affinity antibody production. Although the role played by T follicular helper (Tfh) cells in supporting B cells is established, the mechanisms driving the expansion and maintenance of distinct T-cell clonotypes in the GC perifollicular region remain poorly understood. This review aims to synthesize current knowledge on the differentiation, migration, and clonal expansion of T cells within GCs, with emphasis on Tfh-B-cell interactions. Findings from immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, multiphoton microscopy, and CRISPR/Cas9-based approaches indicate that clonal expansion of T cells carrying defined TCR clonotypes is a regulated process driven by cognate Tfh-B-cell interactions. These interactions promote both B-cell affinity maturation and the concomitant selection and clonal expansion of T cells. The reviewed studies reveal that the TCR repertoire within the GC perifollicular region is refined over time, contributing to the development of long-lived memory and effector cells. The collective results underscore a dynamic reciprocity where T cells shape the antibody response while themselves undergoing antigen-driven selection. Key challenges include clarifying TCR signaling networks, improving in vivo analysis of cellular interactions, and identifying strategies to therapeutically modulate these processes without disrupting immune homeostasis. Overcoming these hurdles will require interdisciplinary approaches and the application of emerging technologies. Future research focused on these areas will be critical for advancing fundamental immunology and developing novel therapeutic strategies for vaccines, autoimmune diseases, and cancer.

title: Glycosylated hypoxic tumour-derived extracellular vesicles as a targeted siRNA delivery system to remodel the immunosuppressive microenvironment in pancreatic cancer.
abstract: N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-modified extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from hypoxic pancreatic cancer cells and loaded with annexin A2 (ANXA2) small interfering RNA (siRNA) were developed to modulate the immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME). Characterisation confirmed successful surface modification and efficient siRNA loading in EVs with a diameter of approximately 100-120 nm. In vitro, these engineered EVs inhibited pancreatic cancer cell proliferation, migration and invasion and promoted apoptosis. Additional cargo-matched comparison showed that GalNAc-modified hypoxic EVs carrying ANXA2 siRNA produced stronger ANXA2 silencing and more pronounced anti-migratory, anti-invasive and pro-apoptotic effects than unmodified hypoxic EVs carrying the same siRNA. In a xenograft model, treatment suppressed tumour growth and improved survival. Multi-omics and immune analyses suggested suppression of the PI3K/AKT signalling pathway and remodelling of the immunosuppressive TME, as reflected by increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration, reduced tissue-associated immunoreactivity for interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-10 (IL-10), and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and increased soluble interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), interleukin-2 (IL-2) and GM-CSF levels. These findings indicate that GalNAc-modified hypoxic EVs carrying ANXA2 siRNA can inhibit tumour progression and modulate the TME in pancreatic cancer, supporting their potential as a therapeutic delivery platform.

title: Advances in siRNA delivery for breast cancer therapy: from molecular design to therapeutic application.
abstract: Breast cancer progression is driven by molecular heterogeneity, drug resistance (DR), and interactions within the tumour microenvironment (TME), creating an urgent need for therapies that can selectively suppress disease-associated genes. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) can silence targets involved in tumour growth, treatment resistance, and immune evasion. Its therapeutic potential, however, depends on overcoming rapid degradation and clearance, limited tumour accumulation, poor cellular uptake, and endosomal entrapment. Lipid-based and polymer-mediated delivery systems (DS) protect siRNA and facilitate its transport, while chemical modifications, molecular conjugates, and physical delivery methods offer additional ways to improve stability or access to target cells. In BC models, these strategies have been investigated for targeted therapy, reversal of DR, and modulation of the TME to support antitumor immunity. Despite encouraging preclinical findings, effective tumour delivery, sustained gene silencing, off-target effects, and immune activation remain significant barriers to clinical translation. This review brings together advances in siRNA delivery and their applications against BC progression, DR, and immune evasion, while defining the barriers that must be overcome to translate effective gene silencing into meaningful clinical benefit.

title: Engineered Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) as Carriers for CRISPR/Cas9 Therapeutics: Recent Advances in Cargo Loading and Targeted Delivery.
abstract: The therapeutic potential of CRISPR/Cas genome editing has advanced the development of precision medicine; however, its clinical translation for many in vivo applications remains limited by challenges in achieving safe, efficient, and targeted delivery. Conventional viral vectors and synthetic nanocarriers are associated with challenges including immunogenicity, limited cargo capacity, prolonged nuclease expression, off-target effects, and manufacturing complexities. Engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) are being investigated as alternative delivery carriers due to their biological origin, capacity for cargo encapsulation, and opportunities for surface functionalization. However, their biocompatibility, immunogenicity, and ability to cross biological barriers depend on vesicle source, formulation, and experimental conditions. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in the design of engineered EVs for CRISPR/Cas delivery, with a particular focus on strategies to improve cargo loading, targeting specificity, and therapeutic efficacy. We discuss the advantages and limitations of different CRISPR cargo formats, including plasmid DNA, mRNA, and ribonucleoprotein complexes, together with endogenous and exogenous loading approaches, hybrid EV platforms, and methods for enhancing intracellular delivery. Advances in EV surface engineering through genetic, chemical, physical, and biomimetic modifications are highlighted as strategies being investigated to improve tissue-specific delivery and functional cargo transport. The review also highlights emerging research directions, including CRISPR-EV theranostic platforms and the application of artificial intelligence to enhance CRISPR-EV therapeutic systems. Finally, key translational challenges, including scalable production, EV heterogeneity, cargo-loading efficiency, biodistribution, regulatory standardization, and quality control, are critically discussed. EV-mediated CRISPR delivery remains at an early preclinical stage, with clinical safety and therapeutic efficacy yet to be established. Further advances in EV engineering, cargo-loading strategies, and manufacturing standardization are needed to support its potential clinical translation.

title: Antiviral nanoparticles: mechanisms, biomedical applications and clinical translation toward next-generation therapies.
abstract: Viral infections represent a major global health challenge due to the rapid emergence of new pathogens, increasing antiviral drug resistance and limited efficacy of traditional treatments against evolving viruses. Nanotechnology is a promising interdisciplinary approach to fighting viral diseases, which can perform direct viral inactivation, targeted drug delivery, immune modulation, vaccine development, rapid diagnostics, and prevention of infection. This review offers an in-depth and critical overview of the major antiviral nanoparticle platforms, including metallic, metal oxide, carbon-based, polymeric, lipid-based, and bio-inspired nanoparticles. In this article, we employ a comparative framework to systematically analyze classes of nanoparticles based on their physicochemical properties, molecular mechanisms of antiviral action, biomedical applications, and translational potential. Antiviral mechanisms are discussed within the framework of the viral life cycle, including the inhibition of viral attachment and entry, destruction of viral envelope and capsid integrity, suppression of intracellular viral replication, reactive oxygen species-mediated viral inactivation, immune-modulation, and nanoparticle-assisted therapeutic delivery. Moreover, the review critically discusses the increasing biomedical applications of antiviral nanoparticles in therapeutics, vaccine delivery, diagnostics, antiviral coatings, gene therapy and precision nanomedicine, while highlighting the clinically successful technologies such as lipid nanoparticle-based mRNA vaccines. Special attention is paid to the main obstacles in clinical translation, such as nanotoxicity, biodistribution, manufacturing scalability, regulatory challenges, and the lack of standard evaluation protocols. Finally, major knowledge gaps and future research priorities are highlighted, focusing on the design of multifunctional, clinically translatable and regulatory-compliant nanoplatforms. This review offers insights on antiviral nanomedicines and practical insights for the rational design and successful clinical translation of next-generation antiviral nanoparticle.

title: Engineering smart liposomes to combat antimicrobial resistance: from mechanistic design to clinical translation.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a critical global health threat, surpassing the pace of discovery and clinical development of new antimicrobial agents. Therefore, innovative therapeutic strategies are urgently needed to enhance antibiotic efficacy, overcome multidrug-resistant infections, and limit resistance development. Smart liposomal nanoplatforms have emerged as promising tools capable of improving antimicrobial therapy through targeted delivery, enhanced bacterial uptake, biofilm penetration, protection against enzymatic degradation, and controlled drug release.
AREAS COVERED: This review examines recent advances in the rational design of evolved liposomes, including stimuli-responsive and programmable systems, for combating resistant bacterial infections. It discusses their ability to improve pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles, overcome biological barriers, and enable precision antimicrobial delivery. Current translational challenges, including large-scale manufacturing, physicochemical characterization, regulatory requirements, and clinically relevant preclinical models, are critically evaluated. Emerging strategies, such as artificial intelligence-driven formulation optimization, continuous microfluidic manufacturing, multifunctional therapeutic platforms incorporating gene editing, and next-generation antibiotic-adjuvant combination strategies, are also explored.
EXPERT OPINION: Liposomal drug-delivery systems may improve the exposure, distribution, and intracellular or local delivery of antimicrobial agents, but improved delivery should not be equated with reversal of bacterial resistance. Successful clinical translation will depend on formulation- and infection-specific evidence, clinically relevant preclinical models, controlled and scalable manufacturing, and appropriate regulatory frameworks, while artificial intelligence, digital-twin, and precision-medicine approaches are best viewed as decision-support tools that complement experimental and clinical validation.

title: The Zα domain of ADAR1: emerging roles in cancer biology and evidence as a promising therapeutic target.
abstract: Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) has emerged as an important cancer dependency and suppressor of innate immunity. While early therapeutic strategies focused on global enzymatic inhibition, these approaches may compromise essential homeostatic functions of the constitutively expressed ADAR1-p110 isoform. Growing evidence highlights editing-independent functions uniquely mediated by the interferon-inducible ADAR1-p150 isoform. Through its conformation-specific Zα domain, ADAR1-p150 binds Z-nucleic acids and suppresses MDA5-, PKR-, and ZBP1-driven innate immune activation, thereby promoting tumor immune evasion and adaptation to inflammatory stress. Consequently, selectively disrupting this p150-mediated suppression may represent a more therapeutically tractable strategy than global ADAR1 inhibition, with the Zα domain providing a potentially selective mechanistic interface. This review synthesizes current understanding of Zα-mediated immune regulation, evaluates emerging domain-specific therapeutic approaches, and provides a comprehensive guide to the biophysical and cell-based assays used to interrogate Zα interactions, highlighting key mechanistic gaps that may inform future p150-selective translational interventions.

title: Exercise-induced lactylation in WDR41 initiates autophagy and improves fatty liver diseases.
abstract: Excess lipid accumulation and a sedentary lifestyle are associated with metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD), but the causal mechanisms and preventive methods are not fully understood. Macroautophagy/autophagy is a lysosomal degradation pathway robustly induced by exercise and plays a key role in lipid metabolism. Understanding the mechanisms by which exercise activates autophagy and elicits metabolic benefits in the liver will provide important insights into the pathogenesis of MAFLD. Here, we discovered negative correlations between expression and lactylation of WDR41 (WD repeat domain 41) and pathogenesis of a series of human hepatic metabolic diseases. We found that WDR41 was a pro-autophagy protein that underwent lactylation in response to autophagy-inducing conditions, such as exercise. WDR41 was lactylated at lysine 319 (K319), a modification facilitated by LDHA (lactate dehydrogenase A) upon autophagy induction, and delactylated by SIRT2 (sirtuin 2). Lactylated WDR41 promoted autophagy initiation by directly interacting with the autophagy proteins ATG13 (autophagy related 13) and RB1CC1/FIP200 (RB1 inducible coiled-coil 1) and driving the ULK1 (unc-51 like autophagy activating kinase 1) complex assembly. Physiologically, WDR41 and WDR41K319 lactylation, were important for exercise-induced improvements in insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism against excess lipid accumulation in the liver. title: Dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR delivery systems for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma.
abstract: Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy, and effective gene therapy remains limited by ocular barriers, tumor heterogeneity, and inefficient nucleic acid delivery. This review critically analyses the molecular rationale, engineering principles, emerging nanoarchitectures, biological validation, and translational prospects of dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR delivery systems for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma. The manuscript also highlights key challenges and future strategies for clinical implementation. Current evidence indicates that dual-vector platforms enable independent optimization of mRNA and CRISPR cargos while maintaining coordinated spatiotemporal therapeutic activity. We conducted a literature search in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for relevant studies published from January 2015 to September 2026. Functional cargo partitioning, vector modularity, programmable intracellular trafficking, and ocular-targeted nanoengineering improve delivery precision and reduce biological compromise associated with co-encapsulation. Lipid, polymeric, hybrid, biomimetic, and viral-nonviral architectures each provide distinct engineering advantages depending on therapeutic objectives. Preclinical studies support enhanced genome editing, transient protein restoration, improved tumor suppression, and reduced off-target effects. Nevertheless, manufacturing scalability, regulatory standardization, long-term safety, and clinical validation remain major barriers to translation. Dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR systems represent a promising next-generation platform for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma by enabling coordinated and programmable therapeutic delivery. Continued advances in modular nanoengineering, personalized cargo selection, and clinically scalable manufacturing will be essential for successful translation into precision ocular oncology.

title: Cytokine networks in the tumor microenvironment: nanotherapeutic modulation of immune-cell communication and signaling networks.
abstract: Cancer remains a leading global mortality cause, driven by complex interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) that facilitate progression, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance. Cytokines form the central regulatory network governing TME intercellular communication, exerting highly context-dependent pro- and anti-tumorigenic effects. Dysregulated cytokine signaling drives chronic inflammation and immunosuppression, limiting durable therapeutic responses. While cytokine-based immunotherapies show clinical potential, their widespread use is hindered by poor stability, rapid clearance, limited specificity, and dose-limiting toxicities. Advances in nanomedicine offer innovative solutions by improving cytokine pharmacokinetics, tumor-selective delivery, and spatiotemporally controlled release. Beyond passive delivery, engineered nanoplatforms act as active modulators of the tumor immune ecosystem, remodeling cytokine networks to restore antitumor immunity. Nanotechnology interventions effectively regulate key signaling pathways- including JAK/STAT, TGF-β/SMAD, NF-κB, MAPK/ERK, and PI3K/AKT- disrupting pathological feedback mechanisms and crosstalk. Furthermore, localized cytokine delivery, gene silencing, mRNA therapeutics, and CRISPR-enabled genome engineering are expanding precision immunotherapy. Despite significant translational challenges such as tumor heterogeneity, biological barriers, immunogenicity, and manufacturing complexity emerging biomimetic and personalized nanoplatforms offer promising avenues for precise immune modulation and biomarker-guided patient stratification. Literature searches were conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect (with Google Scholar for citation tracking) covering peer-reviewed publications from 2003 to 2026.

title: Paving the way for translational relevance in advanced therapies in Brazil: conference report from SBINT 2025.
abstract: The 2nd Symposium on Pharmaceutical Bioengineering and Nanobiotechnology Applied to Advanced Therapies (SBINT 2025) was held in Goiânia, Brazil, under the theme "Challenges in preclinical evaluation: paving the way to translational relevance of advanced therapies." The meeting brought together approximately 150 participants from academia, industry, clinical institutions and regulatory agencies to discuss scientific, technological and regulatory barriers shaping advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs) in Brazil. Keynote lectures addressed human-relevant bioengineered platforms, organ-on-a-chip and microphysiological systems, regenerative biomaterials, extracellular vesicle-based therapies, nanobiotechnology-enabled nucleic acid delivery, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based genome and epigenome editing, and the Brazilian regulatory framework for ATMPs. The discussions highlighted the need for predictive preclinical models capable of capturing human-specific mechanisms, as conventional animal models may have limited translational value for personalized cell, gene and tissue-engineered products. Regulatory and roundtable sessions emphasized risk-based assessment, Good Manufacturing Practice-compatible infrastructure, product characterization, traceability, and the development of national biotechnological raw materials, analytical services and vector production capacity. Overall, SBINT 2025 underscored Brazil's scientific maturity and structural bottlenecks in regenerative medicine, highlighting the importance of coordinated action among academia, industry, clinical centers, regulators and funding agencies to support ATMP translation in Latin America.

title: Natural and engineered bacteriophages against multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens: current landscape and clinical translation.
abstract: The worldwide emergence of antimicrobial resistance and the need for non-conventional alternatives to conventional antibiotics have been increased by multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens, which cause the majority of nosocomial infections and are starting to develop resistance to even the most potent drugs. Engineered bacteriophages are promising precision antimicrobials because of their ability to selectively infect and lyse bacterial hosts, multiply at infection sites, and co-evolve with bacterial populations to overcome resistance. Advances in synthetic biology, such as tail fiber modification, depolymerase and endolysin enhancement, genome editing using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), and computationally designed phage cocktails, have opened new possibilities for therapeutics that were hindered by the limitations of natural phages. These engineering strategies expand host range, enhance biofilm penetration, and target resistance genes. In spite of promising evidence in preclinical models, the use of engineered phages in routine clinical practice remains difficult. Specific key challenges include unclear regulations, lack of good manufacturing practice (GMP)grade production, variable pharmacokinetics and limited clinical trial data. This review critically examines engineering approaches to improve phage activity against ESKAPE pathogens, identifies the scientific and regulatory barriers limiting clinical use, and outlines the key steps needed for wider adoption.

title: Synthetic mRNA engineering beyond prophylactic infectious disease vaccines: epigenomic and molecular reprogramming of diseased cells.
abstract: The clinical validation of mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines in 2020-2021 accelerated the development of synthetic messenger RNA as a precision therapeutic platform beyond infectious disease prevention. Unlike gene therapy approaches that permanently modify genomic DNA, synthetic mRNA enables transient protein expression through programmable molecular engineering. This narrative review examines therapeutic applications of engineered mRNA, emphasizing its epigenomic potential. It discusses key engineering strategies, including nucleoside modifications, codon optimization, untranslated region engineering, cap chemistry, and advances in lipid nanoparticle and alternative delivery systems. Six therapeutic domains are explored: cancer immunotherapy, cardiac regeneration, monogenic diseases, genome and epigenome editing, autoimmune disease, and somatic cell reprogramming. Particular attention is given to mRNA-mediated replacement of chromatin regulators, dCas9-based epigenome editing, epigenetically derived tumor antigens, and transcription-factor-driven cellular reprogramming. The review distinguishes chemical nucleoside modifications from endogenous epitranscriptomic regulation and examines the differences between transient protein expression, heritable but reversible chromatin changes, and permanent genomic modifications. Clinical evidence, discontinued programs, and preclinical developments are critically evaluated. Despite promising advances, major challenges remain regarding delivery specificity, durability, safety, and clinical translation. Overall, synthetic mRNA represents an emerging platform for molecular and epigenetic therapeutic reprogramming beyond vaccination.

title: Macrophage-directed immunotherapy in Inflammatory bowel disease: advances in reprogramming intestinal phagocytes.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorder characterized by dysregulation of the intestinal immune system, in which functional abnormalities of phagocytes such as macrophages play a critical role in pathogenesis. Although conventional therapies such as anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) antibodies are widely used in clinical practice, they have limitations including low response rates and significant side effects, creating an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies. In recent years, macrophage-directed immunotherapy has emerged as a cutting-edge approach for IBD treatment by reprogramming intestinal phagocytes to restore immune homeostasis. Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on the M1/M2 polarization framework, this review integrates recent single-cell discoveries of novel macrophage subsets (e.g. SPP1+ and TREM2+ macrophages), systematically examines the crosstalk among signaling, epigenetic, and metabolic regulatory layers, and critically evaluates translational barriers from preclinical models to clinical application. By evaluating preclinical and clinical studies, we assess the potential and challenges of these strategies. Through in-depth analysis, this review aims to provide a theoretical basis for the development of more precise and effective immunotherapies for IBD and to point out future research directions. (Literature search: PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase; January 2000-December 2025.).

title: Mathematical modeling in mRNA therapeutics: towards a pathway to individualized treatment protocols.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) therapeutics represent a transformative pharmacological paradigm in which the delivery vehicle, genetic payload, and expressed protein form a tightly coupled system. This multicomponent structure introduces nonlinear, multiscale dynamics that challenge traditional pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic frameworks, making quantitative modeling essential.
AREAS COVERED: This review provides a structured biological framework for mRNA-LNP therapeutics, detailing the key processes governing delivery, endosomal escape, mRNA stability, and translation, and highlighting their associated temporal and spatial scales, providing the key aspects to consider for modeling. Building on this foundation, we summarize mathematical modeling approaches, including pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK), and quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) models, used to represent these mechanisms. The literature was surveyed to identify representative preclinical and translational studies, focusing on model structure, assumptions, and their use in human projection and dose optimization.
EXPERT OPINION: Mathematical models are increasingly critical to interpret and predict mRNA therapeutic behavior, yet challenges remain in parameter identifiability, data availability, and model standardization. Future advances will depend on biologically grounded modeling frameworks, improved integration of mechanistic insight with quantitative approaches, and tighter coupling between experimental design and model development. These developments will support more efficient translation and enable precision medicine applications.

title: Engineered bacteriophages as precision antimicrobials against multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens: molecular engineering strategies, clinical translation, and the crystallizing global regulatory landscape.
abstract: The global antimicrobial resistance crisis, driven primarily by the ESKAPE pathogen consortium has catalyzed the translation of engineered bacteriophage therapeutics from experimental platforms to clinical-stage precision medicines. Unlike their wild-type counterparts, which are constrained by narrow host ranges, susceptibility to reticuloendothelial clearance, and limited biofilm penetrability, synthetically engineered phages exploit receptor-binding protein remodeling, phage-derived enzymatic depolymerases, CRISPR-Cas3 chromosomal shredding payloads, sequence-independent SASPject delivery vectors, and in vivo microbiome base editors to overcome the multilayered resistance arsenals of MDR ESKAPE organisms. Recent clinical development has generated human evidence across both genetically engineered phage platforms and advanced fixed phage-cocktails. Engineered programmes include CRISPR-Cas3-based LBP-EC01 and SNIPR001, while AP-SA02 represents an analytically characterized fixed multi-phage cocktail targeting Staphylococcus aureus. This review examines engineering strategies, pharmacokinetics, immune-mediated clearance, delivery challenges, clinical evidence, manufacturing, and regulatory pathways. It also discusses emerging regulatory approaches and distinctions between natural and genetically modified phage products. The literature search was conducted from January-June 2026 using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, supplemented by searches of ClinicalTrials.gov and the websites of the US-FDA and EMA. Overall, this review evaluates the translational potential of engineered phages, identifies barriers to clinical adoption, and considers future developments in precision antimicrobial therapy against multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: RIG-I is essential for radiation-induced IFN-β production and PD-L1/PD-L2 upregulation in HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells.
abstract: The RIG-I pathway, a key component of the innate immune system that classically detects cytosolic viral RNA, has also been implicated in regulating tumor cell viability, radiosensitivity, and patient survival across multiple cancer types. However, these effects appear to be context-dependent and partly contradictory. Whether radiotherapy modulates tumor-intrinsic RIG-I signaling in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) depending on HPV status, and whether such modulation is associated with changes in the tumor immune phenotype, remains unknown. Four human HNSCC cell lines (two HPV-negative and two HPV-positive), along with siRNA-mediated RIG-I knockdown and a CRISPR/Cas9-generated RIG-I knockout derivative, were treated with radiotherapy. Tumor cells were analyzed for their immune phenotype, including RIG-I expression via Western blot and flow cytometry, IFN-β secretion via ELISA, and PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression via flow cytometry. Radiotherapy, dose- and fraction-dependent, induced the upregulation of RIG-I expression and IFN-β secretion from HPV-negative HNSCC cells. The knockdown and knockout of the RIG-I-encoding gene DDX58 in the HPV-negative cell line HSC4 minimized both IFN-β secretion and PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression. These effects could be replicated by pre-exposing HPV-negative cell lines to the RIG-I inhibitor RIG012 before irradiation. Interestingly, HPV-positive cells showed less radiotherapy-mediated modulation of RIG-I and of the tumor cell phenotype of immune-related surface markers and showed no significant reaction to the inhibitor treatment. The previously unrecognized RIG-I-IFN-β axis is a central regulator of RT-induced immune checkpoint modulation for HPV-negative HNSCC. These results provide new opportunities to reshape the immune response following RT in HNSCC.

title: ADAR-mediated RNA editing of Influenza A virus genomes may be age-dependent and inversely correlates with viral load.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Seasonal influenza epidemics cause significant mortality, especially among the elderly. Influenza A virus triggers the host innate immune system through various mechanisms. Human enzymes belonging to the group of RNA-acting adenosine deaminases (ADARs) play a role in the innate antiviral immune response, partly by inducing mutations in viral RNA. The effect of this mechanismin influenza A virus infection remains unexplained in humans.
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to assess the clinical impact of ADAR-induced mutations on influenza A virus in hospitalised patients.
METHODS: Full-genome deep sequencing of Influenza A virus was performed on respiratory samples from 75 hospitalised, Influenza A(H3N2) virus infected patients, aged 41 to 95 years. ADAR-associated mutations in minor viral subpopulations were analysed in relation to demographic and clinical factors.
RESULTS: ADAR-associated mutations showed a significant inverse correlation with viral load (p < 0.0001) and age (p = 0.0051), especially in patients older than 75 years. The association between ADAR-associated mutations and viral load was independent of age, inflammation, and disease severity (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: We found an association between ADAR-induced mutations and viral load, which may indicate an antiviral function of ADAR on influenza A virus. The lower mutation rate and associated higher viral load in the elderly suggest an age-dependent reduced ADAR activity, which may contribute to increased disease severity.

title: The complete chloroplast genome of the Korean endemic fern Hypodematium angustifolium C.S. Lee & K.H. Lee (Hypodematiaceae).
abstract: Hypodematium angustifolium, a fern species endemic to Korea, has no reported genomic characteristics or phylogenetic position. In this study, the complete chloroplast genome of H. angustifolium was assembled and characterized: 150,022 bp in length with a typical quadripartite structure. Overall, 128 genes were identified (87 protein-coding genes (PCGs), eight ribosomal RNAs, and 33 transfer RNAs). Additionally, 73 RNA editing sites were predicted. Phylogenetic analysis based on 84 PCGs showed that H. angustifolium was clearly distinguishable from H. crenatum. These genomic data provide a resource for future phylogenetic and evolutionary studies of Hypodematium.

title: Pulmonary Ionocytes Regulate CFTR-Mediated Chloride Transport in Human iPSC-Derived Epithelium.
abstract:
RATIONALE: Pulmonary ionocytes, representing approximately 1% of airway epithelial cells, exhibit high CFTR expression and unique transcriptional markers, including FOXI1, ASCL3, and V-ATPase. Their exact role in human airway physiology is incompletely understood.
OBJECTIVE: This study employs induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived airway epithelial models (iPSC-airways) to elucidate the role of FOXI1 in pulmonary ionocyte differentiation and function.
METHODS: CRISPR-Cas9 was used to generate FOXI1-knockout iPSCs, into which a doxycycline-inducible FOXI1-overexpression cassette was introduced. Edited and control lines were differentiated into airway epithelia to evaluate ionocyte formation, epithelial composition, and ion transport. Rescue studies assessed the effects of FOXI1 re-expression in a FOXI1-KO background, and the addition of inducible WT-CFTR ionocytes to F508del/F508del cystic fibrosis (CF) cultures on restoring chloride transport.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: FOXI1 deletion abolishes ionocyte formation and alters airway epithelial composition, with increased mucus-secreting goblet cells and decreased ciliated cells. Functional assays confirmed ionocytes as key regulators of chloride homeostasis, with FOXI1-deficient airways displaying diminished ion transport. Induction of FOXI1-overexpression restored CFTR-mediated chloride transport. Introduction of WT ionocytes into CF airway models rescued chloride transport deficits, with no rescue observed in vehicle-treated controls lacking ionocyte induction.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings highlight FOXI1's essential role in pulmonary ionocyte development, airway cell composition, and airway chloride transport. We present a fully manipulable, gene-edited iPSC-derived system that enables investigation of ionocyte biology and function within a human airway context, highlighting them as promising therapeutic targets for respiratory disorders.

title: RNA-binding proteins as emerging regulators in interstitial lung diseases.
abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are emerging as critical post-transcriptional regulators that control multiple stages of RNA life cycle, thereby linking post-transcriptional programs to cellular function. Increasing evidence implicates dysregulated RBP-RNA interactions in key pathological mechanisms underlying interstitial lung diseases (ILDs), including epithelial injury, fibroblast activation, immune dysregulation and impaired tissue repair. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), cytoplasmic retention of the RBP Fused in Sarcoma (FUS) in patient derived fibroblasts is associated with preferential binding to profibrotic transcripts, while antisense oligonucleotide mediated suppression of FUS attenuates fibrotic signaling and enhances epithelial regenerative programs in cellular, ex vivo and 3D models. Emerging findings across ILD subtypes suggest that RBP dysregulation may represent a broader post-transcriptional phenomenon. Here, we review the principles governing RBP-RNA interactions, approaches for identifying and measuring these interactions and the links between RBPs, aging and lung pathology. We further discuss the emerging role of RBPs as post-transcriptional orchestrators of ILD pathogenesis and consider their potential as therapeutic targets.

title: PrEditR: a protein-centric platform for CRISPR-mediated base editor sgRNA design.
abstract:
MOTIVATION: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are critical to protein activity, yet the biological role of most known modification sites remains uncharacterized. CRISPR-mediated phenotypic screens using base editors offer a powerful approach to dissecting PTM function at scale. However, existing single-guide RNA (sgRNA) design tools for base editing applications are DNA-centric and lack the throughput required to integrate seamlessly with mass-spectrometry-based proteomics experimental outputs.
RESULTS: We introduce protein editing in R, PrEditR, an open-source, protein-centric tool for high-throughput sgRNA design for custom base editor screens. PrEditR enables users to designate specific amino acid residues in proteins and design protospacer sequences that target the corresponding gene and annotate every resulting amino acid change (missense, nonsense, or silent), including bystander edits.
AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: PrEditR is available on GitHub and Docker Hub.

title: PRIDA: Cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction based on biological language models and conditional domain-adversarial learning.
abstract:
MOTIVATION: The interaction between RNA and proteins is a complex process that involves atom-level details and dynamic changes. Accurate prediction of protein-RNA interactions helps researchers to develop protein-targeted small nucleic acid drugs. However, the scarcity of protein-RNA complexes and experimental data limits the ability of existing data-driven supervised learning methods to learn latent patterns, leading to limited performance.
RESULTS: In this study, we propose PRIDA (Protein-RNA Interaction prediction based on Domain-Adversarial learning), a protein-RNA interaction framework that combines bilinear attention with conditional domain-adversarial learning. Powered by pretrained protein and RNA language models, PRIDA improves interaction prediction under protein-level distribution shifts and limited labeled data. By integrating PRIDA with Monte Carlo Tree Search, we apply it to a virtual screening pipeline to generate RNA aptamer candidates for specific target proteins. Experimental results show that PRIDA achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction and provides effective guidance for RNA aptamer virtual screening.
AVAILABILITY: The data and source code of the proposed method are available at GitHub (https://github.com/zhouyyang/PRIDA) and Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/23644677).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Redirecting full-length FLT1 expression towards its soluble isoform by targeting alternative polyadenylation promotes postischaemic angiogenesis.
abstract:
AIMS: Vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGFs) and their endothelial tyrosine kinase receptors are crucial mediators of vasculogenesis and angiogenesis, with FLT1 (VEGFR1) acting as a decoy receptor for VEGFs. Alternative polyadenylation (APA) of Flt1 transcripts produces a truncated mRNA transcript encoding soluble (s) FLT1, which contains only the extracellular ligand-binding domain. The relative roles of full-length (fl) FLT1 and sFLT1 in angiogenesis are incompletely understood. Alternative polyadenylation is an important post-transcriptional mechanism of gene regulation that is increasingly recognized to affect the expression of many genes related to cardiovascular diseases. However, there are no in vivo models available to target APA and to examine the physiological roles of gene isoforms.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We here generated mice by introducing silent mutations into the Flt1 exon 13/intron 13 5' splice site through homology-directed repair with CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. Embryonic development, postnatal retinal vascular development, and reparative angiogenesis were evaluated in models of hindlimb ischaemia and myocardial infarction, complemented by assessments of cardiac functional recovery and cell phenotypes through snRNAseq, as well as in vitro assays examining endothelial cell phenotype and function. The introduction of specific splice site mutations within Flt1 to activate APA led to a complete loss of flFLT1 and an increase in sFLT1 expression. Using this mouse model, we demonstrate that sFLT1 alone is sufficient for developmental vasculogenesis, whereas the specific loss of flFLT1 enhances reparative revascularization and angiogenesis and improves cardiac recovery after myocardial infarction.
CONCLUSION: Our findings show that APA can be effectively targeted to modulate FLT1 isoform expression in vivo. Our mouse model may help to understand diseases driven by an imbalance in FLT1 isoform expression. Given the widespread presence of APA signals, our approach could furthermore serve as a model for studying the function of other truncated gene isoforms.

title: Baseline characteristics of patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy in the CARDIO-TTRansform trial of eplontersen.
abstract:
AIMS: Eplontersen is an antisense oligonucleotide that suppresses hepatic production of circulating transthyretin (TTR) by targeting TTR mRNA. We present baseline data from an ongoing trial, CARDIO-TTRansform, evaluating eplontersen in patients with TTR amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) and compare findings across previous ATTR-CM trials.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We evaluated 1432 patients enrolled in CARDIO-TTRansform from March 2020 to July 2023 who received ≥1 dose of study intervention (eplontersen or placebo) and had ≥1 post-baseline measurement. Mean (standard deviation) age was 76.4 (7.1) years; 9.4% were female; 88.8% were White. A total of 211 (14.7%) patients had hereditary/variant ATTR-CM (ATTRv-CM); Val122Ile (p.Val142Ile) was the most common genotype (n = 130). Patients spanned New York Heart Association functional classes I (n = 192), II (n = 997), and III (n = 243); 62.6% were National Amyloidosis Centre disease stage 1. Median (interquartile range) N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide was 2025 (1296-3465) pg/ml; n = 51 measured >8500 pg/ml. Median (interquartile range) high-sensitivity troponin T was 50 (35-69) pg/ml and mean left ventricular ejection fraction was 55.7% (9.7%). At baseline, 57.2% were on TTR stabilizer; 18.4% were on sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors.
CONCLUSION: The baseline characteristics of CARDIO-TTRansform were consistent with previous ATTR-CM trials; however, CARDIO-TTRansform evaluated patients with a wide range of disease severity and receiving the contemporary standard of care for ATTR-CM. Overall, blinded baseline data suggest that CARDIO-TTRansform provides a unique opportunity to determine the clinical benefits of eplontersen in a contemporary setting and in clinically relevant subgroups of patients with ATTR-CM.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT04136171.

title: Engineering mRNA-Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines against multidrug resistant bacteria: current and future prospects.
abstract: This review highlights the significant potential of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology for application in bacterial vaccines, with a long-term goal to provide critical tools in controlling problematic microbial infections regardless of their antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profile. The current landscape of bacterial vaccine development, including methods for identification of candidate antigens, are discussed along with emerging design principles for LNP delivery systems. We focus on mRNA-LNP systems for delivery of bacterial vaccine antigens in large part due to their extensive clinical validation, compatibility with reverse vaccinology, and growing prominence in modern vaccinology. Attention is also given to emerging opportunities to develop effective tools to combat severe infections, particularly those caused by AMR bacterial infections. Specific advantages and challenges of RNA-based vaccine platforms and LNP delivery systems compared to other vaccine modalities including strategies are highlighted, with a focus on particular strengths in conserved antigen identification via genome sequencing and recent advances in optimizing LNP composition for induction of strongly protective immunity for vaccine delivery. We argue that mRNA-LNP technology combined with reverse vaccinology approaches has the potential to improve and accelerate bacterial vaccine development, particularly for broadly protective immunity less dependent on bacterial strain surface composition and which are entirely dependent on host immunity, making them agnostic to the issue of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Yeast-Based Platforms for Next-Generation Human Health Applications.
abstract: Yeast platforms are rapidly transitioning from traditional eukaryotic model organisms to versatile, programmable chassis for next-generation human health applications. This review systematically examines the translational evolution of conventional and non-conventional yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Komagataella phaffii, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Yarrowia lipolytica and redefines them as scalable biomanufacturing factories and advanced living therapeutics. We highlight milestone advancements in synthetic biology toolkits that lower technical barriers, such as CRISPR-mediated multiplex editing, modular cloning frameworks, and high-throughput secretion screening. We focus on sophisticated glycoengineering strategies for humanized N-glycosylation, alongside data-driven paradigms that leverage artificial intelligence to predict gene expression and streamline strain design. In clinical domains, we detail the established success of yeast in producing subunit or virus-like particle vaccines (e.g. HBV and HPV) and therapeutic enzymes (e.g. ecallantide), alongside its emerging role as gut-adapted live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) engineered for in situ delivery and biosensing. Finally, we explore specialized non-conventional platforms, focusing on lipid- and acetyl-CoA-rich hosts for lipophilic drug discovery, and stress-tolerant systems optimized for economical, feedstock-flexible bioprocesses. In summary, this review underscores the integrated value of yeast systems across disease modeling, industrial manufacturing, and clinical intervention, charting future directions to address global health challenges.

title: Gene therapy strategy to treat Cornelia de Lange syndrome due to Hdac8 Deficiency.
abstract: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is a rare, multi-system genetic disorder characterized by developmental and cognitive impairments with systemic manifestations. Among the genes associated with CdLS, loss-of-function variants in HDAC8 account for approximately 4% of cases (referred to as CdLS5), causing the dysregulation of the cohesin complex, a core pathogenic mechanism of the disorder. Currently, no gene-based therapeutic strategy exists to directly address CdLS resulting from HDAC8 deficiency. Here, we created a new CdLS5 mouse model by introducing a clinically reported HDAC8 p.Ile19Ser variant in the mouse Hdac8 gene using CRISPR-Cas9 technology. Comprehensive molecular, morphological, and behavioral characterization revealed that the new Hdac8I19S mouse strain exhibits a robust phenotype, including marked alterations in deacetylase activity and pronounced developmental and behavioral deficits. This model was subsequently used to evaluate a gene augmentation approach aimed at increasing HDAC8 protein levels and restoring cohesin function through delivery of human HDAC8 transgene. Two AAV vectors driving expression of human HDAC8 were assessed. Although efficient delivery and robust expression were achieved, only modest effects on Smc3 acetylation, a key HDAC8 substrate, were observed, and no significant improvement in cognitive or behavioral phenotypes was detected. Overall, these findings demonstrate that postnatal HDAC8 gene augmentation resulted in limited biochemical correction and minimal phenotypic improvement under the conditions tested. These results highlight important biological considerations, including target engagement and developmental timing, that should be considered in the development of effective therapies for cohesin-related disorders.

title: Genetic principles enabling the creation of bacteria-based therapeutics.
abstract: Genetic engineering can transform bacteria (including Salmonella, Escherichia coli, Listeria, and Yersinia) from naturally occurring microbes into programmable therapeutics. Unlike passive platforms, engineered bacteria can localize to defined biological niches, sense environmental cues, regulate programmed activity in situ, interact with host tissues in novel ways, and persist for controlled periods. These properties make bacteria versatile medicines but require genetic control of precision, safety, stability, and activity under clinical conditions. Major design layers include strain or "chassis" selection, attenuation and biocontainment, control of therapeutic activity, targeting and persistence, and genotype-to-phenotype stability during manufacturing and in vivo use. These features also create liabilities, including off-target behavior, unstable expression, and evolutionary loss of function under selection. Progress depends on safe, clinically translatable chassis with integrated, bounded, and durable behaviors. This review examines the genetic design principles and liabilities of bacteria-based therapeutics, approaches used to produce clinical and near-clinical candidates, and the emergence of programmed bacteria delivering complete gene editing systems to therapeutically relevant cells.

title: A review-based guide to selecting an appropriate strategy for transgene-free genome editing in plants.
abstract: The field of plant genetic engineering has advanced considerably since the development of the first transgenic crop plants, and even though transgenic varieties of various crops are now commercially available, consumer reluctance and environmental concerns over transgene escape pose limits on their expansion. Gene editing offers the opportunity to selectively and precisely alter DNA sequences without reliance on stably integrated transgenes, assuaging both concerns. Considerable progress has been made with the advent of programmable nucleases such as Cas9 and its derivatives. The transgenes encoding the gene editing components can be expressed transiently without integration in the plant's genome or removed from the genome via outcrossing or haploid induction to result in gene-edited plants that are no longer considered transgenic. Nonetheless, gene editing systems remain challenging to implement in some plant species, notably those that have long generation times or are vegetatively propagated, precluding the removal of editing tools through crosses. In these cases, a transgene-free method for introduction of all components needed to enable gene editing will bring the promise of modern breeding tools within reach. Transgene-free genome editing can be accomplished through the delivery of editing components as DNA, RNA, or ribonucleoproteins with delivery via Agrobacterium, microprojectiles, nanocarriers, DNA and RNA viruses, and grafting. Between technical constraints and scientific goals, it can be challenging to determine an appropriate transgene-free genome editing method. Following a review of the literature, a decision tree is provided to help select an appropriate method for a given plant species and to show how emerging tools, including smaller editors, can advance the field.

title: Mobile group II intron reverse transcriptases: evolution, biochemical activities, and applications.
abstract: Bacterial mobile group II intron-encoded reverse transcriptases are structurally similar to an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and may have evolved at the time of transition from an RNA to DNA world. Mobile group II intron reverse transcriptases remain prevalent in bacteria, where they diversified into different subtypes, as well as into chromosomally encoded reverse transcriptases that acquired a variety of cellular functions, including phage defense, RNA spacer acquisition in CRISPR systems, and host cell DNA double-strand break and oxidative DNA damage repair. Mobile group II intron and related reverse transcriptases have remarkably beneficial biochemical properties for biotechnological applications, including high-throughput RNA sequencing. Thermostable Group II Intron-encoded Reverse Transcriptases from bacterial thermophiles, the first of these enzymes shown to have such properties, were used to develop a comprehensive RNA sequencing method that enables simultaneous profiling of virtually all RNA biotypes in human cells, extracellular vesicles, and plasma. In recent studies, Thermostable Group II Intron Reverse Transcriptase sequencing identified a novel large class of short (<300 nt) largely structured Full-Length EXcised linear Intron RNAs in human cells and plasma; enabled parallel analysis of transcriptional and post-transcriptional gene regulation by mapping Thermostable Group II Intron Reverse Transcriptase sequencing reads to genome and transcriptome reference sequences and calculating intron/exon depth ratios; and detected numerous differentially expressed RNAs in inflammatory breast cancer patient tumors and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Differentially expressed RNAs with high intron/exon depth ratios in inflammatory breast cancer patient tumors and peripheral blood mononuclear cells were correlated with pre-mRNA and intron RNA fragments detected in plasma and included the first potential inflammatory breast cancer biomarkers.

title: Differences in ectopic adiposity of skeletal muscle and the liver among Black Caribbeans, Black Americans, and White Americans.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ectopic adiposity of skeletal muscle and the liver share common pathophysiological mechanisms predictive of physical disability. Here, we sought to characterize muscle and liver adiposity among Black Caribbeans, Black Americans, and White Americans and determine whether muscle and liver adiposity predict future gait speed.
METHODS: Computed tomography-derived abdominal lean muscle attenuation, intermuscular adipose tissue volume, and liver attenuation were measured in 749 Black Caribbean men ages 50-91 from the Tobago Longitudinal Study of Aging and 1061 Black and White American men and women ages 42-57 from the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study. Gait speed was measured 7-13 years later.
RESULTS: On average, Black Caribbean men had lean muscle attenuation that was ≥8 Hounsfield Unit (HU) higher and intermuscular adipose tissue that was ≥11 cm3 lower than Americans (p-values<0.0001), even after adjusting for age, height, walking, smoking, alcohol, energy intake, total muscle volume, and visceral adiposity. White and Black American women had lean muscle attenuation that was ≥3 HU lower and intermuscular adipose tissue that was ≥2% more of their total muscle volume (p-values<0.0001). White American men had liver attenuation that was ≥4 HU lower (p-values<0.0002), which was explained by higher visceral adiposity. Higher lean muscle attenuation and lower intermuscular adiposity were associated with faster future gait speeds (p-values≤0.007).
CONCLUSIONS: Black Caribbean men had a more favorable muscle composition, specifically higher lean muscle attenuation and lower intermuscular adiposity; characteristics that predicted better physical performance. Identifying factors explaining less myosteatosis may indicate targets to prevent physical disability.

title: Targeted antisense oligonucleotide mediated exon skipping therapies for a recurrent CEP290 mutation.
abstract: Joubert Syndrome (JBTS) is a ciliopathy and disease-causing variants in CEP290 are the leading cause of JBTS presenting with cerebello-retinal-renal phenotypes. We investigated a Brazilian child with JBTS and compound heterozygous variants in CEP290. Using patient derived fibroblasts, we characterised the c.6271-8T>G intron 46 splice site allele using RT-PCR, confirming it led to a 7 bp intronic inclusion leading to a frameshift and downstream nonsense variant p.(Asn2091Leufs*12). Patient fibroblasts displayed elongated and tortuous primary cilia and a decreased primary ciliation rate. We reviewed other Brazilian cohorts where the CEP290 c.6271-8T>G allele had been reported in homozygosity or in compound heterozygosity with a second pathogenic variant. Phenotypes associated with this allele included Leber congenital amaurosis, nephronophthisis and JBTS. Finally, we used antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) mediated exon skipping of exon 46, an 87 base pair exon which if skipped is not predicted to disrupt reading frame or CEP290 protein structure, in patient fibroblasts to rescue ciliary phenotypes and CEP290 protein expression at ciliary the transition zone. These findings confirm that the CEP290 c.6271-8T>G is a pathogenic splice-site variant and pathogenic alleles within or disrupting exon 46 splicing including c.6271-8T>G are amenable to targeted ASO mediated exon skipping as a future therapeutic strategy.

title: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis following CRISPR/Cas9 knockdown demonstrates a novel role for human T cell-intrinsic IL-1β in determining T cell metabolic landscape.
abstract: T helper 17 (Th17) CD4+ T cells are key mediators of autoimmune pathology. Interleukin (IL)-1β is a potent proinflammatory cytokine known to promote Th17 differentiation and pathogenicity, in combination with other cytokines. Whereas recent studies have shown that T cells are capable of expressing IL-1β themselves, the role of this T cell-endogenous IL-1β is poorly understood. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of IL1B in naïve human CD4+ T cells along with cytokine neutralization and IL-1 receptor blockade, we found that T cell-intrinsic IL-1β is not essential for Th17 differentiation or effector resistance. Remarkably, single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that IL1B deletion profoundly rewires the transcriptional and metabolic landscape within the T cells, suppressing glycolytic and hypoxia-responsive pathways. These findings uncouple T cell-intrinsic IL-1β from Th17 effector resistance while uncovering an important contribution toward sustaining metabolic roles. This refines our understanding of IL-1β biology and informs therapeutic strategies in immune-mediated disease settings.

title: Robust CD8 T-cell response generated via attenuated Plasmodium sporozoite prime and multi-epitope mRNA vaccine boost.
abstract: Plasmodium infections and subsequent malaria disease remain a global health scourge. Liver-resident and circulating memory CD8 T cells elicited by whole parasite vaccines such as genetically or radiation-attenuated sporozoites can provide potent immunity to Plasmodium infection and prevent the development of the symptomatic blood stage of infection in humans, nonhuman primates, and mice. However, this requires multiple, large doses of attenuated sporozoites, posing numerous logistical challenges. To partially address these logistical challenges, here, we prime CB6F1 mice with a human weight-normalized, subprotective single dose of genetically or radiation-attenuated Plasmodium berghei sporozoites to elicit liver-resident and circulating memory T cells prior to boosting with a novel lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccine encoding multiple CD8 T-cell epitopes from liver-stage proteins. We show that boosting primed mice with this mRNA vaccine engenders sterilizing immunity against sporozoite challenge by generating a robust liver-stage-specific CD8 T-cell response when administered intravascularly or intramuscularly. Thus, combining a single, dose-sparing attenuated sporozoite immunization with a multi-epitope translationally relevant mRNA vaccine can engender protective immunity against P. berghei sporozoite challenge via the generation of a potent circulating and resident memory liver CD8 T-cell response. Minimizing the number of attenuated sporozoite doses required to prime CD8 T cells with a full complement of liver-stage malaria-specific epitopes effectively mitigates some logistical challenges associated with attenuated sporozoite vaccination.

title: The recognition pathway: reconceiving inventorship and obviousness for iterative CRISPR-AI convergence.
abstract: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats -Artificial Intelligence (CRISPR-AI) convergence generate therapeutic candidates via iterative human-machine workflows that disrupt the inventorship criterion of patent law based on conception. In CRISPR-AI studies, AI systems suggest thousands of guide RNAs or Cas variants; human researchers select, confirm, and optimize them via experimental feedback loops that conceal the locus of conception. The existing patent doctrine, which demands a clear and final concept in the human mind, fails to align with inventions in which AI comes up with solutions that human researchers had not anticipated. This Article advances a recognition pathway for CRISPR-AI inventorship that maintains the natural-person baseline while attributing inventorship to humans who exercise claim-defining technical judgment in identifying patentable value within AI outputs. The Article reconceives the person having ordinary skill in the art standard for AI-enhanced biotechnology, rejecting both inflexible pre-AI baselines and the 'computer having ordinary skill in the art' proposal. A five-factor test is employed to assess AI-generated CRISPR inventions on non-obviousness in terms of problem structure, predictability of solutions, and quality of human judgment. The framework provides a computational biotechnology human-accountability grammar that is administrable, but not legally granted to machines.

title: IL-15/IL-15Rα-targeted CRISPRa boosts NK cell effector function against HIV-infected cells.
abstract: Like many other immune cell types, natural killer (NK) cells exhibit impaired functionality in people with HIV (PWH), limiting their ability to efficiently target and eliminate HIV-infected cells and contributing to the persistence of the HIV reservoir. Recently, adoptive NK cell therapy using activated or engineered NK cells has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer; however, its application to HIV remains in the early stages of development. NK cells primarily rely on interleukin-15 (IL-15) signaling for their development, survival, and maintenance, and dysregulated IL-15 signaling has been reported in PWH. We hypothesized that simultaneous enhancement of IL-15 and IL-15 receptor alpha (IL-15Rα) expression would improve NK cell effector function and promote clearance of HIV reservoir. Utilizing dCas9-VPR-mediated multiplex CRISPR activation (CRISPRa), we successfully upregulated both IL-15 and IL-15Rα expression in the same primary NK cells without altering the genomic sequence. CRISPRa-treated NK cells displayed increased IL-15 and IL-15Rα transcript levels, as measured by RT-qPCR and significantly elevated surface expression of IL-15Rα, as determined by flow cytometry. Enhanced IL-15/IL-15Rα expression increased NK cell metabolic activity and cytotoxicity against target K562 cells, a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line, indicating improved effector function. Furthermore, in co-culture experiments using an HIV-positive T-cell line, IL-15/IL-15Rα-CRISPRa-treated NK cells demonstrated enhanced target cell elimination and increased secretion of IFN-γ. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept that multiplex CRISPRa can be used to enhance NK cell function, representing a novel strategy to improve persistence and therapeutic efficacy in HIV and other disease settings.

title: Crosstalk between immune cells and keratinocytes in atopic dermatitis: mechanism and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a prevalent chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by genetic susceptibility, epidermal barrier dysfunction, and immune dysregulation. This review systematically expounds and analyzes the intricate cellular interactions between immune cells and keratinocytes (KCs) and their central roles in AD pathogenesis. The analysis emphasizes bidirectional crosstalk among diverse immune populations, such as Th2, Th17, regulatory T, and cytotoxic T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages, mediated by cytokines, chemokines, and surface molecules, as well as how this cellular communication orchestrates key disease features, including inflammation, barrier breakdown, and chronic itch. Key signaling pathways, such as the JAK-STAT, NF-κB, and MAPK pathways, along with molecular targets including thymic stromal lymphopoietin, interleukin-4 receptor alpha subunit (IL-4Rα), OX40/OX40 ligand, protease-activated receptor 2, transient receptor potential vanilloid channels, and aryl hydrocarbon receptor, are critically evaluated for their contributions to disease mechanisms. The review also surveys current and emerging therapeutic approaches, ranging from biologics targeting IL-4Rα/IL-13 and small-molecule inhibitors to combination regimens and novel strategies involving microbiome modulation and gene editing. Future investigations should advance personalized medicine paradigms to improve the long-term control and management of AD.

title: ATMLP regulates MDVs mediated inflammation induced by radiotherapy in lung cancer.
abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, and radiotherapy, a commonly used treatment for lung cancer, is associated with a variety of complications while treating cancer, among which radiotherapy-induced pneumonia is a common complication whose underlying mechanism remains unclear and requires further investigation. To address this, cell lines with ATMLP overexpression and knockdown were created using gene editing techniques, and Western blot, immunofluorescence and trans-well co-culture were used to explore the role of mitochondria-derived vesicles (MDVs) in mediating radiotherapy-induced inflammation, as well as the effects of ATMLP, DRP-1 and PGAM5 on MDVs. Ionizing radiation promoted the expression of ATMLP and the release of ATMLP-mediated MDVs. Up-regulation of ATMLP expression led to increased levels of PGAM5 and activation of phosphorylation at the Ser616 site of DRP-1. The increased number of MDVs further promoted macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype. Overall, ionizing radiation induces ATMLP expression, which enhances MDVs release through the PGAM5/DRP-1 axis. This process leads to macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype, contributing to the inflammatory response.

title: Fully modified SpyCas9 guide RNAs enable robust genome editing in cells and in vivo.
abstract: Precision engineering of CRISPR/Cas9 components has advanced genome editing toward therapeutic applications. Fully chemically modified guide RNAs (gRNAs) have the potential to improve stability and broaden therapeutic delivery strategies. However, extensive chemical modification of CRISPR guides can compromise genome editing activity by disrupting gRNA-Cas9 interactions. Here, we employed an iterative, structure-guided optimization strategy to systematically evaluate chemical modifications throughout SpyCas9 gRNAs. Extending beyond commonly used nucleotide modifications, we incorporated 2'-amino-RNA, 4'-thio-RNA, and extended nucleic acid (exNA) to generate gRNAs in which 90%-100% of nucleotides are sugar- or backbone-modified. Although the performance of individual modification patterns varied among target sequences, we established a repertoire of guides that support robust genome editing in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, these findings provide a systematic framework for rational engineering of heavily and fully modified gRNAs using diverse nucleotide chemistries for nonviral CRISPR genome editing.
