title: A p32 family RNA editing factor acts in mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis.
abstract: Biogenesis of mitochondrial ribosomes (mitoribosomes) in the unicellular parasite Trypanosoma brucei requires an exceptionally large toolkit of assembly factors, identified in stable precursors of large and small mitoribosomal subunits (mtLSU and mtSSU) by cryoEM. Here, using genetic modifications and proteomic characterization of the immunoprecipitated assemblosome, the earliest characterized mtSSU precursor, we determined that a cap of its distinctive protrusion of hitherto unknown composition consists of a p22 homotrimer. This protein was previously implicated in the uridine-insertion editing of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit II transcript. Our functional analysis confirmed this role but revealed that its ablation also causes a loss of mtSSU and a systemic reduction in mitochondrial translation, phenocopying the depletion of established mitoribosomal assembly factors. Consequently, the oxidative phosphorylation system and mitochondrial function are compromised. The p22 protein belongs to the p32 family. We showed that five of its six trypanosomal members are involved in mtSSU biogenesis. Notably, p32 proteins are associated with mitoribosomes in two other distant eukaryotic lineages. A eukaryote-wide mapping of p32 proteins documented that their presence correlates with the retention of mitochondrial genomes. Together, our findings redefine trypanosomal p22 as a dual-function coordinator of mitochondrial gene expression and reveal that the ancestral role of the p32 family is associated with mitochondrial translation.

title: A non-nucleotide activator reveals a second allosteric regulatory site in the type III CRISPR ribonuclease Csm6.
abstract: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems rely on cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signaling to activate ancillary nucleases such as Csm6, which serve as core effectors in antiviral immunity. While cOA-mediated Csm6 activation has been widely harnessed for molecular diagnostics, its broader application is constrained by inherent limitations, including poor cellular permeability and susceptibility to degradation by ring nucleases. Here, we conducted a high-throughput fluorescence-based screen and identified DMPCH (7,8-dimethyl-4-phenylchroman-2-one) as a non-nucleotide allosteric activator of Thermus thermophilus (Tt) Csm6. DMPCH selectively stimulates TtCsm6 ribonuclease activity by binding to the higher eukaryotes and prokaryotes nucleotide-binding domain dimerization interface, leading to expansion of the catalytic pocket and remodeling of the R-X4-6-H catalytic motif. Moreover, DMPCH acts synergistically with cA4 to activate TtCsm6, enabling rapid and sensitive RNA detection in a Cas13a-Csm6 system. Cell-based assays confirm that DMPCH activates TtCsm6 ribonuclease activity in live bacteria cells. When combined with DMPCH, an engineered miniCsm6 fused to pyocin S2 (PyS2) exerts potent and specific bactericidal activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Our work establishes a framework for discovering non-nucleotide activators of CRISPR-associated ribonucleases and highlights their potential as chemical tools in cell-based research and as therapeutic agents against bacterial pathogens.

title: Marker-based CRISPR screens identify POU2F1 as a regulator of DLL3 and neuroendocrine identity in small cell lung cancer.
abstract: Small cell lung cancers (SCLCs) often exhibit a neuroendocrine lineage identity marked by high expression of Delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3). Because DLL3 shows minimal expression in normal adult tissues, it serves as an SCLC-selective tumor antigen and is the basis for clinically efficacious targeted therapies. Understanding the mechanisms that regulate DLL3 expression is therefore critical for advancing therapeutic strategies in this disease. Here, we performed transcription factor-focused and genome-wide CRISPR screens to identify regulators of DLL3 expression in SCLC. Both approaches converged on POU2F1 as a top activator of DLL3 in this tumor context. Despite its ubiquitous expression, we identify an SCLC-specific role for POU2F1 in activating DLL3 and a broader set of neuroendocrine lineage genes. Epigenomic analyses reveal tandem POU2F1-ASCL1 motifs within the DLL3 promoter that underlie the functional cooperativity between POU2F1 and the neuroendocrine master regulator ASCL1 for high-level DLL3 expression in SCLC. We provide evidence that tandem POU2F1-ASCL1 elements are part of a cis-regulatory code for the lung neuroendocrine cell fate. Together, these findings define a previously unrecognized transcriptional logic controlling DLL3 expression and establish POU2F1 as a context-specific regulator of neuroendocrine lineage in SCLC.

title: A versatile tool for gene editing in the diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana.
abstract: Diatoms are major contributors to marine primary production, with the centric diatom Thalassiosira pseudonana a powerful model for understanding biogeochemical processes including carbon fixation and silicification. While there are molecular tools available for fluorescent protein (FP) tagging and CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing in T. pseudonana, these require the delivery of multiple vectors or have limited versatility. Additionally, scarless endogenous tagging, that results in a FP fusion expressed from its native genomic location, has yet to be developed. Here, we describe a versatile modular Golden Gate-based toolkit for T. pseudonana that through the delivery of a single-episome via bacterial conjugation enables: (i) FP tagging, (ii) dual FP tagging, (iii) CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, (iv) simultaneous FP tagging with gene editing, and (v) scarless endogenous FP tagging. We further expand the available parts for T. pseudonana by validating 3 additional FPs and 2 untested promoter/terminator pairs. We demonstrate the versatility of our system by knocking out diatom pyrenoid component 1 (DPC1) while simultaneously GFP tagging the rbcS (Rubisco small subunit), and by endogenously GFP tagging the bestrophin-like protein BST2. While DPC1 knockout does not result in a major pyrenoid structural defect due to unperturbed rbcS-GFP localization to the pyrenoid, we confirm that BST2 localizes to the pyrenoid and exhibits increased fluorescence under low CO2-supporting a role in diatom carbon fixation. Our developed genetic tools provide a robust framework for exploring cellular processes in diatoms, accelerating routine studies and enabling systematic, quantitative and large-scale studies.

title: Moss is more: The moss Physcomitrium patens as an ideal chassis for plant synthetic biology.
abstract: Physcomitrium patens, commonly known as the spreading earthmoss or Physco, has gained increasing attention as a chassis for synthetic biology in plants. This review explores its advantages over flowering plants traditionally used more often for biotechnology, such as Arabidopsis thaliana and maize, including shorter life cycles and ease to handle experimentally, being haploid, and much higher efficiency for integration of transgenes into its genome by homologous recombination. In addition, Physco's ability to maintain episomes also introduces an additional possibility for transgene expression and manipulation. With these advantageous traits, Physco has already been used for synthetic genomes, recombinant protein production, metabolic engineering and artificial organelle engineering. These applications have been enabled by various toolkits developed for construction of transformation cassettes, DNA and RNA editing, as well as different reporters to allow microscopy imaging or quantification of gene expression. While Physco does have limitations, such as its high number of duplicated genes which can present issues when tweaking of native genes is involved, these certainly do not prevent Physco becoming a useful synthetic biology model for further applications on Earth and future space explorations.

title: CRISPR screening identifies GNPTAB as a noncanonical STING activator driving cellular senescence.
abstract: Cellular senescence is accompanied by profound lysosomal alterations, yet whether lysosome-associated factors actively drive aging remains unclear. Through a focused CRISPR/Cas9 screen in human mesenchymal progenitor cells (hMPCs), we identified N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase subunits alpha and beta (GNPTAB), an enzyme responsible for lysosomal hydrolase targeting, as a positive regulator of cellular senescence. Genetic ablation of GNPTAB attenuated senescence, whereas its overexpression accelerated senescence. This pro-senescent function occurred independently of GNPTAB's canonical enzymatic role. Instead, GNPTAB binds to the innate immune adaptor stimulator of interferon genes (STING) through an interface involving the critical residue E1119, leading to activation of STING and its downstream TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), as well as pro-inflammatory gene expression. A STING-binding-deficient GNPTAB mutant (E1119A) preserved canonical lysosomal functions but failed to induce senescence, while STING depletion abolished GNPTAB-driven senescence. Together, these findings uncover a new signaling pathway wherein GNPTAB engages STING to facilitate its activation, suggesting that the GNPTAB-STING interaction interface may serve as a potential therapeutic target for ameliorating age-related cellular dysfunction.

title: Dysregulation of macrophage colony stimulating factor in Paget's disease of bone.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether common genetic variants at the chromosome 1p13 locus that predisposes to Paget's disease of bone (PDB) regulate macrophage colony stimulating factor (M-CSF) expression in bone cells and to determine whether there is dysregulation of M-CSF in patients with PDB.
METHODS: The regions surrounding single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) previously associated with PDB at a genome wide significant level were deleted in clones of MG63 osteoblast-like cells using CRISPR/Cas, and levels of M-CSF mRNA and protein were evaluated in cells with and without deletions. Serum M-CSF was measured by ELISA in PDB and controls, and values in patients were related to clinical features of PDB and biochemical markers of bone remodelling.
RESULTS: Deletion of the region surrounding rs484959 increased expression of M-CSF mRNA by 1.31-fold (95% CI: 1.04, 1.58; P = 0.026) and M-CSF protein by 1.91-fold (95% CI: 1.25, 2.57; P = 0.013), compared with control cells. Serum M-CSF was significantly elevated in PDB vs controls (mean [S.D.] 781.7 [678] vs 541 [491] pg/ml, P < 0.001). Furthermore, M-CSF levels were associated with number of affected bones (P = 0.029), bodily pain assessed by SF-36 (P = 0.026) and biochemical markers of bone turnover.
CONCLUSION: The rs484959 SNP is a regulatory variant that modulates M-CSF mRNA and protein expression in osteoblasts. Serum M-CSF is increased in PDB and is associated with pain, disease extent and biochemical markers of bone remodelling. This suggests that there is dysregulation of M-CSF in PDB and that this cytokine may play a role in pathogenesis of the disease.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-Mediated Mutagenesis of Two Alleles Encoding a Glutathione S-Transferase Confirms Their Identity as Fhb7 Conferring Fusarium Head Blight Resistance in Wheat.
abstract: Fhb7 is a gene derived from the homoeologous group-7 chromosomes of tall wheatgrass (Thinopyrum species), which confers resistance to Fusarium head blight (FHB) in wheat. Two resistance alleles at the Fhb7 locus (Fhb7Thp and Fhb7The2) were identified from Th. ponticum and Th. elongatum, respectively, and introgressed into the wheat genome by homoeologous recombination. Fhb7Thp was first cloned and reported to encode a glutathione S-transferase (GST), which detoxifies trichothecenes through de-epoxidation. However, a recent study has questioned the role of GST in Fhb7-mediated FHB resistance. To decipher the function of two GST-encoding alleles, Fhb7Thp and Fhb7The2, in FHB resistance, we generated haploid plants from three spring wheat lines (CS-Fhb7, WGC002, and FW23-009-80) carrying Fhb7Thp or Fhb7The2 through wide hybridizations with transgenic maize expressing Cas9 and guide RNA (gRNA) targeting GST. Of 57, 35, and 74 haploid plants derived from CS-Fhb7, WGC002, and FW23-009-80, respectively, 16, 5, and 9 had an insertion/deletion at the target sites of GST. Greenhouse evaluation of doubled haploid (DH) lines derived from the haploid plants for FHB resistance indicated that the GST-edited DH lines were significantly more susceptible and accumulated more deoxynivalenol (DON) than their corresponding wildtypes and non-edited DH lines, confirming GST as the causal gene for Fhb7-mediated FHB resistance. This study also demonstrated the power of wheat × maize hybridization coupled with genome editing in validating gene function in wheat.

title: A High-Sensitivity RPA/Cas12a Assay for Rapid Detection of the Select Agent Ralstonia solanacearum R3b2.
abstract: Ralstonia solanacearum is a globally distributed, soil-borne species complex that causes bacterial wilt in many economically important crops. Race 3 biovar 2 (R3b2) is a cold-tolerant, highly aggressive subgroup within this complex that is responsible for an estimated $1 billion in annual global losses. Because R3b2 remains exotic to North America, it is classified as a USDA Select Agent due to its high potential to devastate U.S. solanaceous crops and ornamental industries. However, current diagnostic methods for this pathogen involve trade-offs among cost, sensitivity, specificity, and ease of use, particularly for point-of-care (POC) detection in field settings. CRISPR-based detection platforms have recently emerged as promising tools for high-sensitivity POC diagnostics. Here we developed an isothermal recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA)/Cas12a assay for specific, sensitive and rapid detection of R3b2. By targeting a genomic region associated with the cool-virulence phenotype, the assay reliably differentiates R3b2 from plant hosts and other diverse R. solanacearum strains. Incorporation of a dual-guide RNA system and an 8-mer single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) fluorescent reporter further improved sensitivity and reduced detection time. Using dilution series of R3b2-spiked Pelargonium DNA extracts, the assay detected as few as 4 CFU per reaction. To facilitate POC applications, the system was adapted into a one-pot, contamination-resistan¬t format compatible with portable fluorescence readers such as Genie III device and P51 viewer. By improving both sensitivity and portability, this assay enhances current diagnostic capabilities and, pending validation in real-world conditions, supports early surveillance efforts aimed at preventing the introduction of R3b2 into the United States.

title: ADAR1 Inhibits ZBP1-Driven Neuronal Necroptosis After Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
abstract: Necroptosis is a critical response to secondary brain injury following intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Z-DNA Binding Protein 1 (ZBP1) binds to dsRNA and promotes the activation of Receptor-Interacting Protein Kinase 3 (RIPK3). This study investigated whether Adenosine Deaminase Acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) inhibits neuronal necroptosis after ICH. ADAR1-knockdown mice and ZBP1flox/flox/Thy1-Cre+/- mice were subjected to collagenase VII-induced ICH. Brain edema and neurobehavioral deficits were assessed. The expressions of ADAR1 and ZBP1 were investigated by qPCR, western blot, immunofluorescence, and ELISA. Protein interactions were performed using co-immunoprecipitation. ADAR1p150 was reduced in both ICH patients and mice. ZBP1 and ADAR1 both bound to dsRNA. ADAR1p150 suppressed ZBP1 activation, potentially through functional antagonism and dsRNA editing, although causality remains to be established. Knockout of ZBP1 resulted in increased ADAR1p150 expression and reduced brain edema. Etanercept and shRNA-mediated ADAR1 knockdown promoted ZBP1 expression. Complementation of the ADAR1 Zα truncation did not reduce ZBP1 in ADAR1-knockdown cells. The inhibitory effect of ADAR1 on ZBP1 was attenuated in ADAR1Zα-/- cells. These data show that the Zα domain is required for ADAR1 to suppress ZBP1, but they do not establish whether this suppression depends on RNA editing or on dsRNA binding alone.

title: Hypoxia-Driven CA2 Promotes Trophoblast Dysfunction in Preeclampsia.
abstract: Explore the potential function of Carbonic Anhydrase 2 (CA2) in the pathophysiology of preeclampsia. Peripheral blood and placental samples were collected from healthy pregnant women and patients with preeclampsia. Placental CA2 expression was validated in independent clinical cohorts and experimental mouse models. HTR-8/SVneo cells were cultured and transfected with a CA2 overexpression plasmid to evaluate trophoblast dysfunction. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed to identify downstream genes associated with CA2 overexpression, followed by VEGFA rescue experiments. Hypoxia-related regulation of CA2 was investigated. Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated siRNA against CA2 was constructed in an L-NAME-induced PE model to evaluate therapeutic effects. CA2 expression was significantly increased in placental tissues and maternal serum from women with PE and was also elevated in experimental PE mouse models. CA2 predominantly localized in trophoblast cells, and correlated positively with serum creatinine and urea and correlated negatively with fetal birth weight. CA2 overexpression markedly suppressed trophoblast proliferation, migration, and invasion, without affecting apoptosis. Transcriptomic analysis suggested that vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) acted as a downstream mediator of CA2, and VEGFA overexpression partially rescued CA2-induced trophoblast dysfunction. CA2 expression was upregulated under hypoxic conditions and regulated by hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α). LNP-mediated CA2 silencing partially improved placental structure and fetal outcomes in vivo. CA2 is upregulated in the preeclamptic placenta and is associated with placental dysfunction and adverse fetal outcomes. Mechanistically, CA2 may act downstream of HIF-1α and contribute to trophoblast dysfunction partly through modulation of VEGFA signaling, and CA2 silencing partially improved maternal and fetal outcomes, highlighting CA2 as a potential therapeutic target for preeclampsia.

title: RNA-Targeted Therapeutics in Cardiovascular Risk Reduction: From Gene Silencing to Precision Cardiology.
abstract: Advances in cardiovascular prevention and treatment have substantially improved patient outcomes. However, residual cardiovascular risk remains a major clinical challenge. Traditional lipid-lowering and antihypertensive therapies, although effective, remain limited by suboptimal adherence, adverse effects, and persistent residual cardiovascular risk. RNA-targeted therapeutics have emerged as a transformative therapeutic paradigm, offering durable and highly specific gene silencing through small interfering RNA and antisense oligonucleotide platforms. This review evaluates the current evidence on RNA-targeted therapeutics for cardiovascular risk reduction, with an emphasis on their mechanisms of action, clinical efficacy, safety, and emerging therapeutic applications. A review was conducted using PubMed, Embase, Scopus, ScienceDirect, the Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to June 2026. A total of 154 eligible studies were included and narratively synthesized by therapeutic class and molecular target. Inclisiran reduced low-density lipoprotein cholesterol by approximately 50% with twice-yearly dosing, while pooled ORION analyses suggested a reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events. Pelacarsen, olpasiran, and lepodisiran achieved 80-98% reductions in lipoprotein(a), whereas zilebesiran lowered systolic blood pressure by more than 15 mm Hg with sustained effects for up to 24 weeks. Across studies, RNA therapeutics demonstrated favorable safety profiles, with predominantly mild injection-site reactions. Although definitive cardiovascular outcome data remain unavailable for several emerging agents, RNA-targeted therapeutics represent a promising advance in precision cardiovascular medicine by providing durable, mechanism-based therapies capable of addressing important residual cardiovascular risk.

title: Urine as a liquid allograft biopsy: emerging technologies for noninvasive monitoring in kidney transplantation.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Long-term kidney allograft survival remains limited by immune and nonimmune injury, while conventional surveillance tools are constrained by delayed detection, limited specificity, or invasiveness. Urine provides an accessible window into the allograft, containing inflammatory mediators, cells, extracellular vesicles, nucleic acids, proteins, peptides, and metabolites reflecting intra-graft processes.
RECENT FINDINGS: Over the past two decades, urinary biomarkers have evolved from single-analyte discovery to molecular signatures matched to kidney biopsy findings. Urinary CXCL9/CXCL10, urinary-cell mRNA, extracellular-vesicle transcriptomics, donor-derived cell-free DNA, proteomics, and metabolomics provide complementary measures of allograft injury and have demonstrated encouraging diagnostic performance. Although some remain limited by variable specificity, analytical standardization, reproducibility, or insufficient prospective validation, others have undergone multicenter validation, assay standardization, and progression toward clinical implementation.
SUMMARY: Urinary biomarkers are unlikely to replace biopsy with a single universal test. Their greatest potential lies in context-specific applications, including risk stratification, surveillance, biopsy triage, differential diagnosis, prognostication, and treatment-response monitoring. High negative predictive value across several platforms may support reducing unnecessary biopsies. Clinical translation will depend on standardized, transferable assays, external validation in representative populations, clearly defined contexts of use, and evidence that biomarker-guided strategies improve patient and allograft outcomes.

title: The role of genetic testing in heart transplant candidates.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Inherited cardiomyopathies are increasingly recognized among patients with advanced heart failure, yet genetic testing remains substantially underutilized. This review examines the evolving clinical utility of genetic testing across advanced heart failure and transplantation and highlights opportunities to integrate genetics into routine advanced heart failure care.
RECENT FINDINGS: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic cardiomyopathy variants are identified in approximately one-third of heart transplant recipients and in up to 44% of explanted hearts from patients with idiopathic cardiomyopathy. Recent studies have linked genotype to heart failure progression, ventricular arrhythmias, and outcomes after advanced therapies, including a higher risk of right ventricular failure following left ventricular assist device implantation. Genetic diagnoses can also uncover multisystem disease relevant to transplant evaluation and posttransplant management. At the same time, the emergence of gene replacement, gene editing, and RNA-based therapies is creating new therapeutic implications for establishing a molecular diagnosis before end-stage disease.
SUMMARY: Genetic testing is becoming an increasingly actionable component of advanced heart failure care. Integrating genetics into advanced heart failure programs may improve recognition of inherited disease, individualize management, and better position patients and their families for emerging precision therapies.

title: The small protein PhrS-P, encoded by the dual-function small RNA PhrS, augments fitness of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the presence of aminoglycosides.
abstract: PhrS (Pseudomonas Hfq-binding RNA S) is a dual-function small RNA of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The base-pairing small regulatory RNA PhrS-R positively regulates pyocyanin biosynthesis. PhrS-R stimulates the production of the Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) by indirectly activating the translation of pqsR mRNA, encoding the quorum sensing regulator PqsR (MvfR), and by inhibiting the synthesis of the anthranilate degradation regulator AntR. Furthermore, PhrS-R was shown to promote biofilm formation, swarming motility and CRISPR-Cas immunity. In addition, PhrS encodes a 37 amino acid long and conserved small protein (PhrS-P), the function of which remained unknown. Here, we provide evidence that PhrS-P is an inner membrane protein which does not contribute to the known physiological roles of its RNA counterpart. RNA-Seq-based transcriptome analyses revealed that multiple aminoglycoside resistance genes, including those of the AmgR regulon, are differentially expressed depending on PhrS-P. AmgR is the response regulator of the AmgRS two-component system (TCS), which affects aminoglycoside and zinc resistance in P. aeruginosa. A PhrS-P-deficient mutant strain exhibited reduced fitness when exposed to sub-inhibitory concentrations of the aminoglycosides tobramycin and amikacin as well as zinc. Based on our findings, we present a working model wherein PhrS-P positively regulates the AmgRS TCS activity through an unknown mechanism, leading to increased bacterial fitness in the presence of aminoglycosides.

title: The Arms Race Between Bacteria and Their Viruses: Update on Phage Countermeasures Against Bacterial Defence Systems.
abstract: In this editorial, I summarize recent progress on phage-encoded anti-defence against bacterial anti-phage systems (APS). Computational approaches based on structural predictions of co-folding bacterial and phage proteins identified many new PAD sponge proteins. New anti-CRISPR-Cas systems were characterized that destroy cas12a mRNA, inactivate Cas12a by acetylation, engage the seed region of the crRNA, or prevent Cas3 from cleaving DNA. The phage defence protein Gad1 forms an octamer web that wraps around the complex of the Gabija APS. Tad1 and 2 are phage sponge proteins that sequester signalling nucleotides of the Thoeris APS. Tad3 to 7 interact directly with the ThsB sensor and Tad8 with the ThsA effector of the Thoeris APS. Phage sponge proteins were also described inactivating the CBASS and Pycsar APS. Still other phages use phosphodiesterases that cleave cyclic nucleotide signals to inactivate APS. Many bacterial APS effectors are NADase, destroying the essential metabolite NAD+. Phages evolved enzymes that resynthesize NAD+ from its cleavage products or proteins directly inactivating the NADase. Many phages degrade the bacterial genome which creates signals activating the Metis or the Kongming APS. Phages counteracted these APS by suppressing pathways leading to the creation of particular mononucleotides degradation products detected by these APS. Several APS cleave specific tRNA, phages responded by mutating cleavage sites in tRNA (anti-PARIS) or increasing tRNA expression to compensate for their destruction (anti-Septu). Phages counteract toxin-antitoxin APS by evolving their own antitoxin or by blocking the toxin protein. Researchers described cases where phages escaped detection by mutating phage proteins detected by bacterial sensors. Against the stringent response phages responded by destroying alarmones or inactivating enzymes producing these stress signals. The arms race between bacteria and phages can involve complicated layers of defence and anti-defences and both bacteria and phages encode multiple defence systems.

title: An inhibitor of the mitochondrial respiratory chain exerts synergistic anti-tumour effects when combined with alkylating agents.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Cancer cells exhibit the Warburg effect, but oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is also important for cancer cell proliferation. Metabolic reprogramming from glycolysis to OXPHOS is one mechanism of resistance to anti-tumour drugs. Here, we have synthesized and characterized OPB-111077, a novel, first-in-class orally available small-molecule compound, and investigated its anti-tumour activity and therapeutic potential in combination with alkylating agents.
EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Inhibition of mitochondrial function by OPB-111077 were assessed by measuring the oxygen consumption rate, ATP production and Complex I enzymatic activity. anti-tumour effects were evaluated in human haematological and solid tumour cell lines and in cell line-derived xenograft and lymphoma patient-derived xenograft models. Mechanistic studies included CRISPR screening, metabolomic analyses, and measurements of the oxygen consumption and extracellular acidification rates. Effects of OPB-111077 combined with alkylating agents were also assessed in mice.
KEY RESULTS: OPB-111077 inhibited mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex I, suppressed OXPHOS, and exerted anti-tumour effects in several models. OPB-111077 demonstrated synergism with the alkylating agent bendamustine, with simultaneous inhibition of both OXPHOS and glycolysis. Bendamustine reprogrammed cancer cells into an OXPHOS-dominant state, thereby enhancing the efficacy of OPB-111077.
CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: Based on these findings, we propose a novel anticancer therapeutic strategy of combining OXPHOS inhibitors with alkylating agents. OPB-111077 has demonstrated potential in combination therapy and was recently evaluated with bendamustine and rituximab in a Phase 1 clinical trial for patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (NCT04049825).

title: The road ahead for stem cell therapies in type 1 diabetes.
abstract:
AIMS: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells. Although exogenous insulin remains the standard treatment, it does not restore physiological glucose regulation. Differentiation of human pluripotent stem cells into β-cells offers a scalable alternative to cadaveric islet transplantation and has progressed rapidly over the past decade, resulting in nine clinical trials at various stages of completion. Despite this progress, durable graft function remains constrained by two major challenges: the absence of key islet microenvironment components, such as vasculature, extracellular matrix and supporting cell types and continued vulnerability to autoimmune and alloimmune rejection.
METHODS & RESULTS: This review considers emerging technological approaches to overcome these barriers. Bioengineered niches, including multilineage organoids, functionalized hydrogels, decellularized matrices and bioprinting, aim to recreate the native islet microenvironment, while synthetic biology approaches, such as hypoimmune gene editing, CRISPR-based transcriptional control and stimulus-responsive survival circuits, seek to enhance grafts' resilience. Computational and single-cell approaches, including gene regulatory network analysis and digital twin frameworks, are beginning to provide predictive tools for benchmarking differentiation quality and forecasting graft outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Together, these complementary strategies, potentially tailored to individual patients, represent a realistic path towards safer, more effective and durable β-cell replacement therapies for type 1 diabetes.

title: Beyond Dendritic Cells: A Cellular Pharmacology Agenda for mRNA Cancer Vaccines in Hematologic Malignancies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: mRNA-based vaccines are emerging as a promising platform for cancer immunotherapy, including in hematologic malignancies. Current vaccine development has largely focused on antigen selection, mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation, and combination with established immunotherapies. However, increasing evidence indicates that the cellular and tissue distribution of antigen expression may critically influence the quality and durability of the immune response. In this context, the term "cellular pharmacology" refers to the principle that the pharmacodynamic effect of an mRNA vaccine is shaped not only by the encoded antigen and formulation but also by the cell types in which antigen expression occurs.
OBJECTIVES: Here, we propose a cellular pharmacology framework for mRNA vaccines in hematologic malignancies, moving beyond the traditional dendritic-cell-centric model and considering antigen expression as a determinant of immune activation, tolerance, and T-cell exhaustion.
DISCUSSION: Three functionally distinct compartments can be considered: professional antigen-presenting cells, immunogenic non-immune cells at the injection site, and tolerogenic tissues, particularly hepatocytes. This tripartite model is intended as a simplified functional framework rather than a complete anatomical or cellular classification. While antigen expression in dendritic cells and other antigen-presenting cells supports effective T-cell priming, antigen production by skeletal myocytes and stromal cells may provide a sustained source of antigen for uptake and cross-presentation. Importantly, myocytes should not be regarded as professional antigen-presenting cells, but rather as potential antigen-producing cells whose antigens can be presented by professional APCs. Conversely, hepatic antigen expression may promote peripheral tolerance and impair antitumor CD8+ T-cell responses. Recent preclinical evidence indicates that microRNA-guided hepatocyte detargeting may enhance vaccine-induced immunity and tumor control in experimental models, although its clinical relevance in hematologic malignancies remains to be established. This concept may be particularly relevant in hematologic malignancies, characterized by disseminated disease, chronic antigen exposure, immune dysfunction, and frequent treatment-related organ vulnerability. We discuss how cellular targeting could be incorporated into mRNA vaccine strategies for lymphomas, acute leukemias, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and multiple myeloma, as well as into combination approaches with CAR-T cells, bispecific antibodies, and immune checkpoint inhibitors.
CONCLUSIONS: The therapeutic potential of mRNA vaccines in hematologic malignancies may depend not only on the antigen encoded but also on the cellular compartment in which it is expressed. Incorporating tissue biodistribution and cell-type specificity into vaccine design could represent a new strategy to improve immunogenicity while limiting tolerogenic signals and potentially reducing unwanted tissue exposure. At present, however, hepatocyte detargeting should be considered a promising and testable translational strategy rather than a clinically validated approach. Prospective clinical studies integrating biodistribution, immune correlates, and tissue-specific antigen expression will be essential to translate this cellular pharmacology concept into clinical practice.

title: Clinical Prospect of Novel Therapies for Functional Cure in Chronic Hepatitis B.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a major global health problem. Functional cure is defined as sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) seroclearance with undetectable HBV DNA 24 weeks after cessation of therapy. It has emerged as a clinically meaningful endpoint, associated with regression of liver fibrosis, reduced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk, and a lower treatment burden. However, current CHB therapies, including nucleos(t)ide analogues (NUCs) and pegylated interferon-α (Peg-IFNα), rarely lead to functional cure despite adequate viral suppression, leading to a notable portion of patients remaining at risk for adverse liver-related outcomes, including hepatic decompensation and HCC. Hence, novel therapeutic agents are aimed at accelerating towards functional cure. They are categorized as virus-targeting and immunomodulatory therapies.
METHODS: This review summarizes the clinical evidence for emerging therapies aimed at acheiving functional cure, with a particular focus on RNA-targeting therapies. It also discusses practical considerations relevant to treatment selection.
RESULTS: Among these novel therapies, RNA-targeting therapies are currently the most promising, with bepirovirsen (an unconjugated antisense oligonucleotide) standing out as the only agent completed in Phase III study showing efficacious results. Combination regimens that use RNA-targeting therapies as backbone are increasingly pursued, leveraging potential synergistic effects to achieve higher rates of HBsAg seroclearance.
CONCLUSION: RNA-targetting therapies and combination regimens offer promising approaches in attaining functional cure in CHB. Further research should emphasize on the long-term efficacy and safety for these novel agents.

title: RNA binding by ADARs prevents RNA interference from attacking self-produced dsRNA.
abstract: The ability of an organism to identify self and foreign RNA is central to eliciting an immune response in times of need while avoiding autoimmunity. As viral pathogens typically employ double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), host identification, modulation, and response to dsRNA is key. However, dsRNA is also abundant in host transcriptomes, raising the question of how these molecules can be differentiated. Two host pathways that regulate dsRNA are A-to-I RNA editing by adenosine deaminases (ADARs), and RNA interference (RNAi). Both mechanisms are important for normal organism development and function by regulating gene expression. Herein, we studied the structure and amount of siRNAs at editing sites and the ability of ADARs to prevent exogenous RNAi using the model organism, Caenorhabditis elegans. We found that the number of siRNAs targeting edited genes is significantly upregulated in ADAR mutant animals. We also found that despite an almost complete depletion of primary siRNAs generated from editing sites in wildtype animals, secondary siRNAs are generated from edited transcripts, suggesting ADARs antagonize only the first step of RNAi processing. We show that ADARs interfere with the efficacy of exogenous RNAi in vivo, probably to prevent trans-silencing, and have indications that ADR-2 binding to the dsRNA is needed for the efficient prevention of RNAi. This work sheds light on how the RNA editing process protects self-produced dsRNAs from aberrant recognition by the immune processes in the cell and from by-product degradation.

title: Lynx1 suppression reopens the window for effective rehabilitation after stroke in mice.
abstract: Rehabilitation is an effective and reliable approach for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, its efficacy decreases during the transition from the subacute to the chronic phase after stroke, posing a major barrier to complete functional recovery. This limited efficacy during the chronic phase is believed to result from declining neural plasticity. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating neural plasticity and its temporal changes after stroke remain unclear. To address this gap, we established a focal ischemic stroke mouse model that allows causal interrogation of the mechanisms responsible for the reduced efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase. Using this model, we identified Lynx1, an endogenous negative allosteric modulator of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, as a negative regulator of post-stroke neural plasticity. Lynx1 expression in layer 5 pyramidal neurons was transiently down-regulated and returned to normal levels in the peri-infarct area. Longitudinal intravital imaging revealed that Lynx1 suppression promoted synaptic clustering with increased dendritic spine turnover in the peri-infarct area, an emerging structural basis for memory formation. As anticipated, Lynx1 suppression improved spontaneous motor recovery and the efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase after stroke. Furthermore, we developed a Lynx1-targeting antisense oligonucleotide and found that its administration during the chronic phase after stroke enhanced the efficacy of rehabilitation. These findings suggest that dendritic spine dynamics in the peri-infarct area are a key determinant of rehabilitation responsiveness through the regulation of clustered spine formation and that Lynx1 may represent a promising therapeutic target for augmenting dendritic plasticity after stroke.

title: FOSL1-associated condensates modulate superenhancer-mediated selected IL-1 family gene activation in psoriasis.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte gene expression, yet the upstream epigenetic mechanisms driving these alterations remain unclear. Here we performed multiomics analyses (chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA sequencing) on psoriatic lesions, perilesional skin, healthy skin, and M5-stimulated HaCaT cells. Functional validation was performed using CRISPR-mediated superenhancer (SE) editing, epigenetic modulation, circular chromosome conformation capture sequencing, assay for chromatin-bound condensates by exploratory sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. We found widespread activation of enhancers and SEs in lesions, including an interleukin 1 (IL-1)-SE regulating IL1A, IL1B, and IL36G transcription. BET inhibition reduced SE activity, repressed IL-1 cytokines, and relieved psoriasis-like inflammation in vivo. Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1) was identified as a key transcription factor enriched in active SEs and associated with condensate formation, contributing to the maintenance of EP300 occupancy and histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation deposition. Macrophage-derived IL-1 up-regulated FOSL1 through mitogen-activated protein kinase/ERK signaling, forming a positive feedback loop that amplified inflammation. This study revealed an FOSL1-SE-centered regulatory network driving keratinocyte inflammatory responses, providing previously unknown therapeutic targets for psoriasis.

title: Targeting cancer immune evasion with anti-FOLR1 antibody-drug conjugate potentiates anti-PD-1 efficacy in colorectal cancer.
abstract: Loss of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) antigen presentation in tumor cells drives immune evasion and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) in colorectal cancer (CRC). To identify therapeutic targets reversing this, we conducted fluorescence-activated cell sorting-based CRISPR activation screens using a druggable genome library and identified folate receptor α (FOLR1) as a top negative regulator. FOLR1 was heterogeneously expressed in CRC tumors but undetectable in adjacent normal tissues. High expression of FOLR1 predicted a poor ICB response, enhanced cancer stemness, and unfavorable patient outcomes. Functional assays showed that FOLR1 promoted CRC stemness-associated properties and fostered an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) with impaired CD8+ T cell infiltration and cytotoxicity, thereby driving tumor progression. Proteomic analyses revealed that FOLR1 stabilized the lactyltransferase AARS1 (alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1), which lactylated signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) at lysine-193 (K193), facilitating its interaction with TCPTP (T cell protein-tyrosine phosphatase) and inducing STAT1 dephosphorylation at tyrosine-701. Consequently, impaired STAT1 signaling down-regulated MHC-I and up-regulated MYC proto-oncogene protein (c-MYC), facilitating evasion of T cell surveillance and enhancing cancer stemness. The anti-FOLR1 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) mirvetuximab soravtansine (IMGN853) exhibited potent activity against FOLR1-positive CRC cells, reprogramming the TME to an immune-active status. Combining IMGN853 with anti-PD-1 (programmed cell death protein-1) therapy boosted antitumor immunity, sensitized tumors to immunotherapy, and induced robust tumor regression in vivo. Our findings support anti-FOLR1 ADC as a clinically actionable approach to overcome immune evasion and unlock immunotherapy efficacy in CRC.

title: Rescue of glutaric aciduria type I by GalNAc-conjugated siRNA against aminoadipate semialdehyde synthase.
abstract: Glutaric aciduria type I (GA-1) is a severe metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase (GCDH), leading to accumulation of organic acids in the brain and resulting in striatal injury and progressive movement disorders. Although early diagnosis and dietary management reduce risk, one-third of patients still develop debilitating neurological complications. We previously demonstrated that liver-specific deletion of aminoadipate semialdehyde synthase (AASS), an upstream enzyme in lysine degradation, is a promising therapeutic strategy. Here, we tested an N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated siRNA against Aass. Treatment of neonatal Gcdh-/- mice rescued lethality and improved the brain pathology while reducing toxic metabolites in the brain and other organs. Serum biomarkers, including glutaric acid, 3-hydroxyglutaric acid, and glutarylcarnitine, predicted neurological outcomes, supporting their use for therapeutic monitoring. Although systemic metabolite concentrations declined, their urinary excretion remained elevated, consistent with a renal washout phenomenon and preserved excretory capacity. These findings demonstrate the potential of liver-targeted small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapy as a treatment for GA-1.

title: Non-canonical function of SCIMP restricts JAK1 activity to counteract immune evasion in bladder cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite the fact that immunotherapy is reshaping the therapeutic landscape of bladder cancer, immune evasion remains a major obstacle to durable clinical benefit. Therefore, elucidating the mechanisms underlying immune resistance is essential for developing novel therapeutic strategies.
METHODS: In this study, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in bladder cancer cells co-cultured with CD8+ T cells and identified the SLP adaptor and CSK-interacting membrane protein (SCIMP) as a key gene that enhances CD8+ T cell antitumor immunity.
RESULTS: SCIMP serves as a favorable prognostic biomarker in patients with bladder cancer treated with immunotherapy. Mechanistically, SCIMP restricts JAK1 phosphorylation in an adaptor-independent manner, suppressing the IFN-γ/JAK1/STAT5A/PD-L1 signaling axis. Meanwhile, YTHDF2 destabilizes the m6A-tagged SCIMP transcripts to reduce their expression. Remarkably, SCIMP synergizes with PD-1 blockade in suppressing tumor growth.
CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unexplored non-canonical role of SCIMP in preventing immune evasion and provide a potential therapeutic target for bladder cancer.

title: RNA Therapeutics in Cardiovascular Medicine: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Practice.
abstract: RNA therapeutics are an exciting class of medications that target RNA and/or are themselves made from RNA. Most RNA therapeutics that have been approved for clinical use are antisense oligonucleotides or small interfering RNAs. To date, eight RNA therapeutics with cardiovascular relevance have received US Food and Drug Administration approval, but not all of them have specific indications for treating cardiovascular disease. There is a promising pipeline of additional cardiovascular RNA therapies targeting lipoprotein(a), angiopoietin-like protein 3, and angiotensinogen. Chemical modifications to therapeutic nucleic acids are important for conferring nuclease resistance and limiting immunostimulation in vivo, and enhanced delivery can be achieved using N-acetylgalactosamine conjugation and/or lipid nanoparticles. Emerging approaches include stereopure oligonucleotide chemistry, circular RNAs, adenosine-to-inosine RNA base editing, and nonhepatic targeting. This review summarizes the mechanistic basis of each modality, the clinical evidence for approved cardiovascular RNA therapeutics, selected pipeline candidates in advanced trials, and directions for future development.

title: Therapeutic Targeting of Oxidative Stress in Hematopoietic Stem Cells: Current Strategies and Future Directions.
abstract: The maintenance of blood homeostasis relies heavily on hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), whose function is highly sensitive to oxidative stress caused by disrupted equilibrium between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and antioxidant systems. This review provides a comprehensive examination of the current strategies aimed at therapeutically targeting oxidative stress in HSC, outlining both the challenges and the advancements in this domain. We discuss the intricate mechanisms by which oxidative stress disrupts HSC self-renewal, quiescence, and differentiation, as well as the implications for aging and hematological malignancies. The function of the hypoxic bone marrow microenvironment in reducing oxidative damage is highlighted alongside the metabolic adaptations that support HSC viability. Furthermore, we explore emerging therapeutic approaches, including antioxidants, gene editing technologies, and niche modulation, that aim to enhance HSC function and resilience in the face of oxidative stress. Drawing on recent preclinical and clinical findings, this review highlights the need for novel strategies that integrate a deeper understanding of redox biology with therapeutic interventions to enhance outcomes in HSC transplantation and regeneration. This integration of current findings and emerging strategies provides valuable insights for developing targeted therapies aimed at preserving HSC integrity in the treatment of hematologic diseases.

title: Integrated Organoid CRISPR Screening Reveals NF1 as a Gatekeeper of Cervical Squamous Malignant Transformation.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Cervical cancer can progress from high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions driven by persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Identifying the gatekeepers restraining malignant transformation could reveal strategies to prevent and treat cervical cancer. In this study, we integrated single-cell transcriptomics, CRISPR-Cas9 screening, and organoid modeling to dissect this process. Single-cell analysis of patient samples revealed progressive activation of rat sarcoma virus (RAS) and proliferation programs along epithelial differentiation paths. A focused CRISPR screen in HPV-positive pretumoroids identified neurofibromin 1 (NF1) as the top suppressor of malignant transition. NF1 loss accelerated carcinogenesis in organoids, substantially shortening the experimental interval required for the emergence of malignant phenotypes and recapitulating basal cell expansion, altered differentiation marker expression, and tumorigenicity. Mechanistically, NF1 loss enhanced RAS-mitogen-activated protein kinase and phosphoinositide 3-kinase-protein kinase B signaling, promoted proliferative programs, and remodeled chromatin accessibility at regulatory regions enriched for activator protein 1 motifs. Conversely, NF1 restoration in cancer organoids induced apoptosis and suppressed malignant maintenance. Artificial intelligence-guided modeling was used to design a minimal NF1-derived peptide predicted to interact with RAS GTP-binding protein. The NF1-GAP-mimetic peptide reduced tumor organoid viability and cervical lesion-associated bioluminescence in an HPV16-driven mouse model and was associated with local immune-related changes without marked alterations in selected splenic T-cell populations. Together, these findings establish NF1 as a critical constraint on HPV-associated epithelial evolution and provide a time-compressed organoid model of cervical carcinogenesis, offering proof of concept for NF1-inspired therapeutic interception of RAS-associated signaling.
SIGNIFICANCE: Single-cell atlas and organoid screening identified NF1 loss as a driver of cervical carcinogenesis, which can be rescued with an AI-designed NF1 mimetic peptide that offers a therapeutic paradigm to intercept tumorigenesis.

title: Aging Rewires Genetic Dependencies in Antitumor T Cells.
abstract: The aged tumor microenvironment can impair antitumor T-cell function, but the molecular regulators that become limiting in this setting remain poorly defined. In a recent issue of Cell, Chen and colleagues harness in vivo CRISPR screening to compare the effects of genetic perturbations in tumor-reactive CD8+ T cells across young and aged hosts. The screen reveals that increased T-cell persistence or an effector-like transcriptional state does not necessarily translate into improved tumor control and identifies Dusp5 and Zfp219 as distinct functional regulators. DUSP5 broadly restrains ERK-dependent proliferation, and its loss improves tumor control in both young and aged mice. ZFP219, by contrast, preferentially limits cytotoxicity in aged hosts; its deletion increases granzyme expression and improves tumor control specifically in the aged setting. Human tumor datasets show that ZNF219 expression in intratumoral CD8+ T cells increases with age and is associated with poorer clinical outcomes. Moreover, Zfp219 loss enhances the response to PD-1 blockade in aged mice, producing complete tumor clearance in a subset of animals and durable protection after rechallenge. Together, these findings show that host age can reshape the functional consequences of T-cell perturbations and reveal age-dependent genetic vulnerabilities with potential therapeutic relevance.

title: Safety and Efficacy of Intratumoral MEDI1191, an IL12 mRNA Lipid Nanoparticle, plus Intravenous Durvalumab in Patients with Advanced Solid Tumors: A First-in-Human Study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: MEDI1191 is a lipid nanoparticle-formulated messenger RNA (mRNA) designed to induce local interleukin (IL) 12 production and intensify antitumor T-cell responses. We report dose-escalation results from a first-in-human, open-label, phase I study of intratumoral MEDI1191 plus intravenous durvalumab (NCT03946800).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients were ≥18 years with advanced/metastatic solid tumors and had progressed on ≥1 line of prior therapy (immunotherapy permitted). Cutaneous/subcutaneous (parts 1A and 1B) or deep-seated lesions (part 1D) were injected; patients had ≥1 noninjected lesion measurable per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST v1.1). Target lesions were noninjected. MEDI1191 and durvalumab were given sequentially (part 1A) or concurrently (parts 1B and 1D). Primary objectives were safety and determination of maximum tolerated dose (MTD). Secondary objectives included efficacy.
RESULTS: As of February 27, 2023, 61 patients were treated. Patients had a median of four prior regimens (range, 1-17); 39 (63.9%) received prior anti-programmed cell death protein 1/programmed cell death ligand 1 [PD-(L)1] immunotherapy. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) occurred in 96.7% of patients, and 41.0% experienced grade 3/4 TEAEs. There were no dose-limiting toxicities. The MTD was not reached. The objective response rate was 9.8%, including 1 confirmed complete response and 5 confirmed partial responses (PR). The duration of response was 2.7 to 22.3 months; the median was not reached. Responses occurred in injected lesions, local noninjected lesions, and distant lesions. Three of the 39 patients with prior anti-PD-(L)1 therapy had PRs.
CONCLUSIONS: MEDI1191 and durvalumab were tolerated. Preliminary antitumor activity was encouraging in these heavily pretreated patients, including patients previously treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors.

title: Danvatirsen plus Pembrolizumab versus Pembrolizumab for Recurrent and/or Metastatic Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma (PEMDA-HN): A Randomized, Phase II Trial.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) is important in promoting a pro-oncogenic tumor microenvironment. This first randomized trial of a STAT3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide with pembrolizumab assessed whether this first-line combination would improve outcomes compared with pembrolizumab alone in recurrent/metastatic (R/M) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: This multicenter, randomized, open-label, controlled study (NCT05814666) enrolled patients with previously untreated R/M HNSCC with positive PD-L1 expression [combined positive score (CPS) ≥1]. Patients were stratified by CPS (1-19; ≥20) and randomized 2:1 to danvatirsen 3 mg/kg intravenously weekly (with two loading doses in week 1) plus pembrolizumab 200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks or pembrolizumab alone. Patients received 21-day treatment cycles until progressive disease, unacceptable toxicity, or voluntary withdrawal. Primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR; partial + complete response per RECIST v1.1).
RESULTS: Sixty-nine patients were randomized, and 66 were treated [51 (77.3%) male]: 45 with danvatirsen + pembrolizumab and 21 with pembrolizumab alone. Enrollment was stopped due to lack of response in the CPS 1 to 19 cohort after ≥1 scan (∼6 weeks of treatment) and in the CPS ≥20 cohort after ≥2 scans (∼12 weeks). In the final analysis, ORRs were 15.6% and 14.3%, respectively (risk difference 1.3; P = 1). The treatment-emergent adverse event rate was increased in the combination arm (97.8% vs. 85.7%), and the combination side effect profile was similar to previous danvatirsen studies.
CONCLUSIONS: Combination danvatirsen + pembrolizumab did not improve ORR compared with pembrolizumab alone in first-line treatment of R/M HNSCC. Further exploration of STAT3-targeted approaches is needed within the context of immunotherapy.

title: Dual Inhibition of PARP and ATR Induces Synthetic Lethal Vulnerability in Prostate Cancer with CDK12 Deficiency.
abstract: Prostate cancers harboring CDK12 alterations exhibit aggressive clinical behavior and poor responses to current therapeutic strategies. Although CDK12 is categorized as a homologous recombination repair (HRR)-related gene, clinical evidence indicates limited benefit of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor monotherapy in CDK12-defective tumors. To clarify the functional consequences of CDK12 loss and identify a mechanistically rational therapeutic approach, we generated CDK12-knockout (KO) prostate cancer cell lines using CRISPR/Cas9 and assessed cell-cycle regulation, DNA damage repair, and replication stress via flow cytometry, γH2AX immunofluorescence, and DNA fiber assays. CDK12 KO abrogated the G0-G1 checkpoint, permitting cell-cycle progression into the M-phase despite the persistence of unrepaired DNA double-strand breaks (DSB), and reduced ATM transcription, resulting in a DSB response phenotype resembling ATM deficiency. CDK12 loss also increased intrinsic replication stress and sensitized prostate cancer cells to ATR inhibition. In patient-derived xenograft models harboring CDK12 alterations, combined PARP and ATR inhibition led to enhanced DSB accumulation and selectively suppressed tumor growth in CDK12-defective models. These findings highlight the importance of interrogating individual genes within the HRR pathway to define distinct mechanistic vulnerabilities and provide a strong rationale for combined PARP and ATR inhibition as a novel therapeutic strategy for patients with CDK12-altered prostate cancer.

title: Preclinical modeling of trastuzumab deruxtecan in a mouse model of brain metastatic triple-negative breast cancer identifies two contributors to efficacy.
abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has demonstrated clinical efficacy in advanced HER2-low to -ultralow breast cancer. We employed a mouse model of triple-negative breast cancer in the difficult-to-treat brain metastasis setting to determine T-DXd efficacy and investigate mechanism(s). T-DXd (10 and 3 mg/kg) was compared to an identical ADC except HER2-nonbinding (control) in a hematogenous model of HER2-ultralow brain-tropic triple-negative breast cancer, MDA-MB-231-BR7 (231-BR). The roles of HER2 and the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) were determined by CRISPR-Cas9 deletion and shRNA knockdown, respectively. 231-BR cells exhibited HER2 0+ staining, with occasional membrane expression. T-DXd at 10 mg/kg reduced 231-BR brain metastases by 49% (P=0.002), while a dose reduction showed a 30% (ns) metastasis reduction, each compared to the control-ADC. HER2-specific and -nonspecific ADC uptake into metastases was accompanied by a 23-47% tumor cell Ki-67 decline, and 5-fold increase in tumor apoptosis. A HER2 CRISPR-Cas9 knockout 231-BR formed multiple brain metastases but was insensitive to T-DXd in vivo. 231-BR tumor cells expressed FcRn, potentially enabling nonspecific ADC uptake. Analysis of human tumors showed TNBC tumors expressed FcRn mRNA. T-DXd failed to inhibit brain metastases in two 231-BR FcRn knockdown clones compared to a 231-BR clone transduced with a scrambled shRNA where T-DXd inhibited brain metastases (67% reduction, P=0.01). Despite ultralow HER2 expression, the HER2 binding capacity of T-DXd is a significant contributor to its efficacy. Breast cancers variably express FcRn, suggesting that nonspecific tumor cell uptake of T-DXd via FcRn is also a potential mechanism of T-DXd action.

title: CDK8 Inhibition Releases the Muscle Differentiation Block in Fusion-Driven Alveolar Rhabdomyosarcoma.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (aRMS) is a fusion-driven pediatric cancer with poor survival and limited therapeutic options. To uncover novel vulnerabilities, we used complex-Map functional genomic data, identifying CDK8 as a dependency in aRMS. Both CDK8 knockout and pharmacologic inhibition impaired tumor cell growth and induced myogenic differentiation in vitro and in vivo. Compared with genetic loss, CDK8 pharmacologic inhibition induced more dynamic transcriptional changes. With a genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 drug modifier screen, we determined that the maximal antitumor activity of the CDK8 inhibitor requires the presence of the Mediator kinase module, including CDK8, and transcriptional cooperation with the SAGA complex. We further identified SIX4 as a key transcription factor mediating CDK8 inhibitor-induced transcriptional activation of myogenic differentiation genes and impaired tumor proliferation. These findings suggest a distinct gain-of-function mechanism of the CDK8 inhibitor and establish a strong rationale for CDK8 inhibition as a differentiation-inducing therapeutic strategy in aRMS.
SIGNIFICANCE: We provide a framework for uncovering therapeutic targets by network-based analysis of functional genomic screens. We identify CDK8 as a druggable target in aRMS and determine that CDK8 inhibition drives myogenic differentiation and impairs tumor progression via a collaborative mechanism involving the Mediator kinase module, SAGA complex, and SIX4. See related commentary by Stevens and Hatley, p. 2210.

title: Immune Checkpoint Blockade Sensitivity Is Linked to Endogenous Retroelement Transcriptional Changes in Cancer.
abstract: Endogenous retrotransposable elements (ERE) can modulate immune responses. We explored ERE transcription in relation to response to immune checkpoint inhibition in advanced solid tumors. ERE expression was measured in pre- and on-treatment samples from patients treated in a clinical trial with pembrolizumab. We evaluated immune cell infiltration and correlated ERE expression with interferon (IFN)-stimulated gene profiles and cytolytic activity. Two independent datasets were retrospectively analyzed as external validation. ERE transcription, notably Alu repetitive elements followed by long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE), is upregulated in immunotherapy responders, and higher ERE expression correlates with durable clinical benefit and improved long-term outcomes. In responders, this dynamic increase correlates with CD8+ T-cell infiltration and cytolytic activity, particularly during treatment. A trend toward increased A-to-I RNA editing was observed in responders. External validation in melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer cohorts confirmed a consistent pattern in ERE transcription. Therefore, ERE transcription is emerging as a potential biomarker for personalized immunotherapy in solid tumors.

title: Therapy-Persistent Leukemia Is Selectively Vulnerable to SLC23A1 Restoration via Targeting KHSRP.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is prone to relapse driven by therapy-persistent residual cells. To discover specific vulnerabilities in this population, we performed genome-wide CRISPR interference screens in leukemia cells treated with multiple agents. KHSRP was the top hit, the depletion of which sensitized AML cells to therapy and substantially prolonged survival in treated AML-bearing mice. Analysis of in vivo residual disease after venetoclax/azacitidine treatment identified downregulation of the vitamin C and uric acid transporter SLC23A1, which mediated resistance to multiple therapies. KHSRP depletion restored SLC23A1 expression by preventing its ZC3H4-mediated nuclear mRNA degradation. KHSRP depletion therefore enhanced the synergistic cytotoxicity of vitamin C and uric acid, particularly in therapy-persistent leukemia cells. Re-expression of TET2 overrode the chemosensitizing effect of KHSRP depletion in TET2-mutant leukemia, suggesting that KHSRP-linked phenotypes were related to vitamin C- and uric acid-mediated TET activation. These findings suggest targeting KHSRP to enhance treatment efficacy and selectively eradicate residual AML.
SIGNIFICANCE: Residual AML cells that persist following therapy have distinct biological properties compared with initial disease or overt relapse. Here, we nominate KHSRP as a target to improve therapy efficacy and exploit selective vulnerabilities of AML residual disease.

title: Adeno-Associated Virus-Induced Humanized Hypertensive Mouse Model Validates N-Acetylgalactosamine-Conjugated Small Interfering RNA Targeting Angiotensinogen as a Long-Acting Antihypertensive Therapy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertension remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, yet current therapeutic strategies lack sustained efficacy and long-term stability. Our study aimed to construct a humanized rodent model for drugs development especially currently prevalent small interfering RNA medication.
METHODS: A humanized hypertensive mouse model was generated by subcutaneous injection of neonatal mice with adeno-associated viruses encoding hAGT (human angiotensinogen) and hRENIN (human renin). Blood pressure was monitored weekly via tail-cuff plethysmography. Expression of hAGT and hRENIN was assessed by ELISA, Western blot, and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Cardiac function was evaluated by echocardiography at 4 and 6 months postinjection. Hypertension-associated comorbidities were examined through histological analysis and ELISA. A modified N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA targeting human hepatic AGT (GalNAc-siAGT) was screened and subcutaneously administered to humanized hypertensive mice, either alone or in combination with valsartan, to evaluate therapeutic efficacy.
RESULTS: The dual adeno-associated virus-induced humanized hypertensive model exhibited a sustained hypertension for 6 months and manifested prevalent comorbidities, including heart failure and kidney disease. This modified GalNAc-siAGT demonstrated significant activity in knocking down hAGT both in vitro and in vivo. Only a single subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siAGT in humanized hypertensive mice led to a sustained reduction in blood pressure lasting for 2 months, accompanied by cardio- and renoprotective effects. Moreover, combining GalNAc-siAGT with the renin-angiotensin system blocker, valsartan, significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study validated the antihypertensive therapeutic effect of GalNAc-siAGT in a humanized hypertensive murine model while highlighting the translational potential of this model for clinical drug development.

title: A universal platform for TCRα/β removal enables safer and more potent TCR therapies and autoimmune modeling.
abstract: Adoptive T-cell therapies using tumour-specific T-cell receptors (TCRs) are limited by competition with endogenous receptors, impairing efficacy and posing risks of off-target autoreactivity. Here we present a CRISPR-based platform that selectively eliminates both endogenous TCR-α and -β chains without affecting transgenic TCRs, irrespective of codon optimization. This approach achieves >90% deletion efficiency in Jurkat and primary human T cells, enhancing expression and functional potency of transgenic receptors. Using an HLA-A*02:01-restricted DMF5 TCR, we show that dual TCR ablation boosts antigen-specific activation and cytotoxicity in vitro and enhances tumor clearance in vivo in human immune system (HIS) mice and prevents graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Targeted locus amplification showed that CRISPR-induced double-strand breaks did not alter lentiviral integration profiles, supporting genomic safety. Extending this approach to four insulin-reactive TCRs demonstrated that endogenous receptor removal increased transduction efficiency and functional activity, with one (1E6) showing selective activation and infiltration of islet grafts (SC-islets) in vivo. This study establishes a universal, safe, and scalable genome-editing platform for generating functionally precise human T cells. By integrating cancer immunotherapy and autoimmune disease modelling within a single framework, it provides a preclinical rationale for dual endogenous TCR removal to improve specificity, safety, and therapeutic efficacy in TCR-based cell therapies.

title: Genomic, single-cell, and functional profiling of the CD48-CD244 axis and NK cell dysfunction in multiple myeloma.
abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) orchestrates immune evasion by subverting natural killer (NK) cell function. CD48, one of the most abundant NK ligands on MM cells, paradoxically enhances NK cell activation yet is associated with high-risk cytogenetics and poor patient survival. We integrated multiomics (bulk and single-cell RNA-seq, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing [ATAC-seq], chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing [ChIP-seq]), genome-wide CRISPR knockout/activation screens, and machine learning to dissect CD48 regulation and function. In human MM and Vκ*MYC mouse scRNA-seq datasets, NK cells exhibit stepwise increases in inflammatory and exhaustion signatures and loss of cytotoxic potential as disease progresses. In vitro coculture assays show that CD48 overexpression on MM enhances NK cell cytokine secretion, whereas chronic exposure leads to ex vivo NK dysfunction. In vivo, CD48-overexpressing Vκ*MYC tumors progress more slowly and extend host survival, while NK cell depletion accelerates disease. These findings support a context-dependent role for CD48, potentiating acute NK responses while coexisting with chronic NK exhaustion, and suggest strategies to modulate CD48 for therapeutic benefit.

title: A single liver-sparing myotropic AAV ameliorates muscular dystrophy in humanized mice by base editing.
abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, most of which are large exon deletions that result in loss of dystrophin protein. Adenine base editing (ABE) enables permanent gene correction by modifying splice sites to cause exon skipping and restoration of the DMD open reading frame. We previously demonstrated that adeno-associated virus 9-mediated (AAV9-mediated) delivery of adenine base editors allows efficient gene editing in mouse models of DMD. However, conventional AAV-based gene delivery approaches are complicated by their limited packaging capacity and high-dose-related toxicity. Here, we describe a single AAV vector encoding a compact adenine base editor, SlugABE8e, and a single-guide RNA, which enable efficient editing in a humanized DMD mouse model at a lower dose using the muscle-tropic MyoAAV4 capsid. Systemic MyoAAV4A delivery in juvenile DMD mice efficiently restored dystrophin expression in the heart and skeletal muscles. This molecular rescue was accompanied by reduced serum creatine kinase activity and diminished muscle pathology. A liver-detargeted MyoAAV4E-off capsid eliminated viral entry and editing in the liver. We also explored a high-fidelity base editor, SlugHF-ABE8e(V106W), which showed similar on-target and off-target editing to SlugABE8e. Together, these findings establish an all-in-one AAV strategy that efficiently mitigates DMD disease progression.

title: Epigenetic regulation of DOT1L methyltransferase activityremodels lipid metabolism to alleviate ferroptosis-induced liver injury.
abstract: Epigenetic modifications contribute to lipid-related disorders by modulating the expression of key genes involved in lipid metabolism. Accumulating evidence suggests that lipid metabolism-mediated ferroptosis drives the progression of metabolic associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and liver injury. However, whether epigenetic mechanisms remodel lipid metabolism to regulate ferroptosis-induced liver damage remains unclear. Here, through pharmacological screening of epigenetics-related compounds and CRISPR-Cas9-based screening targeting epigenetic factors, we identified DOT1 Like Histone Lysine Methyltransferase (DOT1L) as a key sensitizer of hepatocytes to ferroptosis and subsequent liver injury, whereas inhibition of DOT1L reverses the phenomenon. DOT1L loss remodeled the phospholipid landscape by decreasing PUFA-containing phospholipids while increasing monounsaturated and lysophospholipid species. Mechanistically, DOT1L depletion reduced H3K79me1 and H3K79me2 occupancy at the PLA2G7, ALDH3B1, and PLCXD3 loci, particularly across gene-body regions, while increasing promoter-proximal accessibility and expression of these phospholipid-remodeling genes. These genes suppress ferroptosis by reducing the levels of phospholipids containing polyunsaturated fatty acids (PL-PUFAs). Furthermore, we demonstrated that AMPK phosphorylates DOT1L at Ser786, weakens its association with AF9, and suppresses H3K79 methyltransferase activity and ferroptosis sensitivity. Collectively, our findings reveal the AMPK-DOT1L-H3K79 methylation axis as a novel lipid metabolic pathway that regulates ferroptosis and maintains hepatic homeostasis, offering new therapeutic insights for ferroptosis-related liver injury.

title: OSTM1 restrains B-cell lymphomagenesis by promoting PDE3B degradation and activating cAMP/PKA/CREB signaling.
abstract: Through a genome-wide forward CRISPR/Cas9 screen in interleukin-3 (IL3)-dependent Ba/F3 cells, we identified osteoclastogenesis-associated transmembrane protein 1 (OSTM1) as a previously unrecognized tumor suppressor. Analysis of patient datasets revealed that OSTM1 is frequently deleted or downregulated in human B-cell malignancies (BCM). In mice, Cd19-Cre-driven B cell-specific monoallelic or biallelic deletion of Ostm1 cooperated with Cdkn2a loss to drive lymphomagenesis with near-complete penetrance. Mechanistically, OSTM1 directly interacts with phosphodiesterase 3B (PDE3B) and promotes its proteasomal degradation. Because PDE3B hydrolyzes cyclic AMP (cAMP), loss of OSTM1 stabilizes PDE3B, leading to suppression of tumor-suppressive cAMP-dependent PKA/CREB signaling and promotion of oncogenic transformation. Consistent with this mechanism, PDE3B is frequently amplified or upregulated in BCM, and expression of CREB/CREBBP transcriptional targets correlates positively with OSTM1 expression but inversely with PDE3B across BCM cohorts. Importantly, silencing Pde3b reverses oncogenic transformation driven by Ostm1 loss. Together, these findings establish OSTM1 as a tumor suppressor and uncover an OSTM1/PDE3B/cAMP signaling axis that restrains B-cell lymphomagenesis and may represent a therapeutically actionable vulnerability.

title: A Comparison of the Sensitivity of Cynomolgus Monkeys and Beagle Dogs to the Pro-Inflammatory Effects of an Inhaled Antisense Oligonucleotide.
abstract: Chronic pulmonary diseases are often associated with high morbidity and/or mortality, and many lack effective therapies. Direct delivery of antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) to the lung shows promise for the treatment of pulmonary diseases. Despite their overall low risk profiles, systemically delivered ASOs can be associated with pro-inflammatory responses including activation of the alternative complement pathway, particularly near administration sites. Nonhuman primates (NHPs) and Beagle dogs have both been used in ASO toxicity studies, but comparative suitability of these species for ASO safety assessment has not been established. Herein, we compare the tolerability of a phosphorothioate (PS) gapmer ASO in these species after dosing with a nebulized ASO delivered by inhalation at 15 mg/kg once weekly for 13 weeks via face mask. Although lung concentrations of ASO were similar in cynomolgus monkeys and Beagle dogs, ASO inhalation was associated with greater pro-inflammatory responses in the monkey. Anti-drug antibody production, C-reactive protein elevation, complement activation, increased bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cellularity, increased lung weights, and microscopic evidence of pulmonary inflammation were present in the monkey but not the dog. Therefore, although NHPs and dogs can be used in toxicity testing of inhaled ASOs, NHPs exhibit a predisposition to complement activation and development of pulmonary inflammation.

title: Killers by Design: How Innovative Gene-Engineering Fine-Tunes NK Cells as Next Generation Immunotherapies.
abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells have emerged as promising candidates for adoptive immunotherapies. Their natural cytotoxic capabilities and low incidence of side-effects such as cytokine release syndrome and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity, render NK cells a favorable alternative to T cells. Incorporation of a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) has been shown to greatly enhance NK cell's antitumor capacity. Nevertheless, CAR-NK cell therapies still face several challenges, such as low in vivo persistence, low tumor homing of the transfused cells and the effects of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Genetic modifications of key cellular mediators show great potential to overcome these hurdles. While well-established viral engineering strategies are currently the most commonly used techniques, biosafety concerns, high costs, and labour-intensive protocols have encouraged innovation toward nonviral strategies. In this review, we describe recently established viral and nonviral technologies used for NK cell engineering, focusing on their respective advantages and disadvantages. In addition, we highlight the most important functional refinements and mechanistic characterizations of NK cells and genetically optimized NK cells in the context of the TME and how these advances can be progressed toward therapeutic translation.
