title: Recombinant AAV-Based Gene Therapy for Central Nervous System Disorders: From Gene Replacement to Precision Editing and Circuit Modulation.
abstract: Recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) vectors have moved central nervous system (CNS) gene therapy from experimental proof of concept to clinically validated treatment, yet therapeutic design remains highly dependent on disease mechanism, cellular distribution, and treatment timing. This narrative review examines recent progress in rAAV-based interventions for neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) and neurodegenerative disorders. For monogenic NDDs, gene replacement is most applicable to loss-of-function conditions with compatible payload size and tolerable expression, whereas dominant-negative, gain-of-function, and dosage-sensitive disorders may require allele-selective silencing or precise DNA or RNA editing. Rett syndrome illustrates both the reversibility of postnatal dysfunction and the need for tightly regulated transgene expression. Spinal muscular atrophy provides the leading translational paradigm: rAAV9-mediated SMN1 replacement demonstrates the value of early diagnosis, adequate tissue exposure, and treatment before irreversible neuronal loss. For complex neurodegenerative diseases, emerging strategies extend beyond simple gene addition. APOE-directed editing and protective-variant replacement may enable genotype-informed intervention in Alzheimer's disease, whereas Parkinson's disease programs combine restoration of dopamine synthesis, neuroprotection, and genetically encoded circuit modulation. Across these indications, major barriers include incomplete and nonselective CNS delivery, immune and dose-related toxicity, limited redosing, durable control of transgene or editor activity, off-target effects, and uncertain translation from animal models to humans. Progress over the next decade will depend on human-compatible vectors, cell-selective and regulatable expression, rigorous long-term safety assessment, biomarker-guided trials, and rational combinations that connect molecular target engagement to meaningful neurological benefit.

title: Liver concentrations of JNJ-73763989 siRNA triggers in patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB): The INSIGHT study panel 3 results.
abstract: BackgroundJNJ-73763989 is a 2:1 combination of 2 N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated short interfering RNAs (siRNA) targeting the S (daplusiran) and X (tomligisiran) regions of the hepatitis B virus genome. In phase 2b studies, 48 weeks of JNJ-73763989-based combination treatments led to dose-dependent reductions in viral markers, including hepatitis B surface antigen. The objective of the INSIGHT study Panel 3 was to quantify intrahepatic concentrations of the siRNAs in human livers during and after treatment.MethodsIn the open-label, single-arm, single-center study, participants with chronic hepatitis B received 48 weeks of treatment with JNJ-73763989 200 mg every 4 weeks and nucleos(t)ide analog, with optional pegylated interferon α2a 180 µg weekly added after Treatment Week (TW) 40. Core liver biopsies were collected at TW12, TW40, and at Follow-up Week (FUW) 24.ResultsLiver biopsies were available from all 4 participants at TW12 and from 3 at TW40 and FUW24. Between TW12 and TW40, liver concentrations of daplusiran and tomligisiran increased 1.5- to 2.6-fold, consistent with intrahepatic accumulation. Twenty-eight weeks after the last injection of JNJ-73763989, the triggers were still measurable in 2 of 3 participants with 4.5- to 15-fold reduced concentrations from peak levels; the estimated liver half-life ranged from approximately 2.9 to 16.1 weeks.ConclusionsIn this first study to assess liver concentrations of GalNAc-siRNA in humans with sequential biopsies, long persistence of JNJ-73763989 triggers in human livers may partially explain the prolonged suppressive effect on viral parameters observed in phase 2 studies.

title: Beyond Seizure Control: Building the Infrastructure for Disease-Modifying Therapies in Epilepsy.
abstract: Rapid advances in disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) for epilepsy, including gene-based therapies, antisense oligonucleotides, and stem cell-derived approaches, are reshaping the treatment landscape. As these therapies move through clinical trials and toward regulatory review, they introduce complex clinical, operational, ethical, and equity considerations that extend well beyond traditional antiseizure medication management. Successful integration will require careful attention to patient selection, genetic and biomarker testing, multidisciplinary care models, infrastructure readiness, referral pathways, long-term safety monitoring, informed consent for novel and potentially irreversible interventions, access to clinical trials, and cost and reimbursement challenges. Significant investments in personnel, systems, and facilities may be necessary, raising important questions about implementation across diverse practice settings and the risk of widening disparities in care. Here, we review the evolving therapeutic pipeline and outline key considerations for safe, ethical, and equitable implementation.

title: Considerations of Gene Expression Analysis Methods for Gapmer Antisense Oligonucleotide-Treated Samples.
abstract: Probe-based PCR assays are commonly used to evaluate gene expression in antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-treated samples, but assay design and postextraction processing may introduce substantial measurement bias. We investigated workflow-dependent differences in measured knockdown across PCR-based and RNA-sequencing assays using an allele-specific gapmer ASO, targeting a linked single nucleotide polymorphism of a dominant-negative SPTAN1 variant. Exogenous ribonuclease H (RNase H) activity during reverse transcription or ribosomal RNA (rRNA)-depletion inflated apparent knockdown and reduced RNA-sequencing coverage at the ASO-binding site. In droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), allele-specific detection probes overlapping the ASO-binding site produced substantially greater apparent knockdown than nonoverlapping probes, particularly following workflows with active RNase H. Spike-in experiments showed that this bias was not reproduced by adding ASO to purified RNA before complementary DNA (cDNA) synthesis or to cDNA before ddPCR, but emerged when ASO was present during rRNA depletion. Together, these findings show that exogenous RNase H activity during RNA processing and ASO-probe overlap can distort measurements of gapmer-mediated transcript reduction. Poly(A)-based RNA sequencing, reverse transcriptase with reduced RNase H activity, and nonoverlapping PCR detection probes can minimize measurement bias when evaluating gapmer ASO-mediated knockdown.

title: Improved Efficacy and Tolerability of Antisense Oligonucleotide with Guanidine-Bridged Nucleic Acid.
abstract: Guanidine-bridged nucleic acid (GuNA) is a bridged nucleic acid analog with high binding affinity toward complementary strands along with high nuclease resistance. GuNA has been developed to improve pharmacokinetics and safety profiles of phosphorothioate modified gapmers. Here, we evaluated antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) modified with combination of GuNA and 2'-O-methoxyethyl (MOE) and found that the dual-modification strategy could significantly improve knockdown activity in vitro and in vivo. Long-term efficacy evaluation showed that intracerebroventricularly administered GuNA-modified gapmers stayed active for over 24 weeks in mouse brain. Furthermore, we observed that GuNA-modified gapmers could evade lymphocyte-derived immune responses and kept ASO-induced toxicity in check. Taken together, the results of this study demonstrate that GuNA modification can improve the functional potential of ASOs, especially in the central nervous system.

title: Properties of Stereodefined Variants of Nusinersen.
abstract: In the pharmaceutical industry, stereopure drugs are generally preferred over isomeric mixtures to reduce the risks of side effects and to simplify pharmacodynamics (PD) and pharmacokinetics (PK) properties. This reasoning applies equally to antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs). All current ASO drugs are modified to provide appropriate PK/PD properties. Among the modifications, phosphorothioate (PS) groups provide essential nuclease resistance and advantageous biodistribution properties. However, PS groups are chiral, with Rp- and Sp-centers that are challenging to incorporate stereoselectively during solid-phase synthesis, and thus current ASO drugs are diastereoisomeric mixtures. Here, we describe the synthesis of stereodefined variants of the approved drug nusinersen (Spinraza), a 2'-O-methoxyethyl-modified oligonucleotide that redirects splicing of SMN2 during treatment for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). We found that a single 3'-Sp linkage stabilizes nusinersen from degradation in mouse tissue homogenates. Although Rp-nusinersen has higher target-binding affinity than Sp-nusinersen, it is not more active than parent nusinersen in patient-derived cells. Finally, we show mixed results from comparing stereodefined nusinersen with parent nusinersen in a murine model of SMA. While our data do not provide definitive evidence for the superior performance of stereodefined nusinersen, we conclude that it is likely equally effective as its parent ASO, while bearing the pharmacological advantages of a single stereoisomer.

title: Safety, tolerability, and effect of nusinersen in ambulatory and non-ambulatory adults with 5q-SMA treated up to five years.
abstract: BackgroundNusinersen treatment of adults with 5q-SMA was found to be safe and stabilizes or improves motor function in the short-term (<38 months), but data examining longer-term (>38 months) impact and safety is lacking.ObjectiveTo study the long-term (24-60 months) effects and safety profile of nusinersen in adults with 5q-SMA.MethodsWe conducted a observational study of 5q-SMA patients, age ≥18 years, and receiving nusinersen for ≥24 months. Data were analyzed by ambulatory status. Clinical outcomes included: 6-minute walk test (6MWT), Hammersmith Functional Motor Scale - Expanded (HFMSE) scores, revised upper limb module (RULM) scores, pulmonary function test results, and medication-related adverse effects. Data were collected at baseline and post-treatment initiation at months 2, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, and 60 +/- 2 months. Linear mixed models with random intercept for each patient were used to examine the changes of outcomes across time.ResultsThiry-two individuals with 5q-SMA (17 female) were included. Nineteen were non-ambulatory (mean age 38.3+/- 12.1 years) and 13 were ambulatory (mean age 32.9+/-9.5 years) at treatment onset. Average treatment duration was 53.3 months (range 24-60 months). The ambulatory group showed stability in 6MWT and HFMSE compared to baseline. In non-ambulatory patients, RULM and FVC remained stable. No serious adverse events attributable to nusinersen were reported.ConclusionsLong-term nusinersen treatment is safe in adults with SMA. Patients showed relative clinical stability over 60 months. These findings suggest that nusinersen may provide relative improvement compared to the natural disease progression over 2-5 years of treatment.

title: Recombinant Fusion of Polyglutamic Acid Enhances Cell-Penetrating Peptide-Mediated CRISPR-Cas9 Delivery.
abstract: Genome editing has been revolutionized by Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein 9 (Cas9) technology. However, efficient intracellular delivery of Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) remains a major challenge, particularly in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods. Integrating viral vectors carry a risk of insertional mutagenesis, whereas physical methods such as electroporation are not well suited for in vivo or clinically relevant applications. Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) offer a promising alternative for direct RNP delivery, although their efficiency is often limited by endosomal entrapment and limited cytosolic release. In this study, we developed two recombinant CPP-fused Cas9 proteins, polyglutamate (PE)-trans-activator of transcription (TAT)-nuclear localization signal (NLS)-Cas9 (PETATCas9) and TAT-NLS-Cas9 (TATCas9), designed to improve solubility, membrane penetration, RNP complex formation, and nuclear targeting. PE tag in PETATCas9 was introduced to optimize charge balance and reduce nonspecific electrostatic interactions between TAT and guide RNA (gRNA), thereby enhancing RNP stability and delivery performance. Both recombinant proteins were expressed, purified, and assembled with gRNA into functional RNP complexes for delivery into SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. The optimized CPP-Cas9 RNP system enabled efficient intracellular delivery and glucosylceramidase beta 1 (GBA1) gene editing in SH-SY5Y cells. These findings establish PETATCas9 as a scalable, transient, nonviral, and self-delivering RNP platform for CRISPR-based genome editing in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods.

title: Telomere-Targeting CRISPR-Cas9 Induces Distinct DNA Damage Responses.
abstract: Telomeres are essential for maintaining linear chromosome integrity, making their dysregulation in cancer an attractive target for DNA damage-mediated therapeutic interventions. Here, we explored the effects of targeting telomeric repeat sequences with CRISPR-Cas9 in human cells. At high expression levels achieved through transient transfection, telomere-specific CRISPR-Cas9 (TelCR), one of two possible telomere-targeting CRISPR-Cas9 constructs, triggered acute telomere loss, activated the ATR-CHK1/2-WEE1 G2 DNA damage checkpoint, and promoted apoptosis in HeLa cells. Conversely, an inducible system delivering sublethal levels of TelCR resulted in progressive telomere attrition and an ATM-dependent DNA damage response. TelCR also induced chromosomal instability, characterized by the formation of multicentric chromosomes. Moreover, sublethal telomeric damage elicited a transcriptional program distinct from nonspecific DNA breaks, characterized by enrichment of pathways associated with metabolic adaptation, stress responses, and innate immune signaling. Collectively, these findings reveal distinct cellular and transcriptional responses to telomere-specific CRISPR-Cas9-mediated damage, highlighting its utility as a tool for inducing targeted telomeric damage.

title: USP22 is a novel vulnerability regulating MEIS1 protein abundance and gene transcription in KMT2Ar acute leukemia.
abstract: Patients with acute leukemias harboring translocations involving gene lysine methyltransferase 2A (KMT2A) have a poor prognosis due to chemotherapy resistance with rapid relapse following standard treatments. The resulting KMT2A fusion proteins dysregulate gene expression, leading to an upregulation of leukemogenic transcription factors such as HOXA9 and MEIS1, which drives leukemic transformation. Although menin inhibitors are proving to be promising new therapeutics for patients with KMT2A-rearranged (KMT2Ar) acute leukemia, resistance mechanisms have already been described and new therapeutic approaches for this patient subgroup must be identified. Here, a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen in a KMT2Ar B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia cell line identified the deubiquitinase ubiquitin-specific peptidase 22 (USP22) as a novel regulator of MEIS1 protein stability. USP22 is a member of the Spt-Ada-Gcn5 acetyltransferase multiprotein complex, which has crucial functions in shaping the chromatin landscape and modulating transcription. Genetic depletion of USP22 impaired cellular growth and proliferation in KMT2Ar acute leukemia models. Chromatin immunoprecipitation revealed cooperative binding between USP22 and MEIS1 at critical oncogenic target genes, suggesting that USP22 safeguards leukemogenic transcription by protecting MEIS1 from proteasomal degradation. Genetic or chemical inhibition of USP22 led to the polyubiquitination of MEIS1, resulting in proteasomal degradation and downregulation of the expression of target genes. Our study identifies USP22 as a novel regulator of MEIS1 protein stability that could potentially be exploited as a therapeutic target in the future in KMT2Ar leukemias.

title: NRAS knockdown reverses monocytic cell state and resensitizes resistant FLT3-AML cells to gilteritinib.
abstract: Although the FLT3 inhibitor gilteritinib is initially effective in patients with FLT3-mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML), patients invariably relapse within months of treatment. Gilteritinib resistance is commonly driven by the emergence of NRAS mutations and a shift toward a more monocytic cell state. We hypothesized that directly targeting and depleting NRAS protein would reverse these adaptive differentiation changes and restore therapeutic sensitivity. To test this, we used a mutation-agnostic antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively knock down NRAS expression across gilteritinib-resistant AML cell lines, in vivo cell line-derived xenografts, and primary patient samples. NRAS ASO successfully resensitized gilteritinib-resistant cells with multiple distinct NRAS mutations, displaying superior efficacy compared with downstream MEK inhibition. This therapeutic efficacy was independent of NRAS-mutant variant allele frequency, suggesting that wild-type NRAS may also contribute to resistance. Comprehensive multiomics profiling (transcriptomics, proteomics, and phosphoproteomics) revealed that NRAS knockdown consistently reversed the monocytic phenotype, shifting cells back toward a more primitive cell state. Monocytic differentiation and NRAS mutations are established drivers of resistance to diverse targeted regimens in AML, including FLT3, IDH, and BCL2 inhibitors. Therefore, we also tested venetoclax-resistant primary cells with NRAS mutations. Resistant cells were resensitized to venetoclax after NRAS knockdown, suggesting that NRAS knockdown may be more broadly applicable for overcoming monocytic cell state and drug resistance in AML.

title: Reduced SRSF1 expression correlates with LCK exon skipping and impaired Treg induction in immune thrombocytopenia.
abstract: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by antibody-mediated platelet destruction and impaired regulatory T-cell (Treg) function, yet its molecular basis remains poorly defined. Here, we show that CD4+ naive T cells from patients with ITP exhibit diminished T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling and impaired in vitro Treg induction relative to healthy controls. RNA sequencing revealed widespread dysregulation of alternative splicing, most notably exon 8 skipping in LCK, a kinase central to TCR signaling and Treg differentiation. Using an LCK minigene combined with RNA pull-down mass spectrometry and RNA immunoprecipitation assays, we identified the splicing factor SRSF1 as a direct upstream regulator of LCK exon 8 skipping. Notably, SRSF1 expression was reduced in CD4+ naive T cells from patients with ITP, and its overexpression restored in vitro Treg induction capacity. Antisense oligonucleotide-mediated blockade of SRSF1 binding to LCK enhanced exon 8 skipping and attenuated TCR activation in Jurkat cells. Although murine Lck lacks the human-specific recursive splicing sites required for exon 8 exclusion, the adoptive transfer of CD4+ naive T cells expressing the exon 8-skipped murine Lck into CD61-knockout mice significantly reduced Treg proportions and platelet counts in an active ITP model. Mechanistically, Jurkat cells engineered to express only the exon 8-skipped LCK variant showed markedly reduced binding to ZAP70 and CD3ζ, which may partly account for the attenuated TCR signaling and downstream FOXP3 induction. Together, these findings define a novel SRSF1-LCK splicing axis that may regulate Treg development in ITP.

title: Sapablursen for erythrocytosis control in patients with polycythemia vera.
abstract: Polycythemia vera is characterized by erythrocytosis and an increased risk of thrombosis. Sapablursen is an antisense oligonucleotide that suppresses transmembrane serine protease 6, increases hepcidin production, and reduces iron availability for erythropoiesis. IMPRSSION is an ongoing phase 2a, randomized, open-label study in patients with phlebotomy-dependent polycythemia vera. Cohort A (120 or 80 mg) and cohort B (40 mg) received sapablursen subcutaneously once every 4 weeks. The primary efficacy end point was the reduction in phlebotomy frequency from baseline to weeks 17 to 37 in patients who received ≥1 dose. The baseline mean ± standard deviation weekly phlebotomy rate was 0.15 ± 0.07 in cohort A and 0.17 ± 0.07 in cohort B, with reduction by -0.10 (95% confidence interval [CI], -0.13 to -0.07; n = 32; P< .0001) in cohort A and by -0.10 (95% CI, -0.14 to -0.06; n = 17; P = .0001) in cohort B. Sapablursen reduced the median number of phlebotomies from 5.0 at baseline (26 weeks) to 0 in cohort A and 1.5 in cohort B in the efficacy evaluation window (20 weeks). Most adverse events were mild or moderate; anemia and fatigue were most common. The mean change in the myeloproliferative neoplasm-symptom assessment form total symptom score at week 37 was -6.21 points (95% CI, -10.56 to -1.85; P = .0052) in cohort A and -2.71 points in cohort B (95% CI, -8.33 to 2.91; P = .34). Sapablursen reduced phlebotomy need, improved symptoms, and was safe and well tolerated in patients with polycythemia vera. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT05143957.

title: Muco-obstructive lung disease exhibits distinct hypoxic and inflammatory airway epithelial gene pathways.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intraluminal obstruction produces chronic airway epithelial hypoxia. We investigated how chronic airway epithelial hypoxia and inflammatory stimuli interact in human bronchial epithelial (HBE) cultures and resected human bronchiectatic lungs to produce an airway epithelial environment characteristic of muco-obstructive disease.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: HBE cultures were exposed to normoxia or hypoxia (1% O2) for 5 days, followed by administration of supernatants from cystic fibrosis (CF) lung-derived mucopurulent material (SMM) or PBS for 24 h. A reverse order protocol with SMM followed by hypoxia was also performed. Bulk RNA-sequencing and functional (Na+ transport) studies were performed. HIF1A and EPAS1-mediated transcriptional responses were characterised in CRISPR knockdown HBE cells. RNA in situ hybridisation studies of excised bronchiectatic lungs and bioinformatic analyses of published datasets tested for relevance of in vitro findings to in vivo conditions.
RESULTS: Hypoxia and SMM regulated largely separate airway epithelial transcriptional programmes regardless of treatment order. PTGS2 (COX-2), CCL20, MUC5B, and CXCL8 (IL-8) represented a small number of genes upregulated by both hypoxia and SMM. HIF1A knockdown and EPAS1 knockdown produced distinct, often opposing, effects on hypoxia-responsive pathways. HIF1A dominated upregulation of glycolytic pathway signalling. EPAS1 regulated genes that increase mucus concentration under hypoxia (e.g., SCNN1G). An EPAS1 inhibitor blocked hypoxia-induced upregulation of Na+ transport.
CONCLUSION: Chronic hypoxia and inflammation regulated distinct genes/pathways that combine to produce a complex diseased environment in muco-obstructed airway epithelia. HIF1A and EPAS1 regulated distinct hypoxia-induced transcriptional responses. EPAS1 inhibition may exhibit a favourable therapeutic ratio for treatment of muco-obstructive lung diseases.

title: Immortalisation of human airway epithelial cells for genome editing applications.
abstract:
AIM: In vitro air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures of human airway epithelial cells are widely used to study respiratory biology and disease, as they recapitulate key features of the pseudostratified airway epithelium and reduce reliance on animal models and repeated patient biopsies. However, the limited proliferative capacity of primary airway basal cells restricts long-term studies and genome editing. This study aimed to generate stable, immortalised human airway basal cell lines that retain differentiation capacity and support genetic manipulation.
METHODS: Human airway epithelial basal cells from bronchial and nasal origin were immortalised by lentiviral expression of human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) followed by polyclonal expansion. A panel of cell lines derived from three independent nasal donors was established. Differentiation capacity was assessed in ALI cultures and compared with primary airway epithelial cells. Suitability for genetic manipulation was evaluated using lentiviral overexpression and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene knockout and knock-in strategies.
RESULTS: All immortalised cell lines displayed sustained proliferative capacity and efficiently differentiated into major airway epithelial cell types, including multiciliated and secretory cells. Differentiation patterns and functional characteristics closely resembled those of primary airway epithelial cultures. The cell lines supported efficient lentiviral transduction and CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing, enabling stable gene overexpression, targeted gene disruption, and precise genomic modification.
CONCLUSIONS: hTERT-immortalised human airway basal cell lines preserve key features of primary airway epithelium while enabling long-term culture and versatile genome editing. This resource provides a robust platform for airway biology research, disease modelling, and therapeutic development.

title: Targeted siRNA-lactobionic lipid nanoparticles with novel ionizable lipid inhibit antithrombin III expression in hepatocytes.
abstract: Targeted reduction of hepatic antithrombin (AT) via siRNA offers a promising strategy to enhance thrombin (TMB) generation in bleeding disorders, though efficient hepatocyte delivery remains challenging. This study developed and evaluated a targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation incorporating a novel morpholine-based ionizable lipid (MIL) and a lactobionic-octadecylamine conjugate (LBN) for hepatocyte-specific delivery of AT-siRNA (siAT). Following synthesis of MIL and LBN, siAT-loaded LNP (siAT LNP LBN) were prepared using microfluidics and characterized for size, morphology, zeta potential, polydispersity index, and encapsulation efficiency (EE). Functional assays on HepG2 cells assessed cellular uptake, protein knockdown, and AT activity. The optimized formulation exhibited uniform particles (124 nm, PDI 0.125, zeta potential - 8.9 mV) and high EE (90%). Cytotoxicity assays confirmed safety up to 65 pmol siRNA. LBN-decorated LNP significantly enhanced hepatocyte uptake compared to non-targeted LNP and naked siRNA. Optimal AT mRNA suppression occurred at ~ 65 pmol siRNA and 16 h, with protein knockdown confirmed at 48 h. Functionally, siAT LNP LBN reduced AT activity to 48.1 ± 5.5%, substantially outperforming non-targeted LNP (64.1%) and naked siRNA (86.6%). The developed siAT-LNP-LBN platform demonstrated efficient hepatocyte uptake, robust AT knockdown, and low cytotoxicity in vitro, providing preliminary evidence for its potential as a hepatocyte-targeted siRNA delivery platform. Further in vivo studies are warranted to evaluate its biodistribution, liver-targeting efficiency, pharmacodynamic effects, therapeutic efficacy, and biosafety.

title: Nanoparticle therapeutics for infectious diseases integrating AI-guided design, crispr delivery, phage synergy, and immune modulation.
abstract: Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive.Clinical trial registrationNot applicable.

title: From molecular pathways to nanocarrier design: a translational framework for lipid-based nanoparticles in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease, being a complicated neurodegenerative disoder affects cognitive as well as memory functions. Characterised by amyloid-β aggregation, along with tau hyperphosphorylation, and cholinergic dysfunction, this disease is also associated with oxidative stress and neuroinflammation. Conventional clinical interventions, like acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and novel monoclonal antibodies predominantly rely on symptomatic alleviation of symptoms. Nevertheless, these conventional treatments come across considerable constraints, like temporary effectiveness, lesser therapeutic reach due to the blood brain barrier, apart from additional adverse effects. To overcome these delivery obstacles and achieve intracellular targeting, lipid nanoparticles, such as liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles, and drugs, that can effectively traverse biological barriers, and facilitate precise intracellular release. This review introduces a translational, pathway-integrated framework that connects key molecular mechanisms of the disease with rational design strategies of lipid nanocarriers. The review also illustrates how essential internal factors, such as lipid composition, ionizable lipid pKa, selection of helper lipids, PEG density, along with methods of endosomal escape, and the protein corona, affect brain targeting efficacy and toxicity. It further focuses on pathway-enforced nano lipidic therapeutic approaches, where nanocarrier design is tailored to cater to specific biological targets. Nano lipidic delivery of siRNA, miRNA, mRNA, monoclonal antibodies, and along with other neuroprotective agents has been emphasised. Additionally, advancements in surface functionalization, intranasal administration, as well as receptor-mediated transcytosis, and focused ultrasound-driven blood-brain barrier penetration have also been highlighted in this review. Therefore, it aims to bridge the gap between molecular pathology and formulation design through alignment of design principles that emphasize on nanocarrier properties and its relevance to disease-specific requirements, an approach that has never been comprehensively addressed in previous literature.Registration number of clinical trial: Not applicable.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-based mRNA delivery system for cancer management.
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics have transformed cancer treatment strategies, especially after the success of lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-enabled mRNA vaccines. LNPs are effective non-viral delivery vehicles that protect mRNA, enhance intracellular delivery, and improve therapeutic safety. This review discusses recent advancements in LNP-mediated mRNA therapies, including mRNA vaccines, cytokine delivery, immune modulation, and CAR-based strategies. Innovations in lipid formulations and high-throughput technologies have enhanced delivery efficiency. We also discussed how LNP-mRNA formulations elicit immune responses and improve tumor microenvironments. We highlight promising personalized mRNA vaccines and therapies. However, challenges such as tissue specificity, immunogenicity, and manufacturing remain. Emerging strategies in lipid engineering and personalized medicine aim to address these issues, making LNP-mediated mRNA therapeutics a pivotal approach in precision oncology. This report provides a comprehensive review of recent developments in LNP-mRNA therapeutics for cancer treatment. This report also highlights recent innovations and clinical trials. We further highlight the limitations and challenges associated with LNP-mRNA therapeutics in clinical translation. Finally, we outlined the prospects of LNP-based mRNA therapeutics for personalized cancer treatment.

title: Characterization of the organelle genomes of mycoheterotrophic Thismia angustimitra and evidence suggesting horizontal gene transfer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Our knowledge about mitochondrial genome evolution in plants is lacking far behind our knowledge of plastome evolution. In heterotrophic plants, it is well-known that plastome degradation and reduced or lost photosynthesis go hand in hand, and there is little if any difference between plastome evolution in mycoheterotrophic and haustorial parasites. The mitochondrial genome appears less affected by a heterotrophic lifestyle, although exceptions occur. In contrast to plastome evolution, mitochondrial evolution may differ between mycoheterotrophic and haustorial parasites, in particular with regards to the occurrence of horizontal gene transfer. However, data from mycoheterotrophs are scarce, and complete mitogenomes are only known from three of ten clades.
RESULTS: Here we present data from the complete plastome and mitogenome from Thismia angustimitra, representing a fourth clade of mycoheterotrophs. The 18,215 bp plastome is much reduced and includes only few genes. The mitogenome has a multicircular structure consisting of 22 chromosomes with a total length of 422,400 bp. The gene content and the pattern of RNA editing are normal. The mitogenome includes only few repeats and recombinational activity is limited. A search for foreign DNA did not reveal any fungal sequences, the content of plastid DNA is low, but a large proportion of intergenic DNA shows similarity to distantly related angiosperms. Just a few plastid inserts appear to have originated through intracellular transfer, whereas others most likely stem from horizontal gene transfer. Synteny patterns of the intergenic sequences suggest that horizontal transfer may happen in either direction.
CONCLUSION: The highly reduced plastome of T. angustimitra fits completely the general picture of plastome degradation in heterotrophic plants. Whereas the mitogenome in many aspects appears unaffected by the lifestyle, the recombinational activity is unusually low. Surprisingly, we find evidence suggesting horizontal gene transfer, indicating that this phenomenon may be more common among mycoheterotrophic plants than previously thought.

title: Repurposing of abemaciclib to overcome C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acquired resistance to osimertinib mediated by the EGFR C797S mutation remains a major therapeutic challenge in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with limited effective treatment options. This study explored whether abemaciclib, an FDA-approved CDK4/6 inhibitor, can overcome C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
METHODS: A high-throughput screen of approximately 125,000 compounds was performed using Ba/F3 cells expressing EGFR triple mutations (L858R/T790M/C797S and Del19/T790M/C797S). The impact of abemaciclib on EGFR kinase activity was evaluated via in vitro kinase and Western blot assays. Apoptosis induction was assessed using flow cytometry. The activity of abemaciclib was evaluated using biochemical assays, cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA), molecular docking analyses, CRISPR-engineered isogenic models, xenografts, and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models.
RESULTS: Abemaciclib was identified as a potent inhibitor of EGFR triple-mutant cell growth and exhibited preferential activity toward mutant EGFR-dependent models. IL-3 rescue assays demonstrated that its antiproliferative effects were dependent on suppression of oncogenic EGFR signaling. Abemaciclib inhibited mutant EGFR kinase activity, reduced EGFR phosphorylation, and induced apoptotic cell death in osimertinib-resistant models while exhibiting substantially weaker activity toward wild-type EGFR. CETSA and molecular docking analyses supported direct engagement of mutant EGFR by abemaciclib. Importantly, abemaciclib significantly suppressed tumor growth in CRISPR-engineered isogenic xenografts and PDX models harboring EGFR C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance.
CONCLUSIONS: Abemaciclib selectively suppresses C797S-mutant EGFR signaling and demonstrates robust antitumor activity in preclinical models of osimertinib-resistant EGFR-mutant NSCLC. This breakthrough not only overcomes the existing therapeutic barrier but also demonstrates minimal interference with WT EGFR, offering a transformative and precise therapeutic strategy with significant translational and clinical potential. These findings support the therapeutic repurposing of abemaciclib as a potential treatment strategy for EGFR C797S-mediated resistance and provide a translational strategy for overcoming resistance-associated EGFR alterations using clinically available targeted agents.

title: The multifaceted role of a-to-i rna editing in tumorigenesis: from coding to noncoding RNAs.
abstract: RNA editing, a post-transcriptional process altering RNA sequences, is crucial in cancer progression. Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing, mediated by ADAR enzymes, and cytosine-to-uridine (C-to-U) editing, by APOBEC proteins, diversify the transcriptome and proteome. Dysregulation of RNA editing significantly impacts gene expression, promoting tumorigenesis through alterations in amino acid sequences, transcript stability, and miRNA targeting. Conflicting research highlights the complexity of RNA editing's role in cancer. While hyper-editing often correlates with editase overexpression and aggressive phenotypes, hypo-editing links to lower expression. Specific RNA editing events, rather than overall levels, offer more precise insights. ADAR1 primarily promotes oncogenesis, while ADAR2 generally acts as a tumor suppressor. ADAR3's role remains unclear. RNA editing also influences noncoding RNAs, including miRNAs and lncRNAs, affecting their function and stability. A-to-I editing regulates miRNA biogenesis and mRNA-miRNA interactions, altering target gene selection and processing. LncRNAs, susceptible to A-to-I editing, undergo modifications that disrupt crucial molecular interactions, impacting their roles as miRNA sponges and regulators of gene expression. CircRNAs, through ADAR-mediated regulation, contribute to the complexity of RNA editing's influence on cancer. This review underscores RNA editing's multifaceted role in cancer, impacting key signaling pathways and immune surveillance. Understanding these mechanisms is vital for developing targeted therapies and improving cancer outcomes.

title: RBP1-driven retinol metabolism in tumor-associated lymphatic endothelial cells orchestrates triple-negative breast cancer progression and lymphatic metastasis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive breast cancer subtype and is characterized by a high metastatic potential and limited treatment options. TNBC frequently metastasizes to lymphatic vessels and the presence of breast cancer cells in tumor-draining lymph nodes (LNs) is an important prognostic factor. Nevertheless, the molecular and metabolic reprogramming of TNBC-associated lymphatic vasculature remains poorly understood.
METHODS: A comprehensive single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of 44,000 endothelial cells from human breast tumor datasets was performed. RBP1, a retinol-binding protein, was identified as a metabolic gene highly and specifically upregulated in tumor-associated lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). Then, RBP1 expression in human TNBC biopsies was assessed, and its association with LN status and overall patient survival was investigated in a cohort of 1,474 breast cancer patients. We further evaluated the in vivo relevance of RBP1 by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Rbp1 knockout in a pre-clinical TNBC mouse model. In vitro functional studies were performed using co-culture systems and RBP1-silencing in LECs. Finally, RBP1 mechanism of action in the lymphatic vasculature was determined by bulk-RNA sequencing and validated by applying different cellular and molecular approaches.
RESULTS: Single-cell profiling revealed that the metabolic gene RBP1 was upregulated in LECs within the human breast tumor microenvironment. Further analysis showed that lymphatic RBP1 expression was associated with LN metastases, and correlated with poor prognosis and reduced survival in TNBC patients. In the pre-clinical TNBC mouse model, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Rbp1 knockout reduced lymphangiogenesis, tumor growth and metastatic burden, and increased necrosis. Moreover, functional assays demonstrated that direct co-culture of LECs with TNBC cells, or exposure to their secretome, induced lymphatic RBP1 upregulation and enhanced pro-lymphangiogenic activities, whereas RBP1 silencing compromised their biological, redox and metabolic properties. Mechanistically, bulk RNA sequencing of RBP1-silenced LECs combined with experimental validation revealed that RBP1, through its retinol-binding domain, modulates the VEGFR3 and NOTCH pathways, while also involving lipid mobilization.
CONCLUSIONS: We define lymphatic RBP1 as a key "switch" that couples LEC metabolism to molecular programs, thereby driving tumor-associated lymphangiogenesis, breast tumor growth and lymphatic dissemination in TNBC. Our findings underscore the potential of RBP1 as both a novel prognostic biomarker and a tractable therapeutic target for blocking TNBC progression and lymphatic metastasis.

title: Advances in therapeutic oligonucleotide conjugates.
abstract: Oligonucleotide therapeutics (ONTs) have revolutionized the medical landscape by enabling the precise modulation of genetic pathways. This perspective highlights the major conjugation strategies for ONTs, using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) as representative modalities. We describe diverse classes of targeting ligands, including small molecules, cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs), antibodies, and aptamers. For example, triantennary N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) conjugation has enabled a number of approved oligonucleotide therapeutics. Meanwhile, other emerging conjugation technologies have expanded oligonucleotide delivery to extrahepatic tissues to address a broader range of diseases. We further summarize the clinical translation of these delivery platforms, highlighting approved therapeutics alongside emerging clinical candidates. Finally, we provide an outlook on challenges and opportunities for the next generation of oligonucleotide therapeutics.

title: Human-relevant disease models to accelerate the development of nucleic acid-based therapies and other advanced therapeutics.
abstract: Advanced therapeutics, including programmable nucleic acid-based therapies (NATs), such as small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), CRISPR-Cas 9 editing systems, modified in vitro transcribed messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), have the potential to transform healthcare. However, while there have been considerable successes, there have also been notable clinical failures in early-stage human trials, which slowed down the progression of these therapeutic platforms. Multiple trials of NATs have been halted or discontinued, or approved products carry black box warnings as unforeseen or underestimated toxicities and poor efficacy have been observed in humans. There are a variety of reasons for failure of NATs, one of which is that many preclinical studies lack disease modelling in a human-relevant manner and, therefore, do not capture disease-specific effects on therapy tolerability and efficacy. This Perspective provides a short overview of why better human disease modelling is required to understand the potential therapeutic liabilities of NATs across modalities.

title: Diverse RNA Editing Systems Across Heterolobosea (Discoba).
abstract: Mitochondrial RNA editing events were previously reported in only three unrelated species within the phylum Heterolobosea (Discoba): Naegleria gruberi and Acrasis kona (which performs C-to-U substitutions) and Pharyngomonadida sp. BB2 (which inserts single nucleotides by a yet unknown mechanism). We present novel high-quality genome assemblies obtained via a combination of whole-genome and targeted sequencing approaches and predicted proteomes for two species, Paravahlkampfia ustiana and Heteramoeba clara, representing an understudied clade of the phylum. Surprisingly, we discovered RNA editing events of C-to-U substitutions and mononucleotide insertions co-existing in the mitochondria of P. ustiana, while the two systems were both absent in H. clara. In addition, P. ustiana also exhibits A-to-I editing sites in rRNA transcripts encoded in multicopy circular rDNA plasmids. RNA editing events in P. ustiana were verified by proteomics, Illumina short RNA reads, ONT long cDNA and direct RNA reads. We elaborate on the potential mechanisms of mitochondrial insertional editing by investigating several aspects of the RNA transcription machinery and base modifications in template DNA and mRNA products. We report additional cases of C-to-U RNA editing in other species of Heterolobosea and explore the distribution of various putative components of the C-to-U editosome, including the DYW domain-containing pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, across the phylum expanding the understanding of the evolutionary dynamics underlying this phenomenon, which remains understudied outside land plants. The comparative analysis of available sequence data from Heterolobosea revealed that C-to-U RNA editing was acquired relatively deep in the evolution of Heterolobosea and subsequently underwent repeated losses.

title: Inositol hexakisphosphate is a cofactor and modulator of ADAR1 RNA editing activity.
abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing by ADAR1 is a key post-transcriptional modification, and mutations in ADAR1 lead to Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS), an autoimmune disorder. Despite its biological and clinical relevance, the regulation of ADAR1 activity remains incompletely understood. Using a combination of biochemical approaches, inositol-pentakisphosphate 2-kinase (IPPK)-knockout cells, molecular dynamics simulations, and a cell-permeable inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) prodrug (Pro-IP6), we demonstrate that IP6 depletion drastically reduces global RNA editing, while supplementation with Pro-IP6 restores and even enhances editing levels. Furthermore, we identify the C6-phosphate of IP6 as a critical determinant of ADAR1 catalytic efficiency, functioning within a hydrogen-bonding network that indirectly coordinates a Zn2+-ion. Finally, we show that the AGS-associated ADAR1 mutation N907S impairs RNA editing activity, most likely by altering the hydrogen-bond interaction network linking IP6 to the ADAR1 catalytic center. Together, these findings identify IP6 as an essential cofactor and regulator of ADAR1 activity and highlight cofactor availability and interaction networks as strategies for therapeutically modulating RNA editing.

title: Antisense Oligonucleotides with 5'-decoy technology triggers nonsense-mediated decay of SCN9A to elicit long-lasting analgesia.
abstract: The voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.7 (SCN9A) is a genetically validated target for pain therapy, but achieving therapeutic isoform selectivity remains a formidable challenge for small-molecule inhibitors. Here, we overcome this bottleneck through a highly selective RNA-targeted strategy that dictates SCN9A alternative splicing. We first identified ASO50 as the most potent baseline candidate antisense oligonucleotide (ASO). Subsequent 5'-decoy (5D) sequence screening yielded an upgraded candidate, L9C-ASO50, which is engineered to competitively intercept U1 snRNA, achieving a cooperative spatial hindrance that robustly suppresses exon 5 recognition. This targeted exon exclusion introduces a frameshift that triggers robust, obligate transcript clearance via the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway, ensuring complete functional silencing without cross-reacting with homologous NaV channels. Mechanistically, we define the underlying cis-trans regulatory architecture, revealing a homeostatic tug-of-war where the RNA-binding protein ELAVL2 enforces exon inclusion, paradoxically antagonized by the canonical SR protein family. Crucially, CNS-restricted delivery of L9C-ASO50 produces profound and sustained mechanical and thermal analgesia. These findings establish splice-modulated transcript degradation as a viable therapeutic paradigm for chronic pain and provide a broadly applicable blueprint for engineering targeted RNA therapeutics.

title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo models.
abstract: Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human-animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo. Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro, ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.

title: Phosphatidic acid phosphatase PAP2-2 controls lipid metabolism and membrane homeostasis in Leishmania mexicana.
abstract: Phosphatidic acid phosphatases (PAPs) regulate lipid metabolism by controlling the interconversion of phosphatidic acid (PA) and diacylglycerol (DAG), thereby influencing membrane composition and multiple downstream cellular processes. We investigated the role of PAP2-2 in Leishmania mexicana using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene ablation and genetic complementation. Immunofluorescence analyses revealed partial co-localization of PAP2-2 with the endoplasmic reticulum. Ablation of the PAP2-2-encoding gene LmxM.19.1350 significantly reduced total phosphatidic acid phosphatase activity, resulting in marked accumulation of endogenous PA and alterations in lipid composition, including changes in phosphatidylcholine, cardiolipin, sterols, and selected DAG species. PAP2-2-deficient parasites displayed altered cell morphology, reduced growth, and delayed differentiation into metacyclic promastigotes and amastigotes. Furthermore, loss of PAP2-2 impaired mitochondrial physiology, as evidenced by reduced basal respiration, diminished oxidative phosphorylation capacity, altered electron transport chain activities, and decreased responsiveness to respiratory substrates and inhibitors. Our findings identify PAP2-2 as an important regulator of PA/DAG homeostasis in L. mexicana and demonstrate that disruption of this enzyme triggers extensive lipid remodeling with downstream effects on mitochondrial function, parasite development, and cellular morphology. These results highlight the central role of membrane lipid homeostasis in the physiology of Leishmania and establish PAP2-2 as a previously underappreciated determinant of parasite fitness that may represent a promising target for future mechanistic and therapeutic investigations.

title: Mechanistic insights into benzoxaborole activity against Cryptosporidium parvum: CPSF3 targeting genetically validated for AN3661, with implications for resistance.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cryptosporidiosis is a major enteric disease affecting humans and animals worldwide, with severe consequences in young children and neonatal livestock, yet treatment options remain extremely limited. Benzoxaboroles have emerged as promising broad-spectrum antiparasitic compounds, but their mechanisms of action, molecular targets, and resistance pathways in Cryptosporidium spp. remain incompletely understood, limiting their optimal therapeutic deployment. We previously showed that the benzoxaborole AN3661 inhibits the endonuclease Cleavage and Polyadenylation Specificity Factor 3 (CPSF3) in Cryptosporidium hominis, likely by disrupting pre-mRNA processing and restricting parasite growth. Here, we further investigated the mode of action of AN3661 and compared it with two additional benzoxaboroles, AN13762 and AN7973.
METHODOLOGY: Cell culture assays combined with imaging-based quantification were used to assess drug activity and determine the impact of treatment on parasite growth and development. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing was used to introduce a point mutation into Cryptosporidium parvum CPSF3 and evaluate resistance to benzoxaboroles in vitro and in vivo. Nanopore sequencing was performed to examine the effects of drug exposure on parasite mRNA processing.
PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: We identified a single mutation in C. parvum CPSF3 (Y385N) that conferred strong resistance to AN3661. In contrast, this mutation did not reduce sensitivity to AN13762 or AN7973, which are also suspected to target CPSF3. All three benzoxaboroles impaired mRNA processing, a process mediated by the CPSF machinery, and exhibited parasiticidal activity, with pronounced effects during late-stage maturation of first-generation meronts, including inhibition of parasite egress; two compounds also affected gametogenesis. Notably, AN7973 controlled severe infection in susceptible mice challenged with the AN3661-resistant C. parvum CPSF3 Y385N mutant. In Toxoplasma gondii, AN7973 remained active against strains resistant to AN3661 and AN13762, supporting a distinct mechanism of action. Finally, AN3661 and AN7973 were active against Eimeria tenella, and AN3661 against Giardia duodenalis.
CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: Together, these results identify a resistance mechanism affecting AN3661 in Cryptosporidium, and highlight AN7973 as a promising alternative compound with broad antiparasitic activity and efficacy against AN3661-resistant parasites.

title: TRIB2 supports a high glycolytic phenotype in melanoma cells.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Metabolic adaptation is a crucial driver of melanoma progression and therapy resistance. The pseudokinase Tribbles homolog 2 (TRIB2) is highly expressed in melanoma and is associated with poor outcomes and treatment resistance. However, its specific role in the metabolic profile of melanoma cells remained unexplored. This study aimed to investigate the impact of TRIB2 on cellular metabolism, and its role in metabolic adaptation in melanoma.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The study used UACC-62 human melanoma cells with high endogenous TRIB2 expression and isogenic TRIB2-knockout (KO) clones generated via CRISPR-Cas9. Cell proliferation was assessed using trypan blue exclusion assays under treatment with metabolic drugs including 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG), and dichloroacetate (DCA). Metabolic phenotypes were evaluated by measuring glucose consumption, lactate production, and real-time analysis of glycolytic flux (ECAR) and mitochondrial respiration (OCR) using a Seahorse bioanalyzer. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were measured by dihydroethidium (DHE) fluorescence. Gene expression was analyzed by qPCR, and protein levels were determined by western blot. Citrate synthase activity was measured enzymatically.
RESULTS: TRIB2-KO cells exhibited significantly reduced basal proliferation compared with wild-type (WT) cells. KO cells were also more sensitive to the glycolytic inhibitor 2-DG. Conversely, WT cells were more susceptible to DCA treatment. Metabolic analyses confirmed that TRIB2-KO cells had lower glucose consumption, lactate production, and glycolytic capacity than WT cells. Mitochondrial respiratory function and the protein levels of key respiratory complexes were unchanged. Despite the reduction in glycolytic activity, TRIB2 depletion did not increase mitochondrial respiratory capacity and was associated with elevated basal intracellular superoxide levels. Among the molecular alterations identified, PDK4 was consistently reduced at both the mRNA and protein levels, whereas citrate synthase activity was significantly decreased despite preserved protein abundance, indicating selective alterations in mitochondrial carbon metabolism.
CONCLUSIONS: TRIB2 expression promotes a glycolytic phenotype and contributes to metabolic adaptation in melanoma. Loss of TRIB2 does not induce a metabolic shift towards oxidative phosphorylation but instead results in broader metabolic rewiring characterized by reduced glycolysis together with selective alterations in mitochondrial carbon metabolism. These findings identify the TRIB2-PDK4 axis as a previously unrecognized component of metabolic regulation in melanoma and provide a rationale for further investigating its therapeutic potential.

title: Unveiling the functional landscape of A-to-I RNA editing associated with Marek's disease in chickens.
abstract: Genetic improvement of disease resistance against viral infections represents a longstanding and formidable challenge in animal breeding. The antiviral innate immune response is highly regulated at the RNA level, especially through RNA modifications. Adenosine-to-Inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing modifies the mRNA sequence. Growing evidence shows that this type of RNA editing plays a key role in mediating cellular responses to viral infections and disease resistance. However, the role of RNA editing in cellular response to MD remains unclear. In this study, we examined A-to-I editing in CD4+ T cells during Marek's disease virus (MDV) infection. By comparing MD-resistant and susceptible chicken lines, we identified 642 A-to-I RNA editing events in CD4+ T cells, most of which were located within repeat elements, particularly in the CR1 family. We observed differences in RNA editing levels and counts between the two chicken lines with different infection statuses, indicating distinct editing patterns across genetic backgrounds and infection states. Additionally, ADAR (adenosine deaminases acting on RNA) expression was correlated with RNA editing frequency. We identified 21 RNA editing sites (RESs) associated with gene expression and 42, 14, and 38 RESs with predicted effects on amino acid sequences, alternative splicing, and miRNA-target binding, respectively. A comparative analysis revealed 131 group-specific RESs and 21 RESs shared across groups. Functional enrichment analysis of genes associated with group-specific RESs highlighted several terms related to MD resistance, including the MHC class I protein complex in non-infected MD-resistant birds. Significantly, we identified two L63-specific candidate RNA editing sites, chr6:26,600,122 in MXI1 and chr16:1,716,632 in MHCY57, which were predicted to affect gga-miR-1759-3p binding and amino acid sequence, respectively. Our findings reveal the landscape of A-to-I RNA editing in CD4 ⁺ T cells during MDV infection and provide new insights into its potential association with immune regulation and MD resistance.

title: Rankl contributes to early bone development via the Wnt signaling pathway in zebrafish.
abstract: Receptor activator of nuclear factor-κB ligand (RANKL) is essential for osteoclast differentiation and bone remodeling; however, its role in early osteogenesis remains incompletely understood. This study investigated the contribution of RANKL to early bone development and regeneration and explored whether its effects on osteoblast differentiation are associated with RANK signaling, osteoclast activity, and the Wnt signaling pathway. Two zebrafish rankl mutant alleles were generated using CRISPR/Cas9, and the 19-bp insertion allele was used for phenotypic and mechanistic analyses. Bone mineralization and osteoclast formation were evaluated using Alizarin Red S and tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase staining, respectively. Osteoblast- and osteoclast-related gene expression was examined using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction. Rescue experiments were performed using capped rankl mRNA, acute rank disruption, pharmacological osteoclast inhibition, and Wnt or mTOR pathway inhibitors. Transcriptomic profiling was used to identify signaling pathways associated with rankl deficiency. Compared with wild-type controls, rankl-/- zebrafish exhibited reduced skeletal mineralization at 8, 15, and 30 days post-fertilization and decreased expression of osteoblast-related genes. The number of TRAP-positive osteoclasts and the expression of osteoclast-related genes were also significantly reduced. Adult mutants exhibited increased vertebral thickness and narrowed neural and vascular canals, whereas caudal fin regeneration was delayed. Injection of capped rankl mRNA restored mineralization and osteoclast formation. Acute rank disruption blocked the osteoclast rescue but did not abolish the recovery of bone mineralization, while pharmacological osteoclast inhibition did not reproduce the early mineralization defect. Transcriptomic analysis identified enrichment of Wnt-related signaling, and several Wnt-associated genes were differentially expressed in rankl mutants. XAV939 attenuated the mineralization rescue induced by rankl mRNA, whereas rapamycin did not produce a comparable effect. These findings suggest that RANKL contributes to early zebrafish bone development through distinct effects on osteoclasts and osteoblasts. Osteoclast regulation is RANK-dependent, whereas the effect of RANKL on early osteogenesis may be partly independent of RANK-mediated osteoclastogenesis and associated with Wnt signaling. Further genetic and cell-specific studies are required to establish the underlying mechanism.

title: Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy: Contemporary Pharmacological Management.
abstract: Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy increasingly recognised as a cause of heart failure. Advances in the understanding of its pathophysiology have enabled the development of targeted therapies, making ATTR-CM a paradigm of precision medicine in cardiology. Currently approved disease-modifying therapies, including two stabilisers (tafamidis and acoramidis) and one gene-silencing agent (vutrisiran), slow disease progression and reduce hospitalisations and mortality, particularly when initiated early. Because these therapies do not reverse established amyloid deposition, supportive management remains a critical component of care and presents distinct challenges. These include universal anticoagulation in AF, careful diuretic management, the benefits of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and limited tolerance to other foundational heart failure therapies. On-going intensive research is expanding the therapeutic landscape, with several Phase III trials evaluating next-generation silencers, gene-editing strategies and amyloid-removal therapies. While these advances hold promise for disease reversal and prevention, important unresolved issues arise, including optimal treatment selection, monitoring strategies and economic sustainability.

title: Inhibition of malignant progression in mesenchymal glioblastoma by PARP1 inhibitors.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Among molecular subtypes of glioblastoma (GBM), the mesenchymal subtype (MES) exhibits the most aggressive clinical course, marked by heightened invasiveness and therapeutic resistance. To overcome the challenge of intrinsic drug resistance in MES GBM, we performed a high-throughput screen of Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved compounds on NF1-silenced human GBM cells.
METHODS: We performed a high-throughput screen of 2,697 FDA-approved compounds on NF1-silenced human GBM cells, engineered via CRISPR/Cas9.
RESULTS: This screen nominated poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) inhibitors as top candidates, demonstrating selective cytotoxicity against NF1-deficient cells. Integrated analyses of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) data, immunofluorescence, and immunoblotting revealed significant PARP1 upregulation in GBM tissues, establishing its role as a proto-oncogene that drives tumor cell proliferation and migration. Using orthotopic xenograft models, we confirmed that NF1 knockdown (KD) profoundly sensitized GBM tumors to the anti-tumor and pro-apoptotic effects of PARP1 inhibition in vivo. Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays identified a physical interaction between the NF1 gene product neurofibromin and PARP1, suggesting a direct regulatory nexus.
CONCLUSIONS: This study breaks through the traditional limitation of PARP inhibitors being used only for DNA repair defects, and for the first time reveals a novel selective killing mechanism of PARP1 inhibitors in NF1-deficient GBM. Collectively, our findings delineate NF1-mutant, MES GBM as a distinct clinical subset poised to derive therapeutic benefit from PARP1-targeted therapy.

title: Genetic background determines allele-specific Pfkelch13- mediated artemisinin tolerance and persistence in Plasmodium falciparum.
abstract: Artemisinin-based combination therapies are the frontline treatment for Plasmodium falciparum malaria, but their efficacy is threatened by Artemisinin partial resistance (ART R ). ART R in Plasmodium falciparum is mediated by Pfkelch13 ( k13 ) mutations but remains rare in West Africa. A critical question is whether short-term drug survival intrinsically predicts long-term evolutionary persistence. Here, using CRISPR-Cas9 editing, and nanopore-assisted allele tracking in a contemporary Senegalese isolate, we evaluated ART R receptivity using the ring-stage survival assay (RSA), a proxy for clinical resistance. We demonstrate that ART R survival and drug-free persistence are biologically separable traits. While the WHO-validated Asian I543T mutation conferred the RSA phenotype, it was rapidly counter-selected during drug-free growth. In contrast, emerging African alleles (R561H, M579I) and a regional novel variant (C473S) establish stable resistance without a competitive penalty. These findings reveal that a parasite's genetic background acts as a strict evolutionary filter, uncoupling short-term tolerance from long-term persistence and establishing that genomic context determines allele-specific resistance trajectories.

title: Research Progress of Stem Cell Therapy for Premature Ovarian Insufficiency.
abstract: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) is a heterogeneous reproductive and endocrine disorder characterized by impaired ovarian function before the age of 40 years. Conventional management, particularly hormone therapy, addresses hypoestrogenic symptoms and long-term health risks but does not reliably restore endogenous ovarian activity or fertility. Stem cell-based strategies have therefore attracted considerable interest because of their potential paracrine, immunomodulatory, anti-apoptotic, angiogenic, and microenvironment-remodeling effects. This review summarizes current evidence on stem cell sources, therapeutic mechanisms, preclinical models, clinical studies, extracellular vesicle-based approaches, biomaterials, gene-editing strategies, and translational challenges in POI. Particular emphasis is placed on the distinction between mechanistic and animal evidence, uncontrolled or pilot human studies, and controlled clinical evidence. Across preclinical models, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) frequently improve ovarian histology, hormone profiles, follicular parameters, and reproductive performance; however, these findings cannot be assumed to represent restoration of ovarian reserve or fertility in humans. Clinical evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and predominantly derived from small non-randomized studies, with outcomes ranging from menstrual recovery and changes in AMH, FSH, estradiol, or antral follicle count to a small number of reported pregnancies. These surrogate changes should be distinguished from clinically meaningful endpoints such as ovulation, ongoing pregnancy, and live birth. Emerging approaches involving extracellular vesicles, biomaterials, and gene editing may improve cell retention or therapeutic potency, but most remain preclinical or early translational strategies. Overall, stem cell therapy should currently be regarded as an investigational approach for POI. Progress toward clinical translation will require standardized cell products, clearly defined dosing and administration routes, appropriate comparator groups, clinically meaningful reproductive endpoints, rigorous long-term safety surveillance, and adequately powered controlled trials.

title: Sonodynamic Therapy in Periodontitis: From Mechanisms to Biomaterial-Based Innovations.
abstract: Periodontitis is a common chronic inflammatory disease driven by pathogenic biofilms, leading to progressive periodontal tissue destruction and systemic health risks. Conventional therapies often fail to eradicate biofilms in deep periodontal pockets, promote antimicrobial resistance and offer limited regenerative potential. Although SDT has emerged as a promising alternative, its clinical efficacy is constrained by several material- and microenvironment-related barriers that have not been systematically addressed in previous reviews. Sonodynamic therapy (SDT) employs low-intensity ultrasound to activate sonosensitizers, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inducing mechanical disruption of biofilms, with advantages of deep tissue penetration, broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and low risk of resistance. Nevertheless, conventional sonosensitizers often exhibit poor water solubility, rapid clearance, limited specificity, and suboptimal ROS generation, while hypoxia, continuous fluid turnover, and mechanical disturbance within periodontal pockets further compromise local retention and therapeutic efficacy. Advances in biomaterials address these barriers by engineering high-performance sonosensitizers to enhance ROS efficiency, developing delivery systems to improve solubility and prolonged retention and integrating multimodal antibacterial and regenerative functions. This review summarizes the mechanistic basis of SDT with recent advances in sonosensitizer engineering, local delivery platforms, synergistic therapies, and multifunctional biomaterials, thereby linking antimicrobial performance to periodontal tissue regeneration. We further identify hypoxia, delivery efficiency, biosafety and the lack of standardized evaluation as key translational challenges, and propose future directions including AI-guided sonosensitizer design, precision delivery systems, and CRISPR-assisted antimicrobial combination strategies to accelerate the clinical translation of SDT for periodontitis management.

title: Nanocarrier-Mediated Immunotherapy for Gynecological Malignancies: Mechanisms, Clinical Translation, and Emerging Nucleic Acid-Based Strategies.
abstract: Gynecological cancers, including ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers, remain major contributors to female morbidity and mortality worldwide. Conventional treatments-surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy-have improved outcomes, but advanced or recurrent disease is still associated with poor prognosis, chemoresistance, and tumor heterogeneity. Immunotherapy has emerged as a transformative strategy because of its specificity and potential for durable responses. However, the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and inefficient delivery of immunotherapeutic agents limit clinical benefit. Nanocarriers, including organic, inorganic, and biomimetic platforms, can improve targeted delivery, sustained release, biocompatibility, and tumor microenvironment remodeling, thereby enhancing immunotherapy. This review summarizes major immunotherapeutic modalities for gynecological cancers-immune checkpoint blockade, CAR-T cell therapy, tumor vaccines, and oncolytic viruses-and the classification and characteristics of commonly used nanocarriers. We focus on nanocarrier-mediated immunotherapeutic mechanisms in ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers, and further highlight emerging lipid nanoparticle/mRNA and programmable RNA delivery strategies. Finally, we analyze challenges in clinical translation and provide perspectives for future development, aiming to support fundamental research and clinical application of nano-immunotherapy in gynecological malignancies.

title: The Role of Interferons in Regulating and Mediating NK Cell Anti-Tumor Immunity.
abstract: Interferons (IFNs) are cytokines critical for natural killer (NK) cell development, activation, cytotoxicity, and anti-tumor function. In this review, we examine how type I and type II IFNs shape NK cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity, with an emphasis on recent advances and their implications for NK cell-based cancer therapy. Although IFNs have traditionally been viewed as immune activating cytokines and biomarkers of effective anti-tumor immunity, emerging evidence suggests that their effects in cancer are highly context dependent. By integrating recent CRISPR screening studies in NK cells, mechanistic analyses of IFN signaling in NK cell therapy, and emerging evidence on IFN-NK cell crosstalk within the tumor microenvironment, we highlight a central paradox: while IFNs can enhance NK cell activation and tumor surveillance, they can also drive dysfunction, tumor immune adaptation, and therapeutic resistance under chronic or dysregulated conditions. This distinction is particularly important in solid tumors, where NK cell therapies continue to face major barriers, including poor tumor infiltration, limited persistence, and suppression by the tumor microenvironment. We propose that IFN signaling may be one underappreciated factor contributing to the highly variable efficacy of NK cell therapy across cancer models. Therefore, IFNs should not be understood simply as pro-inflammatory or anti-tumor signals. Instead, they function as dynamic immune regulators whose effects depend on timing, dose, duration, cellular source, and tumor context. We further discuss the current clinical landscape of IFN-NK therapies, including IFN-α and INF-β drugs, CAR-NK cell therapy, STING agonists, and other rational combination strategies. Future research should develop physiologically relevant and tumor-microenvironment representative model systems to investigate the effects of IFN signaling on NK cell anti-tumor function across distinct tumor types. Coordinated investigation of NK, cytokine, and tumor biology will accelerate clinically actionable strategies that leverage the NK-IFN axis.
