title: The "Invisible Killer" of Neurodegeneration: Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurodegenerative Disorders, Mechanisms, Emerging Pathways and Therapeutic Strategies.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), Huntington's disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) place substantial burden on global public health. Mounting evidence identifies mitochondrial dysfunction as a central contributor to neuronal damage and progressive brain functional decline. As a narrative review, this work aims to dissect mitochondrial‑associated pathological features across these major neurodegenerative disorders, summarize under‑recognized emerging mechanisms, and highlight translational bottlenecks for mitochondrial‑targeted therapies. Mitochondria sustain neuronal survival by mediating oxidative‑phosphorylation‑driven energy production, biomolecule biosynthesis, calcium homeostasis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolism, and apoptotic regulation. In PD, aggregated α‑synuclein (α‑syn) damages respiratory‑chain complex I, perturbs mitochondrial dynamics and blocks PINK1/Parkin‑dependent mitophagy. In AD, amyloid‑β together with hyper‑phosphorylated tau (p-Tau) impairs respiratory complex activity, axonal mitochondrial trafficking and mitophagic clearance. Mutant huntingtin induces multiple mitochondrial lesions in HD, while inflammation‑triggered oxidative stress secondarily compromises mitochondrial function in MS. Pathogenic mutations in ALS disrupt respiratory‑chain assembly, mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy. Beyond classic mitochondrial defects including respiratory‑chain impairment, dynamic imbalance and defective mitophagy, emerging mechanisms such as mitocytosis, mitochondrial aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase (mt‑aaRS) dysfunction and mitochondria‑associated membrane (MAM) disruption are discussed. Mitochondrial dysfunction drives neurodegeneration via energy exhaustion, aggravated oxidative stress, pathological protein aggregation and excessive neuronal apoptosis. We further recapitulate mitochondrial‑oriented therapeutic approaches including small‑molecule regulators, mitophagy activators, mitochondrial biogenesis promoters, gene‑editing strategies and mitochondrial transplantation. Notable translational obstacles remain, including limited blood‑brain‑barrier penetration of candidate drugs, narrow therapeutic time‑window post‑symptom onset, and prominent disease heterogeneity. By synthesizing basic experimental findings and pre‑clinical and clinical trial progress, this review provides updated insights into the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases and facilitates the development of precise mitochondrial‑targeted therapeutic regimens.

title: Nanoparticle-Mediated Delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 Rnps Into Cells.
abstract: The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPRassociated protein 9 (Cas9) system has revolutionized genome editing through its precision, simplicity, and programmability. The clinical translation of CRISPR/Cas9 Ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) remains constrained by major delivery challenges, including large molecular size, instability in biological fluids, and limited cellular penetration. Nanoparticle-mediated, non-viral delivery systems have emerged as a compelling strategy to overcome these barriers by providing targeted, transient, and biocompatible transport of Cas9 RNPs into cells. This review systematically evaluates recent advances in lipid-based, polymeric, peptide, and exosome-derived nanocarriers, focusing on their design principles, mechanisms of uptake, and endosomal escape strategies. Particular attention is given to receptor-mediated targeting, intracellular trafficking, and the emerging translation of lipid nanoparticle systems such as NTLA-2001, which exemplify clinical progress in genome editing. Despite these advancements, several challenges persist. Nanoparticle systems exhibit trade-offs between efficiency, biocompatibility, and scalability. For example, lipid nanoparticles may trigger anti- PEG immune reactions, exosome production faces manufacturing constraints, and polymeric systems risk cytotoxicity or limited degradability. Pre-existing immunity to Cas9 proteins and unpredictable immune responses to nanoparticle components remain significant translational hurdles. By integrating current preclinical and early clinical evidence, this review highlights both the promise and the limitations of nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 RNP delivery. Understanding these biological, immunological, and engineering challenges will be crucial for developing safe, efficient, and clinically scalable genome editing platforms.

title: Gene Therapy: Advances in Delivery Systems, Genome Editing Technologies, and Applications in Human and Veterinary Medicine.
abstract: Gene therapy has emerged as a revolutionary therapeutic strategy for the treatment of inherited, acquired, and age-related diseases through the modification, replacement, or correction of defective genes. Advances in molecular biology, viral engineering, and genome-editing technologies have significantly enhanced the efficiency and safety of gene delivery systems. This review provides a comprehensive overview of gene therapy, including its classification, delivery methods, and therapeutic applications in both human and veterinary medicine. Viral vectors such as adenoviral, retroviral, lentiviral, adeno-associated viral, and poxviral vectors remain the most effective delivery platforms owing to their high transduction efficiency, whereas non-viral approaches including physical and chemical delivery systems offer improved biosafety and reduced immunogenicity. Recent developments in gene-editing technologies, particularly clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein systems, have expanded the therapeutic potential of gene therapy by enabling precise genome modifications. The review highlights the successful application of gene therapy in treating genetic disorders, cancer gene therapy, retinal diseases, neuromuscular disorders, hemophilia, and metabolic diseases in humans, as well as inherited and acquired diseases in companion and livestock animals. Despite remarkable progress, challenges related to delivery efficiency, immune responses, off-target effects, manufacturing scalability, regulatory approval, and long-term safety continue to limit widespread clinical implementation. Advances in vector design, genome-editing precision, artificial intelligence-assisted development, and regulatory frameworks are expected to address these limitations. Overall, gene therapy and CRISPRbased technologies represent promising platforms for the development of next-generation precision medicines that could transform disease management in both human and veterinary healthcare.

title: Next-Generation Mycobacterium tuberculosis Diagnostics: A Systematic Review of Molecular, CRISPR, and Biosensor Technologies.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: TB (tuberculosis) due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis continues to be a significant worldwide health issue. Timely and reliable diagnostic tests will improve treatment outcomes and reduce the spread of disease. Traditional TB diagnostics currently available, such as smear microscopy and culture, have significant limitations with regard to sensitivity and turnaround times, especially for smear-negative cases and for tuberculosis in extrapulmonary locations.
OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this review is to analyze the evolution of TB diagnostics from traditional microbiology to new molecular diagnostic methods (including CRISPR, biosensor technology, and microfluidic methods), including an assessment of their diagnostic testing performance, feasibility, and potential for the future.
METHODS: The systematic narrative review aimed to systematically assess literature published from 2020 to 2025 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The review was carried out according to the PRISMA guidelines and included 89 studies after screening and assessing for eligibility. The data were analysed qualitatively (i.e., through thematic analysis) by comparing data from conventional, molecular, and next-generation diagnostic methods.
RESULTS: Molecular tests (e.g., GeneXpert, Line Probe Assays, PCR, and Whole Genome Sequencing) provide greater sensitivity and specificity than traditional methods and allow for faster diagnosis. Additionally, newer CRISPR-based tests, biosensors, and microfluidic devices hold promise for rapid, portable, point-of-care diagnosis of tuberculosis.
DISCUSSION: The findings indicate that molecular diagnostics improve rapid detection and drug-resistance profiling, while CRISPR and biosensor platforms offer potential for rapid point-of-care testing. However, affordability, infrastructure, clinical validation, and scalability remain important barriers.
CONCLUSION: The use of molecular diagnostic testing, CRISPR technology, biosensors, artificial intelligence, and portable platforms will dramatically enhance existing TB surveillance systems and strategies for controlling the disease globally.

title: High Ubiquitin-like Protein 3 Expression Is Associated With Prolonged Recurrence-free Survival in Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/AIM: Current clinicopathological factors inadequately capture the biological heterogeneity of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). This study investigated the prognostic significance of ubiquitin-like protein 3 (UBL3), a molecule involved in extracellular vesicle sorting and immune regulation, in NMIBC.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Following an exploratory analysis of public RNA-sequencing databases, we evaluated tissue samples from patients who underwent transurethral resection for primary NMIBC. A discovery cohort (n=37) was assessed for UBL3 mRNA via qRT-PCR and protein expression via immunohistochemistry (IHC) quantified using digital H-scores (QuPath). A separate internal validation cohort (n=192) was subsequently evaluated by IHC. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival (RFS).
RESULTS: The database analysis indicated that high UBL3 expression was associated with longer RFS in early-stage bladder cancer. In the discovery cohort, higher UBL3 mRNA levels were associated with prolonged RFS [hazard ratio (HR)=0.33, p=0.004]. mRNA levels also were associated with digital H-scores (ρ=0.39, p=0.018). In the separate internal validation cohort, elevated UBL3 protein expression was associated with a reduced risk of recurrence. A multivariable Cox regression confirmed that a higher UBL3 H-score (HR=0.95 per 10-point increase, p=0.023), alongside a negative preoperative urine cytology and immediate intravesical chemotherapy, remained independently associated with RFS.
CONCLUSION: Elevated UBL3 expression was associated with prolonged RFS in patients with NMIBC following transurethral resection of bladder tumor. While UBL3 has potential as a prognostic biomarker, establishing its definitive clinical utility will require mechanistic investigations and validation across independent, multicenter cohorts.

title: miRNA Regulation of the FGF23-Klotho Pathway Mitigates Adverse Cardiac Remodeling During Nocturnal Hemodialysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with ESKD. Dysregulation of the fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23)/Klotho axis has been implicated in uremic cardiomyopathy, however the mechanism linking dialysis intensity to the regulation of this pathway remains poorly defined.
METHODS: We analyzed serum samples from ESKD patients transitioning from conventional to nocturnal hemodialysis (NHD). Left ventricular mass (LVM) was measured by echocardiography before and after transition. Patients were stratified as LVM regressors [ ≥ 10% decrease in LVM; n = 6] or LVM progressors [ ≥ 10% increase in LVM; n = 7]. Circulating microRNAs (miRs) and serum FGF23 and alpha Klotho were quantified. Mechanistic relevance was tested in an angiotensin-II model of cardiac hypertrophy using FGF23 suppression via an antisense oligonucleotide gapmer, or antagomirs targeting miR-200c-3p.
RESULTS: Among 13 patients transitioning to NHD, LVM regressors required fewer antihypertensive medications than at baseline (P<0.001) with improved metabolic parameters (urea 12.9 vs. 16.6 mmol/L, P<0.01) and higher hemoglobin (109 vs. 95 g/L, P<0.01). We identified six differentially expressed miRs (let-7a/g/i, miR-200c, miR-1 and miR-30c) that targeted the FGF23/Klotho signaling axis. LVM regressors also demonstrated significantly lower circulating FGF23 levels than LVM progressors [60 (28, 160) vs 668 (73, 1734) pg/mL, P<0.05]. In the angiotensin-II murine model of cardiac hypertrophy, FGF23 gapmer treatment or miR-200c-3p inhibition reduced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and attenuated interstitial fibrosis while restoring FGF23/Klotho signaling through the suppression of extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 phosphorylation, activation of dual specificity phosphatase-1 and inducing antioxidant gene expression.
CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, these exploratory findings link dialysis intensification to miR-mediated regulation of the FGF23/Klotho axis, demonstrating that targeting this regulatory network is sufficient to suppress pathological cardiac remodeling. These data provide a mechanistic basis for the cardiovascular benefits of nocturnal hemodialysis and identify the FGF23/Klotho axis as a candidate therapeutic target warranting further validation.

title: Sex- and Ketogenesis-Dependent Effects of Intermittent Fasting on Diet-Induced Fatty Liver Disease.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Intermittent fasting (IF) improves metabolic health, yet whether hepatic ketogenesis is required for mediating its effects remains unclear. Here, we investigated how ketogenesis contributes to the systemic and liver-specific metabolic effects of IF in male and female mice. Fasting increased circulating ketone bodies in both sexes, with females showing a greater increase, indicating intrinsic sex differences in ketone metabolism. IF reduced body weight gain and adiposity in both sexes, and these benefits persisted when Hmgcs2 expression was knocked down in adult mice, using an antisense oligonucleotide approach to inhibit ketogenesis. In contrast, hepatic benefits were sex- and ketogenesis-dependent. IF markedly reduced steatosis and fibrosis in male mice, but these improvements were attenuated when Hmgcs2 expression was suppressed. In contrast, female mice showed minimal hepatic benefit from IF and had heightened susceptibility to steatosis, fibrosis, and inflammatory activation upon Hmgcs2 knockdown. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified neutrophils and myofibroblasts as key responders to hepatocyte-derived ketone bodies. IF suppressed neutrophil-driven inflammatory signaling in an Hmgcs2-dependent manner, and ketone bodies attenuated low-grade inflammation in cultured neutrophil-like cells. This ketogenesis-inflammation-fibrosis axis was further supported by human Genotype-Tissue Expression liver coexpression analyses. Together, these findings demonstrate that although body weight and antiobesity actions of IF are largely ketogenesis-independent in both sexes of mice, its hepatic antisteatotic and antifibrotic effects are sexually dimorphic and ketogenesis-dependent in male mice.
ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS: We investigated whether ketogenesis is required for the metabolic benefits of intermittent fasting (IF) and whether these effects differ between sexes. We specifically asked whether ketogenesis drives IF-mediated protection against obesity and fatty liver disease in male and female mice. We found that IF reduced adiposity independently of ketogenesis in both sexes, but its antisteatotic and antifibrotic effects were ketogenesis-dependent in male mice and minimal in female mice. These findings reveal a sex-dependent ketogenesis-inflammation-fibrosis axis and highlight the need to consider sex and ketone metabolism when designing dietary or therapeutic interventions.

title: Optimized gGBE enables robust G-to-Y conversion in mammalian cells and zebrafish embryos.
abstract: Base editing is a powerful and precise genome-editing tool capable of introducing single-base substitutions with high resolution. Depending on the base-modification domains employed, base editors can mediate both transition and transversion base editing in mammalian cells. While deaminase-derived base editors have enabled efficient transition editing in the zebrafish genome, glycosidase-derived transversion editing remains a significant challenge. In this study, guided by structural insights into the Cas9 complex, we engineered a series of glycosidase guanine base editor (gGBE) constructs by inlaying the N-methylpurine DNA glycosylase (MPG) domain into Cas9 protein. Among these variants, we identified a high-performance gGBE in which MPG was inserted between residues G1246 and S1247 of the PI domain in Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9, which we named gGBE-PIGS. This variant improved editing efficiency by up to 3.5-fold in mammalian cells and 13-fold in zebrafish embryos, without compromising editing precision. Furthermore, we developed a gGBE-editing-responsive GFP reporter to monitor editing efficiency and enrich for gGBE-edited cells and embryos. Using a combination of the optimized gGBE-PIGS and the GFP reporter, we successfully generated zebrafish models carrying mutations homologous to human amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated variants. Together, these findings highlight the robustness and versatility of the gGBE platform for precise base editing and underscore its promising potential for in vivo disease modeling and therapeutic genome engineering.

title: Advances in injectable liposome-microspheres platforms for osteoarthritis therapy: from sustained delivery to multifunctional disease modification.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic, whole-joint disorder marked by progressive cartilage degradation, subchondral bone remodeling, synovial inflammation, and capsular fibrosis, affecting over 500 million individuals worldwide. Current pharmacotherapies are mainly palliative, with no approved disease-modifying osteoarthritis drugs (DMOADs). Intra-articular (IA) injection provides direct joint access but is hampered by rapid drug clearance and short residence times. Injectable liposome-microsphere (iLMP) systems have recently emerged as integrative delivery platforms that synergistically combine the high loading capacity, targeting versatility, and stimuli-responsiveness of liposomes with the sustained release, lubrication, mechanical support, and protective shielding of hydrogel microspheres. This "nano-in-micro" hierarchical architecture enables prolonged joint retention, spatiotemporally controlled drug release, active cell/tissue targeting, and even gene editing, thereby shifting OA management from symptom alleviation toward true disease modification. In this review, we systematically examine the rational design of iLMPs, covering liposomal composition and functionalization, microsphere fabrication technologies (microfluidics, electrospraying, 3D bioprinting, emulsification), and assembly strategies (embedding, anchoring, adsorption, and matrix hybridization). We then detail their physicochemical determinants-size, surface charge, rheology, and degradation kinetics-and discuss the multifaceted therapeutic mechanisms, including sustained pharmacokinetic modulation, boundary lubrication, active/passive targeting, enzyme/ROS/pH-responsive release, nucleic acid delivery, and exosome-hybrid biofunctionalization. Finally, we critically analyze current translational barriers (scale-up, long-term stability, safety, and cost) and outline future directions toward intelligent, personalized, and combination regimens. With continued advances in biomaterials, microengineering, and precision medicine, iLMPs are poised to become a cornerstone of next-generation OA therapy.

title: The translational journey of human pluripotent stem cells.
abstract: Human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs), comprising embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), have emerged as a versatile platform connecting developmental biology with disease modelling, drug discovery, and regenerative medicine. Their capacity for indefinite self-renewal and differentiation into derivatives of all three germ layers provides an essentially renewable source of human cells that are otherwise inaccessible from patients. In this review, we discuss the biological principles governing hPSC identity, with emphasis on the transcriptional, epigenetic, metabolic, and extracellular signalling networks that regulate pluripotency and the distinct features of naive and primed states. We further examine culture systems for maintaining pluripotency and directed differentiation strategies for generating lineage-specific cell types. The application of hPSCs to disease modelling and therapeutic discovery is considered through two-dimensional cellular models and increasingly sophisticated three-dimensional organoids and organoid-on-chip systems, which provide progressively greater tissue complexity and physiological relevance. We also highlight the integration of CRISPR-based genome editing with hPSC platforms to generate isogenic disease models, establish genotype-phenotype relationships, identify therapeutic targets, and enable precise correction of disease-associated variants. Finally, we review the emerging clinical applications of hPSC-derived cell therapies and clinical translation, which remains constrained by challenges related to genomic stability, cellular heterogeneity and maturation, immune compatibility, tumorigenicity, manufacturing, and scalability. Addressing these challenges through improved differentiation, quality control, genome engineering, and scalable manufacturing will be essential for translating the broad potential of hPSCs into safe, reproducible, and accessible clinical therapies.

title: Decoding multispecies oral biofilms: molecular architecture, host modulation and systems-guided precision anti-biofilm strategies.
abstract: Oral biofilms are spatially ordered microbial communities whose pathogenic behavior is shaped by more than taxonomic composition. Their development reflects the combined effects of adhesin-receptor recognition, interspecies coaggregation, matrix formation, metabolite exchange, local physicochemical gradients and host-derived selection. Here, we synthesize molecular and ecological evidence on the bacterial cell surface-matrix interface and consider how these interactions contribute to cariogenic, periodontal and peri-implant biofilms. Particular attention is given to glucosyltransferase-dependent polysaccharides, extracellular DNA, amyloidogenic proteins, sortase-anchored surface factors and outer membrane vesicles, together with metabolic interactions involving lactate, arginine, hydrogen peroxide and heme. We further evaluate functional-genomic and systems-level approaches (including transposon sequencing, CRISPR interference, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics, spatial imaging, genome-scale metabolic modeling and machine learning) while distinguishing association and prediction from experimentally demonstrated mechanism. Emerging interventions are assessed according to their biological target and evidence level, including adhesion blockade, specifically targeted antimicrobials, matrix synthesis inhibition and degradation, quorum interference, probiotics, catalytic nanoparticles, antimicrobial photodynamic therapy and antibiofilm dental materials. Across these approaches, reduction in biofilm biomass is not equivalent to ecological restoration or clinical benefit. Key translational barriers include model fidelity, donor-to-donor variation, spatial heterogeneity, treatment durability, endpoint selection and the limited external validation of many computational and preclinical findings. Future precision strategies should therefore integrate microbial identity, matrix architecture, spatial metabolism and host context, with experimental perturbation used to establish causal vulnerabilities before therapeutic translation.

title: The potential for large-scale genome editing in finfish aquaculture via germline stem cell culture and transplantation.
abstract: Genome editing has emerged as a promising tool to complement selective breeding programmes and accelerate genetic gain in aquaculture. Although CRISPR-based genome editing has been successfully applied in several economically important fish species, its application at an industry-relevant scale remains challenging due to limitations of current delivery methods, which primarily rely on manual embryo microinjection. This approach is labour-intensive, technically demanding, and frequently results in high levels of mosaicism in founder individuals, necessitating additional generations of breeding to establish stable genotypes. In this mini review, we discuss the potential of combining germline stem cell (GSC) culture and transplantation approaches as an alternative platform for further improved genome editing in fish. By enabling genetic changes to be introduced, validated, and expanded in vitro prior to germline transmission, this approach has the potential to improve scalability, reduce mosaicism, and shorten breeding timelines. Although several technical challenges remain, continued progress in GSC culture and transplantation methodologies could facilitate the practical implementation of tailored genome editing for improved genetic gain, fish health, and welfare in aquaculture.

title: Programmable RNA therapeutics: converging vaccination and on-demand disease treatment via self-adaptive RNA platforms.
abstract: RNA technology, most prominently messenger RNA (mRNA), has transformed vaccine development by enabling rapid, sequence-specific antigen design, scalable manufacturing, and transient protein expression. Its long-term significance, however, extends beyond prophylactic vaccination. This Perspective argues that mRNA should be conceptualised as a programmable therapeutic platform capable of integrating vaccination, immune modulation, and on-demand disease treatment. Current mRNA vaccines deliver predefined antigenic instructions, whereas emerging RNA systems, including self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA, sequence-engineered mRNA, and targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), may support more adaptable therapeutic functions. Such platforms could prime immunity, replace deficient proteins, encode antibodies, reprogramme immune cells, or induce antigen-specific tolerance. The concept of self-adaptive RNA-based therapeutics remains at an early stage and should not be overstated; most existing systems are programmable at the design stage rather than biologically autonomous after administration. Nonetheless, this conceptual position is no longer purely speculative: the first regulatory approval of a self-amplifying RNA vaccine and controlled-trial evidence of clinical benefit from a personalised neoantigen mRNA therapeutic in resected melanoma indicate that programmable RNA platforms are beginning to move from concept to clinical validation across both the prophylactic and therapeutic ends of the spectrum. Key challenges include tissue-specific delivery, expression control, innate immune activation, repeat dosing, safety assessment, regulatory classification, and equitable access. A self-adaptive RNA-based framework does not replace existing vaccines or biologics but extends them towards responsive, personalised, and temporally controlled therapy.

title: Research progress on the epidemiology and diagnostic technologies of urinary tract infections in kidney transplant recipients.
abstract: In recent years, the increase in poor lifestyle and dietary habits (such as smoking, unhealthy eating) coupled with the high prevalence of chronic comorbidities including diabetes and hypertension has led to a rising number of patients with kidney disease. Kidney transplantation (KT), as an important means to improve the quality of life for patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), has been widely applied in clinical treatment. However, post-kidney transplantation urinary tract infections (Post-KT UTIs), as a serious postoperative complication, severely threatens the safety of transplant recipients and the long-term function of grafts. Post-KT UTIs refer to an inflammatory reaction resulting from pathogen proliferation in the urinary system after transplantation, which may include cystitis, pyelonephritis, and in severe instances, can advance to bacteremia or sepsis, endangering both patient and graft survival. Post-KT UTIs are commonly caused by Gram-negative bacterial infections, notably by species such as Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli (E. coli). Currently, the clinical detection and treatment of Post-KT UTIs remain based primarily on traditional urine culture and empirical antimicrobial therapy. This review introduces advanced detection methods such as next-generation sequencing and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), aiming to offer new strategies for diagnosing Post-KT UTIs. Moreover, it reviews recent advancements in the epidemiology, treatment methods, and preventive strategies of Post-KT UTIs, and the role of gut and urinary microbiota in infection development, aiming to facilitate the development of novel therapeutic agents, vaccine formulations, and refined treatment strategies for precise management of Post-KT UTIs.

title: Gene-edited porcine liver xenotransplantation: advances and key clinical translation barriers.
abstract: Liver allotransplantation constitutes a vital organ-replacement therapy for end-stage liver disease, yet the global shortage of donor livers severely limits treatment capacity. Porcine liver xenotransplantation, which employs genetically edited pig livers as grafts, holds promise for alleviating donor scarcity and providing bridging organ support for patients with acute liver failure. In recent years, considerable progress has been achieved in preclinical non-human primate (NHP) models and human clinical studies. Benefiting from multi-gene editing, optimized immunosuppressive regimens, and refined surgical techniques, this approach can now effectively avert hyperacute rejection (HAR) and achieve short-term graft functional compensation. Nevertheless, clinical translation of liver xenotransplantation still faces multiple obstacles. Technical bottlenecks include delayed immune injury mediated by non-α-1,3-galactose (α-Gal) antigens, intractable coagulopathy, cross-species incompatibility in metabolism and drug disposition, lack of standardized surgical protocols, and risks of cross-species transmission of porcine viruses. Non-technical challenges encompass inconsistent global regulatory standards, informed-consent issues, animal welfare, and medical equity. Risks posed by exogenous viruses such as porcine cytomegalovirus (PCMV) can be mitigated by establishing designated pathogen-free (DPF) donor pig breeding systems combined with pre-transplant pathogen screening; however, such strategies cannot eliminate porcine endogenous retroviruses (PERV) integrated within the porcine genome, which carry risks of latent reactivation, recombination-mediated mutation, and potential cross-species infection. This review summarizes research progress and core limiting factors in liver xenotransplantation, aiming to provide theoretical references for optimizing donor gene-editing targets, improving immune-coagulation disorder prevention and control, standardizing surgical procedures, and constructing ethical supervision frameworks, so as to facilitate safe and orderly clinical translation of liver xenotransplantation.

title: Nonclinical pharmacology and toxicology studies of LY01620, a therapeutic mRNA vaccine against human papillomavirus 16-related cancers.
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and related cancers remain significant public health concerns worldwide. Among high-risk HPV genotypes, HPV16 demonstrates the highest epidemiological prevalence. The viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 are crucial drivers of HPV16-associated carcinogenesis and have become key therapeutic targets for treating HPV16-related cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cancers. HPV prophylactic vaccines have been widely implemented in clinical practice; however, effective therapeutic interventions for infected individuals remain limited. Therefore, the development of therapeutic HPV vaccines is urgently needed. LY01620 is an investigational mRNA therapeutic vaccine targeting HPV16 E6/E7 antigens. To support LY01620's clinical trial application and development, comprehensive nonclinical studies were conducted, including immunogenicity evaluations in mice and rats, anti-tumor activity and mechanistic studies in C3.43 tumor-bearing mice, single-dose tissue distribution study in rats, and a GLP-compliant repeated-dose toxicity study in rats combined with toxicokinetics, local irritation, and immunotoxicity assessments. LY01620 demonstrated strong immunogenicity in mice and rats and exhibited significant anti-tumor activity through inducing a strong Th1-polarized immune response, increasing frequency of antigen-specific T cells, and enhancing infiltration of CD8+ T cells and mature macrophages into tumors. LY01620 mRNA exhibited sustained accumulation in inguinal lymph nodes and spleens, potentially facilitating persistent antigen presentation and prolonged immunological effects. In the repeated-dose toxicity study in SD rats, LY01620 exhibited a favorable safety profile, with the no observed adverse effect level was the highest dose of 300 μg/animal. In conclusion, preclinical studies have demonstrated that LY01620 exhibited favorable mechanism of action-related efficacy and a well-tolerated safety profile, supporting its further development.

title: From aerosol to alveoli: materials, methods, and models to bridge barriers to respiratory delivery of RNA.
abstract: Delivery formulations that facilitate mRNA transfection in the respiratory system aim to provide a flexible platform to address or prevent respiratory disease in a patient-accessible, targeted manner. Recent clinical trials in cystic fibrosis, respiratory oncology, and mucosal vaccination have exposed the unique physicochemical and immunological challenges that differentiate respiratory and parenteral mRNA strategies. This review examines the nanomaterials, barriers, and experimental models central to the rational development of aerosolized mRNA medicines. We begin with an overview of the most promising classes of devices and nanomaterial formulations used for respiratory delivery. We then analyze the physical barriers to nasal and lung delivery, spanning delivery-associated physical stresses and anatomical matrices, and present the major chemical and biological strategies developed to overcome them. A parallel analysis addresses the immunological barriers of the respiratory mucosa, including the innate and adaptive cell populations and the sensing pathways that mRNA delivery engages. Immunoengineering approaches to improve the tolerability of repeat dosing are discussed, including nucleoside modification and alternative RNA constructs, degradable and anti-inflammatory material chemistries, and co-administration of standard-of-care pulmonary drugs. Finally, we address methodologies for the investigation of the nanomaterial-mucosal interface using biophysical characterization techniques, and evaluate preclinical models spanning in vitro mucus mimics, air-liquid interface cultures, ex vivo precision-cut lung slices, in vivo rodent and non-rodent species, three-dimensional (3D) nasal and lung cast replicas, and mathematical models of the intranasal airways and lung. We propose an interdisciplinary bioengineering approach that combines the expertise of chemists, immunologists, and pulmonologists to enable clinical translation of respiratory mRNA medicines.

title: From prophylactic mRNA vaccines against viral infections to therapeutic applications: regulatory science considerations for expanding mRNA platforms.
abstract: Conventional non-amplifying messenger RNA (mRNA) and self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) medicines generally share a core linear RNA architecture-including a 5' cap, untranslated regions, one or more open reading frames, and a poly(A) tail-and are commonly formulated with delivery systems such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) to enable transient intracellular expression of a target protein. Prophylactic mRNA vaccines are designed primarily to express infectious-disease antigens and generate protective immune memory, whereas mRNA therapeutics exert pharmacological effects intended to treat disease, suppress recurrence, replace proteins, modulate immunity, or deliver gene-editing enzymes. Thus, even products based on similar mRNA-LNP technology may have different regulatory classifications and evidence requirements according to their intended use and mechanism of action. The clinical and regulatory landscape has expanded beyond the first coronavirus disease 2019 vaccines to include respiratory syncytial virus and influenza mRNA vaccines, an influenza-coronavirus disease 2019 combination vaccine, an authorized saRNA vaccine, personalized cancer immunotherapies, protein-replacement therapies, in vivo cell programming, and gene-editing delivery systems. This review examines which prophylactic-vaccine evidence can support therapeutic development and where product-specific quality, nonclinical, clinical, and lifecycle evidence remains necessary. For prophylactic mRNA vaccines, major regulatory considerations include quality, immunogenicity, preventive efficacy, lot release, and safety surveillance after large-scale vaccination. For mRNA therapeutics, the principal issues include delivery to target tissues, function of the expressed product, repeat-dose safety, biodistribution, off-target risk, long-term follow-up, and patient-specific manufacture and traceability. In particular, although personalized mRNA cancer vaccines are commonly described as vaccines, they are closer in regulatory purpose to therapeutics that act on the basis of each patient's tumor characteristics than to vaccines that prevent infectious disease. Antigen-selection algorithms, patient-specific sequence design, small-batch and multi-product manufacture, product-patient matching, clinical evaluation of combination strategies, manufacturing delays and analysis populations, and risk-based long-term postauthorization follow-up therefore require explicit regulatory consideration. Platform-level knowledge from prophylactic mRNA vaccine authorization can support therapeutic development, but regulatory questions may vary with each new product type; developers will need to track evolving regulatory instruments across jurisdictions and engage regulatory authorities early.

title: Molecular mechanisms of AcrVA-mediated Cas12a inhibition and their potential applications.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas12a is widely used for genome editing because it is simple, efficient, and suitable for multiplex targeting. However, strong or prolonged Cas12a activity can increase unwanted cleavage at off-target sites. This problem is especially important when Cas12a is used in complex microbial communities, where unintended editing may affect non-target microorganisms or mobile genetic elements. Anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins are natural inhibitors of CRISPR-Cas systems. Acr proteins targeting type V-A CRISPR-Cas12a systems are called AcrV proteins. Recent structural and biochemical studies have shown that AcrVA proteins inhibit Cas12a through highly different mechanisms. AcrVA1 induces cleavage of Cas12a-bound crRNA. AcrVA2 recognizes the nascent Cas12a polypeptide and promotes translation-dependent degradation of cas12a mRNA. AcrVA3 directly cleaves double-stranded DNA and indirectly reduces Cas12a activity. AcrVA4 allosterically blocks target DNA binding, whereas AcrVA5-AcrVA8 inhibit Cas12a by acetylating important lysine residues. These studies provide a structural basis for using AcrVA proteins as potential Cas12a off-switches. Importantly, AcrV proteins may reduce off-target effects by limiting the strength and duration of Cas12a activity after sufficient on-target editing has occurred. In this mini review, we summarize the structural mechanisms of AcrVA proteins and critically discuss the evidence and experimental requirements for their potential use in controlled Cas12a-based microbial engineering.

title: S100A4 facilitates influenza A virus replication by interacting with M2 in human alveolar epithelial cells.
abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) replication depends on host cells and is regulated by numerous host factors. Therefore, investigating and understanding the role of these host factors is a significant topic. In this study, we found the IAV replication was attenuated after host factor S100 calcium-binding protein A4 (S100A4) was knocked down with RNAi or knockout with CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing technology. Conversely, IAV replication was enhanced upon the overexpression in A549 cells. The interaction between S100A4 and the IAV M2 protein was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation. Meanwhile, confocal microscopy experiment demonstrated that the viral M2 protein co-localized with endogenous S100A4 in IAV-infected A549 cells. Truncation analysis confirmed that amino acids 45-62 of the M2 protein constitute the main interaction region with S100A4. Further study showed that viral entry was reduced after S100A4 deletion. And the polymerase activity was significantly decreased in S100A4-knockout A549 cells compared to that in wild-type A549 cells. The S100A4 overexpression resulted in the downregulation of IFN-β, while the mRNA levels of the interferon-stimulated genes ISG15 and BST2 were also significantly reduced. Therefore, the host factor S100A4 was a positive modulator of IAV replication and was involved in the viral entry, polymerase activity maintenance and innate immune regulation. Collectively, our findings shed new light on the molecular mechanisms governing IAV infection and suggest a previously underexplored avenue for antiviral therapeutic intervention.

title: Molecular origami in neuroscience: noncanonical DNA structures and functional nucleic acids in neural regulation and disease.
abstract: Gliomas are increasingly recognized as network diseases in which aberrant interactions between tumor cells, neurons, and immune populations drive hyperexcitability, seizures, cognitive dysfunction, and disease progression. Simultaneously, advances in structural biology and nucleic acid engineering have revealed DNA to be a dynamic molecular architecture capable of sensing, regulating, and modulating cellular states. In this review, we examine how noncanonical DNA structures and functional nucleic acids including Z-DNA, G-quadruplexes, cruciform structures, aptamers, and DNA origami systems, shape neural regulation and glioma associated circuit pathology. We discuss how activity dependent DNA conformational transitions influence transcriptional programs controlling neurotransmission, ion channel expression, synaptic signaling, metabolism, and inflammatory pathways in glioma cells and peritumoral neural networks. Z-DNA formation appears linked to rapid transcriptional activation and enhancer dynamics, whereas G-quadruplex rich regulatory regions modulate genes associated with excitatory signaling, cellular proliferation, and tumor progression. Cruciform DNA structures additionally interface with genome stability and DNA repair, creating mechanistic entry points for therapeutic intervention. Beyond endogenous DNA architectures, we highlight the emergence of aptamer based diagnostics and therapeutics capable of detecting neurotransmitters, cytokines, and metabolites associated with glioma induced network dysfunction. DNA origami platforms further enable programmable multivalent delivery systems for targeted transport of small molecules, oligonucleotides, CRISPR machinery, and ion-channel modulators across the neurovascular unit and tumor microenvironment. We also explore closed-loop neuromodulatory strategies in which electrophysiological signatures guide state dependent therapeutic actuation through nucleic acid based sensing and delivery systems. Finally, we discuss key translational considerations, including blood brain barrier delivery, nuclease stability, immunogenicity, biodistribution, manufacturing reproducibility, and integration with existing neuro-oncology and anti-seizure therapies. By bridging molecular origami, electrophysiology, and neurotechnology, this review proposes a framework for precision neuromedicine in glioma and broader neurological disease, where programmable nucleic acid architectures are coupled to the dynamic circuit states that drive pathology.

title: Targeting autocrine CCL2 signaling reveals oncogenic networks and prognostic biomarkers in medulloblastoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: CCL2 is a well-established mediator of immune cell recruitment to the tumor microenvironment (TME), however, its autocrine role in medulloblastoma remains poorly understood. This study investigated the molecular and prognostic consequences of CCL2 ablation in medulloblastoma cells.
METHODS: CCL2 expression was characterized in HTB-186 medulloblastoma cells, and CRISPR/Cas9 was used to generate CCL2 knockout (KO) cells. Transcriptomic alterations were assessed by RNA sequencing followed by differential gene expression, KEGG pathway, and Gene Ontology analyses. Select signaling pathways were validated by cytokine and protein analyses. The prognostic significance of differentially expressed genes was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox proportional hazards analyses in the Cavalli medulloblastoma cohort (n = 488).
RESULTS: HTB-186 cells expressed high levels of CCL2, and approximately 40% of cells expressed the CCL2 receptor CCR2, supporting the existence of autocrine signaling. CCL2 ablation resulted in 2, 284 differentially expressed genes and significantly altered pathways involved in PI3K/Akt, NF-κB, JAK/STAT, cAMP, and Hippo signaling. These transcriptomic findings were confirmed by reduced IL-6 production and altered activation of Akt, NF-κB, CREB, and YAP. Survival analyses identified four genes upregulated following CCL2 knockout (KSR2, DLG4, DGKA, and PLD2) that were associated with improved overall survival, whereas four downregulated genes (HSPA8, MYC, CCND1, and ETS2) were associated with poorer survival. These associations remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, metastatic status, histology, and molecular subgroup.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings demonstrate that autocrine CCL2 signaling regulates multiple oncogenic pathways in medulloblastoma and promotes transcriptional programs associated with tumor growth, survival, and poor clinical outcome. These results identify CCL2 as a potential therapeutic target and highlight CCL2-regulated gene signatures as candidate prognostic biomarkers in medulloblastoma.

title: Morusin induces GSDME-dependent pyroptosis in non-small cell lung cancer via the angiotensin II receptor type 2.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, its 5-year survival rate continues to be unsatisfactory. Current therapies are often limited by resistance, toxicity, or poor efficacy, highlighting the urgent need for novel strategies.
METHOD: We performed a high-throughput compound screen for inducing cell death in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells. Combined with lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release assays, cell death morphology observation, and propidium iodide (PI) staining, we confirmed the cell death mode as pyroptosis. Then, we conducted a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen to identify the critical regulator of compound-induced pyroptosis.
RESULTS: The screening results showed that morusin is a trigger of gasdermin E (GSDME)-mediated pyroptosis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells. Importantly, morusin suppresses tumor growth in vivo. Through a genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen, we further demonstrated that angiotensin II receptor type 2 (AGTR2) as a critical regulator of morusin-induced pyroptosis, acting via activation of the caspase-3-GSDME signaling cascade. Notably, morusin also upregulated AGTR2 expression in NSCLC cells. In an NSCLC mouse model, morusin treatment potently suppressed wild-type tumor growth, whereas its antitumor efficacy was substantially diminished in AGTR2-knockout tumors.
CONCLUSION: Our study reveals a novel mechanism underlying the antitumor effect of morusin, establishes AGTR2 as a potential therapeutic target, and provides a rationale for pyroptosis-based therapy for NSCLC.

title: Engineering aptamer-based therapeutics for precision cancer immunotherapy: from molecular targeting to clinical applications.
abstract: Although cancer immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer therapy, the clinical efficacy of this approach is restricted due to tumor heterogeneity, immune escape, therapeutic resistance, poor tumor penetration, and toxic side effects. Short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, termed aptamers, have high affinity for a given target, low immunogenicity, and high chemical programmability and are emerging as promising agents for precision cancer therapies and immuno-oncology. This review aims to provide a comprehensive, integrated overview of the development of aptamer-based cancer therapeutics, from molecular engineering and pharmacology to clinical applications and translational potential. The discovery and optimization of tumor and immune-specific aptamers have been enhanced by the development of conventional SELEX, Cell-SELEX, in vivo SELEX, high-throughput sequencing, microfluidic selection, and AI-assisted selection. To enhance nuclease resistance, circulation time, biodistribution, and tumor accumulation, chemical modifications such as PEGylation, 2'-fluoro, 2'-O-methyl, LNAs, phosphorothioate linkages, circularization, and lipid/albumin binding have been developed. Aptamers can directly regulate oncogenic and immune signaling pathways or be used as targeted delivery vehicles for chemotherapeutic drugs, siRNAs, miRNAs, proteins, peptides, and CRISPR-based systems. Moreover, aptamers targeting tumor-associated biomarkers, cancer stem cells, the tumor vasculature, stromal components, and immune regulatory pathways have the potential to selectively remodel the tumor microenvironment. In addition, they are well-suited to other immunotherapy strategies, including immune checkpoint inhibitors, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, photodynamic or photothermal therapy, oncolytic viruses, and cancer vaccines, thereby further supporting a multifunctional, personalized treatment approach. Although there has been significant progress in pre-clinical research, several issues remain regarding pharmacokinetics, tumor penetration, off-target effects, manufacturing, long-term safety, regulatory approval, and clinical validation. Additional advancements in aptamer engineering, nanotechnology, computational design, and biomarker-directed therapy could potentially enable the development of these platforms into successful next-generation precision cancer immunotherapies.

title: From prediction to functional delivery: evaluating artificial intelligence in lipid nanoparticle design.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding the chemical and formulation space explored for nucleic acid lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), but accurate assay prediction does not by itself establish useful delivery in vivo. This critical narrative review examines how evidence links molecular design, complete formulation identity, and biological context to cell-resolved function, with a focus on mRNA. We distinguish tissue accumulation from functional cargo delivery, membrane damage from productive release, and target-cell coverage from panel-restricted on-target precision. Four purposively selected cases illustrate distinct inference problems: AGILE's selected-candidate association and reformulation, Hamilton's non-AI accumulation screen and functional follow-up, LANTERN's benchmark using AGILE-derived data, and Wang's delivery-classification and pKa-regression workflow with changes between screening rounds. We propose a claim-specific evidence audit and a prospective comparison whose primary outcome is the number of confirmed qualifying formulations found within a declared resource ceiling. Manufacturing, storage, and tolerability are considered where they constrain the application. Neither the audit nor the comparison design has been empirically validated. They identify testable requirements for evaluating whether AI improves a declared delivery decision.

title: The first mitochondrial genome assembly of Ardisia gigantifolia Stapf: genome characterization, RNA editing, and phylogenetic analysis.
abstract: Ardisia gigantifolia Stapf, belonging to the genus Ardisia (Primulaceae), is an important traditional medicinal plant with extensive applications in folk medicine. However, its mitochondrial genome remains unexplored. The first mitochondrial genome of A. gigantifolia was sequenced using Illumina NovaSeq 6000 and Oxford Nanopore Technologies platforms and assembled using a hybrid strategy implemented in Unicycler. The genome was assembled into a 639,756 bp circular configuration with a GC content of 42.02%. ONT long reads supported the contig connections within this configuration, although alternative configurations may also exist. The mitochondrial genome contained 38 protein-coding genes, 20 tRNA genes, and 3 rRNA genes. Repetitive sequence analysis identified abundant repeat elements, including 63 simple sequence repeats, 62 tandem repeats, and 73 dispersed repeat regions, which may contribute to mitochondrial genome expansion and structural complexity. In addition, 72 mitochondrial plastid DNA fragments were identified between the mitochondrial and plastid genomes. A total of 451 C-to-U RNA editing sites were predicted across 38 protein-coding genes using Deepred-Mt. Fourteen editing sites in nad4L, including the conversion of its ACG start codon to AUG, and a stop-codon editing site in ccmFC were experimentally validated. Phylogenetic analysis supported a close relationship between A. gigantifolia and Aegiceras corniculatum. This study reports the first mitochondrial genome of A. gigantifolia, providing a valuable genomic resource for understanding mitochondrial genome evolution, phylogenetic relationships, and molecular characteristics of Ardisia.

title: CRISPR-Based Engineering of Mesenchymal Stem Cells: Functional Enhancement, Translational Challenges, and Clinical Perspectives.
abstract: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are promising platforms for regenerative and immunomodulatory therapies, but their clinical performance is limited by donor heterogeneity, variable potency, and limited persistence. CRISPR-based engineering provides programmable approaches to modify MSC function through genome editing and transcriptional regulation. This review examines CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout and knock-in, dCas9-based transcriptional regulation, and emerging base-, prime-, and epigenome-editing technologies for MSC engineering. These approaches can enhance survival and stress resistance, homing and tissue retention, paracrine and extracellular vesicle activity, immunomodulation, immune compatibility, and lineage-associated functions. Key translational challenges include efficient delivery, engineered-population heterogeneity, genomic safety, immunogenicity, phenotypic stability, scalable manufacturing, and mechanism-linked potency assessment. The appropriate engineering strategy should therefore be selected according to the intended therapeutic mechanism and product development requirements. Clinical translation will ultimately depend on demonstrating reproducible functional enhancement, manufacturing consistency, genomic and phenotypic stability, and validated therapeutic potency.

title: Analysis of the Use of shRNA in Atherosclerosis Therapy: Current Status.
abstract: Atherosclerosis remains the principal pathological substrate of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke and peripheral artery disease, and its progression is driven by an interlocking set of processes, including hepatic and vascular lipid metabolism, chronic vascular inflammation, macrophage foam cell formation and vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) proliferation, none of which is fully controlled by currently approved pharmacotherapy. Short hairpin RNA (shRNA) technology, in which a DNA template encoding a stem-loop transcript is delivered to a cell and processed intracellularly into small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) that trigger sequence-specific mRNA degradation, offers a route to durable, vector-encoded gene silencing that is mechanistically distinct from transiently acting synthetic siRNA or antisense oligonucleotides and that, although non-permanent at the level of the target gene, is not readily reversible at the level of the vector, which cannot easily be withdrawn once administered. This review analyzes the current status of shRNA-based strategies for atherosclerosis therapy. We summarize the molecular mechanism and vector design principles of shRNA-mediated RNA interference (RNAi); critically examine preclinical studies in which shRNA delivered by lentiviral or adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors has been used to silence hepatic lipid-metabolism genes (PCSK9, ApoB,), the endothelial gene ANGPTL2, inflammasome and inflammatory mediators (NLRP3, TACE/ADAM17), and genes driving VSMC proliferation in restenosis models (connexin 43); we explicitly distinguish this direct shRNA evidence from complementary target-validation studies that use antisense oligonucleotides (e.g., ANGPTL4), synthetic siRNA, genetic knockout, or antimiR approaches (e.g., lncRNA AK136714, CD36, miR-33, P2X7R); and discuss the principal delivery vectors, their tissue tropism, and the toxicity arising from saturation of the endogenous microRNA-processing machinery. We further place shRNA in the context of competing and complementary RNA-based and gene-editing modalities, including clinically approved synthetic siRNA drugs (inclisiran, patisiran) and CRISPR-based gene editing of PCSK9 and ANGPTL3, both of which have now yielded human phase 1 data, to clarify why, despite two decades of robust preclinical proof-of-concept, no shRNA construct has yet reached clinical use in atherosclerosis; we further compare this with the clinical trajectory of vector-encoded shRNA in other indications, in which anti-CCR5 and anti-HCV constructs have already been administered to patients in phase 1/2 trials, in order to establish that the limiting factor is not the hairpin itself but the risk-benefit case obtainable in a chronic, largely asymptomatic disease for which withdrawable and outcome-validated therapies already exist. We conclude that shRNA remains a mechanistically attractive but clinically immature modality whose translation will depend on vector engineering that limits off-target saturation of the RNAi pathway and achieves durable, cell type-restricted expression in the liver, endothelium, macrophages or vascular wall, and, equally, on the identification of an atherosclerosis indication-most plausibly a small, high-residual-risk or locally treatable population-in which durability outweighs the vector-level irreversibility, immunogenicity and manufacturing burden of a viral vector.

title: Genome Editing for Earliness and Plant Architecture in Cucurbit Crops: Recent Advances and Future Perspectives.
abstract: Earliness and plant architecture are major breeding targets in cucurbit crops because they influence crop duration, early yield, planting density, canopy management, and production efficiency. This review summarizes genetic, molecular, and genome-editing advances related to flowering, sex expression, fruit development, stem elongation, branching, and canopy architecture in cucumber, melon, watermelon, Cucurbita species, and other cucurbits. Current evidence shows that earlier flowering or increased femaleness does not necessarily lead to earlier commercial maturity, while compact growth must be evaluated together with yield, fruit quality, and environmental adaptation. CRISPR/Cas9 knockout remains the most established editing approach, whereas base editing, cis-regulatory editing, multiplex editing, developmental-regulator-assisted regeneration, and DNA-free RNP delivery offer promising routes toward more precise trait optimization. Major constraints include genotype-dependent transformation, pleiotropic effects, limited validation in elite germplasm, and scarce direct evidence for shortening fruit-development duration. An evidence-guided framework is proposed that links trait definition, functional genomics, target prioritization, tailored genome editing, whole-plant evaluation, and breeding deployment. Future progress will depend on quantitatively tuned alleles and coordinated optimization of reproductive timing, canopy architecture, productivity, fruit quality, and environmental stability.

title: Chimeric iPSC-Derived Lung Organoids Reveal the Minimum Wild-Type Cell Fraction Detectable by the Forskolin-Induced Swelling Assay in Cystic Fibrosis.
abstract: Cystic fibrosis is a life-threatening inherited disease caused by pathogenic variants in the CFTR gene that impair chloride and bicarbonate transport across airway epithelia. Gene editing and cell replacement strategies hold promise for restoring CFTR function, yet they inevitably generate heterogeneous cell populations in which only a fraction of cells carry a corrected allele, raising the question of how large this fraction must be for functional rescue to be detectable and whether the forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) assay is sensitive enough to capture partial correction. To address this, we generated chimeric iPSC-derived lung organoids by co-culturing GFP-labeled wild-type airway basal cells with unlabeled F508del-homozygous cystic fibrosis basal cells at seven predefined ratios (0-100% wild-type), verifying the actual wild-type fraction by flow cytometry and quantifying 24-h forskolin-induced swelling as the area ratio. Chimeric organoids showed a dose-dependent increase in swelling with rising wild-type fractions, with a statistically significant FIS response first resolved at approximately 6% wild-type cells in the pooled analysis. Separately, ROC analysis of well-level data identified two area-ratio cutoffs for classifying organoid populations-1.16 (80% sensitivity, 80% specificity) and 1.21 (98% specificity, 70% sensitivity)-which the fitted mean response reaches at approximately 14% and 34% wild-type cells, respectively. The minimum statistically detectable fraction and the classification cutoffs are distinct quantities derived from different analyses and are not interchangeable; both describe the performance of the FIS assay in heterogeneous organoids rather than thresholds for therapeutic benefit and provide a practical reference framework for designing and interpreting gene editing and cell therapy studies in cystic fibrosis.

title: Combined Effect of Hadron Therapy and PCSK9 Inhibition Therapy on the Immune Response in STK11-Deficient Lung Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Lung cancer is the most common type of cancer worldwide. Tumors carrying a mutation in the STK11 gene are associated with severe prognosis and resistance to therapy. New treatments for pulmonary adenocarcinoma highlight the efficacy of High-LET neutron therapy, often combined with drug therapy. PCSK9, whose inhibitors are used to treat dyslipidemia, may also be a new target in lung cancer therapy. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated STK11 mutation was performed in murine LLC1 lung adenocarcinoma cells. Human A549 cells that naturally carry a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the STK11 gene were also used. Cells were irradiated with protons, neutrons, and photons (2 Gy) and analyzed for survival, apoptosis, clonogenic survival assay, and evolocumab (PCSK9 inhibitor) sensitivity. In vivo xenograft (Nude) and syngeneic (C57BL/6) subcutaneous tumor models were neutron-irradiated (5 Gy). Tumor cell proliferation, microenvironment, and protein expression were assessed. High-LET irradiation confirmed the STK11-deficient lines radio resistance, which did not reduce under PCSK9 inhibitor treatment conditions in vitro. In animal models, the PCSK9 inhibitor decreased Ki67 index of tumor cells and infiltration of cancer-associated fibroblasts and macrophages in the combination therapy group. Particle therapy resistance serves as a crucial prognostic marker in the management of lung adenocarcinoma. Using cell lines and animal models, we successfully described this resistance phenotype and demonstrated the promising use of a PCSK9 inhibitor to enhance the efficacy of hadron radiotherapy against lung cancer.

title: Engineering Lipid Nanoparticles Beyond ApoE-Mediated Liver Tropism: Design Strategies for Extrahepatic and Organ-Selective Delivery.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have evolved into a significant delivery technology for nucleic acid therapies, including messenger RNA (mRNA), small interfering RNA (siRNA), and genome editing tools. Although LNPs have demonstrated therapeutic success, they display strong tropism to the liver when systemically delivered, thus restricting their use for targeted delivery to extrahepatic organs. The major factor responsible for the liver targeting of LNPs is the binding of apolipoprotein E (ApoE) to the nanoparticle surface, which enables their recognition by lipoprotein receptors and uptake by liver cells. However, increasing evidence suggests that the tropism of LNPs can be altered by controlling lipid composition, physical and chemical properties, and acquired biological properties. This review discusses the mechanisms responsible for the liver tropism of LNPs as well as recent trends in modulating LNP tropism to extrahepatic organs. How ionizable lipids, helper lipids and sterols, PEG-lipids, LNP properties, and interaction with the protein corona can impact the organ tropism of LNPs as well as approaches for active and endogenous targeting of LNPs for organ- and cell-specific delivery are discussed. The challenges associated with organ- and cell-selective delivery of nucleic acids, such as delivery to functionally specific cell populations, endosomal release, species-specific translation, safety, repeated dosing, and clinical translation, are also described.

title: SLC38A2-Driven Glutamine Metabolic Reprogramming Promotes Hypoxic Survival in Glioblastoma.
abstract: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) is highly refractory to standard therapies, including anti-angiogenic agents such as bevacizumab. While bevacizumab prunes tumor vasculature, it exacerbates intratumoral hypoxia, which drives a metabolically resilient phenotype that limits survival benefits. This study aimed to identify the metabolic dependencies underlying GBM adaptation to hypoxia and to evaluate whether targeting these dependencies could enhance the antitumor efficacy of bevacizumab. Methods: We analyzed the spatial distribution of key metabolites in GBM patients and orthotopic xenograft mouse models using magnetic resonance spectroscopy and chemical shift imaging. A dual-vector hypoxia fate-mapping system paired with an in vivo genome-wide clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) knockout screen was employed to identify metabolic vulnerabilities within the hypoxic niche. Metabolic flux was analyzed utilizing 13C5-labeled glutamine tracers. The molecular mechanisms governing solute carrier family 38 member 2 (SLC38A2) regulation were investigated using chromatin immunoprecipitation, cycloheximide chase assays, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and co-immunoprecipitation. The efficacy of targeting SLC38A2 was evaluated through structure-based virtual screening and in vivo orthotopic xenograft models treated concurrently with zonisamide and bevacizumab. Results: Imaging and tissue metabolite analyses revealed a spatial metabolic mismatch in the hypoxic tumor core, characterized by lactate accumulation alongside glutamine depletion. In vivo CRISPR-Cas9 screening identified SLC38A2 as an essential metabolic dependency for GBM cell survival under hypoxic stress. Under hypoxic conditions, hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF-1α) promoted SLC38A2 transcription, while elevated lactate stabilized the SLC38A2 protein through alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 (AARS1)-mediated lactylation at Lys472. These changes were accompanied by increased glutamine uptake and glutathione biosynthesis, reduced reactive oxygen species levels, and decreased mitochondrial-fission-mediated apoptosis. Pharmacological screening identified the US Food and Drug Administration-approved, brain-penetrant anticonvulsant zonisamide as an inhibitor of SLC38A2. In orthotopic GBM xenograft models, combined treatment with zonisamide and bevacizumab markedly suppressed tumor growth compared with bevacizumab alone. Conclusions: This study defines a spatially organized lactate-glutamine metabolic axis essential for hypoxic adaptation in GBM. The dual transcriptional and posttranslational up-regulation of SLC38A2 represents a critical survival mechanism. This axis can be pharmacologically dismantled by zonisamide, offering a clinically actionable combinational strategy to overcome anti-angiogenic therapy resistance.

title: Development of mitochondrial base editing technology and its application in animals.
abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations constitute major genetic determinants of mitochondrial disorders and contribute to the progressive dysfunction of energy-demanding tissues. However, precise manipulation of the mitochondrial genome remains a formidable challenge for decades due to the unique structural and biological features of mitochondria. Recent breakthroughs in mitochondrial base-editing technologies address longstanding barriers in mitochondrial genome engineering by enabling programmable nucleotide conversion without introducing DNA double-strand breaks. Mitochondrial base editing evolves rapidly from a proof-of-concept strategy in cultured cells into a versatile platform for generating animal models, dissecting mitochondrial gene function and exploring therapeutic interventions for mitochondrial diseases. Recent advances enable the creation of animals carrying defined pathogenic mtDNA variants and provide initial evidence supporting the feasibility of in vivo mitochondrial genome correction and disease amelioration. Here, we review the evolution of mitochondrial base-editing technologies and summarize the major editing platforms, with particular emphasis on recent advances in editor engineering, expansion of targeting capabilities, generation of animal disease models and emerging therapeutic applications. We further discuss the remaining challenges, including editing precision, target-site accessibility, delivery efficiency, and comprehensive safety evaluation. Finally, we highlight future opportunities for developing next-generation mitochondrial genome-editing systems and advancing their translation toward clinical applications.

title: Plant molecular farming: from gene design to scalable expression of therapeutic recombinant proteins.
abstract: Plant-based expression systems have emerged as low-cost, scalable, and safe alternatives for producing therapeutic recombinant proteins. Among them, Nicotiana benthamiana stands out as a versatile chassis due to its rapid growth, high biomass, efficient transient expression, and weak RNA silencing. In this review, we systematically summarize the key technical procedures and recent advances in the expression of therapeutic recombinant proteins in N. benthamiana, covering gene design and subcellular targeting, expression vector engineering and delivery, host engineering for enhanced yield, and cultivation optimization. We discuss strategies to address major bottlenecks, including codon optimization, endoplasmic reticulum retention, protease knockout, glycoengineering to eliminate immunogenic plant-specific glycans, and the use of viral-based transient expression systems such as magnICON, pEAQ-HT, and geminiviral replicons. Additionally, we highlight emerging approaches such as CRISPR-based multiplexed chassis engineering, artificial intelligence-assisted vector design, and hydroponic cultivation for scalable production. Despite significant progress, challenges remain in achieving coordinated high-level expression of multiple proteins and reducing downstream processing costs. This review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the current state and future directions of plant molecular farming in N. benthamiana, emphasizing its irreplaceable value for rapid emergency response, personalized vaccines, and safe biopharmaceutical manufacturing.

title: Pyroptosis in cancer nanotherapy: Molecular mechanisms and advanced nanosystems (Review).
abstract: Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death characterized by activation of inflammasome complexes and caspase signaling cascades, ultimately leading to the cleavage and activation of pore‑forming executioners such as gasdermin D (GSDMD), ‑E and ‑B. Accumulating evidence indicates that pyroptosis induction in cancer cells exerts potent antitumor effects. As a result, recent therapeutic strategies such as cancer nanotherapy have increasingly focused on harnessing pyroptotic cell death to improve cancer treatment outcomes. This review aimed to explore recent advances in nanotechnology‑based approaches designed to induce pyroptosis in cancer cells, with an emphasis on their potential to enhance antitumor immunity and overcome treatment resistance. It explored four distinct nanoplatforms: i) Chemo‑photodynamic systems that trigger GSDME‑mediated death by generating reactive oxygen species; ii) magneto‑plasmonic nanoparticles that use GSDME activation to modulate the tumor microenvironment, turning 'cold' tumors 'hot'; iii) bioorthogonal chemical delivery tools leveraging click chemistry for site‑specific gasdermin release; and iv) nano‑CRISPR activation scaffolds designed to boost GSDME expression and work alongside cisplatin. Beyond these platforms, the present review highlights how immune cell‑derived granzymes and interferon‑γ drive vital downstream pyroptotic pathways via GSDME and GSDMB activation. Lastly, the review weighs clinical risks, such as chronic systemic inflammation and tumor‑promoting environments, providing a realistic perspective on how to safely progress these preclinical nanotherapies into selective, effective clinical immunotherapies.

title: CRISPR opens the door to targeted therapy against glioblastoma (Review).
abstract: The progression in molecular understanding of glioblastoma (GBM) enables the identification of key therapeutic targets, allowing the advances of targeted therapy in GBM. However, to date, most clinical trial results have been disappointing. The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) system is a revolutionary genome‑editing tool that has the potential to improve basic research and therapy for GBM. In the present review, the current status and challenges of targeted therapy in GBM are examined. As a potential approach to address the challenges, the development process and application scope of CRISPR are investigated. Furthermore, the application of CRISPR in the study of GBM is explored, mainly by conducting CRISPR screens and employing CRISPR to target genes associated with the malignant phenotype of GBM. Finally, delivery of CRISPR/CRISPR‑associated protein 9 (Cas9) for the treatment of GBM is briefly reviewed.

title: Gene therapy for epilepsy: From SCN1A to broadened therapeutic horizons (Review).
abstract: Genetic epilepsy, for which the molecular mechanisms are relatively well defined in numerous monogenic forms, represents an attractive model for the transition from symptomatic seizure control to mechanism‑driven correction. However, gene therapy strategies differ in their mechanisms of action, adaptability to specific mutations and translational maturity, making rational selection of interventions based on variant‑specific functional consequences an important clinical challenge. The present review examined five nucleic acid‑based therapeutic strategies, namely gene supplementation, enhancement of endogenous gene expression, gene silencing, DNA editing and RNA editing, for major causative genes, using mutation‑specific functional consequences [loss‑of‑function (LOF) vs. gain‑of‑function] as the primary framework for therapeutic decision‑making. The mechanisms and suitability of each approach are analysed, and their performance in terms of cell‑type specificity, delivery vectors and safety is evaluated by integrating evidence from animal models, induced pluripotent stem cell‑derived neurons and organoids and clinical trials. The present review also summarised key translational barriers, including vector cargo constraints, blood‑brain barrier penetration, off‑target and immune‑associated risks, therapeutic dosing windows and the timing of developmental intervention. Antisense oligonucleotides and regulatory adeno‑associated viral approaches, supported by mature delivery platforms and manageable safety profiles, have progressed furthest towards clinical validation. Endogenous gene activation strategies, such as CRISPR activation, offer a gene replacement‑free approach for LOF disorders but remain preclinical. DNA and RNA editing, while potentially capable of durable disease modification, require further evidence on delivery efficiency and long‑term homeostatic safety. Gene therapy for genetic epilepsy is undergoing a key transition from proof‑of‑concept studies to individualised clinical application. Future progress will depend on integrating personalised intervention design, multi‑target therapeutic combinations, artificial intelligence‑assisted sequence optimisation and standardised translational models, with the potential to drive a paradigm shift from seizure suppression to mechanistic correction.
