title: Decoding proteomic complexity of transcript variants and homologous isoforms for precision therapeutics.
abstract: The traditional "one gene, one protein" paradigm is insufficient to capture the vast phenotypic and physiological complexity of eukaryotes. This review aims to comprehensively elucidate the molecular mechanisms of transcriptomic diversification, namely, alternative splicing, alternative usage of promoter, and alternative polyadenylation, and their profound impacts on cellular homeostasis and human disease. By synthesizing recent breakthroughs in targeted long-read RNA sequencing, single-cell isoform-specific multiomics, and AI-driven 3D structural modeling, we systematically examine how transcript variants are generated and functionally annotated. Our analysis highlights that multiple transcript variants originating from a single genetic locus are not merely redundant copies; rather, subtle sequence alterations dynamically rewire protein-protein interaction networks and dictate precise subcellular localization. The exquisite spatiotemporal regulation of these variants controls critical cell fate decisions and organ development. Consequently, the pathological dysregulation of these processes, frequently termed spliceopathies, acts as a primary driver in severe pathologies, including cancer multidrug resistance, metabolic reprogramming, and neurodegenerative disorders. In conclusion, understanding the eukaryotic proteome requires a fundamental shift from conventional gene-level to isoform-level perspectives. Decoding the complex regulatory syntax of transcript variants paves the way for next-generation precision medicine, highlighting the therapeutic potential of RNA-targeted interventions, such as antisense oligonucleotides and CRISPR-based RNA editing, to correct pathogenic isoforms.

title: Tofersen in the treatment of SOD1 ALS - a two-year experience from the Polish Early Access Program.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The use of tofersen, an antisense oligonucleotide against SOD1, has been recommended for the treatment of SOD1-ALS by current European guidelines. Before full approval by national health funding agencies, patients received tofersen through the Early Access Program (EAP) and/or as rescue therapy.
AIM OF THE STUDY: The aim of the study was to prospectively analyze clinical outcomes and neurofilament light chain (NfL) concentration in patients participating in the EAP in Poland between October 2023 and October 2025.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: Twenty patients with SOD1-ALS (11 with familial and 9 with sporadic ALS; male:female ratio, 2.2:1) were enrolled in the EAP. They carried 11 SOD1 pathological variants, the most frequent being L145S and K4E. As 1 patient withdrew after the first dose of treatment, data were collected from 19 individuals. The median age at disease onset was 49 years (33-69 years). Disease duration before treatment was 39 months (8-110 months), and the median age at initiation of tofersen treatment was 51 years (39-74 years). The analysis included demographic and genetic data, ALS functional rating scale-revised (ALSFRS- -R), ALS progression rate, forced vital capacity (FVC), adverse events, and NfL concentration in cerebrospinal fluid.
RESULTS: The median duration of tofersen treatment was 16 months (7-24 months). ALSFRS-R stabilized or increased in 68% of cases. Median delta ALSFRS-R during the treatment period was 0/month. The overall median progression rate decreased significantly from 0.218/month before treatment to 0.145/month at the last assessment (p < 0.0001). The decrease was observed in all patients, including fast-progressing individuals with continuous functional decline, as well as those with the most benign disease course. Two patients developed respiratory insufficiency, while FVC did not deteriorate in the remaining subjects. NfL concentration decreased in all analyzed patients, with significant reductions after 9 and 14 months. Serious treatment-related adverse events (SAEs) occurred in 3 patients and resolved without clinical consequences in 2 individuals. Two patients died due to disease progression and/or exacerbation of a preexisting condition/SAE.
CONCLUSIONS: The long-term follow-up data support the clinical efficacy and acceptable safety profile of tofersen treatment and demonstrate a biomarker response reflecting reduced axonal injury in both slow- and fast-progressing SOD1-ALS.

title: Genome Editing of Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurological Disease: Progress and Translational Barriers.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared mechanism across neurological disease. Specifically, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial DNA damage are factors in primary mitochondrial disorders and major neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson, Alzheimer, and Huntington diseases, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. This review surveys the mechanisms driving mitochondrial dysfunction and evaluates the current landscape of gene-editing technologies developed to address them. We examine mitochondria-targeted editors and nuclear-targeted editors, examining the editing capability, delivery constraints, and off-target risk of each. Heteroplasmy-shifting nucleases currently offer the strongest in vivo evidence for mtDNA-directed therapy, while base editors extend correction to homoplasmic mutations at the cost of a narrower editing scope and off-target editing. Nuclear editing platforms avoid the mitochondrial gRNA import barrier entirely, allowing current technologies to achieve the most progress toward functional, behavioral rescue in animal models. Across all platforms, delivery efficiency, off-target specificity, and translation from rodent to primate models remain unresolved barriers to clinical application. Gene editing for mitochondrial dysfunction is highly creditable as a precision therapy for genetically defined disease subsets, including primary mitochondrial disease and other neurodegenerative disorders with a known nuclear driver, rather than as a universal strategy for sporadic neurodegeneration, where mitochondrial dysfunction arises from multifactorial and poorly localized causes.

title: Knockdown of the long non-coding RNA DNAAF3-AS1 activates the p53 pathway and remodels the H3K36me3 landscape
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs are increasingly recognised as chromatin regulators, yet most remain functionally uncharacterised. DNAAF3-AS1, transcribed antisense to the ciliary dynein assembly factor gene DNAAF3, is almost exclusively associated with H3K36me3 in the HiMoRNA database. H3K36me3 ChIP-seq in human dermal fibroblasts following DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown with two independent antisense oligonucleotides revealed a marked reduction of gene-body H3K36me3, with residual signal shifted towards promoters. In FANTOM6 CAGE, DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown activated the p53 pathway and triggered differential promoter usage in genes enriched for p53 and apoptotic regulators. Consistently, genes that gained gene-body H3K36me3 upon knockdown were enriched for apoptosis-related pathways. In line with high expression of DNAAF3-AS1 in testis, analysis based on the adult human testis single-cell atlas suggests that DNAAF3-AS1 may contribute to promoter-level H3K36me3 regulation during late spermatogenesis. Together, these results identify DNAAF3-AS1 as a chromatin-associated lncRNA that links H3K36me3 maintenance to p53 signalling.

title: Naked antisense oligonucleotides access the cytosol during early endocytic trafficking
abstract: Phosphorothioate-modified antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) enter cells, but their site of productive escape remains uncertain. We combined live-cell imaging and ratiometric pH measurements to follow a Malat1-targeting ASO internalized without a delivery vehicle. In U2OS cells, less than 4% of internalized ASO reached the nucleus under conditions that reduced Malat1 RNA by >90%. Most ASO accumulated in late endosomes, endolysosomes and lysosomes as foci and broadly distributed luminal signal. These compartments underwent neutralization without detectable membrane rupture or galectin-3 recruitment. ASO foci showed constrained motion, consistent with association with endolysosomal constituents. L-leucyl-L-leucine methyl ester-induced membrane damage or Calcium dependent lysosome exocytosis released dextran while retaining luminal ASO. Loss of the stress-granule scaffolding proteins G3BP1/2 modestly enhanced ASO activity without detectable endolysosomal damage. Tantalosin, a small molecule that perturbs endosomal recycling, redistributed the ESCRT-III protein IST1 to endosomes. It enhanced early escape of SYTOX Green and ASOs, detected by nuclear accumulation, and increased Malat1 knockdown, with cell-type-dependent responses. Tantalosin did not detectably increase nuclear ASO accumulation after sequestration in late compartments. These findings place productive ASO escape early in endocytic trafficking, most likely in early or recycling endosomes, before sequestration in largely nonproductive late compartments.

title: Double-Stranded RNA Profiling with Mass Photometry
abstract: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is a potent immunogenic impurity and its detection is a critical quality attribute in characterizing mRNA therapeutics. Standard analytical methods (e.g., sandwich ELISA) are only able to resolve the bulk presence of dsRNA and cannot characterize the different sub-species that may be present within a mRNA sample.. In this study, we use mass photometry (MP) as a single-molecule analytical platform for the simultaneous detection and characterization of dsRNA impurities in mRNA samples. We demonstrate how ionic strength can interfere with the stability of the mAb/dsRNA complex and measure the binding affinity (1 nM) under a set of parameters for reproducible characterization of the complex. We then leverage the J2 antibody to identify antibody/dsRNA complexes that then resolve dsRNA-positive species within an mRNA sample based on discrete molecular weight profiles. Furthermore, we introduce a novel MP assay that harnesses the repulsive surface chemistry of uncoated glass to exclude the bulk mRNA analyte to enable the use of higher loading concentrations to sensitively profile trace dsRNA impurities as antibody-bound species. This work establishes MP as a valuable next generation mRNA analytical tool for analyzing dsRNA byproducts within mRNA samples.

title: Fundamentals on the Kinetic and Thermodynamic Analysis of Oligonucleotide DNA Hybridization by Surface Plasmon Resonance: A Guide for HIF1α Antisense Design.
abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) are nucleotide polymers that hybridize to sense strands and have been successful in treating a variety of diseases. A wide range of strategies have been investigated to optimize and develop ASO for clinical studies. A key objective for this study was to provide an overview of the range of detailed data that can be obtained and provide an updated method review on how to design surface plasmon resonance (SPR) kinetic experiments for DNA oligonucleotide hybridization studies that can also be applied to other ASO including peptide nucleic acids (PNA). We describe many lessons learned from published literature and provide a state-of-the-art strategy and methods for generating not only kinetic but also thermodynamic characterizations of oligonucleotide hybridization. In this study we have performed an SPR kinetic and thermodynamic analysis for the hybridization of HIF1 antisense DNA strands to its immobilized Intron2-Exon3 splice site sense DNA strand to provide insight, in general, on the optimal length and insight into optimal design of DNA ASOs. We provide a process on how to design experiments to: 1.) obtain oligonucleotide-length dependent kinetics, 2.) analyze reactions to obtain association and dissociation rate kinetics (ka, kd), assess if hybridization follows a 2-state model and to obtain kinetic dissociation constants (Kd), 3.) perform temperature-dependent hybridization kinetics to obtain thermodynamic values ({Delta}H{degrees}, {Delta}S{degrees} and {Delta}G{degrees}) that can give insight into the molecular interactions driving hybridization, 4.) compare experimental thermodynamic values to values derived from nearest-neighbor prediction models to identify atypical reactions and importantly 5.) enable calculations to predict oligomer hybridization affinity at the physiological 37 {degrees}C temperature to assess if the design of the oligomer will have the required cellular activity for a therapeutic effect. The strategy and results presented throughout the paper are compared to previous SPR reports and suggestions made to optimize kinetic studies.

title: Dysregulation of miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis links endocytic trafficking dysfunction to ER stress in Parkinson's disease
abstract: Background: Parkinson's disease is defined by progressive dopaminergic neurodegeneration and -synuclein pathology. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and clathrin-mediated endocytosis dysfunction are implicated in disease pathogenesis, but the molecular mechanisms connecting these processes remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate a miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis as a regulator link between endocytic trafficking and ER stress in Parkinson's disease. Methods: MiR-103a-3p and AGFG1 were examined in plasma and postmortem substantia nigra from patients with Parkinson's disease and controls. Gain- and loss-of-function studies, target validation and live-cell imaging were used to define the role of the miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis in ER stress and endocytic trafficking. The pathway was further investigated in SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S hiPSC-derived neurons. Therapeutic targeting of AGFG1 was evaluated using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) in vitro and in a 6-hydroxydopamine mouse model. Results: MiR-103a-3p was significantly reduced in Parkinson's disease plasma and substantia nigra, whereas AGFG1 was increased in nigral tissue. MiR-103a-3p directly repressed AGFG1 and attenuated thapsigargin-induced ER stress, while miR-103a-3p inhibition or AGFG1 overexpression exacerbated stress signalling. AGFG1 knockdown reversed the effects of miR-103a-3p inhibition, establishing AGFG1 as a functional downstream effector. Mechanistically, AGFG1 associated and co-trafficked with clathrin-positive vesicles, whereas ER stress progressively disrupted AGFG1-clathrin vesicle dynamics, revealing an association between endocytic trafficking and stress signalling. In genetic Parkinson's disease models, SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S neurons showed mutation-dependent differences in AGFG1 expression and stress regulation. eIF2 phosphorylation increased in both SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S neurons, whereas AGFG1 and GADD34 upregulation was selective to SNCA A53T neurons. Importantly, ASO-mediated AGFG1 suppression attenuated ER stress in vitro and preserved nigral dopaminergic neurons with improved motor performance in vivo. Conclusion: Our findings identify the miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis as a previously unrecognised molecular link between endocytic trafficking dysfunction and ER stress in Parkinson's disease, and support AGFG1 as a mechanistically potential therapeutic target.

title: In Step, the sole Drosophila TENT5 poly(A) polymerase, is required for spermatid elongation and individualization.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Cytoplasmic poly(A) tail length is a key regulator of mRNA translation and stability, controlled in part by non-canonical poly(A) polymerases of the TENT5 family, which are required for gametogenesis in mice. We characterize the sole Drosophila melanogaster TENT5 ortholog, which we name in step ( isep ). Although identified as a candidate target of the eye-specification factor Eyeless, isep mutants have normal eyes; instead, isep is essential for male fertility. The isep gene and its protein are expressed in spermatocytes and in elongating spermatids and are concentrated at the distal end of spermatid cysts. Mutant spermatids fail to elongate normally and to individualize. Whole-testis poly(A) tail sequencing revealed that, unexpectedly for the loss of a poly(A) polymerase, median tail length increased in mutants, with lengthened transcripts enriched for roles in axoneme assembly. Both wild-type and a predicted catalytically inactive Isep rescued sterility. We propose that Isep controls localized translation of axonemal transcripts at the spermatid tip, largely independently of its poly(A) polymerase activity.
ARTICLE SUMMARY: This work contributes to the Drosophila spermatogenesis community by identifying a previously unknown factor, isep , the fly's only TENT5 , which makes flies a model to study this enzyme family. This work traces the expression pattern of both isep's transcripts and protein. Loss-of-function alleles generated by CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis result in complete male sterility, and immunofluorescence shows defects in spermatid elongation and individualization (separation into individual sperm). Mutant testes have longer median poly(A) tails, and lengthened transcripts are enriched for spermatogenesis and axonemal (sperm tail) genes. This work also suggests that the predicted poly(A) polymerase activity may be dispensable for spermatogenesis.

title: The human-specific lncRNA HD-LINC drives lipid droplet-associated neurodegeneration in Huntington's disease
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is characterized by degeneration of striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs), yet the human-specific regulatory mechanisms that contribute to neuronal vulnerability remain poorly understood. Here, we identify HD-LINC (LINC01139), a human-specific long intergenic noncoding RNA selectively induced in symptomatic HD patient-derived MSNs (HD-MSNs) and human HD caudate. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis in HD-MSNs revealed that HD-LINC was enriched in a symptomatic HD neuronal state associated with lipid metabolic and protein clearance regulation, while not observed in non-degenerative reprogrammed MSNs derived from pre-manifest HD individuals. Reducing HD-LINC attenuated mutant HTT aggregation, dystrophic neurites, DNA damage, and neuronal death, whereas HD-LINC overexpression exacerbated these phenotypes. Transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses further implicated HD-LINC in neuronal lipid regulation. We found that HD-MSNs exhibited aberrant accumulation of enlarged, low-mobility lipid droplets (LDs) within neurites, a previously unrecognized phenotype in patient-derived neurons. Critically, increased lipid peroxidation was observed within LD-enriched dystrophic neurites in HD-MSNs. HD-LINC knockdown cleared neuritic LD accumulation, restored soma-enriched LD distribution, and reduced lipid peroxidation. Finally, we developed antisense oligonucleotides that effectively reduced HD-LINC and reversed HD-LINC-associated phenotypes, nominating HD-LINC lowering as a potential therapeutic strategy in HD. These results identify HD-LINC as a human-specific regulator of neuronal LD spatial organization, lipid peroxidation, and neuronal degeneration in HD. They further reveal dysregulated neuritic LD accumulation driven by HD-LINC, and highlight lincRNA-mediated lipid dysregulation as a significant contributor to neuronal vulnerability to degeneration.

title: Synthetic Poly(2-Oxazoline) Chimera "Lipo-Polymers" as Replacements for Key Lipids in Lipid Nanoparticles.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) rely on specialized lipid components, many of which are proprietary and difficult to access or modify. Here, we introduce a polymer-based alternative to key LNP constituents through the development of chimera poly(2-oxazoline) (POx) synthetic lipid polymers (SLPs) and synthetic lipid oligomers (SLOs). These chimeric lipid-mimetic materials are designed for seamless incorporation into existing LNP architectures, enabling direct replacement of PEG-lipid conjugates and ionizable lipids, respectively. Chimeric SLPs comprise hydrophilic shell-forming POx blocks linked to hydrophobic lipid-inserting domains, whereas SLOs consist of hydrophobic POx oligomers terminated with ionizable amine-containing groups. Using mRNA-loaded LNPs, we demonstrate that first-generation POx-Chimera SLPs and SLOs functionally replace industry-standard lipid components while maintaining robust transfection activity in vitro and in vivo. Notably, SLO-containing formulations achieved expression levels comparable to, and in some cases exceeding, those of conventional lipid formulations. Together, these results establish POx-Chimera SLPs and SLOs as a versatile platform for polymer-centric LNP engineering, creating new opportunities to tune nanoparticle composition, biodistribution, and transgene expression while reducing reliance on proprietary lipids.

title: Stabilizing the CHI3L1-Gal3BP complex remodels the glioblastoma immune microenvironment and synergizes with PD-1 blockade.
abstract: CHI3L1 (YKL-40) is associated with mesenchymal, treatment-resistant glioblastoma (GBM) and shapes macrophage programs through interactions with galectin-3 or galectin-3-binding protein (Gal3BP). However, the CHI3L1-Gal3BP interaction has not been previously targeted. A surface plasmon resonance screen identified LZ6. Ternary complex formation was assessed by fluorescence-based, biophysical, and mass spectrometry methods. Activity was evaluated in five patient-derived GBM lines, myeloid cultures from eight donors, CRISPR interference with guide-resistant rescue, and a four-arm factorial study of orthotopic GL261 tumors. LZ6 increased Gal3BP engagement 3.4-fold while reducing galectin-3 in vitro. In GBM-conditioned cultures, LZ6 raised phagocytosis 22% to 44% and MHC class II 24% to 39% and lowered CD206 45% to 31% and IL-10 105 to 67 pg/mL, with concordant transcripts. Gal3BP knockdown reduced the response 41%; guide-resistant rescue restored it. Oral LZ6 raised the intratumoral Gal3BP:galectin-3 ratio from 1.02 to 1.56 at unchanged CHI3L1. In tumor tissue LZ6 shifted 20 of 24 immune endpoints, lowering CD206 and IL-10 and raising MHC class II and CD8 effector function. Median survival with LZ6 was 52.4 versus 26.3 days ( P = 0.0012), and in combination with anti-PD-1 most animals survived to the end of follow-up (median not reached), with a significant factorial interaction (hazard ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.10-0.57, P = 0.0014). LZ6 is a molecular glue of the CHI3L1-Gal3BP complex that engages its target in brain tumor after oral dosing and extends survival alone and synergistically with PD-1 blockade.

title: Therapeutic Targeting of the TGFβ Pathway Augments CAR T cell Efficacy in Glioblastoma.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T therapy represents a promising approach to improve outcomes for patients with high-grade gliomas (HGG). Recently, we reported on a phase I trial assessing the local delivery of CAR T cells for HGG. Despite notable clinical benefits to CAR T treatment, clinical responses were highly variable between patients. Here we report that TGFβ levels in the tumor cavity fluid (TCF) decreased following CAR T treatment and that lower TGFβ levels positively correlated with improved patient responses to CAR T therapy. Patients were stratified based on baseline TGFβ levels in the TCF before CAR T therapy. Single-cell RNA sequencing of patient tumor tissues identified significant upregulation of genes associated with angiogenesis and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and IL6 and SLRP pathways in TGFβ high patients, while IL2, chemokine signaling and NK-mediated cytotoxicity pathways were significantly upregulated in TGFβ low patients. Preclinically, we demonstrated that systemic treatment with a TGFβR1 inhibitor markedly improved CAR T efficacy in syngeneic murine glioma models, correlating with changes in the tumor microenvironment (TME) that benefited both endogenous and CAR T cell phenotype and trafficking. Further studies demonstrated that inhibition of the TGFβ pathway in CAR T cells, through either TGFβR1 inhibitor or CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of TGFβR2 (TGFβR2-KO), significantly enhanced CAR T cell expansion and antitumor activity. Collectively, our clinical and preclinical findings strongly indicate that targeting the TGFβ pathway could significantly enhance CAR T therapy for patients with high-grade gliomas.
ONE SENTENCE SUMMARY: High TGFβ levels in tumor is linked to resistance to CAR T therapy in GBM patients supporting targeting this pathway to enhance CAR T therapy for GBM.

title: Decoy and antisense RNA oligonucleotides targeting the EGFR exon 3 splice site suppress proliferation of A172 glioblastoma cells
abstract: Short RNA oligonucleotides directed at the 3' splice site region of EGFR exon 3 reduced the proliferation of A172 glioblastoma cells, while the same oligonucleotides had no detectable effect on A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells. Glioblastoma carries EGFR amplification in roughly a third of IDH-wildtype cases, and the A172 line harbours a tandem duplication in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. Because exon definition in human genes depends on RNA-binding proteins that engage exonic sequence near splice sites, we used the SpliceAid database to identify candidate RNA-binding proteins at EGFR exons 2 and 3. Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1, encoded by YBX1), reported to drive glioblastoma growth through its RNA-binding function, scored highly immediately adjacent to the exon 3 3' splice site. We designed four 2'-modified RNA oligonucleotides carrying a nuclear localisation signal: two antisense oligonucleotides against the exon 3 region (asRNA1, spanning the splice site; asRNA2, downstream of it), a decoy complementary to the asRNA2 target (dRNA2), and a decoy carrying the YB-1 consensus binding sequence (dYB-1). In A172 cells, all four reduced EGFR protein in a single Western blot experiment, and asRNA1, asRNA2 and dRNA2 reduced proliferation relative to scrambled RNA at days 1 to 3; dYB-1 produced a comparable reduction at day 3. None of these effects was seen in A549 cells. YB-1 protein level and subcellular distribution were unchanged by the oligonucleotides, arguing against an indirect route through altered YB-1 abundance. These observations are preliminary. Every experiment reported here was performed once: the proliferation data come from single plates with three wells per group, analysed by Dunnett's test against the scrambled-RNA control, and the Western blot, RT-PCR and immunocytochemistry panels are single runs presented as representative observations. Direct binding of YB-1 to the targeted EGFR sequence has not been demonstrated. We post this work as a preprint so that the design strategy and the initial observations are available while these questions remain open.

title: A bivalent Lassa virus mRNA vaccine protects guinea pigs from lethal infection with Lassa virus
abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4 and CD8 T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever.

title: Structural basis for repeat-associated non-AUG translation initiation on C9orf72 mRNA
abstract: A GGGGCC (G4C2) hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the first intron of C9orf72 is the most common monogenic cause of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD). This element serves as a template for repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation, which generates neurotoxic dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins that aggregate in patient brains and contribute to neurodegeneration in model systems. To understand the mechanisms underlying RAN translation initiation, we used cryo-electron microscopy to determine the structure of an in vitro assembled human late-stage C9orf72 translation initiation complex at 3.2 A resolution and a near-native complex purified from human cell lysate at 3.5 A resolution. RAN translation on C9orf72 mRNA initiates predominantly at a near-cognate CUG codon that is located 24 nucleotides upstream of the G4C2 repeat and is flanked by a strong endogenous Kozak sequence. The structures further reveal a direct interaction between the G4C2 repeat and 18S ribosomal RNA expansion segment 9 (ES9S) on the 40S small ribosomal subunit through a kissing-loop interaction. Preventing this RNA-RNA interaction using complementary antisense oligonucleotides significantly reduces RAN translation in vitro and in patient-derived iNeurons, indicating that this structural interaction is functionally important. These findings provide mechanistic insights into RAN translation initiation and highlight a novel potential therapeutic approach to mitigate toxic DPR production in C9orf72-associated neurodegenerative disease.

title: Population-scale genome-wide prioritization of targets for allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide therapy design
abstract: Background: Allele-specific antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are increasingly used to selectively suppress transcripts containing pathogenic gain-of-function or dominant negative (GOF/DN) variants. However, most current approaches rely on patient-specific target selection of SNVs in cis with the disease-causing variant. This individualized approach may limit broader ASO applicability and could exacerbate inequities in access. Population-level selection of ASO-targetable SNVs is an alternative approach not previously explored at scale. Methods: For a curated set of >400 disease genes with putative toxic GOF/DN mechanisms, we applied a greedy algorithm to identify ASO-targetable SNVs that maximize population coverage in the 1000 Genomes Project dataset. Population coverage was evaluated across ''superpopulation'' ancestry groups and assessed in multiple diverse replication datasets. For each prioritized SNV we attempted to design allele-specific 15-mer and 20-mer ASOs meeting standard chemistry and sequence criteria. The presence of prioritized SNVs was assessed in two local cohorts with GOF/DN disorders: infants with epilepsy diagnosed by rapid short-read genome sequencing, and children with long-read genome sequencing data generated for bespoke ASO development. Results: We identified 7,927 SNVs (median 17.5 per gene) achieving a median cumulative heterozygous population coverage of 88.9% across 408 disease genes. More than two-thirds of genes (70.6%) reached [≥]80% coverage using a median of only four prioritized SNVs. Coverage was consistently high for all ''superpopulation'' ancestry groups, with median coverage proportions of [≥]85%. Prioritized SNVs generalized to independent ancestrally diverse replication datasets, achieving median coverage of 86.4% in the Human Genome Diversity Project and 90.3% in the All of Us Research Program. Many prioritized targets were compatible with established ASO design principles, enabling generation of candidate allele-specific 15-mer and 20-mer ASOs at scale for future experimental validation. The presence of prioritized targets in the rapid short-read sequencing cohort, and the overlap between prioritized targets and manually curated long-read genome sequencing targets, supports the clinical relevance of population-informed target selection. All SNV targets and candidate allele-specific ASO sequences are available at hawk-eye.research.sickkids.ca/knockdown. Conclusions: Prioritization of common SNV targets may facilitate the development of ASO therapies with broader population coverage, helping move the field beyond single-patient applications and toward more equitable opportunities for access.

title: An OmpX mRNA-LNP vaccine induces protective humoral and cellular immunity against Klebsiella pneumoniae in a C57BL/6 mouse model
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP) poses a significant threat to global public health, and effective preventive measures are urgently needed. The widespread antibiotic resistance of KP underscores the critical need for vaccine-based strategies. Although numerous vaccine candidates against KP have been investigated, none has yet been licensed. mRNA-LNP vaccines against KP have only recently begun to be explored, and their ability to deliver conserved outer membrane protein antigens remains largely untested. In this study, we constructed an mRNA vaccine encoding the highly conserved outer membrane protein X (OmpX) of KP-the first mRNA-LNP vaccine targeting this antigen-and evaluated its immunogenicity and protective efficacy in mice. Immunoinformatics analyses predicted concordance between the in silico and in vivo outcomes: bioinformatics tools were used to evaluate the antigenicity, immunogenicity, physicochemical parameters, and secondary and tertiary structures of OmpX, and the C-ImmSim server was used to simulate the vaccine-elicited immune responses. We then performed mouse immunization and challenge experiments to characterize the humoral and cellular immune responses induced by the OmpX vaccine. The mRNA vaccine was immunogenic in mice, eliciting high titers of OmpX-specific antibodies. OmpX-Fc mRNA-LNPs also induced robust cell-mediated immunity, with significantly elevated IFN-{gamma} and IL-4 levels indicative of combined Th1/Th2 cellular responses. Serum from OmpX-immunized mice promoted significantly greater complement-mediated KP cell lysis than serum from the alum or luciferase mRNA-LNP control groups. Notably, OmpX-Fc mRNA-LNP immunization conferred complete protection against lethal KP challenge, with 100% survival and a significant reduction in visceral bacterial burden. These data establish a promising mRNA vaccine strategy for inducing broad immune responses and promoting serotype-independent immunity against KP.

title: Systematic analysis of genetic vulnerabilities caused by chromosome loss events in cancer.
abstract: Chromosome loss events are common across tumor types but rarely occur in normal tissue, raising the possibility that these alterations could be exploited as cancer-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities. Here, we integrate genome-scale CRISPR screening data with chromosome-level copy number profiles from 1,150 cancer cell lines and identify 389 dependencies that are selectively associated with individual chromosome loss events. The most significant vulnerabilities uncovered by our analysis are paralogous gene pairs, in which the loss of a paralog on an aneuploid chromosome establishes a unique dependency on its redundant paralog encoded elsewhere in the genome. We experimentally validate two paralog dependencies: loss of chromosome 8p, which encodes the phosphatase PPP2CB , creates a specific dependency on its paralog PPP2CA , while loss of the Y chromosome, which encodes the helicase DDX3Y , creates a specific dependency on its paralog DDX3X . Systematic benchmarking of CRISPR screening data indicates that the selective dependency on DDX3X in loss-of-Y cells exceeds other published aneuploidy-associated vulnerabilities and matches or exceeds most clinically-validated biomarker-target relationships. Furthermore, we found that the acute degradation of DDX3X was sufficient to trigger apoptosis in vitro and tumor regressions in mice. Collectively, these findings establish chromosome loss as a recurrent source of biomarker-defined therapeutic targets, identify paralog insufficiency as a general vulnerability in aneuploid cells, and provide in vivo proof-of-concept for targeting DDX3X in cancers with Y chromosome loss.

title: Vaccination of pregnant mares with mRNA encoding a GPI-anchored form of the virulence-associated protein A of Rhodococcus equi induces strong IgG responses that are transferred to their foals
abstract: The bacterium Rhodococcus equi is a common cause of severe pneumonia in foals worldwide. Foals are exposed to R. equi from birth and are most susceptible in the first weeks of life. In North America, control measures are limited to transfusion to newborn foals of hyperimmune plasma whose potency is assessed by surpassing a threshold of IgG against the virulence-associated protein A (VapA) of R. equi. Here we report results of vaccination of pregnant mares with mRNA encoding a GPI-anchored virulence-associated protein A (VapA) of R. equi induced VapA-specific IgG subisotypes transferred to their foals during the 63-day period after birth. Pregnant mares were randomly assigned to receive either VapA mRNA vaccine (n=10) at 8 and 10 months of gestation or no vaccine (n=10). Serum was collected from mares at 8 months of gestation (before vaccination for immunized mares) and {approx}24 hours after foaling and from foals at ages 1, 35, and 63 days. Mean relative concentrations of were low before immunization in all mares and did not change over time in unvaccinated mares; however, mean relative concentrations of anti-VapA IgG1, IgG4/7, and IgG3/5 of mares were significantly increased after VapA mRNA immunization and strongly correlated with the corresponding concentrations in their foals sera at age {approx}24 hours. Concentrations of anti-VapA IgGs remained increased in foals of vaccinated mares compared with control foals for at least 35 days.

title: Refactored intracellular domains enhance CAR expression and function
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) intracellular domains (ICDs) couple antigen recognition to T-cell activation. Here we worked with AI agents to refactor CAR ICDs, proposing designs and refining them as measurements accumulated over three rounds. This approach yielded KRGR-{zeta}1-40, a 45-amino-acid ICD less than a third the length of the clinical 4-1BB-CD3{zeta} (BB{zeta}) ICD. Compared with BB{zeta}, KRGR-{zeta}1-40 increased CAR surface expression and antigen-driven IFN-{gamma} release, without detectable antigen-independent IFN-{gamma} release. KRGR-{zeta}1-40 extended CAR expression and target-cell killing after transient mRNA delivery, supported the expression of four CARs from a shared mRNA dose, and enhanced B-cell depletion after lentiviral and lipid-nanoparticle delivery. These results show that iterative agent-guided design with experimental feedback can yield compact ICDs that enhance CAR expression and sustain CAR T-cell function.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA encoding CagW, a conserved component of the Helicobacter pylori type IV secretion system, protects mice against H. pylori challenge
abstract: Background: Roughly one person in two carries Helicobacter pylori, a pathogen classified by the World Health Organization as a group I carcinogen, and the steady loss of antibiotic efficacy has made prophylaxis an urgent rather than an optional goal. No mRNA vaccine against this organism has yet been tested in the clinic, and CagW, a conserved inner-membrane subunit of the H. pylori type IV secretion system (T4SS), has never been evaluated as an mRNA-encoded antigen. Methods: A codon-optimised construct carrying a signal peptide, the CagW coding sequence and a human IgG Fc tag was synthesised, transcribed into mRNA, encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and shown to direct antigen expression in HEK293T cells. C57BL/6 mice received three intramuscular doses of CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs (5 ug mRNA each) at 14-day intervals; animals given alum alone, luciferase mRNA-LNPs or CagW protein adsorbed to alum served as comparators. Humoral readouts (IgG, IgG1, IgG2a, IgM, IgA and secretory IgA), lymphocyte proliferation, CD4+/CD8+ subsets, intracellular IFN-{gamma}, IL-4 and IL-17A and circulating cytokines were quantified before challenge, and protection was assessed after live challenge. Results: The formulation (93.2 nm; PDI 0.13; approximately 90% encapsulation) produced CagW-specific protein in vitro. Vaccination raised high-titre CagW-specific IgG (maximal on day 42), IgM and mucosal sIgA, and drove Th1/Th2-type cellular activation (IL-2, IL-4, IL-12, IFN-{gamma} and IL-17A). After challenge, immunised animals carried markedly fewer gastric bacteria and showed lower urease activity than controls. Conclusions: CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs are therefore a credible mRNA vaccine platform for H. pylori and warrant further preclinical development.

title: Single-cell transcriptome-wide association analysis reveals epithelial cell-specific genetic susceptibility to colorectal cancer.
abstract: Bulk-tissue transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) have identified colorectal cancer (CRC) susceptibility genes, but cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we performed single-cell TWAS integrating matched germline genotypes and single-cell transcriptomes from normal colorectal mucosa (381 donors) and polyps (84 donors), cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility, and GWAS from 132,261 cases and 1,752,398 controls. We identified 546 gene-cell-type associations implicating 347 candidate susceptibility genes across seven normal and nine polyp epithelial populations, including 213 previously unreported genes, with 74% exhibiting cell-type-specific associations. Integrated co-expression and ChIP-seq analyses revealed distinct TF-risk gene networks, highlighting GATA6, MAX and RAD21 in normal mucosa, and TFAP4- and CEBPB-associated networks in premalignant polyp populations. Further multi-omics analyses supported dysregulation of 233 genes (67%), while drug-target analyses identified 63 potentially druggable genes. DepMap and CRISPR-Cas9 analyses implicated 35 genes in CRC cell viability. These findings reveal cell-type-specific susceptibility mechanisms and prioritize candidate therapeutic targets for CRC prevention.

title: Cell-resolved pharmacodynamic profiling reveals tissue- and cell-population-specific activity of antisense oligonucleotide chemical conjugates in vivo
abstract: Chemical conjugation can modulate antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) pharmacology and improve organ-specific delivery, yet whole-tissue measurements provide limited information on cell-specific activity. Here, we used metastasis-associated lung adenocarcinoma transcript 1 (Malat1) knockdown as a pharmacodynamic readout to compare whole-tissue and cell-resolved activity of chemically conjugated ASOs in platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha-enhanced green fluorescent protein (PDGFR-eGFP) mouse model to assess their in vivo uptake in PDGFR-expressing (GFP+) cells. This reporter mouse model uses PDGFR as an exemplar cellular marker and provides an accessible tool for evaluating ASO conjugate activity within mesenchymal stromal and progenitor populations, mainly tissue fibroblasts. Following subcutaneous administration, Malat1 was quantified in whole tissues and cell-sorted PDGFR+/GFP or PDGFR-/GFP- populations. ASO-mediated Malat1 reduction varied by tissue and conjugate chemistry, with palmitate conjugation producing the broadest extrahepatic activity and pronounced whole-tissue activity in heart and skeletal muscle. Cell-resolved analysis further revealed preferential palmitate-ASO activity within PDGFR skeletal-muscle populations. Preliminary safety assessment also showed conjugate-dependent differences, with body-weight loss and ALT elevation in tocopherol-ASO-treated male mice and spleen enlargement in both sexes. These findings present an in vivo modelling system for evaluating cell-specific ASO activity and demonstrate the advantages of cell-resolved assessment over whole-tissue measurements.

title: Cell-in-drop genotyping detects megabase-scale loss of heterozygosity as a quantitative marker for CRISPR-Cas9 on-target toxicity.
abstract: Targeted DNA double strand breaks catalyzed by CRISPR-Cas9 have been demonstrated to cause megabase-scale segmental deletions and whole chromosome losses in a wide variety of mouse and human cell lines. This raises safety concerns for CRISPR-Cas9 based therapeutics and highlights the need for scalable methods to assess its on-target genotoxicity in clinical contexts. In this report, we present cell-in-drop genotyping, as a high throughput approach that combines single cell encapsulation with droplet-based PCR genotyping of endogenous polymorphisms to detect loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at a targeted chromosome without any genome manipulation. With this approach, we detected megabase scale LOH induced by Cas9 DSBs, mostly frequently by segmental loss. This approach also detected LOH from loss of a critical DNA repair factor, BLM helicase, and LOH induced by other genotoxic conditions, in particular, the chemotherapeutic drugs Paclitaxel and Mitomycin C, which were demonstrated to induce LOH by different mechanisms. A modified version of the assay also captured rare local short range LOH arising from DSB-induced interhomologue recombination. Because it requires no genome manipulation, cell-in-drop genotyping offers a practical, scalable tool for evaluating genotoxic risk of CRISPR-Cas9 and other agents in research and clinical development.

title: Tiled base editing screens uncover rare second-site mutations that rescue a misfolded disease protein.
abstract: Therapeutic base editing can directly revert ∼30% of disease-causing missense mutations to the wild-type sequence. One strategy to broaden its reach is to install second-site corrector mutations that improve protein stability or function across multiple pathogenic alleles. Here, we use tiled adenine and cytosine base editing screens to identify such corrector mutations in NPC1, a lysosomal cholesterol transporter whose misfolding causes Niemann-Pick type C disease. Tiling mutagenesis of the endogenous NPC1 locus in haploid human cells carrying the prevalent NPC1 I1061T disease allele, combined with phenotypic reporters for cholesterol transport and protein abundance, uncovered rare intragenic suppressor mutations distributed across multiple domains. Unexpectedly, we identified a promiscuous second-site variant that can correct many different pathogenic NPC1 mutations. These correctors improve protein stability, promote ER exit and lysosomal trafficking, and restore cholesterol clearance in patient-derived fibroblasts and induced neurons. Our results establish in situ base editing screens for the discovery of second-site corrector mutations that are actionable for therapeutic base editing when the original mutation cannot be corrected.

title: Therapeutic vulnerabilities of the drug-resistant fungal meningitis pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans.
abstract: Treatment options are limited for the priority fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans . We describe CRISPR-insert, a scalable gene inactivation method for global interrogation of drug targets. Genome-wide screens using this methodology combined with machine learning predict 1,297 essential genes under liberal criteria. Unexpectedly absent from this list is FKS1 , encoding the target of echinocandin drugs to which C. neoformans is resistant. Contrary to longstanding literature, targeted deletion shows that FKS1 is not essential. Solid-state NMR reveals that fks1 Δ mutants lack β-1,3-glucan, arguing against compensation by another synthase. We experimentally test essentiality predictions for genes lacking human orthologs, identifying high-priority drug target candidates. To uncover targets for combination therapies, we establish genome-scale quantitative genetic interaction mapping. We use this method to uncover synthetic lethal dependencies of echinocandin resistance determinants, including the druggable calcineurin and Cdc50-Apt1 pathways. CRISPR-insert illuminates therapeutic vulnerabilities of an invasive fungal pathogen.

title: ExPert infers causal perturbations from cell states across biological and clinical contexts.
abstract: Pooled single-cell CRISPR screens have driven substantial effort toward models predicting the response to a perturbation. We posed the inverse question: which perturbation produced an observed cell state? Here we developed ExPert (Extracting Perturbations), which learns one prototype per perturbation in a latent space shared by 12 cellular contexts, trained on 8,964 perturbations and 19.5 million cells, and ranks 19,895 candidate genes per query, over half absent from training. ExPert more than doubled held-out-context recall over the best existing method with 1,000-fold less compute, and transferred without retraining to drugs, protein degradation and combinations. In alcohol-associated liver disease it implicated mRNA export, unchanged in expression, and we experimentally confirmed nuclear poly(A) retention and isoform switching. In primary mitochondrial disease it recovered the affected complex from blood, localized the signal to monocytes, and flagged a misdiagnosed control. Perturbation atlases can thus be queried in reverse, from state to likely driver.

title: NanoPAMDA enables rapid PAM characterization of metagenome-derived Cas9 effectors.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 orthologs remain functionally underexplored despite the rapidly growing scale of publicly available metagenomic sequencing data. Here, we applied a multi-stage computational discovery pipeline to two independent sources of metagenomic sequence data, a multi-biome collection of 620,185 metagenome-assembled genomes spanning 17 public catalogs, and raw sequencing reads from human microbiome studies assembled de novo, to identify novel Cas9 orthologs. Candidates were filtered for guide RNA architectural plausibility, sequence novelty, conservation of catalytic residues, and structural integrity, yielding 14 candidates spanning both data sources for experimental characterization. To determine PAM preference at scale, we developed a cost-effective Nanopore long-read-based adaptation of the high-throughput PAM determination assay (NanoPAMDA), enabling rapid, time-resolved, kinetic PAM profiling across many candidates in parallel. One Cas9 effector, E10, showed PAM-specific activity in vitro and was catalytically active in E. coli . Together, these findings demonstrate a scalable, long-read sequencing-based framework for discovering and biochemically characterizing novel Cas9 orthologs from metagenomic data.

title: Druggable CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory axis links Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome with MECP2 -related disorders.
abstract: The brain is exquisitely sensitive to methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2) abundance. Too little causes Rett syndrome (RTT), too much causes MECP2 duplication syndrome (MDS), and in both, severity tracks with the amount of functional MeCP2. Even modest deviations are detrimental, yet how MeCP2 abundance is controlled remains poorly understood. Using genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens, we identified hundreds of proteins regulating MeCP2, revealing a casein kinase 2 alpha 1 (CSNK2A1)-driven regulatory axis stabilizing MeCP2. We show this axis is druggable and therapeutically relevant, using a novel CSNK2A1 inhibitor in human cells and targeting Csnk2a1 in an MDS mouse model. We further connect CSNK2A1-MeCP2 regulatory disruption to Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), caused by mutations in CSNK2A1 , finding ∼50% less hippocampal MeCP2 in an OCNDS mouse model. Together, these data identify a druggable regulatory axis modulating MeCP2 and implicate MeCP2 dysregulation in the molecular pathogenesis of OCNDS and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha promotes fitness of cytokine-activated human natural killer cells.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Natural Killer (NK) cells are innate effector cells with potent antiviral, antitumor, and immunoregulatory functions that are relevant for the treatment of human diseases. There is a pressing need to better understand the mechanisms governing cellular fitness and functional persistence of NK cells to generate NK cell-based therapeutics of sufficient durability to achieve meaningful clinical benefit. Given the central role of interleukin-2 (IL-2) and IL-15 in the survival and proliferation of NK cells, we sought to identify transcription factors induced by these cytokines that are essential for maintaining the fitness of human NK cells. Culture in IL-2 or IL-15 increased protein expression of hypoxia inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF-2α, encoded by EPAS1 ) but not HIF-1α in NK cells from healthy human blood donors. Unexpectedly, induction of HIF-2α was independent of limiting oxygen. CRISPR targeting of EPAS1 or pharmacological inhibition of HIF-2α protein expression markedly compromised the survival of cytokine-activated human NK cells. In contrast, inhibition of canonical HIF-2α transcription factor activity via blocking HIF-2α /HIF-1β heterodimer formation had no apparent effects on NK cell viability, function, or metabolic fitness. These results suggest that cytokines, rather than hypoxia, activate an unconventional HIF-1β independent, HIF-2α pathway that helps to maintain NK cells during cellular activation, revealing the potential promise of manipulating HIF-2α to improve the efficacy of adoptive NK cell therapies.
KEY POINTS: Cytokine activation of human NK cells induces hypoxia-independent HIF-2α protein expressionConventional HIF-2α/HIF-1β heterodimer driven gene regulation is dispensable in NK cellsAn unconventional activity of HIF-2α promotes survival of cytokine-activated NK cells.

title: Allele-agnostic KCNH1 suppression rescues gain-of-function developmental epileptic encephalopathy.
abstract: Gain-of-function variants in KCNH1, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv10.1, cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) characterized by seizures, developmental delay and intellectual disability. While pathogenic variants enhance channel activity, loss of KCNH1 is tolerated in humans and mice, suggesting that allele-agnostic gene suppression may represent a viable therapeutic strategy. Here, we developed a gapmer antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting KCNH1 and evaluated its efficacy in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and a knock-in mouse model of KCNH1-related disorder. Neurons carrying the pathogenic KCNH1 variants I494V or G375R exhibited a shared phenotype characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential and abnormalities in neuronal network activity despite largely preserved intrinsic firing properties. ASOs efficiently reduced KCNH1 expression without disrupting network activity in control neurons. In contrast, ASO treatment normalized network dysfunction across both mutant genotypes, demonstrating that distinct KCNH1 gain-of-function variants converge on a reversible disease state. To assess the efficacy of ASOs in vivo, we generated a new Kcnh1-R357Q knock-in mouse model that exhibited profound seizures and early mortality. A single ASO treatment reduced seizure burden significantly and restored survival to near-normal levels. Together, these findings establish KCNH1 suppression as a precision therapeutic strategy for KCNH1-related DEEs and provide a framework for treating gain-of-function epilepsies in which partial gene reduction is clinically tolerated.

title: In situ single-cell CRISPR screens uncover context-dependent rewiring of glioma states and immune recruitment.
abstract: In vivo single-cell CRISPR screens can resolve perturbation effects in native tissues, but few combine cell-type-restricted delivery, somatic tumor initiation, and combinatorial perturbation. Here we developed an RCAS-TVA-based single-cell CRISPR screening approach coupling oncogenic transformation with single- or dual-guide perturbation in defined neural progenitors. In glioma, tumor suppressor loss produced distinct genotype-dependent transcriptional states, including an NF1 -loss-associated increase in mesenchymal programs. Introducing a fixed Cdkn2a (ARF) perturbastion altered malignant-cell state composition, immune-cell abundance, and the effects of additional tumor-suppressor perturbations, including increased representation of Pten - and Rb1 -deficient cells, suggestive of the relief of an ARF-dependent genetic barrier. These perturbations converged on transcriptional states resembling pharmacologic p53 activation in human glioblastoma. Across mouse tumors and human glioblastoma models, this response was associated with increased astrocyte-like state representation. These findings establish a framework for single-cell analysis of context-dependent somatic perturbations during tumor initiation in vivo .

title: Ontology-Based SEA-CDM Integration for Vaccine Clinical Trials: Query, Similarity, and Design Recommendation.
abstract: gov provides valuable information for vaccine research, but fragmented data structures and inconsistent vaccine naming complicate systematic cross-trial analysis. The Study-Experiment-Assay Common Data Model (SEA-CDM) provides a standardized structure for biomedical study data, while biomedical ontologies supply semantic relationships among concepts. We extracted 9,147 vaccine-related study records from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT) database, mapped their records into SEA-CDM, and linked vaccine products and reported adverse events (AEs) to the Vaccine Ontology (VO) and Ontology of Adverse Events (OAE), respectively. Building on the existing Ontology-based SEA Network (OSEAN), we organized the integrated data into relational tables and a Neo4j knowledge graph while retaining links to original registrations. We evaluated three applications to assess semantic trial retrieval, context-aware AE ranking and trial similarity, and trial design recommendation. First, VO-based query expansion retrieved 41 candidate RNA vaccine trials compared with 16 using exact VO identifier matching. Second, a context-aware AE ranking model incorporating SEA-CDM features and VO-derived vaccine families improved recall@10 from 0.317 to 0.383 over a frequency-based baseline. TransE and CompGCN embeddings achieved Hits@10 of 0.950 and 0.946, respectively, for retrieving trials sharing the same VO identifier within disease-specific candidate sets. Third, an ontology-based clinical trial design recommendation model was developed using several machine learning methods under leave-one-Material-out evaluation across 23 vaccine classes, although performance varied across classes. These findings demonstrate how structural and semantic integration can support multiple clinical trial analyses using vaccine studies as a case study. This framework provides a foundation for extending ontology-supported data integration and analysis to other clinical research domains.

title: Still the one: Transcriptional control across leukopoiesis by SPI1/PU.1.
abstract: The transcription factor (TF) SPI1 (historically called PU.1) is a critical pioneer TF and regulator of hematopoiesis. It exerts exquisitely dose-dependent and stage-specific control over lymphoid, myeloid, and central nervous system-resident lineages. Structurally characterized by an intrinsically disordered N-terminal transactivation region and a highly conserved C-terminal DNA-binding E26 transformation-specific domain, SPI1 can operate alone as a monomer, via homodimerization, through epigenetic interactions, and in context-dependent transcriptional partnerships. While early animal models established its essentiality for leukopoiesis, modern human genomics has unveiled direct links between altered SPI1 function and disease. Heterozygous loss-of-function germline variants cause PU.1-mediated agammaglobulinemia, whereas somatic mutations and/or regulatory alterations can drive hematologic malignancies. Dysregulated SPI1 activity is also implicated in autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, and neurodegenerative disorders. This review reconciles foundational murine paradigms with emerging human translational data, highlights current therapeutic landscapes, and projects how single-cell multi-omics and advanced gene editing may shape future directions in the SPI1 biomedical field.

title: A Phase 2 Study of Trametinib in Combination With Radioiodine (RAI) for RAS Mutant or RAS/RAF Wild-Type, RAI-Refractory Recurrent and/or Metastatic Thyroid Cancers
abstract: This phase II trial studies how well trametinib works in increasing tumoral iodine incorporation in patients with thyroid cancer that has come back or spread to another place in the body. Trametinib may stop the growth of tumor cells by blocking some of the enzymes needed for cell growth and may help make treatment with iodine I-131 more effective.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing radioiodine (RAI) activity by determining the proportion of patients alive at 6 months without disease progression by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 (RECIST version \[v\]1.1) criteria following treatment with RAI in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort A) II. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing RAI activity by determining the objective response rate (ORR) at 6 months following treatment with radioiodine (RAI) in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort A) III. To determine the proportion of patients following trametinib therapy with increased tumoral iodine incorporation as quantified by iodine iodine-124 (I-124) positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) lesional dosimetry. (Cohort B)

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine the proportion of patients following trametinib therapy with increased tumoral iodine incorporation as quantified with I-124 PET/CT lesional dosimetry. (Cohort A) II. To evaluate the safety/tolerability of trametinib with or without RAI. (Cohort A) III. To evaluate changes in thyroglobulin levels in patients treated with RAI. (Cohort A) IV. To explore potential correlations between genomic alterations present in the tumor and/or tumoral pharmacodynamic changes induced by trametinib to clinical outcomes. (Exploratory) (Cohort A) V. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing RAI activity by determining the ORR at 6 months following treatment with RAI in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort B) VI. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing RAI activity by determining the proportion of patients alive at 6 months without disease progression by RECIST v 1.1 criteria following treatment with RAI in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort B) VII. To evaluate the safety/tolerability of trametinib with or without RAI. (Cohort B) VIII. To evaluate changes in thyroglobulin levels in patients treated with RAI. (Cohort B) IX. To explore potential correlations between genomic alterations present in the tumor and/or tumoral pharmacodynamic changes induced by trametinib to clinical outcomes. (Exploratory) (Cohort B) X. Preliminary evaluation of best objective response (BOR) rate for patients treated with trametinib alone. (Exploratory) (Cohort C) XI. Preliminary evaluation of the proportion of patients following treatment with trametinib alive at 6 months without disease progression by RECIST v 1.1 criteria. (exploratory) (Cohort C) XII. To evaluate the safety/tolerability of trametinib. (Cohort C) XIII. To evaluate changes in thyroglobulin levels in patients treated with trametinib. (Cohort C) XIV. To explore potential correlations between genomic alterations present in the tumor and/or tumoral pharmacodynamic changes induced by trametinib to clinical outcomes. (Exploratory) (Cohort C) XV. To explore the impact of continued trametinib upon RAI avidity and efficacy. (Exploratory) (Cohort C)

OUTLINE: Patients with RAS gene mutations are assigned to Cohort A, while patients without BRAF/RAS gene mutations are assigned to Cohort B.

COHORT A: Patients undergo iodine I-124 PET/CT on day 5 of week 1. Beginning day 6, patients receive trametinib orally (PO) daily for 4 weeks in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo second iodine I-124 PET/CT on week 5. If I-124 PET/CT shows enough iodine absorption, patients may receive iodine I-131 PO and continue receiving trametinib for another 2 days. If I-124 shows that the thyroid is not absorbing iodine, patients have the option to be assigned to Cohort C.

COHORT B: Patients undergo iodine I-124 PET/CT on day 5 of week 1. Beginning day 6, patients receive trametinib PO daily for 4 weeks in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo second iodine I-124 PET/CT on week 5. If I-124 PET/CT shows enough iodine absorption, patients may receive iodine I-131 PO and continue receiving trametinib for another 2 days. If I-124 shows that the thyroid is not absorbing iodine, patients have the option to be assigned to Cohort C.

COHORT C: Patients may continue trametinib at the doctor's discretion and do not receive iodine I-131.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up for 30 days.

title: Effect of Aspirin on Biomarkers of Barrett's Esophagus After Successful Eradication of Barrett's Esophagus With Radiofrequency Ablation
abstract: This randomized phase II trial studies the safety of and how well aspirin works in preventing Barrett's esophagus from returning after it has been successfully eliminated by radiofrequency ablation. Studying samples of tissue from patients with Barrett's esophagus for the levels of a specific protein that is linked to developing Barrett's esophagus may help doctors learn whether aspirin can prevent it from returning after it has been successfully treated.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To conduct a randomized, double blind, placebo-controlled phase II chemoprevention trial, investigating whether supplementation with aspirin 325 mg/day for 12 months is safe and reduces the expression of CDX2 messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) (a biomarker which has been associated with the risk of developing Barrett's esophagus \[BE\]) in comparison to placebo after successful radiofrequency ablation (RFA).

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To assess safety at 12 months. II. To assess differences in the expression of CDX2 at 18 months, activation status of NF-kB by assessing levels of total and phosphorylated (phospho)-p65 and cytoplasmic to nuclear translocation of phospho-p65 which is likely to be affected by aspirin.

III. To assess the prostanoid marker, prostaglandin E2, and prostaglandin synthases, which are known to respond to aspirin and to correlation with clinicopathological factors in the esophageal cancer.

IV. To assess differences in the expression of proinflammatory cytokines known to induce activation of NFkB, i.e., TNFalpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-10, IL-17A, IL-23 will be measured.

OUTLINE: Patients are randomized to 1 of 2 treatment arms.

ARM A: Patients receive aspirin orally (PO) once daily (QD) for 12 months.

ARM B: Patients receive placebo PO QD for 12 months.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up at 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, and 18 months.

title: Stress Hydrocortisone In Pediatric Septic Shock
abstract:
SHIPSS is a multi-institutional, prospective, controlled, randomized, double-blinded interventional trial that will examine the potential benefits and risks of adjunctive hydrocortisone prescribed for children with fluid and vasoactive-inotropic refractory septic shock.

It is hypothesized that adjunctive hydrocortisone will significantly reduce the incidence of new and progressive organ dysfunction (primary outcome) and proportion of children with poor outcomes, defined as death or severely impaired health-related quality of life (HRQL) (secondary outcome), as assessed at 28 days following study enrollment (randomization).
description:
Sepsis represents the most common cause of childhood mortality worldwide. In the United States alone, 200 cases of pediatric sepsis are diagnosed each day, with an associated hospital mortality rate of 5-10% and health care expenditures now approaching $5 billion annually. Moreover, nearly one third of children admitted to pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) for septic shock have not regained their baseline health-related quality of life one year following the sepsis event.

During early resuscitation of the child with septic shock, in addition to antibiotics, volume replacement, and vasoactive-inotropic support, the most recent pediatric treatment guidelines advise the practitioner to consider adjunctive hydrocortisone therapy if the patient "is at risk of absolute adrenal insufficiency or adrenal pituitary axis failure". However, the potential benefits and risks of this recommendation have not been rigorously examined. On the one hand, corticosteroids are inexpensive and have been frequently demonstrated to improve hemodynamic status in children and adults with sepsis. Conversely, this drug class is known to alter transcription of approximately 30% of the human genome. Notably, corticosteroids down regulate most aspects of the immune response, but particularly adaptive immunity. Moreover, recent data suggests that children with particular gene expression profiles in sepsis have increased likelihood of mortality when treated with corticosteroids.

SHIPSS (Stress Hydrocortisone In Pediatric Septic Shock) is a prospective, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial examining the potential benefits and risks of adjunctive hydrocortisone prescribed to critically ill children with fluid and vasoactive-inotropic refractory septic shock. Up to 500 children will be enrolled, randomized, and evaluated at baseline, and 28 and 90 days following study enrollment.

The primary hypothesis is that hydrocortisone, compared to placebo, will decrease the the incidence of new or progressive organ dysfunction (primary outcome) and the proportion of subjects with poor outcomes, defined as death or severely impaired (≥25% decrease from baseline) HRQL (secondary outcome). Subjects will be monitored daily while receiving care in the PICU for the occurrence of adverse events, including the following protocol specified events:hyperglycemia treated with any insulin; gastrointestinal hemorrhage treated with blood product transfusion or vasopressin or octreotide infusion; delirium requiring medical treatment; and hospital-acquired infection treated with new antimicrobials. Finally, the investigators will test the hypothesis that biomarker-based prognostic and predictive enrichment strategies can improve our ability to identify which children with septic shock are more likely to benefit from adjunctive hydrocortisone, and which may be harmed. This trial will have a significant impact on public health by providing the heretofore missing evidence to inform guidelines regarding therapy for septic shock in children.

The SHIPSS trial will enroll patients from PICUs in Canada, the United States, Saudi Arabia, Israel, Brazil, Vietnam, Pakistan, Japan, Malaysia, and Singapore. Health Canada approval is not required as hydrocortisone is approved for use in septic shock in children, and this trial meets the criteria of a Phase IV study. In the United States, this trial is considered a Phase III trial as hydrocortisone is not approved for use in pediatric septic shock.

outcomes.measure: New or progressive multiple organ dysfunction syndrome as assessed utilizing the Pediatric Logistic Organ Dysfunction (PELOD-2) instrument.
outcomes.description: Appearance of new or progression of existing organ dysfunctions according to PELOD-2 definitions. PELOD-2 considers 5 organ dysfunctions (neurological, cardiovascular, renal, respiratory, and hematological) with 10 total variables, with dysfunction scored 0 up to 6 for each organ category. Total minimum/maximal scores are 0/33, with increasing score indicating increasing risk of mortality. Logit (mortality) = -6.61 + 0.47 × PELOD-2 score. Probability of death = 1/(1 + exp \[-logit(mortality)\]). A new organ dysfunction or progression of organ dysfunction is defined as an increase score in any organ category from baseline.

outcomes.measure: 28-day hospital mortality or ≥25% decrease from baseline in health-related quality of life (HRQL) assessed utilizing the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory, (PedsQL)
outcomes.description: Mortality or ≥25% decrease in PedsQL from baseline

outcomes.measure: SHIPSS specified adverse events
outcomes.description: Occurrence of adverse events plausibly associated with corticosteroid administration. SHIPSS specified events include hyperglycemia, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, delirium, and hospital-acquired infection

outcomes.measure: Risk stratification sepsis biomarkers and pediatric sepsis endotype
outcomes.description: Risk stratification sepsis biomarkers will be measured in serum obtained at enrollment and on Day 2. The PERSEVERE (PEdiatRic SEpsis biomarkEr Risk modEl) will be used to determine the patient's risk of mortality. mRNA will be isolated from blood samples collected at enrollment and on Day 2 to classify the patient as pediatric septic shock Endotype B or A. A composite outcome of sepsis endotype and PERSEVERE risk of mortality will be used to determine if a biomarker-based prognostic model and predictive enrichment strategies allow identification of children with septic shock more likely to benefit from adjunctive hydrocortisone. We hypothesize that pediatric septic shock "endotype B" subjects having an intermediate to high Pediatric Sepsis Biomarker Risk Model (PERSEVERE)-based risk of mortality will derive significant benefit from adjunctive corticosteroids, compared to endotype B subjects having a low risk and endotype A subjects at all risk levels.

outcomes.measure: Trichotomous mortality/morbidity outcome
outcomes.description: This is a 3-level ordinal endpoint, with levels death, survival with severely impaired HRQL (≥25% decrease from baseline), and survival without severely impaired HRQL, assessed at 28 and 90 days. This approach is similar to that recently reported for assessment of functional status among children encountering critical illness, utilizing the Functional Status Scale. This endpoint is expected to be highly correlated with the primary efficacy endpoint.

title: Clinical Study to Assess Efficacy and Safety of LN-145/LN-145-S1 (Autologous Centrally Manufactured Tumor Infiltrating Lymphocytes) Across Multiple Tumor Types
abstract:
This phase II trial studies how well autologous tumor infiltrating lymphocytes LN-145 (LN-145) or LN-145-S1 works in treating patients with ovarian cancer, triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), anaplastic thyroid cancer, osteosarcoma, or other bone and soft tissue sarcomas that do not respond to treatment (refractory) or that has come back (relapsed).

LN-145 is made by collecting and growing specialized white blood cells (called T-cells) that are collected from the patient's tumor. LN-145-S1 is made using a modified process that chooses a specific portion of the T-cells. The T cells may specifically recognize, target, and kill the tumor cells.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To evaluate efficacy using objective response rate (ORR) using Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version (v)1.1 in each cohort.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. Determine the disease control rate (DCR) within and across cohorts. II. Determine the duration of response (DOR). III. Determine progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). IV. Further characterize the safety profile of adoptive cell therapy with tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL) across multiple tumor types.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. Establish duration of tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) persistence. II. Compare the molecular and immunological features of tumors before and after TIL therapy.

III. Prospectively evaluate the existing immunotherapy response criteria (immune-related \[ir\]RECIST) as the best response assessment tool for TIL therapy among a diverse group of solid tumors.

IV. To investigate TIL attributes (CD8 percentage \[%\], CD27 and CD28 expression) and correlation with response to therapy.

V. Assess tumor marker (CA-125) response in patients who produce this tumor marker.

VI. To assess Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQOL).

OUTLINE: Patients are assigned to 1 of 2 cohorts.

THYROID CANCER COHORT: Patients receive cyclophosphamide intravenously (IV) over 2 hours on days -7 and -6, fludarabine IV over 15-30 minutes daily on days -5 to -1, autologous tumor infiltrating lymphocytes LN-145 IV over 45 minutes on day 0 and aldesleukin IV over 30 minutes on days 1-4 for up to 6 doses.

ICI OVARIAN CANCER, OSTEOSARCOMA, Triple Negative Breast Cancer, or OTHER BONE AND SOFT TISSUE SARCOMAS COHORT: Within 2-4 weeks prior to surgery, patients receive a single dose of nivolumab IV over 30 minutes, followed by a single dose of ipilimumab IV over 30 minutes Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 2 hours on days -7 and -6, fludarabine IV over 15-30 minutes daily on days -5 to -1, LN-145-S1 IV over 45 minutes on day 0 and aldesleukin IV over 30 minutes on days 1-4 for up to 6 doses. Within 12 weeks after receiving LN-145-S1, patients receive nivolumab IV over 30 minutes every 4 weeks in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

For cohorts treated without immune checkpoint inhibitors, completion of treatment is defined as having received any volume of LN-145/LN-145-S1 infusion followed by at least 1 dose of adjuvant IL-2. For cohorts treated with TIL + ICI, completion of treatment will correspond to the last dose of nivolumab or IL2 (if the subject is deemed unsuitable to receive adjuvant nivolumab). Patients are followed up at 18 weeks, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 24 months, then every 3 months for at least 3 years.
